# TO GOD C. N° 5. [Handwritten note] [Library stamp: BIBLIOTHEQUE DU TRIBUNAT]

# THE BEST, THE GREATEST,
TO MY INCOMPREHENSIBLE CREATOR,
MAY THERE BE GLORY, PRAISE, HONOR, BLESSING
AND TRIUMPHAL VICTORY,
FOR AGES OF AGES,
AMEN. 5781 [Handwritten note]

[Large decorative initial T] Yours it is, O creative Nature, infinite and
glorious, to regenerate my soul, languishing in
ignorance, by the power of your splendor.
Yours it is, by the admirable clarity of the holy
Spirit of discipline, to awaken, vivify, and
elevate to the true summit or peak of knowledge
the sparks of reason, surviving after Adam's fall
and miserably long immersed in the abyss of
bodily darkness. Your will be done in the celestial and immortal part of me, a human, as in the terrestrial and mortal, so that whatever is produced by them and in them, all of it, with due consideration, may be a partaker of your goodness. Thus will this heartfelt offering, consecration, and as it were, sacrifice of mine be pleasing to your sacred divinity: thus the fruit of your goodness in me, receiving the rays of its own growth, flowing from your luminous brow of all and unique goodness, with your divine Spirit leading the way, will fly up in true resurrection with its whole transfigured self into the heights, and will rejoice to visit its supercelestial homeland, in which you, Supreme Prince and Greatest Emperor, live and reign forever. Convert the hearts of malevolent Readers to better things, I beseech you; let them distinguish with open eyes your true light from the darkness of the Devil. Be, O good God, favorable and propitious to me, You who live forever.

Your Creature
most unworthy of all.
I, MAN.

*to* the Emperor of the Heavens and Earth, Thrice Greatest, and *to* his Incomprehensible Creator:
Health of soul and body, joy in JESUS CHRIST, the abolition of darkness, and the enjoyment of super-celestial light, through the illumination of the Holy SPIRIT.

[Large decorative initial C] O whom it is denied to understand the sacred secrets and mysteries of naked and revealed Nature, offered to us by God, the best and greatest; O most powerful King, and most fortified by knowledge, it will be impossible for him to know himself, and to aspire to the true enjoyment of the most holy Spirit of understanding. Therefore, diligently, with contemplation leading the way, let the storehouse of nature be uncovered, so that we may at last arrive at the sanctuary of GOD and His wisdom. Great things now, with Your Majesty's kind permission be it said, I speak, and things which cannot be acquired or obtained by royal power, violence, majesty, or any human art of the whole world, but are drawn only from the fount of God's good and sincere will, are rained down from the holy heavens, and are granted to the worthy according to divine pleasure. May you be, O MOST SERENE KING, illuminated by the ray of divine light, clarified from human mists and filth, adorned in mind with celestial gifts, a despiser of earthly things, a contemplator of heavenly and divine things, immune to Diabolical arrogance, endowed with Christian humility, and full of Most Holy justice. May you have, O MOST MERCIFUL KING JAMES, true knowledge of Nature, the unique ladder of Jacob the Patriarch directing the way to heaven: For without this means, there is no passage from earth to heaven. Blessed be GOD, and may He bless you and your Empire, so that we, His creatures and your subjects, may live happily under Him with justice, not feigned but sincere.

Your Majesty's
most devoted and most obedient	R. FLUDD.

# To the benevolent Reader.

WHEN, in exotic and overseas regions, having first obtained the degree of Master in the arts, I traversed Gaul, Spain, Italy, and Germany for almost six full years, I devoted my principal effort to the liberal arts, inasmuch as I was solicited by several Princes and noble friends of mine, and especially by the French, to instruct them in some way in those sciences.

First therefore of all, I composed a compendium of Arithmetic, described in this treatise, for Charles de Lorraine, Duke of Guise, and dedicated it to him, and also privately instructed him in its knowledge.

Moreover, I compiled Geometry, Perspective, and the secrets of military art for the most noble and most promising youth and magnanimous Prince, Francis de Lorraine, Knight of Guise, but who was snatched away by an untimely (alas!) death, violently removed from human society by an unfortunate shot from a disastrously dispersed projectile; which sciences indeed he ce-

--- Page 12 ---
4 AUTHOR. EPISTLE.
I also corrected and augmented my own [work], and assigned it the status of a distinct art within this treatise of mine. I also wrote the art of Geomancy [handwritten insertion] in the penultimate year of the aforesaid Queen Elizabeth for the most noble Vice-Legate of Avignon, who was descended from Papal blood and most skilled in Mathematical sciences. And finally, I also composed the art of motion, as well as Astrology itself, for the sake of my dearest friend Reinaud of Avignon, a most learned youth, and distinguished by the sweetness or amiability of his manners; And so in other matters.

Therefore, just as I have particularly presented all these things to those whose names are mentioned above, so now I willingly and gladly communicate them to you in general, dear Reader, hoping that you will receive this work of mine with a cheerful and serene countenance, since everyone knows that no perfect science can be acquired or attained without knowledge of the liberal arts. Therefore, I ask that you examine these our nightly labors with an impartial mind, and if any error occurs in them (as will undoubtedly happen in such a large work), do not attribute it entirely to our lack of skill or ignorance, but rather partly to the weakness of our body, almost exhausted by constant labor, and therefore unable to explore everything with such exact precision, and partly to our other occupations, by which we are called away to various things, and so, led by ardent love, restrain yourself from a viperous tongue, as a minister of darkness and malice, nay, even of the Devil himself, approving and praising those things which you find well and correctly written, but correcting all errors (which I know are not few) with a calm expression and a judgment free from all envy, and not dealing with me in this matter otherwise than you would wish to be dealt with in a similar case: if you do this, you will indeed deserve to be called a son of light, and this book of ours will become more fortunate through your kindness. Farewell.

TREATISE-

6 TRACTAT. II. PART. I. LIBER. I.

[Decorative initial N] A Physical Number is a measure by which we judge concerning the distinction of a smaller or larger quantity of some substance.

We call that a numbered or material number which is a thing or some numbered multitude, such as a pile of bricks, a handful of barley, etc.

But we call the rational soul itself the principal numbering number, because it distinguishes from one another both species and individuals; Whence it is manifest that the souls of brutes can by no means number or discern anything at all.

But that the soul is a number is confirmed by Plato in his Timaeus, where he therefore calls it a harmonic number, because it is constituted from the Monad or unity, the binary, the ternary, and the quaternary number. Nor indeed does Pythagoras disagree with Plato's opinion, who asserts that the soul is composed from the simple, double, triple, and quadruple proportion, and as it were from a point, line, surface, and cube, by which Pythagorean symbol the intellect of the soul, and its powers, seem to be signified. For the Monad signifies the intellect, which is most simple and unique. The Binary (signifies) knowledge discerning two things, namely truth and falsehood. The Ternary (signifies) doubtful opinion judging between three things, namely truth, falsehood, and probability. But the Quaternary expresses sense; For this perceives only corporeal things, since incorporeal things are by no means presented to the senses. Finally, through numbers the elements of species are denoted, which the soul, conceiving them as known, numbers and discerns, either through principles, or through the effects of principles.

A Mathematical Number is a discrete quantity collected from two or more. Therefore no number is a unit, because the smallest number is greater than a unit.

A unit is a term from which every number is derived, and in which it is defined; So in Geometry the terms of lines are points; For as a line is formed from the flow and series of points, so also a number is formed from the congregation of units.

A unit in Arithmetic, and a point in Geometry are indivisible, And indeed a unit multiplied by itself will produce nothing; but that which is not multiplied, that cannot be divided in any way.

An Abstract Number is one which has no denomination annexed to it, such as 5. or 10. without any other thing joined to them.

A Contracted Number is one which has some denomination coupled to it, such as 5. lines, or 10. degrees.

A properly so-called Contracted Number is an integer number, such as 6, 10. An improperly so-called Contracted Number is a fractional number, which is less than a whole unit, such as $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{2}{3}$.

An Absolute Abstract Number is one which has no respect or relation to another, but is considered by itself alone and absolutely.

An Absolute Even Number is one which can be distributed into two equal parts; such as 4, 6, 12, 20, etc.

An Evenly Even Number is one which is divided into equal parts, down to unity, such as 16 into 8, and 8 into 4, and 4 into 2, and 2 into 1.

An Evenly Odd Number is one which cannot be divided into equal parts down to unity by equal division, such as 18 into 9, and not further thus. 10 into 5, etc.

An Evenly Even and Odd Number is one which, when divided, gives even numbers, whose parts, when further divided, will produce odd numbers; such as 60 into 30, which members are even, and 30 into 15, which are odd.

An Odd Number is one which cannot be led into equal parts without the fraction of a unit: Thus 9, equally divided, will produce 4 and $\frac{1}{2}$. And fifteen will give 7 and $\frac{1}{2}$ in the quotient.

Numeration is that by which the due value of each number is estimated, and by suitable figures and proper places it is either raised or lowered.
  A significant figure is that by whose value a unit or a digit is signified.
  A non-significant figure by itself signifies nothing, like the cipher. What a unit is, what a number is, has been said above.
  A digit is every simple number which is comprehended between unity and the first simple article, as 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
  An article is every number which is divided into ten equal parts without remainder, as 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100, 1000.
                                                                    Nume-

--- Page 16 ---
8	TRACT. II. PART. I. LIB. I.
	*A mixed or composite number is one which consists either solely of simple significant figures, such as 12, 345, or partly of significant and partly of non-significant figures, such as 470 or 24021.*
	*A cipher is that which by itself, or placed to the left of any digit or digits, signifies nothing, as in 04, 037. But placed to the right of a digit, it signifies as many tens as the preceding digit denotes units, as in 40, 50, 240, etc.*
	*The certain value of numbers is when a digit is considered by itself and in its own nature, that is, according to the multitude of units it contains, as 2, or 3, or 4, or 5 taken by itself. For 2 has the value of two units, 3 of three, etc.*
	*The uncertain value of numbers is when the same digit expressed in different places has a different value and estimation. For example, in this number 142: 2 signifies no more than two. But 4 signifies forty, and 1 a hundred. But expressing the same digits in this way, 214: here 4 signifies only 4 units. But 1 signifies ten, and 2 two hundred.*
	*A place is a seat, or interval, in which each figure of a number is expressed. For as many figures as are constituted in a number, so many places are also attributed to it, whose orders the following diagram will clearly explain.*
	*The numerator is the estimator and value of the digit of each place in a ternary division.*
	*The denominator gives a name and limits to every place of a ternary division and its figures, by which the numerator can estimate them precisely. For the first ternary division is of units, the second of thousands, etc. For example, in this number 204, the denominator is of units, because it is a ternary division of the first order. But in 204000, the denominator is of thousands, and the estimator (numerator) is 204. For it is a ternary division of the second order.*
	*It should be noted that this kind of denominator differs from that of contracted numbers. For the former is proper to the ternary places of figures, but the latter refers to things joined to the denomination of figures, as, when I say 4000, here "thousand" is the denominator, and 4 is the numerator; but if I connect pounds, inches, or feet to the said number, there will be a double denomination here, of which the former is proper to abstract numbers, the latter makes abstract numbers contracted.*

How, by means of this mirror, the value of each number may be found?

When a number of many places is presented to us, which we cannot readily denominate, one must proceed from right to left in continuous numbering order, observing the ternary places, of which three are numerators, and one denominator.

--- Page 18 ---
10 TRACT. II. PART. I. BOOK I.
Let the given number be, for example.
     246.     354.     228.
               246.     354.     228.
                |        |        |
              Third   Second   First
                \________|________/
                         |
                 Ternary division.

Where eight is the smallest number, from which the order is to be continued towards the left.

In the first section, 8 denotes units, 2 denotes tens, and 2 denotes hundreds; the denomination of these three places, however, is of units.

Likewise, in the second division, 4 denotes units, 5 denotes tens, and 3 denotes hundreds; its denomination, however, is of thousands, and so in the others. Such, therefore, should be the practice of this mirror.

In the first place of the spheres of digits, I find the digit 8, which is the first number of the given number. It is therefore denominated by as many units as it signifies. Similarly, in the second sphere of the second place, I find 2, where the numerator gives as many tens as the simple digit 2 signifies units; for the second place is denominated by units. Afterwards, in the same sphere, in the third place, 2 is to be sought, which counts hundreds as many times as the figure 2 counts units. Then one must proceed into the second division, which is of thousands, always counting as in the previous one; but denominating by thousands: for 4 signifies as many thousands as its simple nature contains units; and so in the others.

**P**roportion of equality is, when two equal numbers are compared together, which
nevertheless less properly bears the name of proportion.
   Proportion of inequality is, when two unequal numbers are compared together,
such as 4 to 2, or 3 to 5.
   Proportion of greater inequality is, when a greater number is compared to a lesser,
such as 5 to 3, and 15 to 12.
   Proportion of lesser inequality is, when a lesser number is compared to a greater, such as
2 to 8, and 3 to 5. Where it is to be noted that the principle of greater and lesser proportion
is the same.
   Simple multiple proportion is that which exactly contains the lesser number two or
more times within itself.
                { Double proportion comprehends the lesser number exactly twice, such as 4 to 2, 6 to 3, &
Therefore, { 12 to 6.
                { Triple proportion embraces the lesser number thrice, such as 6 to 2, 9 to 3, 12 to 4.
                { Quadruple proportion contains the lesser number four times, such as 4 to 1, 8 to 2, 12 to 3, &c.
   Superparticular proportion comprehends the whole lesser number with some
part of it.

14 TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.

*That every species of proportion can be extended to infinity in the order of this mirror.*

Rule I.

*In multiple proportion, a number multiplying itself or some odd number,*
*will produce infinite duplicate (double) proportions, where the number to be multiplied is taken as the smaller, and the product*
*as the larger proportional number. Thus, two multiplied by two make 4. to 2. and 4.*
*by 2. will produce 8. to 4. and 8. by 2. will give 16. to 8. Similarly, 3. by 2. will pro-*
*duce 6. and 6 to 3. is a double proportion. & 12 to 6. & 24. to 12.*
Triple proportion is also produced to infinity by multiplying some
digit in the preceding manner by 3. Therefore, multiply 2. by 3. and it will give 6. and 6. to 2.
is a triple proportion: And 6. by 3. will make 18. which also to 6. is a triple proportion: Thus
3. by 3. makes 9. to 3. and 9 by 3. 27. to 9.
The same rule will also be observed in quadruple proportion by multiplying some
digit by 4. in quintuple by 5. in sextuple by 6. and so in the rest.

Rule II.

*If two even numbers are compared in equal proportion, such as, 4. to 4. 6. to 6. 8. to 8. &c.*
*and the first half part is added, then between those relative numbers there will be a sesquialtera (one and a half) proportion;*
*thus the half part of 4. is 2. which numbers joined together make 6. and 6. to 4. will give the aforesaid pro-*
*portion: 4. also added to 8. makes 12. which to 8. is referred by the preceding pro-*
*portion.*
Similarly, where 3. to 3. are compared, or where two equal numbers composed of 3.
are related, such as 6: to 6. & 9. to 9. if a third part of one is added to the former, it will give
a sesquitertia (one and a third) proportion, such as 4. to 3. 8. to 6. & 12. to 9.
The same applies to sesquiquarta (one and a fourth), where a fourth part is always added, and sesquiquinta (one and a fifth), where a
fifth, and sesquisexta (one and a sixth), where a sixth part of one is added to the other.

Rule III.

*Every superpartient proportion refers to parts of the smaller number: such as super-*
*bipartient, that is, the smaller [number] and its two parts [added]. Supertripartient, that is, the smaller [number] and its*
*three parts [added]. Superquadrupartient, that is, the smaller [number] and its four parts [added], and so on for the rest.*
Similarly, the denomination of such proportions is made by the smaller
number, as the superbipartient thirds proportion signifies the smaller [number], and its two thirds [parts added],
and the superbipartient fourths proportion means the smaller [number] and its two fourths [parts added], and
so on for the rest.
In the same way, supertripartient fourths denotes the smaller [number], and its three
fourths [parts added], Superbipartient fifths the smaller [number] with its three fifths [parts added]. &c.

Rule IV.

*A double sesquialtera proportion can be expressed in three ways, namely as 5. to 2.*
or $\frac{5}{2}$ or $2 \frac{1}{2}$.
Similarly, a triple sesquiquinta proportion can be expressed under these formulas.
16. to 5, or $\frac{16}{5}$. or $3 \frac{1}{5}$. and we can observe this kind of order in every other proportion.

Rule

--- Page 23 ---
DE NUMERO ET NUMERATIONE. 1

Rule V:

*The same proportion, with respect to different aspects, assumes different names.* For example, the *superquadrupartiens tertias* proportion will be a two-and-a-third proportion, as 7 to 3 and 14 to 6. Thus, the *quadrupartiens decimas* proportion will be a *superbipartiens quintas* proportion; and the *superquadrupartiens duodecimas* proportion will be a one-and-a-third proportion; and the *superquintupartiens quintas* proportion will be a double proportion; and the *sextupartiens tertias* proportion will be triple; and so for others.

18          TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.

     Cossic Numbers are those which are contracted to the denomination of some Cossic sign, such as 1. Number, 1. Root, 1. Square: 1. Cube. &c.
     What a numerator is, what a denominator is, what a digit, an articulus, and a number are, and also what the value of numbers is, has been demonstrated previously.

On the Root.

     *A root is the side of any figurate number, exactly square, or a root is a*
*linear number, from which a tetragonal number, a cubic number, and a composite number derived from these, is derived, such as*

[Three diagrams: 1. A horizontal line with 8 segments and the number 8 above it. 2. A horizontal line with 8 segments, dots above each mark, and numbers 1 through 8 below. 3. A square with 8 segments on each side, with the number 8 written on the bottom and right sides.]

Rule I.

     *A root multiplied by itself once or more often will produce that number of which it is the root; for*
*if multiplied by itself once, it will produce its square; if twice, its cube; if thrice, its square of*
*squares, &c. For example, let the root be 2, which multiplied by itself yields 4, which is*
*its square number; Again, 2 multiplied by itself twice will produce 8, which is the Cube of the aforesaid*
*root: if multiplied thrice, it will give 16 in its product; And so for the others.*
     *Therefore, as many times as the root is multiplied by itself, so many times will the product claim a*
*different denomination for itself.*

Rule II.

     *Numbers produced by multiplication are incommensurable; whose roots are also*
*infinite: Therefore, a square number has no other root than a square root,*
*nor a cube than a cubic root. And so on to infinity.*

On the square number.

     *A square number is one which will have some number as its divisor for its*
*quotient. Or,*
     *A square number is one which is made by the multiplication of some number by itself. Thus 8*
*multiplied by itself will produce 64, which is the square number of the root 8. Therefore, the root dividing*
*the square will always be the quotient number.*

On the Cube.

     *A cube is a number produced by a double multiplication of some root by itself,*
*as 2 multiplied by itself twice will constitute 8, which is a Cubic number. Therefore, the root multiplying itself,*
*and multiplying the product a second time, produces a cube. Or.*
     *A cube is a number which, divided by its root, will have its square as its quotient number; Thus 27 divided by 3, will yield 9 in the quotient,*
*which is the square of the number 3.*

On the Square of Squares.

     *A square of squares is a number produced by multiplying some cube by its*
*root. Thus 27 multiplied by 3 will yield 81.*

TRACT. II. PART. I. LIB. I. 19

**Concerning the Surfolidus.**

A Surfolidus is a number produced by the multiplication of a square of squares
by its own unique root, for the multiplier will be the root, the multiplicand
the square of squares, and the product, the Surfolidus number. Thus 81, which is
a square of squares number, multiplied by 3, its root, will give 243, which will be
the Surfolidus number of root 3.

**Rule concerning the Surfolidus.**

If the root of a Surfolidus number is a digit, then the leading digit of the Surfolidus will be the root;
if it is an articulus, then that Surfolidus has five times as many trailing zeros as its root [has zeros]:
For the Surfolidus number arises from the quintuple multiplication of its root by itself;
if it is a mixed number, then the leading digit of the Surfolidus will be the leading digit of the
root.

**Concerning the Square of Cubes.**

A square of cubes is a number which is produced after the multiplication of a Cube by itself
squarely, or it is the product of a Surfolidus number multiplied by its root,
as 27 by 27 will yield 729, or 243, which multiplied by 3, will produce 729.

A MIRROR OF COSSIC NUMBERS,
in which their value is perceived by those who regard the natures of their roots more than their forms.

[A circular diagram consisting of ten concentric rings divided into ten radial sectors. The sectors correspond to the base numbers (radices) from 1 to 10. The rings represent powers of these bases, increasing from the center outwards. At the top of the diagram are labels: "Radix: ℞", "Quadratus: Q.", and "Cubus: C.". The innermost circle contains the number 1 in each sector. The subsequent rings contain the values for $n^1, n^2, n^3, \dots, n^{10}$ for each base $n$.]

Rule I.
One must proceed in the same way with mixed roots as with digits or simple roots.

Rule II.
How may we find the root of each number?
You must examine the nature of the number, namely of what denomination it is, and that given number must be sought in the arc of that quantity; once this is found, moreover, the root of that sphere must be sought, in which the said number is found. For in the arc of roots, and in the same sphere, you will find the radical number of the same given number: Let therefore the given number be 7776, which will be the numerator, whose denominator will be Surfolidus. Therefore, the said denominator must be thoroughly searched for in the arc of Surfolids, namely 7776. Then it will be necessary to proceed through the same sphere towards the left; for the root found there will be the radical number of the given number 7776: namely 6.

Rule:

--- Page 29 ---
TRACT. II. PART. I. LIB. I. 21
Regul. III.
As often as the root is found in the aforesaid numbers, all of which are produced by the successive multiplication of the root, so many times is the radical line present in that Geometric form; for example, this root [diagram of a line with numbers 1 and 2] is found four times in this square [diagram of a square with numbers 1 and 2], and eight times in this cube [diagram of a cube with numbers 1 and 2], and sixteen times in [symbol of a square with a 2 inside], etc.

Regula. IV.
The progression and augmentation of the numbers contained in the Mirror occurs by multiplying the immediately preceding smaller number by the root. By this method, every number of each ring arises from the preceding number in the same ring, multiplied by the root found in that sphere (or ring); for example, the number preceding a cube is a square. Therefore, by multiplying the square by its root, namely by the root of the same sphere, the Cube of the said sphere is produced. And thus it is possible to proceed to infinity.

Regul. V.
Of the alteration of certain number denominations.
Those who commonly expounded the art of Cossic numbers attributed to them names and characters more suited to the natures of their roots than to their Geometric forms; but I, indeed, will name some (of them) from the similarity of their Geometric forms, so that the demonstration of this art may become clearer.

A harmonic number is that by which musical consonances, produced from sounds or voices emitted at the proper time, and distinguished by various and simple intervals, and proportioned to each other, are simultaneously enumerated.
Intervals are the distances of positions from which all consonances are composed.

From Schisma

--- Page 42 ---
34 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; TREATISE II. PART I. BOOK I.
*A Schisma is the half of a comma.*
*A Comma is that proportion by which a major semitone differs from a minor one.*
*A Diesis is half a semitone, which is very much in use in tetrachords.*
*A Hemitone or major semitone is an interval which contains more than half a*
tone; why it is called a hemitone, we will explain later.
*A minor hemitone is that which does not comprise the entire half of a tone.*
*A Tone is that part of consonance which sounds in a sesquioctave proportion,*
as is found by the experience of hammers, glasses, pots & reeds.
*Musical Consonances are those which consist of voices & intervals.*
*A Diatessaron therefore is of 4 voices & three intervals; for it consists of two*
tones & a minor hemitone.
*A Diapente is of 5 voices & four intervals; for it consists of three*
tones & a minor hemitone.

11. | Eleven is signified by a pestle with a spear, or by two pestles, or by a double spear: and it ought to be signified by appropriate actions.
[Marginal note: 9136.] This number is prefigured in memory by a preceding snake, and a man pursuing it with a spear, and in his pursuit passing through a gallows, and killing with his spear a snail climbing upon it.
[Marginal note: 2000.] A number of this kind is also intentionally expressed by the conception of three donkeys pursuing a man carrying a gallows with open mouths, and threatening: And thus it will be necessary to proceed in all remaining figures.

---

Regula I.

For each digit we have described two figures for the sake of variety; because two numbers of the same kind often coincide, which, if they were expressed by the same figure in memorial places joined together, would undoubtedly disturb the memory; for memory is refreshed by diversity; Thus 224 or 111 are not to be expressed by two gallows or three spears; because too many similar things will confuse the impressed images.

Regula II.

Memorial numbers ought always to be demonstrated by a lively action in the appropriate places; so that they may be retained longer and more firmly in the mind.

Regula III.

A memorial number is sometimes to be expressed by association; as if the number two is to be designated, we will imagine a barber placed there by himself without scissors, with a suitable action; but if the number one, a soldier; if the number three, an executioner; For the barber will be referred to by scissors, the soldier by a spear, and the executioner by a gallows.

Regula IV.

The true order of figures will follow the sequence of actions. For the principal actor will possess the first place, counting from the left; Then he who immediately suffers his action will be the second actor, and will claim the second place for himself, and so on for the following; As if 48 is to be retained, let there be a certain Doctor clothed in a square cap; but the cap falling strikes his glasses, in the second place, which by its fall is broken.

# BOOK SECOND.
## On Vulgar Arithmetic or Algorithm.

### CHAPTER I.
*On Arithmetic.*

[Decorative initial A]Rithmetic is the science of numbers, and, as it were, the foundation of all other branches of Mathematics; Its usefulness is considered so necessary, that, according to Plato's opinion, no one can well and conveniently engage in Philosophy, military affairs, Geometry, Music, Cosmography, Geography, Astrology, and similar pursuits without such an excellent and noble art: Just as Grammar has its beginning from letters, Logic from the noun and the verb; So also Arithmetic takes its beginning from the monad or unit.
The first inventor of this science among the Greeks was Pythagoras; Apuleius and Boethius, however, translated it into the Latin language, and moreover added much.

*Addition* is the collection of different numbers into one.
*Subtraction* is the removal of a smaller number from a larger one with the writing down of the remainder.
*Multiplication* is that by which one number, led into another, increases as many times as the multiplying number has units: Under this species, therefore, is comprehended duplation.
*Division* is the partition of a larger number by a smaller one: under this species, therefore, is contained mediation.

                                                                *Progression*

--- Page 47 ---
DE ALGORITHMO.                                43
An Arithmetical Progression is that in which numbers following themselves proceed with a similar interval and equal difference.
The Rule of Three Proportions, which on account of its excellence is called the golden rule, is when by three known numbers a fourth unknown is elicited.
A fractional number is a unit contracted and divided into parts.

Rule VI.
On the method of quickly understanding the product of multiplied digits.

If the multiplicand digit and the multiplier are even numbers, take half or a quarter
of its part or its third, and by that multiply the multiplicand digit: If therefore you have
taken half, as: 3 is half of the digit 6, which is to be multiplied by 8; multiply the whole,
namely: 8 by 3, and double the product; As 3 multiplied by 8 will produce 24, which,
doubled, will give 48. Therefore, six times 8 is 48.
If you have taken the third part, as the third part of the number 6 is 2, and it will give 16,
which you triple and the product will be 48.
If you want the fourth part, (thus the fourth part of 8 is 2,) let 6 be multiplied by 2, and it will
give 12, which, quadrupled, will also give 48. Similarly, if you have doubled 12, and again
double the product, the product will be 48.

                    Rule VII.
    One must proceed similarly where one of the digits is even and the other odd, as half of
8 is 4, and four times 7 will give 28. Therefore, eight times 7 will give 56.
    If its fourth part is multiplied by 7, it will give 14, which if quadrupled, will pro-
duce 56. Therefore seven times 8 or eight times 7 are 56.

                    Rule VIII.
    Where both digits are odd, if one of them is 9, its third part must be taken, which
is 3, as three times five are 15. This number, tripled, will give 45.
    If both are such that they cannot be divided into equal parts without a fractional
number, such as: 5, 7, or 7 & 7, or 5 & 5, then one unit must be kept in mind, and the re-
mainder will be divided equally into two or three parts. For example, if we take half of the digit 5 (after retaining one unit), it is 2; or if we take half of the digit 7 (after retaining one unit), it is 3. Therefore, twice 7 (using the '2' derived from the 5) will be 14. This number, doubled, makes 28. To this, for the retained unit, I add the other digit to be multiplied; which is 7, and it will give in the product 35, which
is five times 7.
    Similarly, three times 5 (using the '3' derived from the 7) are 15, which, doubled, make 30. To which the other multiplied digit (5) added will produce 35, which are seven times five.

Rule II.

Rule III.
When the denominator is greater than the numerator, then it always signifies less than a whole; Thus 1/2 signifies half of a whole; and 1/3 denotes its third part; For every fraction originates from units, which can be divided into infinite parts; as

**Regula I.**

*Where two fractional numbers are to be multiplied, first one denominator must be multiplied*

# BOOK THREE.
## Of Cossic Arithmetic.

### CONTENTS OF BOOK III.

In Cossic Arithmetic we must consider:
*   Certain things necessary for its explanation, such as:
    *   Characters --
        *   Simple, such as:
            *   ⊕ (Unit/Constant)
            *   ℞ (Root)
            *   ϱ (Quantity/Number)
            *   q (Res, x)
            *   c (Cubus, x³)
            *   qq (Zensus, x²)
            *   qc (Res de Cubus, x⁴)
            *   cc (Cubus de Cubus, x⁶)
            *   qqq (Res de Res de Res, x³) &c.
        *   Compound from simple ones, such as:
            *   q.q. (q times q, x²)
            *   q.c. (q times c, x⁴)
            *   c.c. (c times c, x⁶)
            *   q.q.q. &c. (q times q times q, x³) &c.
*   Two Differences:
    *   P. (Plus)
    *   M. (Minus)
*   Its Species, and their use & these are either:
    *   Simple, such as:
        *   Addition.
        *   Subtraction.
        *   Multiplication.

Regula I.
The last number of each species must always be designated, either actually or mentally, with the Plus difference, which is thus signed P. in other places. Multiplication makes this rule clearer:
      4. squares P. 5. roots
      7. squares P. 3. roots
-----------------------
   P. 12. cubes P. 15. roots.
28. quadrato-quadrates P. 35. cubes:

Regula II.
Minus (which difference is thus depicted M.) always diminishes, just as P causes augmentation.

Regula III.
If both dissimilar differences, that is, of different natures, concur simultaneously in addition, they subtract; but in subtraction, they add: but in multiplication, M. always prevails, etc.

Regula IV.
Similar differences in addition add, in subtraction subtract, and in multiplication multiply.

Regula V.
Two differences P. occurring in subtraction, where the number to be subtracted is greater than the number from which it is to be subtracted, are converted into the difference M., which must be subscribed. Similarly, two M. are changed into P.

Regula VII.
When two different differences are found simultaneously in subtraction, the superior difference must always be subscribed.

Rule III.

Where the differences of the numbers to be added are found to be of different natures, there
the smaller value of the numbers to be added, whether it be the upper or the lower, is subtracted
from the larger, and the difference of the larger number with its character is always to be written underneath, as:

the notation will be made according to the order and value of the dimensions. The progressive
order, however, is from ℞. to q. & from q. to ℭ. &c. as:

Rule I.
On the use of this mirror.
By means of this wheel, you will very easily find a new character, which is to be joined to the number produced after multiplication. Therefore, in its upper sphere, numbers are expressed according to the order of natural progression, and below that sphere, Cossic characters are arranged in order. Thus, the smaller character is to be multiplied by the larger, for example, a square by a root. Then add the number above the multiplying character (that is, the one placed above the multiplicand, expressed as 2). And the product, namely 3, will indicate below itself the product character, namely C; Hence q. multiplied by ℞. will produce C.

Rule I.

Where dissimilar differences occur together, there numbers are to be added, as is had in the kind of subtraction; Conversely, numbers are to be subtracted, where the differences are similar.

Rule II.

The first number of the quotient towards the left claims for itself the difference P. (as it is in the third rule of multiplication) which multiplied by P. will give P. Similarly M. by M. will give P. But one difference multiplied by its opposite will produce M. by the second rule of the same. However, M. by P. or, P. by M. is added. But P. by P. or, M. by M. is subtracted, by the fifth rule of subtraction.

Rule III.

In the subtraction of the lower number from the upper; the value of the lower character is also to be taken away from the upper, namely from the dividend, and the character of the remainder's value is to be expressed. It must always be understood, however, concerning the first character towards the left of the number, whose quotient is sought. For the characters towards the right do not diminish the upper values. It is also to be noted, that the remainder of the value of the upper character is to be placed in the quotient, with its difference disposed according to the second rule of this [chapter/section].

Rule IV.

Q. is the smallest Cossic sign or character, which is divisible: for R. is like a unit, which cannot be divided. However, the remainder of the value, which the sign

**EPILOGUE.**

As for the reduction of Cossic fractions and their operations, namely addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division; likewise the rule of three, which Artists call golden because of its unique nature, the extraction of roots, and the Algebraic rule, which is called the Rule of Equation, I believe you should be referred to Stifel, Record, and countless other authors, who have written most clearly about these matters; I am content with having written something openly and clearly about only these principles or primary operations, concerning which other writers, as if envying the world this so excellent and hidden science, lest it should ever become known, have treated too succinctly and obscurely: For with the principles of any science unknown, the science itself is likewise rendered hidden and concealed in every way. And hence it is that this art, so distinguished and noble, is found with such difficulty and by so few: Now, however, these four operations having been sufficiently clearly explained to the world, it will be very easy to investigate the rest, which follow them, with sharpness of intellect, and to master the entire science for one who desires it.

[Decorative initial N] A linear number is one which, starting from two and always adding a unit, constitutes a line; Therefore, one must start from two, because just as a line is constituted from points, so a number is constituted from units.
        A superficial number is one contained by two sides, namely length and width, or it is a number starting from three; because no surface is enclosed by fewer than three lines.
                                                                    Number

--- Page 85 ---
ON GEOMETRIC ARITHMETIC. 81.

A triangular number is one which, when formed in width by units, is enclosed by 3 angles with sides of equal dimension.

[Three triangles formed by dots. The first contains the number "15.", the second "21.", and the third "28."]

A square number is one which, formed in width by units, has 4 angles with sides of equal dimension.

[Three squares formed by dots of increasing size: 5x5, 6x6, and 7x7.]

A pentagonal number is one which, when formed in width by units, is enclosed by five angles, with sides of equal dimension.

[A pentagon formed by an outline of dots.]

A corporeal number is, or a solid number, which is contained by three sides, namely length, width, and depth: Or it is one which, when arranged by its units lengthwise and in depth, will represent the figure of some body.

Rule V.
Hexagons, two of whose sides are equal and differ from the other four equal sides, are measured by reducing them into squares in this way; for the triangles of the square, a.f.e. and e.b.g., are equal to the triangles of the Hexagon (e.f.g.c.d.h.), namely c.h.i. and d.h.i.

Rule VI.
A Parallelogram is reduced into a square or a Rhombus in this way; for the triangles, a.e.c. and b.e.d., of the square, a.b.c.d., are equal to the triangles, a.f.g. and b.f.g., of the Rhombus, a.e.b.f.

By similar reasoning, a Rhombus or a square can be reduced into a parallelogram.

C H A P. X.

On multiplication with division.

Rule I.

A line of altitude (height) is measured with a staff three feet in length by multiplying and dividing, in this manner.

Let the staff be erected perpendicularly upon the ground, and let the eye be moved back and forth (or closer and further away) along the surface of the ground, until the top of the object whose height is sought appears through the top of the staff. Multipli- N 3 -cand

--- Page 106 ---
102          TRACT. II. PART. I. BOOK. IV.

...Therefore, the space between the eye and the base of the height must be multiplied by the height of the staff, and the product must be divided by the interval between the eye and the base of the staff; for the resulting number will be the height of the thing: Let the height of the staff be three feet, the interval from the eye to the foot of the tower 14. and the distance from the eye to the foot of the staff 4. Therefore, the height of the tower will be 10 feet and $\frac{2}{4}$.

[A geometrical diagram showing two similar right-angled triangles. Point A is the vertex (eye). A smaller vertical line BC represents a staff (baculus) with height 3. A larger vertical structure DE represents a tower (turris) with height $10 \frac{2}{4}$. The distance AC is 4, and the total distance AE is 14. A small sketch of a tree is between the staff and the tower.]

The same thing is done by the rule of three proportions, because triangle A. B. C. is proportional to triangle A. D. E. For it produces the same angles, as, if 4 gives 3, what will 14 give? in this way.

Rule II.
*In exactly the same way, the height of a thing is perceived in a mirror, by approaching the mirror until the top of the tower appears in the middle of the mirror, and by multiplying the interval from the center of the mirror to the foot of the tower by the height of the eye, and dividing the product by the distance from the foot of the man to the center of the mirror. See the following figure No. 1.*

Rule III.
By a similar process, the height of an accessible tower is also collected geometrically: Because, if you multiply the distance from you to the base of the tower by the points of the inverted shadow intersected, and you divide the product by 12, the resulting number will be the height of the tower; let the distance be 18 feet, the intersected points 4. as in No. 2.

Rule IV.

The height of an inaccessible tower is found if you divide 12 by the number of points cut off, namely 3, and keep the quotient, which is 4; and having marked the place of your station, by going backward, establish a second station, and by the points cut off, namely 6, divide 12. The quotient will be 2. This should be subtracted from the first quotient if the second quotient is less than the first, and the remainder kept (but where the second quotient is greater than the first, there the first should be subtracted from the second), so, 2 subtracted from 4, 2 will remain. Finally, let the space between the first and second station be measured, which is 40 feet, which is to be divided by two, and to the quotient should be added the height of the body's stature, which is 5 feet, and the sum will be the height of the thing.

Rule III.

You will divide a right-angled triangle into as many equal parts as you wish, if you form a quadrangle along its orthogonal line; whose square you divide by 4, then you extract the root of the quotient number, whose number, measuring from the vertex of the triangle towards the base, will be the fourth part of the triangle: The second fourth part is obtained by taking half of the square and extracting its root; whose root, descending from the vertex towards the base, will show the second fourth part equal to the first: Finally, the third fourth part will manifest itself by extracting the root of three parts of the square, always descending from the vertex towards the base, and so for the rest.
For example.

[A geometric diagram showing a right-angled triangle with internal construction lines and dotted lines forming rectangles. Along the vertical side, the numbers 6, 8 ½, 10 ⅔, and 12 are marked. The number 12 is also written at the bottom-left vertex.]

Rule IV.

Also in this manner, we can divide non-right-angled triangles into equal parts, by making the side that approaches the perpendicular more closely, the side of the square.

C  H  A  P.     XII.

*On progression or proportion.*

Rule I.

The doubling of the correctly found values from two stations of a staff three feet in length (whose cursor will be half a foot) will be the measure of the object's height; for twice a.b. will be the height of the tower, c.d. For thus it holds, a.b. to c.d. as 2. to 4. & 3. to 6.
*For example.*

[An illustration showing two surveyors using cross-staffs (baculi Jacobi) to measure the height of a tower. The tower is labeled with 'D' at the top and 'C' at the bottom. The surveyors are positioned at different distances from the tower; the first station is marked with 'a' and 'b'. Dotted lines represent lines of sight from the instruments to the top and bottom of the tower.]

Rule II.

Also, by the proportion of the width of the object, the length is determined: for as the triangle A. B. C. is constituted, so also is the triangle of the instrument, c. d. e., proportioned. Therefore, the side of the triangle, A. B. C., namely B. C., is similar to the side c. d. e. of the instrument. Side C. B. therefore relates to side A. B. by a sesquiquarta proportion; therefore, divide side A. B. into 5 equal parts, but subtract one, and that will be the length, B. C. as we have extensively demonstrated in our third book on Geometry, where we made ample mention of a similar Jacob's staff in every kind of measurement, where we also spoke fully of the use of the quadrant, and of the instruments invented by us. Moreover, you will find an example of this rule in that place, where the length alone is investigated by a single station.

Rule III.

The proportion of weights and mobile objects is continued by natural progression, whose terms, if successively multiplied, will produce the weights of the positions in geometric proportion, as is shown in the following figure.

C A P. III.
*Of the rule of three proportions.*
Rule I.

Two proportional numbers being known, a third will also be known by this rule.
For if five parts of the parallel line A. B. yield 14 parts in line C. D., then 40 parts of line A. B. will yield 112 parts of line C. D.
For triangle A. B. E. has similar angles with triangle A. C. D. E. And the equally divided parts of line or side A. B. are proportional to the divided parts of line C. D.

*number more closely. For that digit will be the root of the square, as 6 is the root of the square 36. Similarly, 8 is*
*the root of the square 64, because 6 multiplied by itself will produce 36, which no other digit can*

*concerning which this lower wheel, whose outer sphere denotes roots, and inner [sphere] denotes squares.*

                  *The Use of this type of battle formation.*
   Such a formation of soldiers, which the French call *Bataillons en point ou en lozange* (Battalions in point or in lozenge), is little in use today, unless necessity compels it, when, namely, the flat terrain of some place presents itself to cohorts making their way, whose entrance or exit is very narrow, being almost surrounded by rocks, mountains, forests, rivers, swamps, or lakes, through which it is necessary for the army to pass; Similarly, when hostilely invading a town, such a formation is required, and especially where the streets are too narrow.

Regula VI.

*Whoever wishes to arrange soldiers in battle in such a way that the battle line has double, triple, or quadruple the length than the width, let him divide the total number of soldiers into as many parts as he wishes, so that its length is that many times the width; for example, if the length ought to be three times the width, the number of soldiers must be divided by 3; and the root of the quotient will be the number of men in the shorter side; if four times, let it be divided by 4, etc. Let the number of soldiers therefore be 2310. If this is divided by 3, the quotient will be 770. Its root will be 27, and 41 men remain, who can serve other purposes. The demonstration follows below.*

Rule XII.
A ladder by which soldiers may ascend the walls of a town fortified by a ditch is best adapted in this way: From the edge of the ditch to the foot of the wall, let the exact length be taken; similarly, the height of the wall; For a straight line crossing the ditch will form a right angle with the foot of the wall: Therefore, the length of the diagonal line, by which the ladder should be measured, is elicited in that manner, which is taught in Geometrical Arithmetic, in the chapter on multiplication with subtraction, rule one.

ON MUSICAL ARITHMETIC. 131

CHAPTER I:
On Musical Proportion.

[Decorative initial A]To add in proportions is to multiply, but to subtract is to divide, to double is to multiply by itself; Therefore, multiplication and division have no place in proportions, because proportions do not receive unity; For one does not descend beyond the double: However, the demonstration of this rule can be seen as if with one's own eyes in the division of the monochord.
A multiple proportion is one in which the larger number is compared to the smaller in quantity and measure.
However, how all other proportions relate to each other is shown in the book on numeration and the chapter on proportions.

CHAPTER II.
On the Proportion and Invention of Monochord Letters.

Rule I.
The letter A. and the first tone are found on the monochord if you divide the entire string into nine equal parts; for the first division from the head of the string will be the letter A. and the space between Γ and A. will be a tone; Therefore, if the part Γ A. is removed from the string, an entire tone is removed from the string sounding Γ Π.
Boethius calls this section Hypatehypaton, just as Γ sounds Proslambomenos.

[Diagram: A horizontal line representing a monochord string. Above the line are the labels "Tonus" and "A". Below the line are the Greek letter "Γ" at the start, followed by numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and the Greek letter "Π" at the end.]

Rule II.
The letter B. and the second tone are found on the monochord by dividing the space of string A. Π into nine equal parts; For where the first part ends, there the low B. will be placed, and between the space A. and B. we will find another tone, and in this way, tone upon tone is raised throughout the entire monochord by removing one part. Boethius calls this interval Parhypatehypaton.

[Diagram: A horizontal line representing a monochord string. Above the line are the labels "Γ", "a", "b". Below the line are the labels "Tonus", "Tonus;", and numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and the Greek letter "Π" at the end.]

Rule III.
The letter C. and the consonance Diatessaron are produced on the monochord by dividing the entire string Γ Π into four equal parts: For the end of the first will be the low letter C.; and the space between B. and C. will be a semitone and is called Lichanos hypaton. And the distance Γ C. is the sesquitertian proportion of the string, under which the consonance diatessaron is contained.

Rule VI.
The letter F. and the second semitone are made by dividing the space of the monochord between C. grave and $\Pi$ into 4 equal parts; for where the first ends, there F. grave will be placed; Between E. moreover and F. a semitone will be found; therefore, between E. and F. there will also be the consonance Diatessaron; They call this section Antilichanos meson.

[Diagram 4: A horizontal line with points labeled $\Gamma$, A, B, C, D, E, F. An arc labeled "Diateſſaron" spans from C to F. Labels "Ton:", "Ton:", "Semit:" are below. Numbers 2, 3, 4 mark divisions.]

Rule VII.
The letter G., the consonance Diapason, and the sound after the semitone are found in two ways; First, if the distance between F. and $\Pi$ is divided into 9 equal parts. For the extremity of the first part will be the place of G. grave. Or, let the whole monochord be divided into two equal parts, the end of the first of which will be the place of the letter G. and the space between F. and G. will be the tone after the semitone E. F. And the distance of the string $\Gamma$ G. will be a duple proportion: for as 2. is to 1., so the whole string is to $\Gamma$ G., which is its half part, wherefore it is called Mese, the middle, by the ancients. And in this proportion consists the Diapason.

### Rule VIII.
*In exactly the same way, the sharp notes are to be found as the low notes, namely, by dividing the remainder of the string G. $\Pi$ into 9 parts for the finding of the sharp note A; then the distance A. $\Pi$. into another 9 parts for finding the place of sharp B, and so for the rest.*

### Rule IX.
*We shall also proceed with the same method for the finding of the superexcellent or super-sharp notes, as will appear more fully in the following demonstration.*

### Rule X.
*The ratio of a tone is as 9 to 8; but the ratio of a semitone is the superpartient ratio 256 to 243. For example, if the monochord is divided into 324 [units], that number is a tone: But the second tone is 288. A semitone is 256. A Diatessaron is as 4 to 3. A Diapente is as 3 to 2. And a Diapason is as 2 to one, as is clear in the following example.*

Regula XI.
From the Diapason with the Diapente arises a triple proportion, or a double sesquialtera proportion:
From the bisdiapason, a quadruple proportion, and from 3 diapasons arises an octuple proportion: The Diateßaron consists in a sesquitertian proportion. The Diapente truly remains in a sesquialtera proportion, as is clearly presented to the eyes of observers in the preceding demonstration.

C A P. III.
Concerning the discovery of consonances from the proportion of weights.

Regula I.
Six to twelve is a double proportion. Therefore, in this proportion consisted the weights of Pythagoras's extreme hammers, so that one would resound to the other through the consonance of the Diapason.

[Illustration of two hammers of different sizes and a rectangular block]
6. Ounces. 12. Ounces.

Differences of weight.

Regula II.
Pythagoras composed his third hammer from a weight of 8 ounces, so that it would sound a Diateßaron to the fourth. For 6 to 8 are related by a sesquitertian proportion, by which proportion also he related his second hammer to the first: for a second hammer he formed from 9 ounces, and 9 to 12 are related by a sesquitertian proportion, as:

[Illustration of four hammers of increasing size and a rectangular block]
6 Oz: 8 Oz: 9 Oz: 12 Oz:

Numbers

--- Page 140 ---
536          TREATISE II. PART 1. BOOK VI.

Therefore, numbers comprehending musical consonances were found from the weights of the hammers. Just as there were four hammers, so there are four numbers found from their weights, as has been said, which contain almost all the power of music. These numbers are therefore 6, 8, 9, 12. In these four numbers, therefore, you will find as many proportions, and through this, as many perfect consonances. These proportions are therefore, namely *Duple, Sesquialtera, Sesquitertia, Sesquioctava.* Duple proportion is when the larger number, compared to the smaller, contains it twice within itself, such as 6 to 12, and 4 to 8, and 2 to 4, and 1 to 2. Under this proportion falls the consonance called Diapaſon, as demonstrated below in the monochord.

If you wish to prove this, whether with strings, or pipes, or bells, or large bells and all sounding things, it is necessary that one thing be double another, and thus the other, its half, will undoubtedly resonate a Diapaſon for you.

*Sesquialtera proportion is* when the larger number, related to the smaller, will contain the smaller number entirely within itself, and moreover, half of its part, such as 12 to 8, and 9 to 6, and 6 to 4, and 3 to 2. From this proportion arises that consonance which is called Diapente. Therefore, wherever Diapente is found, there the lower voice of it will always contain the entire other part within itself and its half.

*Sesquitertia proportion is* when the larger number, compared to the smaller, contains it entirely within itself, and a third of its part, such as 12 to 9, and 8 to 6, and 4 to 3. From this agreement of numbers consists the Diateſſaron consonance, where its lower voice contains the entire other part within itself, and its third part.

*Sesquioctava proportion is* when the larger number, related to the smaller, contains the entire smaller number within itself and an eighth of its part, such as 9 to 8, which is a unit, in which proportion the tone is comprehended, and do not doubt that its lower voice contains the entire other part within itself, and its eighth part.

*Note,* that wherever the aforesaid consonances are, you will undoubtedly find those proportional numbers, by which alone, and by no others, we divided the monochord, as above; by these also all musical instruments are formed, such as pipes, cymbals and small bells or large bells; by these, citharas, lyres, and viols resonate. Finally, whatever in the world resonates musically will in no way deviate from these proportions of numbers.

C H A P. IV.

*On temporal proportion.*

Rule I.

IN duple proportion, two notes are equivalent to one similar to themselves in name and quantity, such as two minims to one, and two semibreves to one. Similarly, in triple proportion, 3 notes are equivalent to one. In quadruple proportion, 4 notes are equivalent to one in measure and quantity, and so in others.

Rule II.

*Quintuple proportion is always figured by a semibreve.*

Rule III.

*Sextuple proportion, due to its speed, cannot easily be expressed by fingers or lips through a minim. Therefore, this proportion must always be composed by a semibreve.*

C H A P. IV.

ON THE FINDING OF THE CONJUNCTION, OPPOSITION & QUADRATURE OF THE LUMINARIES.

To the number of your year's Epact add as many days as months have elapsed since the beginning of March, from which number subtract 30 if the number exceeds 30, and the remainder will be the day of the conjunction of that month in which the conjunction is to be sought. To these days, adding seven and a half, the day of the first quadrature will result; to which again adding seven and a half, the day of the opposition will be born: finally, to these adding 7 and a half, the second quadrature will be produced. Let the year therefore be 1600, whose Epact is 15. Let the month be July, in which the time of conjunction is to be sought, which is the fifth month from March: therefore 5 are to be added to 15.

C A P. V.

*On the Finding of Aspects in the Zodiac.*

The Zodiac consists of 360 parts, which by bisection denotes the $\circ-\circ$ aspect; but if it is divided by 3, the quotient will be the third part of the Zodiac, making the $\triangle$ aspect: if by 4, it will produce the $\square$ aspect; if by 6, the quotient will denote the $*$ aspect.

*On the finding of the true hour of any day, in which $\sigma$. $\circ-\circ$. $\square$. $\triangle$.*

BECAUSE it happens that at the hour of an aspect, a celestial figure (horoscope) is erected, either for indicating changes in the air, or for making elections (choosing auspicious times). C A P. IX.
*On finding the* EQUAL HOURS *of any day.*
Let the portion of the day's circle be divided by 15, and the quotient will be the number of equal hours of the day: In this same way, the equal hours of the night are found, if the nocturnal portion is divided by 15.
***
C A P X.
*On the conversion of equal hours into unequal hours.*
Multiply the equal hours by 15, and divide the product by the degrees of the hours of that day; and you will have the unequal hours.
***
C A P XI.
*On the conversion of unequal hours into equal hours.*
Multiply the unequal hours by the parts of the hours of that day itself, and divide what results by fifteen, and you will have the equal hours.
***
C A P XII.
*On finding the* DIURNAL MOTION OF ANY PLANET.
The motion of the Planet is to be considered, namely whether it is retrograde or direct? For if it is retrograde, the minutes and seconds are to be subtracted. But where the Planet is direct, minutes with seconds are to be added, as ♃ is retrograde on the fourth day of November. The difference of its motion from the 3rd to the 4th is between 39 and 34. Similarly, its direct motion on the 3rd of July is between 24 and 13.
♃ retr. 39       ♃ Direct. 24.

C A P. XIII.
*On the CALCULATION OF THE MOTION OF THE PLANETS FOR ANY HOUR.*
The diurnal motion of any Planet and the hours elapsed from noon are to be reduced to minutes: Then multiply the minutes of one by the minutes of the other, and divide the product by 24. Again, let the quotient number be divided by 60, and the true quotient will denote the motion of that Planet. Let therefore the diurnal motion of the Sun be 58 minutes, and the hours in question after noon be 20 and 30 minutes.

Rule I.

C H A P. III.

*On Subtraction.*

Rule I.

¶ Subtraction in this art is performed by the same means, namely by subtracting the bases of the places from the upper series, and placing the transformed result in the fundamental place. Thus character 4, namely *pileus* (cap), subtracted from character 5, that is *cornu* (horn), generates character 1, *hasta* (spear), and so in the others, as is found in common Arithmetic.

C H A P. IV.

*On Multiplication.*

IN multiplication, where the multiplier is an article, the method is plainly the same. But because sometimes the multiplier is composed of many articles, therefore the fundamental place is divided into 3 or more equal parts according to its length, of which one will be green, another white, and the third red. For by these distinctions the multiplicands can be explained better and more clearly, and this is also explained by the following example. Whatever the aggregate may be in multiplication, it must be expressed in the black part.

*On Division.*

Because this last species of Arithmetic is very rarely used in this art, both because of the difficulty of its ready comprehension and because of the multitude of its operations, by which confusion would be generated in the Artist's imagination, we will make no mention of it in this place; but we will leave it to be discovered by the sharper investigations of others, accelerating our steps towards playful Arithmetic, by which we will at last refresh for a while our concept, already wearied by vain imaginations.

T H E M O S T S P L E N D I D

D E S C R I P T I O N

O F T H E P R E F I G U R E D T E M P L E.

[Large decorative initial D] Escribing the structure and location of this temple, poets would sing wondrous things, whose intentions usually revolve constantly around fables and fictions; indeed, they would pursue this subject much more eagerly, since Music derived its name from their Goddesses, namely the Muses, as is found in its Etymology. Therefore, I ask their pardon if I allow myself to be led by the stimulus and invention of poetic frenzy, though not by measure, in the description of this temple. Let us therefore imagine this Musical Temple built on the summit of Mount Parnassus, the seat of the Muses, adorned on every side with groves and fields flourishing with eternal greenery; and surrounded by crystal springs gently flowing here and there; whose murmur often induces peaceful sleep in passers-by, while little birds frequenting those parts and inhabiting the groves seem diligently to lay the foundation with their sharper songs (so that they may pour forth diverse consonances of sounds more symphonically), by whose melody the Nymphs themselves around the temple, the Satyrs led by Sylvanus through its groves, and the Shepherds (with Pan as their leader) are moved to lead dances through the fields. Among these delights, therefore, that divine gift of Apollo is established, preserved, and indeed worshipped with the adoration of all souls; all its constituent parts, dedicated to peace and concord, are so bound to each other by the mysteries of harmony and symphony, which include the concordances of heaven and the elements, that the entire universe must perish and be reduced to nothing by the strife of discord, before its consonances either fail or are corrupted.

[Marginal note: a] Therefore, the President or Goddess of this temple is *Concord*, ineffable
Concord, the great offspring of the Being of Beings, by whose adoration small things
grow, and by whose contempt great things fall apart. Its guardian or priestess
is *Thalia*, the sweetest of the nine Muses; by whose teachings the hidden
mysteries of concord are explained to wanderers and to those who humbly
seek her Oracles.
      Therefore, with eager eyes, the learned person will observe every
part of this structure, nor will he scorn its smallest portion,
because in every part, as in its whole, that harmonious soul of Apollo moves,
and that spirit of Music, gently soothing and gladdening the souls of living
beings through all the nerves of this structure, accustomed to breathe like a
Zephyr, carrying away with it human desires, and restraining the rage of
malignant Daemons with its sweetness, as if imbuing them with a certain
humanity: Eagerly, I say, you should gaze upon the spiral revolution of the
great temple's tower, which denotes the movement of air after it is struck by
sound or voice. The two gates signify ears, the organs of hearing, without
which sound produced is not perceived, nor is there entry into this temple
except through them. In the second place, you will observe its three smaller
towers, representing the dispositions of notes, [Marginal note: b] b round, [Marginal note: #] # square, and
natural; And with the observation of these, three parallelograms are to be
keenly inspected (each built naturally related to its respective tower),
demonstrating the different natures, appellations, and positions of the
aforesaid notes in the system: Moreover, the pipes or organs expressed at the
summit of these parallelograms denote the differences of voices and sounds
of each parallelogram. Nor is the division of the column of this temple to be
scorned, since it will delineate the true proportions of the monochord and
the diverse species of consonances. The clock also is to be diligently
weighed, lest time unexpectedly slip away, or proceed with too slow a pace
(that is, with no proportion or measure observed). Therefore, this clock is,
as it were, the regular guardian of the time of notes, and a very ample
mirror of their simple value. Why also should not the triangle of
commensurable quantity be inspected, which explores the diversity of the
proportion of times both in diminution and in augmentation, and clearly
demonstrates the perfection and imperfection of notes? Also, the symphonic
triangle of the system of intervals, as the final mystery of all the rest, is to be
inspected with no small care, since through it, and from it, all musical
consonances are drawn forth, without which no symphony exists: upon
which triangle is depicted a history, by which the reason for the invention of
these concordances is explained, namely *Pythagoras'*
                                                                                               observation

observation, who, happening by chance to pass through the workshop of a certain blacksmith, and perceiving the consonance of sounds from the blows of four hammers, ordered those hammers to be weighed. From the differences of their weights, he discovered three musical proportions or consonances: Diatessaron, Diapente, and Diapason, which we have explained more clearly through the letters of the three temple windows and the connections of those letters. These also contribute equally to the composition of symphonic harmony, as does that symphonic triangle. If, eager Reader, you have sagaciously examined these parts of this temple, I say, you will be a participant in all its mysteries, and a most expert master in this excellent science.

166          TRACT. II.  PART. II.  LIB. I.

In a not dissimilar knot is the soul connected with the body of the Microcosm;
From which wonderful actions of life proceed, and the harmony of humors both for vivification
and for vegetation. For one function gently and kindly aids another.
That species of Music, however, which is called instrumental, is concerned with discerning
and knowing songs. Therefore it contains Harmonic Music; whose role is to distinguish
sounds into low and high. And this consists in numbers and figures. It is therefore
either local according to the proportion of sounds and voices in continuous quantity,
or temporal according to the proportion of long and short figures in discrete quantity.
From these it is clear that harmonic Music is the discernment of modulation and the science
of truly singing, and an easy path to perfection, and the science of many dissimilar
proportional voices, and consonance; or the science of number related to sounds.
From which it is established that under Harmony, Melody and Symphony are contained;
of which Melody is the harmony of sounds, inflected in a certain system and manner to the
singer's emotion; Symphony, however, is the concordant harmony of distinct sounds
and melodies. Universal harmony, however, is brought into being either by the striking
of the voice; and is called a natural Instrument; or by the vibration of strings, as in a
lute; or by the collision of air through the holes of some hollow body, like a pipe.
And these two species are artificial instruments. Under instrumental Music, Rhythmic
and Metric Music are also comprehended; of which Rhythmic is that part which is
required in the scansion of poems invented for songs, namely whether the words, which
are to be used in singing and reading, cohere well or badly; Metric Music, however,
shows the measures of various meters by probable reason, as is clear in Heroic, Iambic,
Elegiac meter and similar ones.

C A P IV.

*On the Musician.*

He who merely sings is not a Musician. For according to *Boethius, book one, last chapter:* A musician is he who, with forethought reason, manifests the science of singing not only through the service of practice, but also through the command of speculation, which we have seen in the work of buildings and wars. Hence there is a great discrepancy between the definition of a Musician and a Singer: for the Musician knows and composes music. But the latter merely perform; and he who grasps what he does not understand is defined as a beast, as in the following verse.
*A beast, not a Singer, is he who sings not by art, but by habit,*
*It is not the voice that makes a Singer of art, but instruction.*

C H A P. V.
*Concerning the matter or subject of Music, and concerning the sense of hearing.*

The matter or subject of Music is sound, which is an undissolved percussion of air, and a violent vibration of the same in low and high pitches, which, by its spiral and rolling motion in the air, tending upwards obliquely here and there (according to the disposition of the medium), finally penetrates the ears through a forced revolution of the same medium, and invades the inner senses. And hence it is that we have fashioned two temple gates, in the manner of the duality of the ears at the summit of the system. For without the sense of hearing, there is no access to the temple of *Concord*. Similarly, we have represented the spiral revolution of air after the production of sound above both gates, so that the dissolved motion of air might be better comprehended by the mind, all of which we have described in this place.

# BOOK TWO,
## On the Musical System.

### PROEM OF BOOK II.

[Decorative initial Q] That square of the temple of Music, which we described below, formed from three parallelograms, we call the musical system; which is nothing other than that subject constituted by lines and keys, in which the ratio of sounds and the melody of song consists, without the knowledge and degrees of whose square surface, it will be impossible to enter the gate of this temple. For without the commanding and commanded notes, together with syllables and keys, both principal and less principal (on account of whose differences the musical system is found), without doubt no one can attain the perfection of this science. Therefore, the first parallelogram of the square, towards the left, denotes the keys and voices of the song or of the B-flat (soft) system; whence it is expressed under a round tower, in which soft sounds or gravely sounding bells are imagined to hang or sound according to the diversity of syllables and organs. The second parallelogram, or the middle one, however, distinguishes natural notes; which is also depicted quite clearly under a tower naturally in the form of fire, that is, sharply ascending (since fire itself is called nature by Philosophers); in which tower also, bells or voices sounding between low and high are imagined. We have therefore depicted the summit of the tower more acute, as if prominent between the two differences, B-round (B-flat) and natural. The third parallelogram, however, we have placed under a square tower because from this kind of hard system square sounds are produced. Therefore, such bells are found in the same tower, which sound hard and square. That part of the temple of Music, however, is depicted by itself in this place, to the explanation of which we will apply this entire second book.

**ABOUT THE MUSICAL SYSTEM. 173**
*Natural is that which exceeds neither in softness nor in hardness.*
*Ministerial keys are all the rest, whose voices are either necessarily referred to the orders of the principals, or make their own order.*
*Signed keys are those which are expressed in the lines of the song.*
*Understood keys are all the others which are not expressed.*
*Voices are fictitious syllables attributed to the keys, by which the differences of sounds are expressed.*
*Grave keys are those in which all songs are gravely produced.*
*Acute keys are those which sharpen all songs.*
*Peracute keys render higher sounds, and excel the acute ones.*
*Deduction is the place on the monochord where the voice Ut is found.*

**CH A P. I.**
*Concerning the exposition of the three towers of the temple, where the song and its keys are discussed.*

*Just as the Theoretical science of Music teaches the method of finding neumes, and of knowing their numbers and proportions, so that Music may be composed from these; so the practice of the same science revolves around three species of sound, to which we have compared the above-described towers of the temple, of which the first is low, the second is middle, and the last is high, from which all melody is composed. Hence, therefore, it happens that the ancients attributed three different properties to plainchant, one of which is ♮ hard or square, which is said to have a whole tone below itself, and a semitone above itself. And we have compared this kind of song property to the square tower, in which we shall imagine sounds or bells sounding hard and sharp to be found; The other is b soft or round, whose sounds we have conceived to be enclosed in the round tower, which is said to have a semitone below itself, and a whole tone above itself; And the third property of song is called natural; because it is taken without any difference. Hence we have fashioned its tower naturally ascending in the form of fire acutely; for in its movement it exceeds neither in softness nor in hardness, but proceeds with a natural sound; Hence it differs both from b round, which sounds somewhat softer than the natural, and also from the hard (♮), which produces a somewhat harder voice than the natural.*

Rule I.
Concerning the properties of song.
*Every song beginning on C is sung by nature, on F by b soft, on G by ♮ hard. Hence the verse.*
*C gives nature, f marks b soft for you.*
*G also hard, etc.*

Rule II.
Concerning b soft.
*In the soft scale, in which b soft is prefixed in its place, one ascends to c f. by Ut. but to d. and a. one descends by la, according to the ancient verse.*
*Say to ascend c & f, to descend d & a soft.*

			Rule IV.

	In the modulation of plainchant, the place of b flat and b natural must always be observed. For according to the more learned in this science, when someone begins to modulate naturally in the low notes, and makes a mutation to low G, or to high A, if he ascends to high C, or to high D or E, before he descends to low F, it must be sung with b natural. But if the mutation occurs in the aforesaid place, and a descent is made to low F before they ascend to high C, or high D or E, after the mutation, it must be sung with b flat in high B. And just as it has been said concerning the low notes, so it is to be understood concerning the high notes and super-high notes.
