**CHAPTER II.**

**How are B flat and B natural to be placed on the monochord?**

Regarding the position of B natural (♮) on the monochord, we spoke in the description of the monochord in Musical Arithmetic, which we depicted according to the nature of B natural: in which way we also divided our column, because according to the description of B natural, it has a whole tone below it and a semitone above it. Now it remains for us to find the true place of B flat (b rotundum) on the monochord, whose property is contrary to that of B natural, because it will have a whole tone above it and a semitone below it. It is placed on the monochord in this way. Let the entire space of the monochord between F and the bridge be divided into four equal parts, and where the first part ends, there B flat (b rotundum) is to be placed, and there you will find a Diatessaron consisting of two whole tones and a minor semitone. And this is continued throughout the entire Diatonic monochord; as appears in the following description.

[An illustration of a monochord, a musical instrument with a single string stretched over a wooden body. The instrument is marked with various labels including letters 'F' and 'b', numbers '1', '2', '3', and musical symbols for flat (b) and natural (♮). A hand on the left is shown holding a small hammer or plectrum labeled 'malle'.]

**CHAPTER III.**

**About the keys of the system, both marked and implied.**

The letters found in the first square parallelogram towards the right are called keys; because just as a lock is usually opened by keys, so through these letters the melody of all Music is opened. However, the primary key according to the ancients is Gamma (Γ): But in these times, lower keys are in use, especially in instrumental Music. However, there are many differences among these keys, as some are low (graves), both lower and higher, some are high (acutae), simple, and doubled or very high (peracutae), and some are extremely high (perperacutae) and excellent. Low (Graves) are so called because all melodies that revolve around them are sung low. And from these, the Bass part is governed. High (Acutae), because all melodies that revolve around them (such as Tenor, Contratenor, and Altus) are made higher. And Excellent or extremely high (perperacutae), because they render a sound higher than the very high (peracutae), and they excel them both in elevation and in place, and by these the Discant is governed. However, these keys, which are called marked, are always noted on the lines for the system of melody. For just as sailors navigating uncertainly are guided by certain terrestrial signs, such as a tower or a flame of fire, and safely reach their desired goal; so also singers are directed by such expressed signs or keys in the system.

CHAP. IV.

*Of the names of the notes, of their orders or changes, and by what interval they are measured?*

AS the letters found in the aforesaid square claim for themselves the name of keys; so the syllables found between the same parallels next to them are called the voices of the keys, and are applied to them, and in Music are found for distinguishing the recurring degrees of sounds. In these notes, however, a twofold order is to be observed, of which the former is simple, and that is twofold. For *one* is called *Principal*, which, running through the principal keys, has middle notes, and this kind of order is either *soft* or *hard*; The *other* is called *ministerial* or *natural*, which touches neither b nor ♮. The latter difference of order, however, is that order which is called *conjunct*; which occurs when one of the principal ones is so joined with the natural, that three or two extreme syllables run next to each other.

Hence arise certain rules to be observed in the conjunct order, which follow below.

Rule I.
In the *Discanti* scale from the simple soft and natural, for sol, re, ascending, for mi, la, descending.

Rule II.
In the *Alti* scale from the same, la, is turned into re, and in the *Tenoris* scale for sol, re, ascending, for mi, la, descending.

Rule III.
In the *Basis* scale from the same, la, is turned into re, ascending, and again descending re is permuted into la.

Rule IV.
In the *Discanti* scale from the simple hard and natural, la into re ascending, and vice versa; in the *Tenoris* scale, la into re, and vice versa; and in the *Basis* scale, for sol, re, for mi, la.

#### D E F I N I T I O N S.

**S**chisma is half of the difference between the major and minor semitone, that is, half part of a Comma.
    Comma is the space by which the sesquioctave ratio is greater than two dieses, that is, two minor semitones, or it is the space by which 6 sesquioctaves are greater than one Diapason; or Comma is the difference between the major and minor semitone, that is, the excess of the major semitone over the minor.
    Diaschisma is half of a major semitone, that is, Diesis is that space, or that part of a tone, which is called a minor semitone.
    Apotome is that space of a tone which is called a major semitone.
    Tone is a perfect interval between two voices, containing two unequal semitones, or Tone is a certain undissolved percussion of air up to the hearing.
    Semiditone is one ratio between three notes immediately related to each other, such as Mi & Sol, Re & Fa.
    Ditone is a ratio between three notes immediately related to each other, such as Fa & La, Ut & Mi.

CONCERNING MUSICAL CONSONANCES. 185

C H A P. I.
Concerning the small quantities of the Monochord.

A larger space in the column or Monochord between two notes is called a Tonus (Tone), and that from "tonando," that is, "sonando" (sounding), because it is the first in consonances. But a smaller interval, which is found in it, we call a semitonium (semitone), and that not because it is considered to be half a tone, as some believe, since a tone is not divided into two equal parts, that is, into two equal semitones, but into unequal ones, of which the larger is called an Apothema among the Greeks, and the other, smaller, a Diesis. The unequal division of that tone is most clearly demonstrated to us by b flat and b natural on the monochord; For since from A to B natural is a tone, and between A and B flat is a semitone, the space between B flat and B natural will be larger than between A and B flat. From which it is clear that a Tone is not divided into two equal parts, but into a larger and a smaller space, as appears in the following book, chapter two.

Rule I.
If you take away a Diatessaron from three tones, a major semitone will remain.

C H A P. II.
*On the proportions of the major and minor semitone, the comma and*
*schisma.*

The Ditone, Semiditone, and semitone are separated by some from the proportions of numbers described in Musical Arithmetic, since they fall into no, or at least difficult, musical proportions. Boethius, however, in Book 1, Chapter 17, affirms that the major and minor semitone are accommodated into a numerical comparison; For, he says in Book 2, Chapter 27, the minor semitone is as 243 to 256. Similarly, in another place, he affirms that the minor semitone is as 1944 to 2089. The major semitone, however, is as 2187 to 2048. Finally, the Comma is as 531441 to 524288. Regarding the schisma, however, which is half of a Comma, he denies that it can be introduced into a musical proportion; There is also a similar impossibility in introducing the Diaschisma under the same proportions.

[horizontal line]

C H A P. III.
*On consonances from the conjunction of sounds, both simple and*
*compound.*

Simple consonances from the conjunction of sounds are the Diatessaron and Diapente, the former of which is found in four spaces of the monochord; the Diapente, however, in only three; the Diapason, however, contains these two, and comprehends other consonances under itself. The Diatessaron contains within itself a Ditone with a semitone. For its name comes from the fact that it is constituted from four voices; because διὰ in Greek means 'through' or 'by means of', and τέσσαρα, that is, four. The Diapente, however, is called from διὰ, that is, 'through' or 'by means of', and πέντε, which is five; because it is constituted by five voices; the Diapason, however, contains all consonances within itself, such as the Tone, Semitone, Ditone, Diatessaron, Tritone, Diapente, Tone with Diapente, Semiditone with Diapente, Ditone with Diapente, and Diapason. From which it derived its name from the Greeks. For διὰ is 'through' or 'by means of', πᾶν (pan) is 'all'; It is nevertheless manifest that the Diapason does not contain nine voices within itself, namely those four from the Diatessaron and five from the Diapente, because, when these two consonances are joined for the constitution of the Diapason, the same voice will be at the top of the Diatessaron and at the bottom of the Diapente, and vice versa; From which it follows that the Diapason has no more than eight voices. The Diatessaron therefore consists of four voices, three intervals, two tones, and a minor semitone: the Diapente of 5 voices, four intervals, and three tones with a minor semitone; And the Diapason from these two, because it contains 6 tones, excluding the comma, seven spaces; Its voices, however, are only eight, as we said before, all of which are more clearly explained in the following monochord.

C A P. IV.

*On perfect and imperfect consonances.*

Among consonances, some are perfect, namely 4: Diapason, Diapente, Diatessaron, and the Tone. The reason for their perfection is that the monochord is divided only by these consonances, and not by others, which must always and infallibly occur in certain proportions: For the tone is found nowhere except in the sesquioctave proportion; Diatessaron in the sesquitertia proportion; Diapente in the sesquialtera proportion; and Diapason is found in the duple proportion, the principle of which is the unison, which always holds the proportion of equality. The other consonances, however, are called imperfect, namely the Semiditone, Ditone, Semitone with Diapente, and Tone with Diapente, etc.

C A P. V.

*On the Diatessaron.*

Diatessaron, which is a perfect consonance, is called one of the principal consonances, because it is more involved in the proportions and quantities of Music, and the monochord is more frequently measured by it. Similarly, through it the round b (B-flat) and the square ♮ (B-natural) are investigated, and the major and minor semitone are demonstrated by it. And just as it is a principal consonance, so some assert it to be the principal concord. And the reason for this is that it firmly maintains its proportion both when ascending and when descending; similarly, because it is more involved with musical proportions than other consonances. However, it is not a consonance by itself; for if it were to concord with the first low voice, it would concord

Aa 2

--- Page 182 ---
188 TRACT. II. PART. II. LIB. III.
...it would also agree above the eighth note, because the first note and the eighth are equivocal; However, that the consonance of the Diatessaron does not agree above the octave, is clear from Boethius, book two, chapter twenty-fourth. "If," he says, "Diapason and Diatessaron are joined, they will produce no consonance, but discord." Therefore, by themselves they do not agree, but when subordinated to another consonance. However, that not every consonance agrees, Boethius relates in book one, chapter three, where he says that consonance is the agreement of voices dissimilar among themselves, reduced into one. Similarly, concordance is a mixture of high and low sound, sweetly and in unison insinuating itself into the ears.

C H A P T E R V I.
On the consonance of the Diapason, and how it is found from any
note on the monochord?

After the seven notes on the monochord are finished, the eighth always returns, just as after the seven days are finished, the eighth, which was the first, returns. For in the eighth note are comprised qualities, that is, elevations and depressions, and orders of tones, which arose earlier on account of the perfection and unity of consonance: From which it is concluded that the first note and the eighth are of the same quality and the same similarity; Also, that the elevations and depressions in both notes are equal, there is no doubt. Hence, if one singer sings some Antiphon through this consonance using low notes, and another using high notes, you will perceive no diversity of voices, but you will perceive their unity: Therefore there are only 7 distinctions of notes on the monochord; For although there are more lines on it than seven, it is nevertheless only a repetition of the same. For all similar notes agree best in the Diapason. But in order that you may find the Diapason from any note on the monochord, let the whole monochord be divided from the given note to its bridge into two equal parts; And the middle dividing section will be the Diapason to the given note. Let the given note therefore be low A; But the midpoint of the space between A and the bridge will be the Diapason, which will be the eighth note from the letter A, of the same quality and similarity, as appears in the following monochord.

C A P. VII.

*How consonances arise from proportions expressed in Musical Arithmetic, & how proportions arise upon proportion.*

FROM musical proportions, which we mentioned in Musical Arithmetic, others arise, namely Triple and Quadruple. The Triple, or Double Sesquialtera, proportion arises from the Diapason with the diapente: the Quadruple, however, from twice the Diapason, and the octuple from thrice the Diapason, as will be evident in the following demonstration. And from these it is manifest that the Diatessaron is the first major consonance, which remains in the sesquitertia proportion; the Diapente is the second major consonance, which consists in the sesquialtera proportion; the Tone is the distance by which the diapason exceeds the Diatessaron, and is the sesquioctava proportion: And thus there throughout the entire monochord the Diapason remains in the same proportion; which is the third major consonance, which consists in the duple proportion, as has been explained in the following demonstration.

Simple notes are the characters of Musical Times expressed without ligature or dots, and they are Larga, Longa, Brevis, Semibrevis, Minima, Fusa, etc.
The Larga or maxima is the largest among all measurable figures.
A Longa is half part of a Larga.
A Brevis is half part of a Longa.
A Semibrevis is half the quantity of a Brevis.
A Minima is half the quantity of a Semibrevis, whose half is a Semiminima.
Unequal proportion or odd time is of unequal duration, yet comprised within the same beat movement.
Hence it is that its notes are of unequal form.
A ligature note is the conjunction of two or more figures together.
A note with a dot towards the right is the value of the same note with its half, as [musical symbol: dotted square note] denotes [musical symbols: three diamond notes] which are, [musical symbol: square note] with [musical symbol: diamond note].
The figure to be held back is called a Pausa (rest), which is nothing other than the omission of the proper sound, made in the due quantity of some note, as if it were somehow sounded.
That sign, which is an internal indication of time, is in the unusual blackness of the note or in the doubling of rests.
An external sign, which is also an indication of time, is that which is prefixed and consists of circles, dots, and numbers, as we will demonstrate below.
A Fusa is half part of a Semiminima.

C H A P. I.

*Concerning simple figures to be expressed by voice.*

**A**mong the ancients, the Minima relates to time as unity relates to number, or a point to a line. For just as unity is not a number, nor a point a line, but their beginning; So the Minima is not Musical Time, but the beginning of measured time. Hence it is clear that the head of measurable Music is the Minima; just as unity is the head of number, which cannot be divided. More recent authors, however, have invented still smaller notes, and completely overturned the aforesaid opinion of the ancients; Among whom Philip de Vitry, who was called the flower of the whole world in Music, is said to have invented the crochuta or semiminima, which we also called semiminima above; Others after him also produced smaller notes by their art, such as the Fusa, Semifusa, and its half part, about which we will speak below. However, I would rather approve and follow the method of Brother Robert Brunham in this matter, who set forth three species of square figures, from which 6 species of simple notes are formed, from the largest of which consists one species, which is called Larga; from the middle square are made two second species, namely, Longa and brevis; from the supreme square arise the three remaining species, namely, semibrevis, Minima and simpla or Fusa, all of which we have explained in the following shield, adding a seventh and eighth note.

[A marginal mark '+' appears to the left of the first paragraph.]

[An illustration of a shield containing various musical notes labeled with letters a through h. Lines connect the letters to the corresponding notes.]

b. Longa.

d. Semibrevis.

Of the aforesaid simple notes, some are less simple, and others are more simple. For long notes are simpler than breves and semibreves, and others of this kind. Because Breves, semibreves, Minimas, etc., are more difficult to pronounce than Longas.

CH A P. III.

*On the value of simple temporal figures, and on notes'*
*dots, likewise concerning figures to be rested.*

The simple value of temporal notes, together with rests, which are figures to be rested, is gathered from the three outer circles of the Temple Clock; as appears at the beginning of this book, and will be more clearly demonstrated in the following demonstration. A Larga is measured by two Longs, and is described with a long square with a 'property', that is, a tail towards the right, in this manner [musical symbol: Larga]. A simple Long, however, is weighed by two Breves, and has an exactly square body with a 'property' or stem, either ascending or descending towards the right, and is described in this manner [musical symbol: Longa ascending] or [musical symbol: Longa descending]. A Breve is an exactly square figure without a 'property' or tail, which is measured by two Semibreves, which we have depicted in this manner [musical symbol: Brevis]. A Semibreve is a rhomboidal body lacking a stem or tail, which is measured by two Minims. It is expressed in this manner [musical symbol: Semibrevis]. A Minim is a Semibreve body with an addition, namely having a stem drawn either above its head or falling downwards from the lower corner, and is measured by two Crochutas or Drachmas; It is depicted thus [musical symbol: Minima ascending] [musical symbol: Minima descending]. A Crochuta does not differ from a Minim, except in the color of the rhomboidal body, for while that of the Minim is white, that of the Crochuta is black: It is formed from the double value of a Fusa, and is expressed in this manner [musical symbol: Crochuta ascending] [musical symbol: Crochuta descending]. A Fusa is half a Crochuta, produced from two Semifusas: It differs only from a Crochuta because the top of its stem is curved, in this manner [musical symbol: Fusa ascending] [musical symbol: Fusa descending]. A Semifusa differs only from a Fusa because, just as the stem of a Fusa is curved once at the top, so the end of the stem in a Semifusa is curved twice, in this manner [musical symbol: Semifusa ascending] [musical symbol: Semifusa descending].

It very often happens that dots are found in a song, and this next to the right side of the notes, which increase their value by half, so that if [musical symbol: Larga] signifies two Longs, [musical symbol: Larga with dot] will denote three Longs. Thus [musical symbol: Longa with dot] denotes the value of [musical symbol: Longa, Brevis, Semibrevis]. And so in the others. As for the voices to be rested, which are called Rests, it is certain that there are as many species of them as there are temporal notes in Music, namely 8. Of these, one signifies the quantity of a Larga to be rested, that is, the omission of the voice for the exact figure of a Larga; the second is for a Long; the third for a Breve, and so on for the others. Therefore, a Larga rest is noted by touching 4 lines in the song, with a perpendicular line, or when two perpendicular lines touch three lines in this manner.

[Musical staff with two Larga rests]

A Long rest is noted by the contact of three lines of the staff or scale by a single perpendicular line, or when two perpendicular lines touch two lines of the scale, as in the following example.

[Musical staff with two Longa rests]

A Breve rest is noted by the contact of two lines of the staff by a single perpendicular line; a Semibreve, however, by a half perpendicular line of a breve hanging downwards from a line of the staff, just as a Minim from the same half-perpendicular line ascending upwards from some line of the staff, from which also smaller rests are formed, as will clearly appear in the following example, likewise the simple value of all notes.

CHAPTER IV.

On the perfection and imperfection of notes, and
on prolation.

All perfection in mensural Music consists in the ternary number, whether it is in
Longas, Breves, or Semibreves; And although among ancient Musicians the Mini-
m is considered to be so simple that it cannot be divided according to them; Neverthe-
less, they admitted that the Minim itself could be altered; And more recent (musicians)
not only included the Minim, but also the perfection of a quantity of the same lesser nature, in the same ter-
nary (group). Moreover, that the ternary number is a perfect number is
proven because it has a beginning, a middle, and an end: for it consists of three
equal units, wherefore to be divided into three

--- Page 191 ---
DE TEMPORIBUS MUSICIS. 197

thus a minim note, when produced, perfects or does not perfect the next larger [note]; Thus from two minims is made an *imperfect Semibreve*; but from three is made a *perfect Semibreve*. Then from two Semibreves is made an *imperfect Breve*, but from three is made a *perfect Breve*: Similarly from two Breves is made an *imperfect Longa*, and from three Breves is made a *perfect Longa*: Likewise from two Longas is made an *imperfect Larga or Maxima*, and from three Longas is made a *perfect Larga*. Here, however, it must be observed that, if a Longa is perfect, it is called *perfect mode*; But if it is imperfect, it is called *imperfect mode*. Similarly, when a *Breve* contains within itself three semibreves, then it is called *perfect time*, but when two, it is called *imperfect*. But when a semibreve contains within itself three Minims, then it is called *major prolation*; but when two, then it is called *minor prolation*. The examples of all these, in the following circles and shields, will be clear, beginning and increasing by binary and ternary numbers up to the perfect Maxima, which is called a triple Longa.

CHAPTER V.

*On perfect and imperfect notes described in the temporal Triangle*
*of the temple.*

**I**t is to be noted that the uppermost note in the described Triangle of the temple, which we call the simpla, because it signifies only unity, can be called neither perfect nor imperfect, because it is almost imperceptible according to Robert Brunham the Monk. More recent (authors), however, found simpler (notes), such as the semifusa and its half part: I, however, will follow the demonstration of the said Monk, and ascending into the nature of the Fusa, I will insist upon that which we call the simpla. The other notes of greater duration, however, are varied according to the diverse application of points and their absence, because every note in the aforesaid figure, except the simpla, lacking a point is imperfect.
However, every note that has a point above itself is called once perfect, because it is perfect from the next obliquely ascending note, that is, it is worth three such (notes); or because the perfect minima, which is the first species, falls into its composition.
Every note that has a point below itself is called twice perfect; because both it and the next obliquely ascending (note) are perfect, as before, or because both the Semibreve and the perfect Minima fall into its composition. That note which has a point below itself and above itself simultaneously is called thrice perfect, because it is perfect with two obliquely ascending species, or because the Breve, Semibreve, or Minima, all entirely perfect, fall into its composition. That note which has two points below itself is called four times perfect, because it and three obliquely ascending species are perfect, or because the Longa, Brevis, Semibrevis, and minima, all entirely perfect, fall into its composition. Every note that has a point after itself is called entirely perfect, because it and all the oblique notes ascending from it are entirely perfect, except for the imperceptible simpla. The preceding Triangle describes the demonstration of this matter.

Proceeding arithmetically, one must descend from the Simpla note to the Larga notes; But proceeding musically, one must ascend from the Larga notes by dividing them up to the Simpla notes. If therefore from any Larga note in the preceding figure we ascend directly upwards to the supreme note of its degree in the upper oblique line, we make duple proportions, that is, each note is double, and the 5 notes immediately above it: But if from the base of this Triangle, that is, from any Larga note to any corresponding note in the left oblique line of the triangle, we ascend obliquely, we make triple proportions, that is, each lower note is triple, and the 5 notes immediately above it; If, however, from any perfect note in the right line of the Triangle to any imperfect note in the left line of the same, we return directly, we make sesquialtera proportions, that is, each note is worth its neighbor, and its half; If, however, from the left side of the triangle, and from its base, we ascend obliquely up to the notes and spaces of the right line of the triangle, we make sesquitertia proportions, that is, each lower note is worth its neighbor, and its third part.

First Rule.

Each rest corresponds to each note placed in the triangular figure; Hence also, rests not marked with dots refer to such notes: But those which are marked with dots also correspond to such notes, and for this reason we have placed notes below in the figure of Rests written below, so that it may be evident to anyone what are the Rests of these kinds of notes, where also the diversity of rests is noted, both with dots and without dots.

# DEFINITIONS.

Melody is a continuous connection of sounds, such that one sounds after another in a continuous flow, and is properly called the song of a single voice.
  Symphony is a harmonious agreement or congruent consensus of distinct sounds and melodies.
  Basis or Bass is the lowest song or voice, inflected through a system of low sounds, and therefore to be expressed by the deep voice of men.
  Tenor is the middle voice, forming almost the principal melody through middle sounds.
  Alto is a high voice, running through almost high middle sounds, but in such a way that, completing the empty spaces, it is adapted to all voices.

*Contratenor is the middle part between Tenor and Altus.*
*Concordance is a harmonious agreement of sounds through suitable inter-*
*vals of the system, or a proportion, or it is a harmony of dissimilar voices brought together into one.*

                                   C A P. I.

                    *How many concordances there are and how they*
                                   *differ from each other?*

Six species of musical concordances are enumerated, differing in quantity,
namely Unison, Semiditone, Ditone, Diapente, Tone with Diapente, and Diapa-
son; From which it is clear that unison is not a consonance, since consonance is a harmony of dissi-
milar voices brought together into one. And consequently, it is mani-
fest that not every concordance is a consonance; nor vice versa. It
also follows that nothing accords more perfectly than two voices singing in uni-
son. Whence it is clear that among these aforementioned concordances there is great discre-
pancy-

--- Page 205 ---
DE SYMPHONICÆ MELOD. PARTIBUS. 211
pancy; For they are distinguished in two ways, namely either by reason of sound, and thus some are called equisonant, namely those which, sounding together, produce one sound; such are unisons: and others are called consonant, that is, sounding sweetly with a mixed succession, like the other concordances; Or they are distinguished by reason of proportion and succession, and thus some are perfect, namely the Unison and those which arose from it, such as the 8th or Diapason, the 15th or Disdiapason, and the Diapente, and those which arise from it, such as the 12th and 9th. Among these, the Unison and Diapason are more perfect consonances, and the Diapente, and those which arose from it, less so: The reason, however, why such concordances are called perfect, is varied; For the unison is called perfect because of its immobility, and it is a concordance of equality; The Diapason, however, which is the eighth voice, is so called because it claims to occur in a double proportion; The Diapente, which is the fifth voice, because it infallibly occurs in a sesquialtera proportion. The other consonances are called imperfect, because of their instability; For they move from place to place, and by themselves, proportions are not found among the others; Such are the Semiditone and Ditone, and those which arise from them, and

			C H A P. III.
		On the parts of symphonic Melody.

The parts of symphonic melody are twofold, namely, Principal, and those which are formed from the Principal parts when multiplied: The Principal parts, moreover, are enumerated as four: namely, Bass, Tenor, Alto, and Discant; of which the Bass is the lowest song or voice, which is concerned with the lower part of the musical system; therefore it must be expressed by the deeper voice of men or the sound of instruments: The Bass is called such, moreover, because it is the foundation upon which the other parts of symphonic melody are usually built. The Tenor, moreover, is that part of the melody which is concerned with the middle part of the musical system, that is, with the middle sounds; But the Alto is almost always occupied with higher voices, and also runs through the middle sounds of the system, whose principal office in melody is to fill the empty spaces in a composed song with its voices, that is, it proceeds by filling the middle spaces; The Discant, moreover, is the highest song or voice concerned with very high sounds; Therefore it occupies the upper region of the system, which must be moderated by a boy's voice: There is also still another part, which is composed, as it were, from the Tenor and Alto, and is called Contratenor; which is concerned with the intervals of the system placed between the aforementioned two parts; as will appear in its proper place. Concerning the simple composition of each of these, moreover, we will describe some particular rules to be diligently observed, beginning first with the Bass.

							On

--- Page 207 ---
DE SYMPHONICÆ MELOD. PARTIBUS. 211
On the Bass.
Rule I.

*The penultimate note of the Bass usually, for the most part, is distant from the last by four*
*intervals when ascending, but by five when descending.*

Rule II.

*The notes of the Bass in succession should never be distant from the preceding (note), whether ascending*
*or descending, except by eight intervals; however, ascents or descents from the preceding*
*note to the consequent by 6 or 7 intervals sound badly and not naturally; Motion successively*
*from interval to interval, similarly from interval to the third, fourth, or*
*fifth, is harmonically consonant.*

Rule III.

*For the most part, the Bass ends on the same note, or on the octave with the note, by which*
*we began to sing or compose it.*

Examples of these Rules follow.
[Musical notation on a five-line staff]

On the Tenor.
Rule 1.

*The notes in the Tenor, as regards their succession, observe the laws given in the second*
*Rule of the Bass.*

Rule II.

*The Tenor for the most part begins with an octave concordance from the Bass, and likewise also ends.*

On the Discant.
Rule I.

*The Discant also observes the laws of the second rule of the Bass.*

Rule II.

*The penultimate note in the Discant usually, for the most part, is distant from the last by no more than one*
*interval.*

Rule III.

*The Discant begins with an octave or a fifteenth concordance, where there are many parts of the melody;*
*But if there are fewer parts, it usually begins with an imperfect note, namely with a 10th or 17th,*
*and ends with the same concordances.*

On the Contratenor.

Rule I.

The Contratenor, just like the other parts, observes the laws of the second rule of the Bass part.

Rule II.

The penultimate (note) is usually more often distant from the last (note) by four intervals ascending.

Rule III.

For the most part, for the sake of variety, the Contratenor begins with the 5th or 12th, and in this way it is very often accustomed to end.

On the Alto.

Rule I.

The Alto is accustomed to begin and end with the 10th, and then the penultimate final (note) will be distant from the last (note), for the most part by one interval, and this especially where a harmony of many parts will be made.

Rule II.

But where the melody is of fewer parts, there this part begins and ends with the 12th.

CHAPTER IV.

On the general laws to be considered in this part of Music.

Many laws or rules are recounted, both general and special or particular, for the composition of symphonic melody, by the diligent observance of which by the Musician in the Symphony, it will not be difficult for him to produce a harmony of melodies. However, the more general of these rules follow.

Rule I.

Perfect consonances make modulated beginnings of songs, and adorn clauses or endings, in which perfection is especially to be expected.

Rule II.

Two perfect consonances of the same nature, for example, two fifths, or two octaves, and those which arise from them, do not immediately follow in the same song.

Rule III.

A minor imperfect consonance, for example, a 3rd, and those which are generated from it, both ascending and descending, is accustomed to follow immediately in the same song.

Rule

--- Page 209 ---
ON THE PARTS OF SYMPHONIC MELODY. 215
Rule IV.

However, perfect [consonances] ought for the most part to be mixed in a measured way with imperfect ones, such that an imperfect [consonance] is inserted between two perfect ones, and vice versa.

Rule V.

In perfect successions, a hard voice should not be opposed to a soft one, but a soft [voice] should consonate with a soft, and a hard with a hard or natural.

Rule VI.

Several sixths are not continued in ascent, but in descent, with a perfect twelfth following, however; although it may also follow a sixteenth.

Rule VII.

A sixth is rarely used, except in a composition of many parts, for it does not sound as sweetly and gracefully as a third.

Rule VIII.

Dissonances are sometimes used in a composition, namely 2nd, 4th, 7th, and 9th. But this does not happen except in the very fastest run of figures, that is, in Fusa and Semifusa, because then they are not perceived due to their speed. For the error of discrepancy lies hidden.

Rule IX.

A dissonant semibreve is rejected, unless it is diminished by half.

Rule X.

A discord over the same sustained Bass note, to be broken into a concord, very often occurs and is approved.

Rule XI.

To an immobile voice in the Bass, several mobile consonances can be adapted, both ascending and descending.

Rule XII.

A break in the upper parts from a 6th to a 5th consonates very well over a solid Bass. Similarly, a Bass note can be broken from a 6th to a 5th to a sustained note of the upper part.

Rule XIII.

A note of the upper part over a sustained note of the lower part, or of the lower [part] under a sustained [note] of the upper [part], can be divided into as many parts as it has smaller time units within itself. Thus a Breve into two Semibreves, or 4 Minims, or 8 Semiminims, or 16 Fusas, or into two Minims and one Semibreve, or into one Semibreve, one Minim, and two Semiminims, or into two Minims, two Semiminims, and four Fusas; and so forth.

Therefore, to compose a melody above the first note of the Bass, placed on the line $\Gamma$, this letter $\Gamma$ must be sought on the hypotenuse line of the Triangle. Then one must ascend perpendicularly above that letter towards the part you desired, so that it may agree with the bass in some consonance; For example, to construct a melody above the first note of the Bass in the Tenor, the rules and laws of the Tenor designated in chapter 3 of this [work] must be diligently observed, and because by its second rule it will be good to begin with an octave; Therefore, above that Tenor interval, which perpendicularly designates a square above $\Gamma$, will be the place in which the same value of the first Bass note must be expressed, and it should sound an Octave with the note $\Gamma$. Then one must ascend to the placement of the Alto note, which must sound above $\Gamma$ according to the first and second rules of the Alto, described in the aforesaid chapter in a 10th or 12th consonance. Therefore, the tenth or twelfth will demonstrate the place of the Alto scale, in which a note consonant a Tenth to $\Gamma$ must be placed. Then ascending higher in the same perpendicular according to the rules of the Discant proposed in the aforesaid chapter, a 15th is found, which will demonstrate the place in which a note sounding a Fifteenth with $\Gamma$ must be written. Afterwards, we will proceed to the second Bass note or semibreve described on the letter D, which letter, found on the hypotenuse of the Triangle, will demonstrate in its perpendicular line all consonances suitable for it, in which musical harmony may be made in any upper part. But because by the second rule of chapter four of this [work], two perfect consonances of the same nature do not immediately follow each other in the same song; therefore, the consonance of an 8th must not be taken in the second Tenor place, because the first note was distant from the Bass by the same interval; therefore, a 5th or a 3rd can be well used: for a 6th is more rarely used, as is clear by the seventh rule of chapter four of this [work]; Similarly, in the Alto, a 10th or a 5th, or rather an octave, should be chosen for its perfection and proximity: But you

CHAPTER VIII.

*How the secrets of the Triangle may be delineated on a parallelogrammatic surface,
and in that way be more clearly explained.*

First, let a parallelogrammatic surface be made, which is accustomed to be divided into 5 equal parts,
each upper part of which will depict the melody of any higher harmony,
always measuring all proportions from the Bass, or fundamental part and melody. For by this way,
the student can more readily find the places of harmonies, and more quickly
perceive the harmonies of melodies, than by the use of the Triangle: Indeed, by observing this
(the preceding rules having been first considered), it will not be difficult for a person
altogether inexperienced in the art of singing to compose a good harmony of parts;
for he will suddenly perceive the proximity and the distance of the preceding note or harmony with the following one.

CH A P. IX.

*On the natures of the four Temple windows, and how the same can be achieved here*
*in the mechanical composition of song, as*
*in the Triangle.*

IN the four Windows, seven low letters are described, opposed by as many high ones, each of which windows denotes a special concordance: For the first two, counting from the left, demonstrate the dimensions of two perfect concordances, by measuring them from the low letter to the higher letter. The latter two, however, designate two imperfect concordances, and their proportions from letter to letter. And it is always to be observed in this doctrine that the letters expressed towards the right in the said windows signify to us the letters distinguishing the intervals of the Bass, that is, spaces and lines: While the others, opposed to them in the same arches, designate the intervals of the parts or songs in spaces and lines, which ought to be built upon that Bass. Hence, therefore, arise the foundations of this doctrine, namely, that any parts of a song, divided into due intervals, should have letters, both low and high, expressed. From which the proportion and measure of any chord or consonance may be more clearly discerned, so that the melody and harmony of the parts may be rendered exact.

The description of the windows follows.

[An illustration of a classical building facade featuring four arched openings or windows, each filled with a diamond-patterned lattice.]

CHAPTER X.
*Concerning Thalia's Staff, by which not only the parts of songs, but*
*also their true concordances and their positions*
*are properly delineated.*

Let a staff or ruler be made, of half a foot or a whole foot in length; which ought to be divided into 4 or 5 equal parts along its length; And its width should be half an inch, or less; And its thickness should be nearly a fourth part of its width, or thinner. Moreover, it will be necessary for each of its five parts to be distinguished by a certain empty interval, lest confusion of parts follow, which again are to be subdivided by five manifest lines, and four implied ones, yet in such a way that a small and equal space is made between any line of either kind.

It is described in this manner.

[A vertical diagram showing a graduated ruler or scale on the left, divided into five sections labeled "Superior", "Altus.", "Contratenor", "Tenor", and "Bassus.". Each section contains a vertical column of numbers. To the right of the ruler are five musical staves, each corresponding to one of the labeled sections and beginning with a musical clef (G, C, C, C, and F clefs respectively).]

Use

--- Page 219 ---
CONCERNING THE PARTS OF SYMPHONIC MELODY. 229
The use, moreover, of the aforesaid staff or ruler is as follows; namely, let this
ruler be extended upon some paper, on which you desire to delineate four musical
staves for songs; Then let the staves be drawn, serving four parts, yet in such a way
that the interval of the parts, and similarly their lines and distance, may in all respects
agree with those of the ruler or staff, by which they ought to be directed and governed,
just as we will explain below. This done, let the Bass part be composed at your discretion,
upon which, so that the other upper parts may be composed harmonically, the lower
extremity of the staff must be placed upon the position of the first note, that is, either upon the
line $\Gamma$ B. D. F. or A., or upon the space F. A. C. E. G. or B. For example, in
the preceding Example the position of the first note is upon G. Therefore let the staff stand per-
pendicularly upon the $\Gamma$ line; and it will show the concordances, and their places in any
upper part as if with a finger. For if you wish to begin the Contratenor
with the consonance of a 12th or a 5th, that consonance will fall upon the second space.
If the Alto with a 3rd or a 10th, you will find this proportion upon the second space of that
part. If the Discant with a 15th or Diapason, you will also perceive that concordance
placed on the second line of the same song. Then the lowest extremity of the staff is raised,
so that it may stand perpendicularly upon the third line, on which the second note is
expressed. The upper parts of the staff will indicate the proper concordances and their
positions suitable for the upper parts, according to their degrees of height
or depression. Here, however, it must always be observed that the succession
of notes in the same song is the more pleasant and sweeter, the closer the succeeding
note is to the preceding one, with the exception of the Bass, where the ascent is made smoothly,
consequently very often by intervals of an 8th or a 5th. And in this same way one must
proceed with all other notes of the Bass, in whatever part of it they may be placed,
namely, either by raising the extremity of the staff, or by lowering the same, yet in such a way
that the staff is always perpendicular to the given underlying note.

# BOOK SIX

### C H A P. I.
### *On the Barbiton.*

[Decorative initial C] SINCE the Barbiton is, as it were, the prince of all musical instruments, so that no invention of the ancients or moderns can bring a more pleasing harmony, or a more desired and praiseworthy symphony to the ears of listeners, therefore, not undeservedly, we attribute the first place in this book to it; for no age will erase the sweetness of its sounds, nor will the inconstant inventions of artisans, however rare, unheard of, and for a time eagerly embraced with no small industry, draw away the affections of men from it; among which they have fashioned some instruments very similar to the Barbiton, such as those which are commonly called *Theorba*, which produce deeper sounds and have gut strings; *Orpharion* and *Pandora*, whose sounds proceed from copper and iron strings. *Cistrona*, which has only 4 doubled strings, and those of copper and iron, concerning which we will say something in its proper place. But more recent musicians continually add something new to the Barbiton; for first they added a seventh string, then an eighth, then a ninth, all of which, when doubled, make 18. They added these three doubled strings so that they might sound a Bisdiapason with the others, as will be demonstrated below.

### *Figure of the Barbiton.*

[Woodcut illustration of a lute-like instrument (barbiton) lying on a table covered with a patterned cloth. The instrument features a rounded body, a fretted neck, and a decorative rose on the soundboard.]

PRAXIS I.

By how many intervals does any preceding string of the Barbiton differ from another immediately following?

Since the doubled strings on the barbiton are numbered, it must be known by how many intervals each of their sounds (beginning from the lowest) differs from the sound of its succeeding companion. First, therefore, it must be observed that, according to the practice of various musicians, the sounds of the two major strings differ, as they are sometimes tightened or loosened more at the artist's will. The remaining 7, however, always maintain the same distance in their sounds. But here I will explain the differences in sounds by which each string commonly tends to resonate before harmony is made from them. Therefore, between the major string and the second, a single interval is counted; between the second and third, three; and between this (the third) and the fourth, only one. The fourth, however, differs from the fifth by 4 intervals, just as the fifth from the sixth by the same number; the sixth from the seventh by three, and the seventh from the eighth by four, just as the eighth from the ninth and last by the same number.

The demonstration follows.

On the left, the strings are numbered 1 to 9 from bottom to top, with interval numbers 1, 3, 1, 4, 4, 3, 4, 4 placed between the corresponding string lines.]

PRAXIS V.

Concerning the method of transferring a song with its parts from one
key to any other, by means of the doctrine of the
following sphere.

Let the key, in which a song is constructed for use with the Barbitum, be in G ut, and we wish to transfer it to A re or B mi, whether in softer sounds or in harder ones; It is to be noted that the arithmetical figures in each sphere of keys distinguish the strings of the Barbitum; For that [string], in which G is found, is designated by figure 1; The second towards the right by figure 2, the third with 3, and so on up to the Chanterelle, which is denoted by figure 6 in the last place. Similarly, letters denote the different sounds of each string, as declared above. Thus, therefore, one must proceed, when I wish to transfer a song from G ut to A re, namely in the upper wheel, which is the sphere of G ut, the letter of the song in G ut must always be found on the string on which it is found, and perpendicularly under that arc, in which it is found, in the sphere of A re, you will find the letter and the string on which that letter is to be expressed, for reducing that voice from G ut to A re. And thus one must proceed with all the others.

For example.

[Two systems of musical notation and lute tablature. The left system is titled "Cantilena in Gam. ut." and the right system is titled "Reductio in A. re."]

Therefore, for 'a' on the first string in G, I find it in the first arc or place of the L sphere, and, because under it I find C. 1. in the A re sphere. Therefore, I express C on the first string of the Barbitum: Then, by turning the L wheel, I find 'a. 6.' in place 25 of the same sphere, and under it, in the A re sphere, 'c. 6.' Therefore, I express 'c' perpendicularly in the A re song. Afterwards, in the L sphere, I look for 'a. 2.' and find it in place 20, and under it, in the A re sphere, I find 'c', which I also express, as in the preceding example, and so with the others.

PRACTICE VI.

How the proportions of the interval triangle can be related
to the positions of the Lute
and its system.

Let the second practice of this [work] be carefully examined, in which you will perceive the arrangements of the system of keys expressed upon the strings: these having been observed, let some bass melody be outlined through the preceding practice, and let it be transferred to the strings: Then, through the bass keys of that [melody] related to the Triangle, you will most easily find the proportions of the triangle corresponding to the high and very high letters outlined on the Lute's strings; these having been known, it will not be difficult to combine a symphony from diverse melodies, and this extemporaneously, with only the bass melody seen: But the skill for this is acquired only by constant practice.

CHAPTER II.

On the instruments called *Orpharion* & *Pandora*.

That musical instrument called *Orpharion* has the same positions and the same distance and proportion of strings: In this alone it differs from the Barbitus, that its strings are brass wires, and these are either single or doubled. It is therefore evident from this, that the order of the system is the same on its strings and on those of the Barbitus, and the same positions of the notes, both low and high, and it is clear that all things can be performed on this Instrument which can be obtained on the Barbitus. Its image, however, follows.

[An illustration of a stringed musical instrument, likely an Orpharion or Pandora, featuring a scalloped body, a long fretted neck, a decorative rose in the soundboard, and a carved headstock.]

In no way does the *Pandora* also differ from this instrument, except in the difference of the sounds of the strings, for in this its system makes it vary greatly from that of the Barbitus.

The use of the *Pandora*, however, for the most part, is found to be extremely useful in that kind of symphonic harmony which is made from various kinds of instruments. For in consort, as they say, it makes the bass part sweetly heard with the Tenor and Contratenor. Its system's description, however, will follow.

C H A P. III.
Of the Viol.

THis instrument is used either by itself alone, or with others of the same kind, gradually rendering deeper or higher sounds according to their size. Some also play this instrument, and especially the larger kind of it, with other instruments of different types, as we are constantly taught in English consorts. It is struck with a bow strung with horsehair, by the continuous playing of which sounds are produced, both low and high. Its strings do not differ from those of the Barbiton, whose arrangement it also observes in the tension and relaxation of the strings, as well as their position. Its image truly follows.

CHAP. I.
*Concerning our instrument and its general composition.*

[Large decorative initial H] This instrument, newly invented by us, certainly, if it is inspected with curious eyes, will not only bring utility to listeners, but will also affect their senses with the greatest delight. I say delight, because we will demonstrate below that music and the symphonic harmony of various parts can be produced by its aid without a musician; so that it is possible to have music without a musician, or the action of any animal, and therefore without cost and at the owner's pleasure, which indeed, as it seems to me, is by no means common. Therefore, it will seem elegant and quite pleasing and wonderful to those feasting, or present at a banquet, to hear unexpected music in a corner of the dining room without the presence of any moving animal, and for the greater part of dinner or lunch, to perceive a song composed of many symphonic parts, and indeed sounding according to the will of the master. Indeed, so that this may be more easily accomplished, it must be known that three things concur in the structure of such a musical machine, namely: the body of the sounding musical instrument with its necessary ornaments, a sliding mechanism arranged for striking the instrument's strings, and a machine constructed from wheels, by whose proportional motion that mechanism gradually and proportionally descends downwards, and by its descent strikes the strings of the instrument to produce harmonious sounds, by means of quills inserted in its lateral parts or rules or ribs; and consequently produces music consisting of many parts for as long as that mechanism moves towards the base of the dining room.

CHAP. II.
*Concerning the structure of the sounding body.*

[Large initial A] For the constitution of such a body, two things are required, namely: its shape, and the arrangement of the shape, and the proper positioning of the strings upon it. As for the shape of this instrument, it is necessary that it be more conveniently formed from that Geometric figure which they call Triangular, all sides of which ought to be equal. For descending from the apex of such a figure to the base, just as its entire capacity appears to be wider and broader the further it extends to the base, so also it is certain that all its strings, from a point on one side to a point on the opposite side, the more they are extended towards the base from a point more remote from the apex, the graver sound they produce, and the closer they are to the apex, the sharper and more excellent the sound. Therefore, let this triangular body be constructed in such a way that its entire interior is hollow; but the edges are formed triangularly from planks

planks in a square manner, yet in such a way that the plank to which the strings are fixed is made of fir wood, so that it may render sweeter and more melodious sounds. For such woods are used by those carpenters whose duty it is to construct musical instruments. Then, from the apex towards the base, let the two opposite sides be divided into 40 or more parts, in such a way that each part of one side, proportionally distant from the apex, corresponds to a part of the opposite side, also equally proportionally distant from the apex. Afterwards, upon each division point of one side, let bronze strings of one and the same dimension be fastened, which ought to be extended to the points of the opposite side, and there fastened with some iron key in such a way that they can be tightened or loosened, to the true height or depth of a monochord, according to the proportion of the musical system. CHAP. III.

*On the structure of the sliding mechanism.*

But in order that this musical arrangement, described in the preceding Triangle, may be brought into harmonious operation, it is also necessary to find some mechanism by the movement of which these strings, arranged according to the proportion of the Musical system, may render sensible and concordant sounds. And indeed, so that this may be done more conveniently, let some rectangular surface be formed from harder wood, that is, having its extreme (short) sides smaller, but its sides extended lengthwise equal, but larger. Let the extreme sides indeed be of exact magnitude with the radius or diameter of the triangular instrument; so that they extend along their length from the extremity of the slot *A.* of the same to the extremity of the slot of the long opening opposite to it *B.*, so that the radius of the Triangle *A. B.* may be the exact width.

--- Page 242 ---
TREATISE II. PART II. BOOK VII.
the height of the structure itself; and the length of its longer sides will be half the height of the dining room. They shall be so constructed that they can very easily be inserted in such a way into the slots or oblong holes, so that they can slide regularly, and without any deviation in any direction, up and down through those narrow passages. And let the thickness of these sides, or rather their width, be three or four inches, so that they have a hollow space within them. Afterwards, let the end sides be divided from that point where they join with the extremity of the longer sides into as many equal parts as half the number of strings contains; and at the point of each division of both opposite sides, let a small slot, or an oblong hole, be made, so that the thickness of a sufficiently thin wooden rule can enter and exit at the Artist's pleasure. Next, wooden rules are to be prepared, whose length is the entire machine, but their thickness is one-quarter of an inch, and their width is almost equal to one inch; and let their material be of good quality, and not green (unseasoned), lest they later warp in drier air; for they must be very straight, and equal in length, and polished. Their number, moreover, will be according to half the number of strings, as has been said, and their length must be exactly equal. Afterwards, let them be prepared in this way: First, let them be divided into 40 equal parts, and let each of those parts represent that temporal proportion of Music which they call a Breve. Then let each part be subdivided into two equal parts, and let each of them represent a Musical Semibreve. And again, let each portion of those subdivided parts be subdivided, and let these subdivided parts represent a Minim, that is, half the quantity of a Semibreve, which if again subdivided, will produce a Semiminim or a black note: And each of these parts, again subdivided, will produce two Fusas; and finally, each of those subdivided will constitute Semifusas. But these rules are not yet sufficiently prepared to produce the desired effects; Therefore, in the center of each division, tiny cavities or slots must be excavated, into which small plectra can be inserted and pushed, and retained there quite firmly; which plectra can indeed be more suitably made from feathers, because these are more suitable for bending, yielding place to resisting strings, and afterwards returning to their original straightness. Let such feathers therefore be cut out and formed into the shape of a small Triangle, so that the part of each more inclining towards the apex of the Triangle may more easily pluck, yield place to the string, and in its retreat lightly strike the strings, and having done so, be able to return to its original state. The length of the Triangle should be about a quarter of an inch, at the tail or base of which, a small quadrilateral of the same magnitude should be left, which is that part of the Triangle that must be inserted into the slot. And here it must also be observed that the dimension of almost every Triangle must always be the same, that is, so that one does not in any way exceed the other, lest the pulsation be stronger on one string, but weaker on another; for the same form of pulsation must always be maintained.

C A P. VI.

*On the method of arranging the Bass part of any Symphony for this instrument.*

It is to be understood that those ribs or sliders of the sliding mechanism are to be removed and drawn from the grooves of its extremities at the discretion of the Artist. Therefore, when you wish to arrange the Bass part in this order, draw away from that mechanism five of its sliders, beginning from Gamma (G). Or, if any Bass note falls below Gamma, let the sixth slider also be taken, namely F faut (F). Then, the first note of the Bass melody must be sought, specifically in which space or on which line it is placed. For on the slider corresponding to such a place, towards its lowest extremity, which is the starting point, according to that division or proportion which corresponds to the note's duration, some triangular plectrum for striking is to be inserted, specifically at the first point of the starting point. And where the duration of that note has ended on the slider, there a plectrum of silence made of wool cloth is to be affixed, lest the string sound longer than is proper and beyond its note's duration, unless two or three notes are consequently expressed in the same place of the system, that is, in the same space or on the same line; for then the plectrum of silence or mute plectrum is to be inserted at the extremity of the last duration. Afterwards, let the second note of the same melody be sought, and diligently search for its place on one of the five sliders and its corresponding positions. Once it is found, measure from its lower end such a quantity of the slider that the space of the first note is omitted; and at the extremity of the previous space, a second plectrum is to be inserted for striking the duration of the second note. At the end of this duration, a plectrum of silence is also to be applied, for the reason stated above, unless other Bass notes immediately follow in the same place. From here, one must proceed to the third note, and its key must also be sought among the aforesaid sliders. Once it is found, at the end of the limits of the durations of the two preceding notes, a third striking plectrum is to be affixed, expressing the note's duration, and again, at the end of its time, the plectrum of silence is to be deployed. And in this way, one must proceed with all the other notes of the Bass part, until you have adapted the entire Bass part by means of the plectra of that slider.

For example, in the demonstration below, I find the first Bass note to be placed on the first line, where the key Gamma (G) holds its place. I also see that that note is a Semibreve (whole note). Therefore, I seek that slider from these five extracted from the mechanism, on one side of which Gamma is expressed, and on the other, A re (A). At the beginning of this slider, starting from the lower end to the upper, I affix a triangular plectrum. And, because I perceive the note to have the duration of a Semibreve, therefore I measure from the place of the plectrum to the half of a Breve (double whole note); for from that end, the duration of a Semibreve extends to the division made in the middle of the first Breve. Therefore, at that middle point, a plectrum of silence is to be inserted, so that the sound of the string Gamma ut (G ut) is impeded, lest it sound further. Then we find the second Bass note to be placed upon that Bass line which D sol re (D) claims for itself. Therefore, that slider is to be sought, among these five drawn out, on one side of which D sol re is found, and on the other, E la mi (E). And since the space of one semibreve, counting from the beginning, was previously allotted to the prior note, therefore I omit the first space signifying a Semibreve, and at the end of the same, I apply a sounding plectrum. But because this note

--- Page 249 ---
DE INSTRUMENTO NOSTRO MAGNO. 255

I find the third Bass note on the second line of its system, where B.mi. is found. C A P. VIII.

*On the adaptation of the Counter-Tenor and Middle parts for the use of this cursorial mechanism.*

FOR adapting the Counter-Tenor to this cursorial mechanism, two upper rules of the Bass, namely F fa ut with G sol re ut, and A la mi re with B fa ♮ mi. Similarly, two upper rules of the Tenor, namely C sol fa ut with D la sol re, and E la mi with F fa ut, must be selected from the mechanism. Furthermore, one more immediately superior rule is required: G sol re ut with a a la mi re. These five rules receive all the notes of its system, and are to be explained, as was stated in the chapter on the disposition of the Bass. For the explanation of the middle part, however, four upper rules of the Counter-Tenor are required, namely A la mi re with ♭ fa ♮ mi. C sol fa ut with D la sol re. E la mi with F fa ut, and G sol re ut with A la mi re, and one other immediately superior rule, namely B fa ♮ mi with C sol fa ut. If all these things are considered more precisely, and compared with the translation of the Bass part, it will not be difficult for the Artist to adapt the notes of these melodic parts to the ribs of the aforesaid mechanism.

C A P. IX.

*Concerning the adaptation of the upper part or Discant to the use of our
sliding mechanism.*

Five rules are also to be drawn from the mechanism for transferring the sounds
of this part of the melody to the harmony of the mechanism; namely E. la mi, with F. fa
ut; G sol re ut with aa la mi re; bb. fa ♮ mi with cc sol faut; dd la sol re, with ee la mi re, &
ff. faut with gg sol re ut. For the use of plectrums, both striking and mute, it is to be
understood that the same method as with those of the Bass and Tenor parts is to be
followed, and therefore we will not make a greater discourse about adapting any melody
part to our mechanism and instrument, since all this can be most easily known and
observed with diligent and studious investigation.

C A P. X.

*That many other Musical instruments can sound to the movement of this
great instrument.*

We can also adapt other wind instruments and those causing musical harmony
by blowing, to this great instrument of ours, so that the movement of the
mechanism itself is the cause moving their sounds. The cause of the blowing,
however, can be the descent of the mechanism itself, by which some appendix
protruding from its solid side can press down the upper part of a well-adapted
bellows, which part of the bellows, after the protrusion's recession, can be raised by
means of a counterweight. And when a second protuberance of the side arrives, it is
raised again. And in this way, throughout the entire passage of the mechanism,
those artificial bellows will be perceived to emit their blasts, and consequently, by
means of plectrums adapted in the thickness of the rules or ribs, the keys
obstructing the openings of the pipes can be raised from the pipe openings, so that
the bellows' blast, penetrating into their throats, may be able to pour forth or excite
various symphonic sounds consonant with the melody of the larger instrument.
Similarly, small bells or chimes can resonate harmonically with the melody of this
instrument, with plectrums attached to the outer side of the mechanism, both
striking and mute and silent. Innumerable other things can be most easily added
to this invention of ours by those who are studious and eager for new inventions.
Indeed, I would dare to affirm that I can accommodate not only the music of the
Barbiton itself, but also parts of the Viola, Sistrum, Pandora, and similar other
instruments to the movement of this instrument, so that they resonate
symphonically with this instrument of ours. All of which, since to expound upon
them in this place is against our purpose and intention, we will deliberately omit,
and we will restrict ourselves to the simple quality of this instrument of ours.

C H A P.     XI.

*On the movement of this instrument and how it is to be concealed from the eyes of the listeners.*

Since hidden things seem more admirable than those exposed to the senses, therefore it is necessary that the body of this instrument, along with its mechanism and prime mover, be concealed, either by boards artificially put together by a carpenter, or by a tapestry; provided that the rest of the wall of the same dining room is equally covered with it. However, one corner of the dining room, less convenient for use, will suffice for the placement and repositioning of this instrument: From the corner, therefore, a hempen cord attached to the upper part of the side of the mechanism ought to penetrate to the highest surface of the dining room into an upper chamber, and there be bent over one pulley; and a second line parallel to the floor should extend into another chamber to another pulley, and afterwards be wound around the axle of the prime mover according to that proportion by which the mechanism ought to move downwards. Hence, when this movable instrument is set in motion, the machine will descend for as long as it has performed its function.

__________________________________________________________________

C H A P.     XII.

*On the types of Song that should be adapted to this instrument of ours.*

The song that is to be adapted to this instrument ought not to exceed the number of rules of the first partition, because otherwise it will be beyond the capacity of this mechanism, which consists of only 40 regions: Therefore, a Pavan, any part of which consists of eight or 12 semibreves, is very suitable for this machine, because after it you can also perform a Galliard, or at least the same Pavan can be repeated twice with a Galliard, provided that their parts do not consist of many semibreves: Or a Pavan consisting of eight semibreves with its Galliard, Allemande, and Courante can sound successively with the same motion: Similarly, those Italian songs, and compositions by other musicians made up of many symphonic parts, can be performed by virtue of this instrument, provided that they do not exceed the limits of the mechanism.

__________________________________________________________________

C H A P.     XIII.

*On the repetition of the same melody on this instrument.*

If indeed you wish to repeat the same music (for perhaps the listeners might desire such a repetition), let the machine be raised again by winding the movable machine, and this gradually; and during the ascent of the mechanism, you will perceive another music different from the first, so that a completely new and unheard-of music seems to be heard. But when the mechanism has been raised to the ceiling of the dining room, let it be allowed to slide down again by the motion of the movable machine; And in its descent, it will repeat the former music, and in this way it will consume the entire time of the banquet with its action, not without great admiration and pleasant delight from those present. And in this way, an end to this our

--- Page 253 ---

There are also infinite inventions of other instruments, which, because to describe them in this place would perhaps seem too tedious to readers, we will gladly omit, and in this way we will bring an end to this our Musical work; this indeed we acknowledge to be nothing but a certain fantastic invention of ours, by which we have attempted to contract the art of all Music into the figure of a temple or palace, and to explain the demonstrative disposition of this most noble art to the studious and curious.

# BOOK ONE
## On fortifications & bulwarks.

CH. I.
*On the Kinds of Fortification.*

[Large decorative initial L] Fortified places are strengthened either only by nature, or only artificially, or by both nature and art joined together. A place is said to be fortified by nature when it is rendered almost inaccessible by nature; Now, nature's fortification occurs by a twofold subject, namely either by the position of some rock, whence access becomes difficult and perilous, or by the embrace of some wide and deep water surrounding a place and as it were guarding it from all terrestrial invasion. By reason of the first natural subject, we call that a strong fortification which is situated not far from Trent, under the dominion of *Venice*, near the river *Adige*; into which no one can enter or exit, except by some large basket which the guards raise high with a rope and lower from above as they please; nor is it possible, for those traveling directly from *Venice* to *Augsburg in Germany*, to avoid this passage guarded by the said fortification. *Quintus Curtius* also mentions a certain rocky mountain, called *Dorium*, so fortified by nature and the river *Indus*, that because of its inaccessibility, very few Persians disturbed the entire army of *Alexander the Great*, and did not fear in the least to resist his hostile fury. In this respect also, *Orvieto*, a town in *Tuscany*, is said to be naturally fortified: For it is situated on the flat summit of a high and precipitous mountain without walls, in place of which it is surrounded on all sides by steep and high cliffs, created by nature in such a way that from the highest edge they have a most horrible view down into the depths. Its image, moreover, is depicted below. In a similar manner, several citadels are fortified above the city of *Aden*, an emporium of Arabia Felix, rising on the highest peaks of rocks.

[Woodcut illustration of the city of Orvieto situated on a high, flat-topped rocky plateau with steep cliffs, surrounded by buildings and towers.]

Xx

--- Page 260 ---
346          TRACT. II.  PART. VI.  LIB. I.

The second type of natural fortification, namely that of water embracing places by its depth and breadth, is best demonstrated by the positions of *Venice in Italy, Zierikzee in Lower Germany* (besieged by the *Spanish in the year 1576*), and *Mexico City in New Spain*. There is also such a stronghold in the middle of the *Rhone* river near *Rochemaure* in the water, not far from *Marseille*, which is called *le Chasteau Det.* *And so in other places.*

But in purely artificial fortification, we do almost nothing but imitate nature; For either we fortify towns and cities by surrounding them with water, or we fortify them against enemy invasions with ramparts and bulwarks, or we defend them with both simultaneously. For by such strongholds are defended *Milan*, namely the *Rampart* with 9 bastions; similarly *Pescara and Lucca in Italy, Calais, Saint-Omer, Arras, and Péronne in France; Bommel, Gorinchem, Flushing, Ostend*, and countless other towns in *Lower Germany*.

Fortifications, both natural and artificial, are commonly those which have an irregular shape, so that art can more easily conform to the natural situation. Such strongholds are found in many places where nature seems to provide aid with its instruments; namely, water or rocks. It must be observed, however, that art is especially required there, and in that part of the place where nature seems to neglect these things more; just as in the citadel of *Brescia in Lombardy* towards the city, in the correction of the walls of *Marseille* towards the land, in the placement of a rampart or Bastion in the part of *Bologna* towards the mountain, in the elevation of the Bulwark of *Cremona in Lombardy* towards the torrent to guard the bridge, and in countless other places where the exposedness of any part is aided either by Curtains and Bastions, or by ramparts or bastions alone, or by spurs and Ravelins, or by the circumduction of water, or by the elevation of a Cavalier; and by many other such inventions.

---

C A P. II.

*On the terms necessary for this science.*

Every part of a fortification, whether it be interior or exterior, requires its own technical term, by which it may be distinguished from others; Indeed, these terms cannot be derived from Latin, because in the times of the ancient Romans, this doctrine of fortification was entirely unknown. Since therefore in these more recent years, in which bombs and larger military engines have come into widespread use, such fortifications are invented to resist the immense forces of the aforesaid machines, which the old Roman walls could not have long endured, we have coined technical terms sounding like Latin; whose sound and substance, however, are derived from those nations among whom they were constantly used in military discipline, so that readers, being somewhat versed in military matters, may more easily understand my intention; Therefore, I did not disdain to imitate mostly the terms of the French and Italians, with whom I have had much discussion about this art: For that part which the French call *Bastion*, and the Italians *Bulvardo*, we also call *Bastion* and *Bulwark*; and those which (they call) *Caffemattes, Flanques, Espaules, Courtines, parapettes, Contreescarpes, Banqueste*, and which the Italians call *battre le strade, Ravellines, Cavallieres*; we call *Casemates, Flanks, Shoulders, Curtains

--- Page 261 ---
DE MUNIMENTIS ET PROPUGNACULIS. 347

C A P. III.

*On the necessary things in the construction of a fortification.*

Among all things, the best judgment of the Engineer is required to foresee future dangers; for otherwise, the greatest error and irreparable damage would follow. Therefore, it is necessary to choose a place suitable for its purpose, in which one must carefully observe its position, the approaches to it, and weigh offensive and defensive positions with equal scales, and especially, he must consider whether it can be attacked from any higher surrounding place. Next, the time in which the commenced fortification can be finished must be considered; for sometimes necessity compels that a bulwark be suddenly raised beyond all enemy expectation; Hence it must be noted that a fortification of fewer bastions can be erected more quickly and at a lesser cost than one consisting of many. All things necessary for war must also be prepared; such as provisions or food required for the appointed term, and it should be such that it can be preserved from corruption for a long time. Moreover, it should be well fortified with artillery with necessary powder and shot; and especially, it should be guarded by industrious men, well-trained in war, who are ready and fit both to attack the besiegers and also to receive and repel their attacks. Finally, the best and most proportional order must be observed in all parts of the fortification, and especially, that the Curtains are neither too long nor too short, but of moderate length. For then the harquebusiers will be better able to guard the Flanks and the sides of the bastions, as will be more clearly stated below. Here, however, we have incidentally expressed certain rules necessary both for attackers and for the besieged.

*Rule I.*
*He who does not know how to hostilely destroy fortifications, does not know how to fortify them; Likewise, he who does not know the method of attacking fortifications, will also be considered utterly ignorant of the art of fortification.*

*Rule II.*
*In the siege of all places, one must proceed at the beginning with impetus, diligence, and fury both to stun the besieged, and also so that not the slightest opportunity for further fortification is given to them. Hence, therefore, follows an admonition to be noted by the besieged: that nothing imperfect be left in their fortifications, but that all things be completed as expected, all things well fortified, and that no opportunity be presented to the besiegers by which they might inflict any damage either upon themselves or upon the bulwark.*

*Rule III.*
*A place well reconnoitered is almost captured.*
