CHAPTER IV.
*On the exterior parts of a fortification.*

A Ditch is a proportional excavation of the earth, whose exterior edges are equally distant from the base of the fortification. Its use, moreover, is to hinder the approach of invaders and a sudden invasion. Its figure follows.

[An engraving of a star-shaped fortification plan, showing a central square structure surrounded by a wide ditch or moat with pointed bastions.]

A *Ravelin* is a certain triangular earthwork, raised in the ditch before the middle of the curtain, not far from the edge of the earth or Banquette. This part is very useful in every fortification; and especially where some part of the Rampart is exposed to some eminent place, or is weak and easy to access, see *No. 1.*
A *Banquette* or *Retrenchment* is that which is made along the length of the ditch's edge with its counterscarp; which will be 6 feet in height.
Its use is to prevent enemies from approaching the ditch at the beginning of a siege: The Banquette defends the Ramparts, and by them (the Ramparts), the soldiers inhabiting the Banquette are also rendered safe, who for the most part are **Harquebusiers**. It is described, moreover, in this manner.

356          TREATISE II. PART VI. BOOK I.

*Certain Rules concerning Ditches.*

*Rule I.*

*When a ditch is not wide, besiegers with their machines & Cannons cannot safely approach its edges.*

*Rule II.*

*Well-rounded ditches filled with water are better for impeding sudden enemy incursions & surprises: However, ditches of this kind bring great harm to the besieged for three reasons: The first of which is, that they cannot sally forth when an opportunity offers itself to attack the besiegers in their Entrenchments, & if they have sallied forth, they cannot, however, retreat without danger; The second is, that water will undermine the earth-wall; And the third is; because a few besiegers can besiege many this way by impeding the exit, which necessity will make narrow.*

*Rule III.*

*Therefore, a dry ditch is judged better, & especially where there are good soldiers, inclined to defend the besieged place, & apt to provoke the enemy: And in a ditch of this kind, a Banquette is especially required; for through a ditch of this kind, the besieged can both sally forth and retreat at their discretion.*

CH A P. V.

*What ought to be considered before one prepares to fortify a place.*

In fortification, many things must be considered; and this above all must be observed, that the Engineer should have excellent judgment, & no mediocre skill for foreseeing future advantages & disadvantages: For the ignorance & negligence of Engineers very often produce irreparable damages in the construction of fortifications: Then the site in the second place, & in it many other things must be carefully weighed, namely, whether it is sufficiently spacious on its surface, if it is flat or irregular, & if its foundation is watery or dry; if a well can be conveniently made in it; if it is assailed by any external mountain or mound & finally all its parts, both offensive & defensive, must be especially observed; Thirdly, its shape & the material from which it must be raised, must be considered, namely, whether earth with wood, or bricks with earth, or stones offer themselves at a cheaper price in that place.
*Furthermore*, in the construction of a fortification, it is necessary to consider the time; For if sudden necessity and the avoidance of imminent danger compel, it is necessary that, due to the shortness of time, the Engineer adapts the material & shape of easier construction to any given place, such as a Triangular or Tetragonal one. Moreover, it is also necessary that there be a suitable proportion in the parts, & that the bulwarks be so arranged that they can observe all approaches of the besiegers. Nor should the interval between two Bastions be either too long or too short. For it is required in the defense of a place of this kind, that the Harquebusiers defend them or all the flanks of the bastions. And if the bulwarks are too much joined to each other or too close, then the Shoulders & Casemates will be too weak & the bulwark itself too small,

--- Page 271 ---
DE MUNIMENTIS ET PROPUGNACULIS. 357
...too small, to contain a sufficient quantity of artillery and soldiers, nor will there be room for a second retrenchment. The number of bastions also ought to be made with respect to the number of soldiers. Lastly, however, the provision of necessary things for defense must be considered, along with the quantity of provisions also required for a shorter or longer siege. All these things, since they are not of small importance, are especially to be observed in the defense of a place by a diligent Engineer, and by no means to be neglected: concerning which we earnestly exhort.

C A P. VI.

*On the Figures of Fortifications.*

Since the figure of a fortification is regular or irregular, we call that regular which has a regular surface, that is, which is formed from equal Bastions and Curtains, and such a figure is called regular because it is drawn upon a regular Geometric surface: However, this kind of Geometric figure, which is angular, according to which fortifications are built, has many differences; For some are trigonal, others tetragonal, a third pentagonal, a fourth hexagonal, a fifth heptagonal, a sixth octagonal: and so in the others, all of whose angles and sides are equal: The types of figures follow.

[Four geometric diagrams: a square, a pentagon, a hexagon, and a heptagon.]

Yy 3 And

--- Page 272 ---
358 TRACTAT. II. PART. VI. LIB. I.
And such figures are usually drawn only on a flat field or ground, because an uneven surface, due to its protuberance in one place and concavity in another, will make the Curtains and Bastions sometimes longer and sometimes shorter, according to the site and roughness of the place. Hence the parts of the fortification will be faulty in the required proportion, which in this art is considered a defect. There is also a type of irregular figures, by which fortifications with their parts are sometimes delineated, and it is what they call oval, which is depicted here.

[An illustration of an oval or ellipse]

But this type is rarer: There are also other variations of regular figures, which are also used in many places, according to which fortifications are built, such as the Rhomboid, and the star-shaped figure, which are depicted here.

[An illustration of a six-pointed star, or hexagram]

Figure

*An irregular figure is one that has no proportion of its parts: However, due to the unevenness of the site, fortifications are very often constructed according to this kind of surface, and this in various ways according to the invention and discretion of the Engineer, who, according to the location and disposition of the place, is accustomed to inventing an infinite number of such types: all of which are called by the general name of Trapezia. And although these types are not as commendable as those which are called regular, nevertheless, with respect to the natural strength and inaccessibility of the place where they are designed, they far exceed those simply called artificial in strength, because such ramparts are never constructed except where nature itself sufficiently fortifies the place by itself, either because of the position of the place, which is raised upon a rock, or because it is fortified on all sides by deep waters or marshy land. Such figures are explained below.*

C H A P. VII.

*On the method of delineating and drawing any figure of a fortification upon the plain of a field.*

**F**irst, it will be necessary to set up a perfectly square, flat piece of wood: in which two lines will be hollowed out to the width of a cord, so that two (cords) can very easily enter and exit each concavity without impediment. And these lines, with their width, should be extended in such a way that they form an angle on the flat surface with two equal sides, either a right angle for describing a tetragonal figure, or a more obtuse angle for describing a fortification with multiple angles: But where those two wide lines form an angle, there both cords are to be fastened as if at the center, and it will also be necessary that a plumb line, hanging perpendicularly with its lead weight next to the openings of the lines, be, as it were, a faithful guardian of the direct and true movement of each cord; so that, when the plumb line is removed over its perpendicular line, then the cord is held immovably, until, according to its direction, a line is dug from the angle of the wooden surface to the other end of the cord upon the flat surface of the earth, or delineated with some iron instrument: Here, however, it is to be noted,

--- Page 274 ---
360          TRACT. II.  PART. VI.  LIB. I.
that the length of the cords must be according to the length of the side of the figure, according to which you desire to construct the fortification. Therefore, with two lines drawn on the ground (which ought to serve for two curtains of the Boulevard), it is necessary to move that board's line up to one extremity of the lines; And in this way it will not be difficult to determine all other sides of the fortification; However, the wooden board is made in the following manner; Where it is depicted for describing a figure of 5 sides.

[An illustration showing a geometric construction on a flat surface using ropes or cords to form an angle, likely representing part of a pentagonal fortification.]

C. & D. E. are equal to the width of two sides of the polygon: These things having been done, let the compasses be taken, and let a polygonal figure be drawn with them upon the ground in the former manner, namely, by affixing center A. to the ground, and extending two cords; one along the edge of one foot of the compass, namely B. C., and the other along D. E. And in this way, it will not be difficult to depict any figure upon any plane without hesitation.

C A P. VIII.
*By what method are the parts of a simple fortification, both interior and exterior, proportionally delineated, so that they may be well arranged in their proper places?*
*And concerning the types of regular fortification figures.*

Therefore, the figure of the fortification having been produced upon a field or some determined place, according to the doctrine of the preceding chapter, each of its sides must be divided into six equal parts, of which four interior parts will be the length of the Curtain of that side. The Bastion also, with its parts, is made in this way; Upon both extremities of each Curtain, let both exterior parts be raised perpendicularly, which remain of the said six besides those four of the Curtains: The height, therefore, of these perpendiculars will be the sixth part of the side of the figure. It is described, however, in a tetragonal figure in this manner, *Num. 1.*
      Moreover, each part erected perpendicularly, namely 1. & 6., equally divided, will constitute the width of the Casemate, and of the Shoulder, which ought to be of the same dimension: These things therefore completed, obscure lines must be drawn from the inner angle of one perpendicular through the vertex of the other of the same side; And this must be done on every side of the figure; From which all the bulwarks will be produced, as will appear in the following demonstration, *Num. 2.*

On fortifications built upon triangular and quadrilateral figures.

Rule I.
Fortifications erected upon triangular and quadrilateral figures are not much used, because the fronts of their bastions have angles that are too acute.

Rule II.
However, fortifications of this kind are very valuable where necessity compels one to suddenly fortify oneself against the invasions of approaching enemies, or where some narrow pass or passage must be held to impede the passage of enemies or to avoid their incursions.
But just as fortifications of this kind are made more easily, and in a shorter time, than others with more bastions, so they are not thought to endure long against the fury of the enemy.
The same method of delineation applies to the internal as well as external parts of any fortification, built upon any other figure; which was in the fortification of a quadrilateral figure, as has been said. For example, a Pentagonal fortification is delineated in this manner, No. 1.
A Hexagonal fortification with its parts is also described in this manner, No. 2.

The same method also applies for delineating other polygonal fortifications, whether they are simple or composite.

*Concerning Pentagonal Fortifications, and other polygonal ones.*

*Rule I.*
Fortifications of this kind, with equal bastions and curtain walls, are always made on flat plains, just as the towns of Flanders are for the most part fortified, and they are more suitable for holding the passes of a region's borders, or the narrows of a river, and for quickly fortifying oneself, where necessity compels.

*Rule II.*
The more bastions a fortification has, the larger it is in its parts, if a proportional order is observed: Therefore, the larger the cohort of soldiers, both cavalry and infantry, the larger and of more points the Bulwark ought to be.

*Rule III.*
Larger cities and towns require more bastions according to their size in circumference.

C H A P. IX.

*Concerning the irregular figures of fortifications with their parts.*

*Rule I.*
Irregular figures of fortifications, or Trapezia, differ according to the difference of the site's location: However, the location compels a change in figure, either because of water surrounding it, as appears in that fortification, called Schenck-Schantze, situated in the middle of a river, or because of the inequality of the sides of some rock surface, as is shown in the Castle or Citadel of Bourg in Bresse.

*Rule II.*
In fortifications of this kind, however, it must be observed that no part, if possible, be commanded by any overlooking place; moreover, they ought to be fortified with sufficiently deep moats, as is evident in the following description of the Siena fortification.

CH A P. X.
*Concerning composite fortifications.*

A composite fortification is so called when, within larger figures, other smaller ones are contained, upon which also other smaller and interior fortifications are accustomed to be raised, for longer resistance and for easier repulsion of enemies: For, if the exterior bastions have been invaded, the enemies nevertheless cannot advance further on account of the interior fortifications, but are always repelled by them: And these interior bulwarks are best fortified with moats and counterscarps.

CHAP. XI.
Concerning the material of fortifications, their foundation and height,
and concerning their inclination.

The material of fortifications is for the most part fourfold, namely Earth, wood, bricks, and stones. However, earth is always accustomed to be the interior material in regular fortifications, sometimes mixed with timbers arranged transversally; But this kind of rampart of earth [is faced] either with bricks (like those of the city of Arras), or with squares of grassy earth, cut from meadows, mixed with fascines (like those of the town of Calais in Picardy), or with squared stones (like those of Peschiera Lum-

--- Page 287 ---
DE MUNIMENTIS ET PROPUGNACULIS. 373
upon piles with transverse timbers, which also ought to be long: Therefore, the first
layer will be of large or small timbers; whose length will be 12 or 15 feet.
But upon these, let a layer of earth be made; afterwards let another layer be placed upon
that of wood and fascines; and observing this order, namely, placing
layer upon layer up to the proper height, the body of the Rampart will be
completed, which it will not be difficult to face afterwards, either with bricks or with
squared pieces of grassy earth, or with stones. But in the dry foundation of the
bastions of some town or city, let the first layer be made, and especially towards its
front, of stones two or three feet high: This done, let the Engineer have ready a
good quantity of large and small timber with fascines, in such a way that their ends
face the front of the bastion: Then let other timbers be placed transversely upon the
first layer of timbers; Finally, let another layer be made upon these of well-prepared
earth, observing this order up to the proper elevation of the rampart. But in
conclusion, if it should be necessary, or if time permits, it will be necessary to face
these bulwarks with the things designated above.
      In many places, and among others in the Italian city of *Genoa*, I have seen the
construction of bastions and curtain walls: Where, before they fill or raise them with
earth, they raise many partitions made of bricks joined together with gypsum in the
form of a small wall, in such a way, however, that the ends of these partitions face the
front of the points and the curtain wall, as below.

[An illustration showing a cross-section or plan of a fortification wall with internal rectangular cells or partitions.]

      And certainly this is a good invention of the Engineers, where wood is not used,
Because unless this were done, the curtain walls and bastions would very quickly be
destroyed by the continuous blows of artillery, due to the easy dissipation and
displacement of the earth.

--- Page 288 ---
374          TRACT. II. PART. VI. LIB. I.
we are also accustomed to give one foot of inclination for every 12 or 15 feet of perpendicular height in material of bricks, or earth, or small stones: But where the material is stony, that is, of large stones, somewhat more is required.
      But the use of this inclination is that the parts of the aforesaid rampart may be placed more firmly together, that is, that one may better support the other. But here it must be noted that ramparts constructed of large stone work, and without earth, yield more to the Cannon, and admit greater weakening of the wall by artillery, and fill the moats more than if they had been revested with earth or other things.

[An illustration showing a cross-section of a fortification wall or rampart, with a sloped face and a hollow interior.]

C H A P. XVII.

*On examples of composite bulwarks.*

WE call those bulwarks composite which have within themselves other internal
fortifications, so that, if the outer ones have been captured by enemies, a strong
resistance may still be made from the inner ones. For example.
Near Tunis, the royal city of Libya, is a certain double fortification situated between the sea and a large lagoon, called *Guleta*, formerly besieged by King Philip
of Spain, whose inner bulwark consists of four bastions; the outer one, however,
of six, with a blunt ravelin; both are fortified by ditches filled with water from the
sea and the lagoon. Its description follows.

The Castle of Brescia in Lombardy, placed on the summit of a rock, is defended towards the east, south, and west by bastions and curtain walls; because from those parts it slopes steeply towards the city, so that it is accessible; Such accessibility, however, is filled with sharp stones, both to impede the ascent for besiegers, and so that cannonballs falling among these stones may bring greater destruction to them. Moreover, every bastion has its own Cavalier, and within the curtain walls there are other fortifications which serve in place of universal Cavaliers; for they are filled with earth up to the summit, and they also have some ancient and round bastions; Again, within these walls, others are also raised at a higher position, surrounding the center of the citadel. Towards the northern part, however, the rock is very steep and deep, overlooking a very large valley, and that part is also fortified by a large and high curtain wall with two towers and round bastions constructed in the ancient manner; The moats of the other sides are dry; There is one entrance into this fortification, and this is by bridges; for every wall has its own bridge and gate with the insignia of Saint Mark; which are strongly guarded. Moreover, all the Cavaliers and bastions are excellently fortified with their artillery. It is described in this manner.

# BOOK TWO
## On the Siege of Fortified Places.

***

### CHAPTER I.
#### *On the things necessary for the siege of a fortified place.*

[Decorative woodcut initial V]UST as in fortification, so also in the siege of a fortified place, first and foremost, a good talent of engineers is required for foreseeing future dangers, by which the enemy's strength, both within the fortification and outside the site of the fortified place, may be observed, namely, whether it is naturally or artificially strong, and in what place it is more abandoned (weak) by nature or art? Is it watery or not? Is any error found in the structure of the rampart? And where is its greatest weakness? Can it be attacked from some elevated place from outside? Is its material stone, earth, or brick? Is the ditch filled with water or is it dry? In what part of the ditches and ramparts should the besiegers fortify themselves? Which places are safer from danger? In what part should the battery be better constructed? How many and what kind of cannons are most necessary? In what space can a breach and weakening be made by cannons, and how large an opening is required? Then, by what methods should the invasion be made, and indeed with less danger, once a breach or weakening has been made? How many soldiers are required in the ramparts to sustain and impede enemy incursions? Furthermore, scouts should be kept in every part to perceive the enemy's intention: If there is any river, or pond, or lake near the fortification, suitable for safely receiving cohorts (for this will be very convenient for the besiegers, provided it is out of cannon range) it should be noted, that infantry should be arranged for battle, and positioned in the front, that stronger regiments should be placed in that part where attacks against the besiegers are most expected; that cavalry should be positioned in the second place with large wings, so that they may appear more ready, if occasion requires; and that each of them understands his duty; that the ramparts and ditches should be completed with as much speed and vigor as possible, so that thereby the spirits of the enemy may be more cast down and dismayed. And other things of this kind should also be investigated with the utmost industry and observed with great diligence. Moreover, it is necessary that all things necessary for the siege be carefully prepared; such as money, which has always been considered the sinews of war, about 2000 spades, 500 or 600 axes, and as many picks or sickles for making fascines and gabions, furthermore, several pincers and hammers, about 30 planks, over which the cannons may be moved. Let there also be a multitude of pioneers, by whose work ditches and ramparts may be more quickly constructed. And where the rampart is fortified with the best bastions, there at least 12 cannons are required, and two or three culverins with the necessary balls and powder for them. And lest provisions fail, the greatest care should be taken, that all routes be kept open for its more abundant transportation to the camp...

396          TRACT. II. , PART. VI. . LIB. I.

Regula I.

    The siege of places is carried out according to their situation and according to the opportune moment: For in cold times, access to fortifications situated in wet places becomes easier.

C A P. II.

    Concerning the explanation of certain terms of the art.

    We call a Battery a place from which artillery or cannons fire their shot against the bulwarks of a fortification; and such a place is fortified with gabions. Gabions are also like round fences, constructed from very strong stakes and smaller wood, in the manner of baskets, upon flat ground, the hollows of which are filled with well-prepared earth.
    Pioneers, whom the French call "les Pionniers," are the men who use spades for digging out ditches and ramparts and for undermining the walls of fortifications.

C A P. III.

    Concerning the shapes of the ramparts, and how they should be delineated?

    What must be considered above all in the siege of fortifications, we believe, is the manner and situation (which indeed, as far as possible, ought to be covered) of delineating the ramparts and ditches. And first, to withstand the sudden sallies of the besieged at the beginning of the siege, it will be necessary for two ramparts to be made, one of which tends towards one side of the place, and the other towards its other side, in the shape of open pincers, and both extend themselves up to the edge of the fortification's ditch, in the following manner.

**C H A P. IV.**

*How a Battery is usually prepared for breaching a bastion.*

So that a battery may be prepared more securely for breaching a bastion, both at less cost and in shorter time, it is necessary that it be adapted against the point of the bastion,

--- Page 314 ---
490          TRACT. II. PART. VI. LIB. II.
So that a battery may be prepared more securely for breaching a bastion, both at less cost and in shorter time, it is necessary that it be adapted against the point of the bastion; and let cannons and culverins be placed among the gabions, as close to the edge of the fortification ditch as is possible by any means, because the sound of the ordnance shakes the walls of the fortress as much as the impact of a shot, even if they [the walls] are breached a little beforehand. However, the battery ought to be made in three places; namely, upon the two sides of the rampart. For the battery on one side of the rampart destroys the revetment of one side of the bastion, and the battery on the other side of the rampart destroys the revetment of the other side of the bastion. But a battery placed in the middle will always move the earth and will overwhelm the wall of the bastion's point. Such a battery is also applied to crush and break casemates, and to dislodge their ordnance; It also destroys the parapets of both the bastions and the curtain walls, so that the fortress may be more easily invaded and assaulted.

Rule I.
*Experience has always taught that in every fortification, whether it be of stone, brick, earth, or wood, breaches and demolitions occur more easily at the point or acute angle of a bastion than in any other part of it, by always removing material on one side, and on the other, and then in the middle of the bastion.*

C A P. II.

*On the different method of fighting of cavalry of different nations.*

**I**N the ordering of Gallic cavalry (whose formations I name here because of their skill in this art), two methods are considered. The *first* is ancient and almost universally used to this day, by which cavalry cohorts are accustomed to be extended and arranged in a long formation, like a hedge, for fighting. The *other*, by which they dispose themselves in a square formation, before they attack the enemy cohorts: Of these methods, however, the more experienced in war consider the latter to be preferred, *first*, because in the former disposition all are perceived to fight simultaneously, and they deliver a single blow with lances, by which, once that fury is repulsed, no other sudden replication can be expected, and at the same time some significant danger can also befall both the Leaders, and the Standard-bearers, and the better soldiers; by whose downfall, astonished and as if lifeless, they are very easily turned to flight. *Secondly*, because in a square formation the clash will be stronger and with greater violence; and, if any in the front of the square are thrown to the ground, others will immediately be substituted to defend their places. And for this reason, if there were 3 or 4 equal cohorts arranged according to the first method, successively arriving, experience teaches that they are ruined by a single square alone. From which it is seen that every battalion, both of infantry and cavalry, ought to be composed of a suitable density.

Different nations, however, fighting in different ways, embrace different methods and disciplines in their engagements, one superior to another. And hence it is that one method in one manner of conflict is to be preferred and is better than another in a different one.

As for the different ways of handling cavalry lances, we will speak briefly about them here. For the *Hungarians* and *Turks* firmly place and hold the shaft of the lance against the front part of the saddle, when they must charge against enemies; the *Gauls* govern the lance with the strength of their arms; whose custom is far safer than that of the Turks; because the lances are governed by the arms at will: The *cavalry of Lower Germany*, namely of the 17 provinces, use harquebuses instead of lances, with certain supports suitable for holding them lightly and firmly, so that in the same charge they sometimes load the firearm twice with bullets and discharge them at the enemies: The *Gauls* also mostly follow their order today (completely neglecting lances).

Something must also be said about the use of swords: For the Gallic cavalry, after the discharge of their firearm, brandish their swords backwards, and with the back part of the hand: Which discipline is to be considered better than that of the Poles and Turks and Hungarians, who, after they have done their business with their pistols, draw their swords and strike with the front part of the hand; for this execution is not done with as much vigor and agility as that of the Gauls, inasmuch as they, by striking, simultaneously turn the horse to flight, which agility and cunning indeed are very valuable in war.

The *Turks* and *Hungarians* wear spurs above the sole or wooden support of their boots, so that if by some chance their horses fall, they can nevertheless very easily free themselves from the spurs, merely by moving and shaking their feet, so that they can more skillfully fight standing.

C H A P. III.
*On the army and its parts.*

There are those who believe that an Imperial army cannot be formed unless it is composed of many nations experienced in military discipline, and they assert that a gathering of soldiers consisting of only one or two nations should not be called an Imperial army, but rather a mere assembly of soldiers. Indeed, their opinions do not seem far from reason, because in such an army, warlike men, highly experienced in every military matter, must be chosen; some of whom are readier for invasion, more apt for scaling the walls of fortifications, and quicker for making a battery; others are by nature more suited for maintaining the unity of ranks in battle; others are more practiced in cavalry discipline, and should be found far more agile than others in governing horses (in which consisted the entire strength of ancient Roman and Greek armies).

Therefore, for sudden invasions and more perilous occasions, Spaniards, Italians, and English are rather to be chosen, because these are perceived as daring in making a battery; Germans and especially Swiss for maintaining the battle line, because they are known to prefer death rather than corrupt their ranks or violate the formation of the battle line. The Gauls are rather to be taken for cavalry, because they cultivate and love the art of riding: in which art they are no less engaged in our age than the Parthians were in Roman times, who, due to their cavalry prowess and agility, kept themselves unconquered against the Roman Republic.

An army, therefore, formed from the aforesaid nations, is constituted of many parts, of which the *Tuldum* or baggage train is, as it were, the tail of the entire army; and this *Tuldum*, just as it immediately follows the army, so also is it of the greatest importance within it. Hence, for the guarding of the baggage train, industrious and most faithful men, and a most noble leader, are chosen, who usually precede the *Tuldum* in a square formation. Also, one squadron of cavalry is usually placed alongside each of its flanks, not only to defend the baggage train from sudden enemy invasions, but also to keep and guard the rear of the phalanx safe from their ambushes. The body of the army, consisting of infantry carrying spears, we call its phalanx and battle line: This relates to its whole as the human body, namely its belly and chest, relates to its other parts. For just as in the human body its principal strength, vigor, and robustness consist, so also in this part of the army is the greater hope of victory to be placed. This body is fortified by arms, sleeves, or wings, which are usually composed of Harquebusiers. The body or battle line is preceded by troops of devastators, whom we have compared to the teeth of a man; for, just as teeth prepare food lest its passage to the stomach be impeded, so also devastators or Pioneers prepare the way, and remove all obstacles by which the army might be disturbed on its march.

Two squadrons of light cavalry preceding the cohorts of devastators we have likened to a man's imagination, [marginal mark] his reason, and his intellect, which are accustomed to foresee future disadvantages. For these aforesaid troops of cavalry are always prepared to defend the front of the battle line and the cohorts of devastators, and to repel the enemy's attacks. *Forerunners, scouts, or Catascopi* (who are light cavalry), because their duty is to observe the enemy's movements and explore their intentions, we have compared to the eyes of animals, whose function is to direct the mass of the entire body well and to govern it correctly.

C A P. IV.

*Concerning the method which the Italians use in the disposition of an army on the march.*

When Italians pass through a suspicious place or hostile region with an army, where indeed a sudden enemy invasion is feared, they arrange the parts of the army in the following manner: first, the forerunners or scouts occupy the foremost position; these are followed by two squadrons of light cavalry; one indeed on the right side, the other on the left. The cavalry are followed by cohorts of pioneers, arranged in a parallelogrammatic form with their leaders; Then field cannons, which they call Canons, raised on wheels, are drawn by horses. After these, the main body of the army, or its phalanx and battle line, follows in a square formation; The battle line precedes the baggage train, between which and the battle line a squadron of soldiers is arranged to guard the baggage train; and two squares of cavalry on either side guard the flanks of the baggage train from harm, one of which, namely the left, is armed with Harquebuses, while the other is composed of cavalry. Moreover, we have depicted the entire figure on the following page under letter A.

C A P. V.

*How the Spanish arrange an army on the march.*

In the time of Emperor Charles V, when there was war in Germany, under Duke Barrabanus, the phalanx of the army or Rearguard, composed of the Spanish nation, was formed in the shape of an exact square: which phalanx indeed had two sleeves or wings consisting of Harquebusiers, one of which tended more towards the front of the phalanx, the other looked towards its rear; Furthermore, at the head or front of the army, and at its rear, two horns of Harquebusiers were constituted: But after the rear of the phalanx followed a squadron of nobles, excellently armed, upon very robust and powerful horses: Finally, light troops succeeded these, distributed into two as it were sleeves, and with these also the baggage train of the army, and all other necessities were transported; In the anterior part, however, they had forerunners, pioneers, and field cannons, not very differently from the Italians. Moreover, we have depicted the demonstration of this army on the march in this manner under letter B.

C A P. VII.

*On the formation of an army into a Lunar*
*figure.*

The formation of an army's phalanx with other officers and foot soldiers, except for the Harquebusiers, into a lunar shape, is very convenient and expedient at night. This can be done suddenly, either by the circumgyration of a rope, or by intervening cloaks. And then in that first order, that is, in the outer order, the Sergeants or officers of each cohort are to be placed in a lunar shape. *In the second order towards the center will consist armed foot soldiers carrying spears. In the third rank, unarmed (soldiers), carrying spears. In the fourth order, those equipped with Halberds, and so on successively up to the last order, in which drummers are to be positioned.* However, all these orders are to be arranged in such a way that a sufficiently large empty space is left near the center, in which the Captain General with his cavalry can reside; Moreover, in the opening between the two lunar horns, the Sergeant Major is to be positioned, so that he diligently observes the order of the Harquebusiers placed outside the lunar figure. For in four parts, equally distant outside the lunar form, four compact bodies composed of Harquebusiers are arranged, who are thus positioned as if in four corners to preserve the lunar figure from all unexpected danger from invaders. We have depicted the figure of this kind of army disposition in this place, under letter D.

CH A P. VII.

*On the formation of any army into a Crescent shape.*

The formation of a phalanx of any army with other officers and infantry, except for the Harquebusiers, into a crescent shape, is very suitable and expeditious at night. This can be done suddenly, either by the circling of a rope, or by intervening cloths/banners. In the fourth order, those equipped with halberds, and so on up to the last order, in which the drummers are to be placed.* However, all these orders are to be arranged in such a way that near the center a sufficiently large empty space is left, in which the Captain General with his cavalry can reside; Moreover, in the opening between the two crescent horns the Sergeant Major is to be placed, so that he may diligently observe the order of the Harquebusiers placed outside the crescent figure. For in four parts, equally distant outside the crescent shape, four compact bodies of Harquebusiers are arranged, who are thus positioned as if at four corners to preserve the crescent figure from all unexpected danger of invaders. # BOOK FOUR
## Of certain machines very necessary for war.

### CHAPTER I.
#### Of the invention of a certain ladder, which can be very easily carried with any army or a simple cohort for ascending the walls and ramparts of a certain fortification.

[Decorative initial H] A ladder of this kind is not only light in weight, but can also be enclosed in a small space. Therefore, let some pole of very strong construction, or some other wood of the same kind, which is usually made of ash, be divided into many equal parts of one and a half feet and two feet in length. And at one end of each staff, let a sufficiently large hole be made, but at its other end let the wood be so fitted that it can very easily enter the hole of another staff. But upon the end of only one of the aforesaid staffs, let a certain large iron hook be firmly attached, and this indeed strongly, so that it can be placed and held tenaciously and strongly upon the top of a wall. Then let two ropes of the same length and dimension be taken. And with one rope, all the ends of one side of the staffs will be tied together, yet so that the hole of one staff is joined with the end of another, which is suitable for entering that hole, and let the distance between the staffs thus tied be about the measure of one foot. Afterwards, from their opposite ends, let a proportional tying be made with the second rope. Therefore, when an army on the march wishes to carry a ladder of this kind with it, all the staffs are to be tied together in the manner of a bundle. But when this ladder is to be applied to the top of some fortification, then the sharper end of each staff is to be strongly pushed and fastened into the hole of the staff nearest to it; and in this way the ladder will have the shape of a very long pole, whose top, carrying the iron hook, it will not be difficult to reach the firm part of the top of some fortification. But with the hook attached, with light force and pulling, let each staff be separated from its neighbor, and it will have the true shape of a ladder. The ends of the ropes protruding towards the ground are to be fastened with a strong tying to stakes driven sufficiently deep into the ground.
Moreover, we have depicted quite clearly in this place the figure of this ladder, both when tied into a bundle, and also when prepared for elevation to the top of ramparts, and at the same time also in that form in which its staffs are to be separated and extended into the appearance of a ladder.

C A P. II.

*Concerning a certain instrument which soldiers can sometimes carry with them,*
*for tearing out bolts and opening gates, and destroying them,*
*however strong they may be.*

The composition of this instrument should for the most part be of iron, so that it may not break, or at least its sides should be made of very strong wood covered with an iron skin, and joined together with very strong joints. The rod, however, passing through its middle, should be made of iron or rather very strong steel, excavated with very strong teeth along its anterior half; which teeth should be adapted to the teeth of wheel A. marked; whose composition must also be very strong. The entire strength and power of this instrument consists in the multiplication of those instruments which they call "force at the end". Therefore, through the middle of each longer side, the primary moving axle should pass, extended by an iron rod at right angles; on the side of which, near the handle of that axle, spiral teeth are to be made: so that they may be very easily adapted into the wheel of the nearest [unclear word] axle; and in the same axle, sib

C A P. III.

*On the discovery by the besieged, by which they usually understand if the besiegers*
*are digging subterranean passages to overturn*
*and remove the ramparts of the fortification*
*with gunpowder.*

There are several inventions which the besieged use to discover the mines of the besiegers, by which they not only perceive the attempts of the enemy, but also the true location of the fortification or rampart to which they intended to direct their passages. Therefore, when the besieged fear such a stratagem (for usually during the time of excavation, the besiegers are accustomed to fire cannons and make such a noise of drums, that the besieged are less able to hear or perceive their subterranean works), they place a drum upon that rampart which they most suspect, and having placed a needle upon its uppermost surface, if that subterranean work is being carried out near that bastion or wall, for every blow which the excavators will give underground, that needle will be seen to jump, and in that place where the needle is perceived to move more and higher and more vigorously, in that place, danger will be more to be expected. Therefore, having thus learned this, the besieged immediately, to impede the attempts of the besiegers and resist them, construct other counter-mines by which they destroy the enemy's. Some also attach bells to sticks, or by tying them to some thread between two sticks fixed in the ground, they suspend that thread, for thus, at every percussion made underground, the bells will emit a sound. The method, however, of these operations is declared in the following two demonstrations.

CHAPTER IV.

*Concerning the custom by which the ancients transported a man from*
*one side of a river to another without a boat.*

The ancients, when they wished to cross some river, where every means of transportation was lacking, and they desired to retrieve a boat or some other thing from the opposite side of the river, used to cover a certain sufficiently experienced man with a very thick ox hide, and adapt that covering to his body in such a way that no water could enter it. Around his mouth also, a very long tube or channel made from the same hide ought to be inserted and glued with the preceding

--- Page 331 ---
DE MACHIN. NONNUL. BELLICIS. 419
garment, so that the top of the same tube may extend beyond the deepest part of the river: And at the top or summit of that tube, a mass of cork must be artificially connected, so that the opening of the tube is always raised above the surface of the water, to prevent water from entering through that opening: And a staff suitable for this task must also be prepared, so that one may better support oneself in one's passage, and its soles or supports should be almost round and very wide, lest the muddy substances of the river easily adhere to them. And in this way, men were accustomed to cross rivers, as I have learned from certain ancient authors. But I have thus depicted the method.

[A woodcut illustration depicting a man walking along a riverbed underwater. He is holding a long staff and breathing through a tube that is attached to a float on the surface of the water. In the background, there is a landscape with a watermill, houses, and trees.]

C A P. V.

*Of the method or invention by which cavalry can most easily break into the enemy phalanx.*

Let there be made from steel plates, of sufficiently thick substance, a machine having a single angle, and that as sharp as can conveniently be made, and let the height of the angle be to the height of a man riding a horse; But in its lower part, let there be a wheel, upon which this machine can be moved, and let a shaft be affixed to the wheel, so that two or three horses can be attached to each of its sides, yet in such a way that both the riders and the horses are protected by the sides of the angular machine itself. This done, let the horses, vigorously urged by spurs, be caused to move rapidly towards the enemy phalanx: Therefore, the machine will most easily penetrate among the spears due to the sharpness of its angle, and by the force of the horses, which ought to be very strong and spirited, the foot soldiers of that phalanx will be thrown into confusion, and will give entry to the cavalry following this machine; with the order of the phalanx broken and the battle line of the whole army dispersed, it will not be difficult to obtain victory. The design of this machine, moreover, follows under letter E.

C A P. VI.

*Of artificial fire combined with a small cannonball, which not only most easily penetrates any iron breastplate, but also burns the human body clothed in these arms with the violence of its flame.*

I saw this experiment with my own eyes in Paris, so that it most easily penetrated a breastplate placed before it, and after that penetration, the flame of the fire still remained unextinguished. Moreover, a certain friend of mine, who at that time revealed that experiment to me, gave me its composition under oath in this manner; Take as much powdered camphor as you wish, and dissolve it in the best aqua vitae, and to it add a little linseed oil or pig's fat and wax or Burgundy pitch (that is, a little of each of them), and with these, let a waxed cloth be made. This done, let a lead or iron ball or square be taken, and let it first be moistened in that water in which the aforesaid camphor is dissolved without anything else, and afterwards let it be wrapped in a portion of the said cloth, and thus let it be placed in the cannon, and all that which is promised above will be achieved.

C A P. VII.

*Of another preparation of an artificial ball, exceedingly useful in war.*

Among the secret armaments of England, which are preserved in the Tower of London, we have a certain arcane confection of a lethal ball divided into eight principal parts, so that those divisions pass through its poles no differently than vertical lines through the poles of the world: Moreover, these are usually cast from copper or iron, and linked together in such a way that the finest part of its metallic material joins the coarser ones: But at its top or one pole, there is a hole, through which the material of artificial fire can be placed into its innermost cavity, and after

--- Page 333 ---
human being clothed in these arms is consumed by the violence of its flame.

I saw this experiment with my own eyes in Paris, so that it very easily penetrated the breastplate placed before it, and after that penetration, it still remained with an unextinguished flame of fire. Moreover, a certain friend of mine, who at that time revealed that experiment to me, gave me its composition under the faith of an oath in this manner: Take as much powdered camphor as you wish, and dissolve it in the best aqua vitae; and to it add a little linseed oil or pig's fat and wax or Burgundy pitch (that is, of each of them); and with these, let a waxed cloth be made. This done, let a leaden or iron ball or small square be taken, and let it first be moistened in that water in which the aforesaid camphor is dissolved without anything else, and afterwards let it be wrapped in a portion of the said cloth, and thus let it be placed in the cannon, and all that which is promised above will be performed.

	But for the launch of this globule, a very strong crossbow is prepared, whose string, prepared to receive such a globule, is violently stretched by a certain machine. Then the crossbow is raised to a certain altitude by means of a Quadrant, according to the distance of the place to which this globule is to be sent, a distance which can be most easily calculated once the weight of each globule is known, and an experiment has been made with the same (globule) for each degree of the quadrant. Therefore, when that globule is to be launched, the aforesaid wood must be ignited, and without any delay the crossbow's string must be released: Thus the globule, suddenly falling into the designated place, with that artificial material sensing the force of fire, bursts forth as if from the center to the circumference in eight parts, which are violently dispersed in all directions with such vehemence that even planks having the thickness of a full inch are penetrated from all sides without difficulty.
	But here it must be noted that this kind of war machine is most useful to those who are besieged in some fortification, so that through it they may constantly harass the besiegers with danger, especially those (besiegers) who are safe from direct artillery fire from the fortification by means of ditches, gabions, or other defenses; for the crossbow must launch its globule high up, so that when the violence by which it was first driven along a curved line finally ceases, it may at last fall directly by its natural motion, and as if by a perpendicular line, upon the besiegers' ditches and into their midst, and thus circularly destroy them from every side where it falls.
	But we have expressed the forms of the globule and the crossbow in the following manner, but the method of mixture, since it is among the secrets of our country, it is not proper for us to reveal.

C H. VIII.

*On the use of elevating or depressing artillery.*

Since in military matters the knowledge of the elevation or depression of the cannon's muzzle is extremely useful and necessary, therefore we think it worthwhile to discuss in this place the variety of its position and its rationale, inasmuch as according to it the projectile's ejection is either longer or shorter: But so that this may be understood more correctly, we will first set forth two propositions by which the principle of projectile motion will be explained; then we will explain the composition of the instrument, or Quadrant, for a certain and determined knowledge of the elevation or depression of artillery.

Proposition I.

*All bodies of equal weight at the end of some violent motion, which is not in a direction perpendicular to the Horizon, will move with their natural motion, which will be continuous with the curved motion caused by violence. For example; A projectile violently emitted into the air, finding no resistance at the end of its violent motion, will move by natural motion, in this manner.*

[A diagram showing a projectile path. A curved line starts at point A, goes up to point B, then curves down through point C to point D, which is depicted as a sphere or cannonball.]

A. B. C. D. is the description of the entire line, both violent and natural, where A. B. C. will be the path of violent motion, and C. D. the path made by natural motion, which will be continuous and tangent to the curve B. C. at point C.

Proposition II.

*The longest range (effect) that a body of equal weight can cause from its origin by violent motion upon a plane, or some straight line, is that which precisely terminates in the same*
Ggg 2                                        

--- Page 336 ---
424 TREATISE II. PART VI. BOOK IV.
the same plane or straight line, when the ejection occurs with similar power and violence. For example, if a motive force at point A violently emits into the air a body B, equally ponderous, whose trajectory will be A. E. D. B., it must be concluded that point D will be the instant dividing the violent trajectory or mode A. E. D. from the natural trajectory D. B., and that from point A to D, the line A. D. C. should be drawn. Now indeed we say that point D is the furthest effect from point A which body B can produce upon the line A. D. C. or upon the plane where the said line A. D. C. is situated. For if the said body A were to eject body B more upwards above the horizon, then it would produce with it the effect of natural motion upon the said line A. D. C., as appears in the line or trajectory A. F. G. at point G. This effect G will indeed be closer to point A, for body B will not end its violent motion on the line A. D. C. but rather above it at point F. And the higher body B is emitted, the more it will approach its origin A upon the line A. D. C. The reason, however, is because its violent motion is further from its terminus, or end, namely the line A. D. C.

Similarly, if that body B is less elevated from the line or trajectory A. D. C., and body A ejects it so that its trajectory is along the line A. I. H. K., then the effect of its violent motion will be upon the line A. D. C. at point H, which will also be closer to its origin than D, because the end of such violent motion will reach below the line A. D. C. at point K. And finally, the more sloping and lower the ejection of body B will be, the closer will its effect be to that origin A upon the line A. D. C., because its violent motion will end below the line A. D. C.

[A diagram illustrating projectile motion with various trajectories labeled with letters A, E, F, M, D, C, G, H, I, K. Three spheres labeled B B B are shown at the bottom right.]

Concerning the Artillery Quadrant.

The Astronomical Quadrant is divided into 90 parts, in accordance with the quarters of the sphere, which is distributed into 360 degrees: But geometers divide their quadrant into only twelve sections, which those skilled in the art of artillery also follow in the design of their quadrant, who nevertheless construct their instrument in this manner.

Let a gnomon be made of copper or harder wood, in whose interior angle a quadrant must be enclosed, with its plumb line: But here it must be noted that one leg or arm of the gnomon should be longer than the other, so that it can as desired
Ggg 2

--- Page 337 ---
DE MACHIN. NONNUL. BELLICIS. 425
...at will, be quickly inserted by the artisan into the mouth of the cannon. Let the gnomon therefore be B. A. C, whose longer leg is A. B. And the quadrant included in it will be E. F. H. And its whole drawing should be in this manner.

[An illustration of a gnomon or quadrant device with labels A, B, C, E, F, G, H.]

*How should the cannon be positioned to achieve a longer distance with its shot?*

By natural Geometric reasoning, it is established that the cannon must be elevated 45 degrees above the Horizon, which is half of 90 degrees, which constitute a fourth part of the world [a quarter circle]. Hence, so that this may be done more precisely, let the quadrant described before be taken, and let its longer leg, namely A. B., be placed in the mouth of the cannon. Then let the cannon be elevated to such an extent until the thread passes through the middle of the quadrant, that is, so that it cuts the part of the quadrant E. G. F. into two equal parts, namely at point G. For then it can be said that the cannon directly points to 45 degrees above the Horizon or 6 parts on the quadrant. An example follows, *No. 1.*

The proof of this matter was made in the city of *Verona*, where an excellent master in this art named *Leonardus Justinianus*, disputing over this aforesaid assertion with another *Paduan Master*, vigorously defended it against the other, who wanted to depress the cannon by two points out of those 6 given on the quadrant. Therefore, with silver and coins deposited as a wager for the victor's prize, a Culverin from *St. Lucia* was brought forth, and that *Veronese* man fired the first shot according to his elevation, and the distance between the end and the beginning was 1972 measures, each of which consisted of 7 feet according to the Veronese calculation. Afterwards, that *Paduan* man, according to his intention, by depressing the cannon by two points, fired his load from the Culverin, and only 1872 of the aforesaid measures were counted between the beginning and the end of that motion. Hence the judges verified the aforesaid statement, about which they had previously doubted much. An example of the cannon's position according to the *Paduan's* intention is as follows, *No. 2.*

[Left]
However, for verifying the aforesaid, it must be noted that every ball should be a quarter smaller than the bore diameter of its cannon.

[Main Bottom Block]
Since there is a great difference in the strength of gunpowder of various kinds, for example, between that commonly used for larger cannons, which are commonly called Artillery, and that other [powder] which is commonly used for smaller firearms, such as Harquebuses, Muskets, patronels, pistols, and other such [weapons]; indeed, of which the former is granulated today and mixed with a larger body, and is called granulated powder for Cannons, while the latter is called fine granulated powder, and ought to have a strength a fourth part greater than that for large Artillery; therefore, should it happen that you have only a single kind of powder, which is fine granulated powder, so that it must also serve for Artillery, in this case, it is necessary to reduce a fourth part of the powder in the loading of each cannon from the quantity expressed in the preceding table: and similarly, also by rule and compasses and pincers, a fourth part of the length and width of your powder measure has been reduced: And thus you will load the cannons serving your use; for this has been discovered and verified by John Sheriff in a Battery made with a Cannon and a Culverin, in the service of the deceased Queen of England; and this experience of his in military art has been found and proven just, good, and useful without danger....

# BOOK ONE
## Concerning oblong movable instruments.

### CHAPTER I.
#### *Concerning the Roman Steelyard, and concerning instruments invented from the Roman Steelyard.*

**T**he Roman steelyard is an instrument commonly used in Gaul, Italy, and Spain,
by which the just weights of things sold are ascertained. It is described, however,
in this manner.

[An illustration of a Roman steelyard scale. The horizontal beam is marked with letters A through R. A fulcrum is at point B, a scale pan hangs from point A, and a sliding weight hangs from point C.]

The act of outweighing with this Roman instrument consists in the removal of a
weight from its center. Therefore, two equal weights equally distant from the center of the
instrument will stand in equilibrium. But by however many degrees one of them is removed further
from the center than the other, by so many proportions will that one infallibly
outweigh the other, which is less distant from the center.

*Demonstration.*

Let there therefore be two equal weights A and C, namely of one pound; which, because
they are equally distant from the center B of the instrument, are balanced by equal forces. But if
weight C is moved further from the instrument's center, namely to D, E, F, G,
etc., it will be necessary that it outweighs the other weight less distant from the center, namely
weight A.
The more the progression of the weight occurs from the center towards the extremity
of the instrument (if only proportional), the greater also will be its overweighting, and yet pro-
portional: from which it is clear that the multiplication of weight is nothing other than
the elongation of the weight from the center of the moved line.

*Demonstration.*

The meaning of this proposition is made clear by three propositions of geometric or arithmetic
progression/proportion described by us.

C A P. II.

*On wheels, and the parts of wheels, and their proportion.*

Since the wheel is the mother of all instruments, and its construction consists in the circle, and the proportion of the circle, it seems necessary to briefly explain how the proportion and force of the circle is observed in constructing machines, and applied in practice. However, concerning the demonstration of this matter, we wrote something above, when we made mention of the *Romana*, since it ought not to be considered anything else than the radius of some circle, as we will explain in the following.

Regula I.

*Every wheel revolving on its axis, the larger it is, the more easily it moves, when it is touched on its surface, or an agent causing motion is applied to it.*

[A diagram showing several concentric circles with a horizontal axis. Points along the axis are labeled A, B, C, D, E, F. Weights are suspended from points A and F.]

From these it is clear that wheel A. C. moves more easily than wheel A. B., and wheel A. D. than A. C., and so in the others: We stated the reason in proposition 1, chapter 1. For 1 pound at A. and another at B. will stand in equilibrium, but the same weight at C. will overweigh-

From which it is manifest that, the more the semidiameter is distant from its center, the more rapid will be its motion. However, we will give an example of this matter by a common experiment.
     *A. will be the designated center.*
     *B. the load slightly distant from the center.*
     *C. the hand less distant from the center; hence it lifts more weakly.*
     *D. the hand more distant from the center; wherefore it lifts more strongly.*

Rule III.
The axis of any wheel, if it is large and thick, its wheel will turn with difficulty: On the contrary, however, if it is small and thin, its wheel will turn easily.
The reason is, because the surface of the axis, being far distant from the inner point of its center, is easily impeded by the agent on the surface, that is, by the applied material, touching the surface on which the axis rests, or over which the axis turns.

Rule IV.
The higher the wheel, and the smaller its axis, the more easily it is moved, if the motion occurs at its extremity, that is, if it is driven by the surface: But concerning wheels moved from the center, the opposite is to be understood; about which in the following chapter.

*Rule V.*

In all machines generating force, wheels must be placed which are moved from the outside, and the load must be applied to the axle through some suitable means, for example, by a rope; although the lifting proceeds slowly, it is nevertheless done more safely than in other ways, because the entire wheel's force is always transmitted to the axle; for just as every heavy object placed in any location naturally seeks its center and readily falls towards it, so the forces of the entire wheel are gathered in the axle, as will clearly appear in what follows.

C A P. III.

*Concerning the first difference of wheels, that is, concerning wheels*
*moving from the outside.*

There are two principal kinds of this difference of wheels, one of which is moved by a rack, and the other by a force at the end. *The first kind is more common, because it can operate either more quickly and lightly, or also, when necessary, more vigorously, and it is suitable for any method of construction, and is constantly used for the construction of clocks and other machines with which cooks are accustomed to roast food. But the second kind, by force at the end, acts more slowly, but more vigorously, because for any period or revolution, the force at the end can only draw out a single tooth.*

*Rule I.*

*A wheel subjected to force at the end can never operate or move that wheel, as a wheel on a rack does, but rather it would break.*

*Rule II.*

*The force at the end must have at least three threads, so that one can supply the other, as appears below.*

*Rule III.*

*A wheel to which the force at the end is connected can be made in two ways, both of which are good; the first, however, is better than the latter, because it is stronger and more easily prepared: Their figure is this, Num. 1.*

*Rule IV.*

*The higher the wheel, the greater its force, according to the first and second rules of chapter two: but then its motion is slower.*

*Rule V.*

*The force of the wheels is doubled if another wheel is applied to the acting rack, or to the force at the end: for then the weight will not be so great that it cannot be lifted by the hand of one man, which is demonstrated in the following figures, Num. 2.*

Rule VI.

If a third wheel is added to the preceding machine, it will be an instrument of immense power;
However, the wheels ought to be proportioned such that the first driving wheel is always taller than the second; and the second and intermediate wheel is taller than the third.
Thus also, the first should be narrower and finer than the second, and the third should be stronger than the other two.
The reason is that the first suffers less, the second more, but the third suffers the most. However, it is not as important to observe the height of the wheels as it is to note that the last one should be stronger, see Fig. 1.

446      TREATISE. II. PART. VII. BOOK. I.

The principle of motion in this instrument is the same as in the wheels of the first
order, that is, moving from the outside, where the force is dissolved and expanded into
smaller particles, which are proportioned to time, so that for the elevation of any load,
which is done by instruments light at the beginning, time is multiplied along
with the weight: that is, so much more time is consumed, the lighter the instrument
is pulled at the beginning.

Such instruments can therefore be called dividers of weight, attributing to each
man's pull such a weight as can naturally be lifted without instruments;
For example, one lifting a hundredweight from the ground to the height
of one foot without an instrument; now, when he has the instrument, he lifts
ten hundredweights just as easily and with no greater effort. But it is necessary
for the same (person) to cover ten times the distance (of the pull) over ten feet,
whether it be in direct, straight, curved, circular, or however it can be done.
Therefore, in ten minutes, one man lifts with the instrument what ten men lift
in a single minute without the instrument.

A similar principle is observed in the instrument depicted above, because a single man
lifts a very large weight; but to lift to a height of one foot, it is necessary to pull
9 palms of rope, because the added rope is sixfold, the rest (of the rope's behavior) is
accounted for by the width according to the size of the circular wheels.

The cause of the lightness is that the rope, by means of such small wheels, is compelled
to depart from its direct or taut line from the center, and this happens as many times
as you add other small wheels to it.

It should be noted here that there is a twofold progression or multiplication from double
to double; because whatever force you gain by the first small wheel, you have double that
in the second; thus in the third, double the second, and so on, progressing consequently.
That such a recession of the rope from its center, that is, from its taut line of
pull (whether the pull is in a straight or indirect line), brings about lightness, is clear by reason,
because the rope must be longer in such a curved or bent path than
in a straight or direct line; and when the rope is longer, then the operation is slower,
as is clear from the figure.

C H A P. IV.

*On wheels of the second kind, that is, on those which move from the center.*

The use of wheels which move from the center is properly in clocks, and in those machines which cooks constantly use for roasting food, where not force, but speed is required, that is, a multitude of revolutions, so that from the first fundamental wheel, which sometimes in 24 hours (more or less) revolves only once, the speed is multiplied, because the upper small wheel sometimes revolves two hundred times; and this through 3 or 4 wheels with as many cogs, and not with more, except very rarely in clocks with duplicated weights, so that they may operate longer.

*Rule I.*

*All clocks are moved either by a spring, like those small ones which are carried around the neck, or are placed on a table or board, or operate by the gravity of a weight, as are all the larger ones which are built in houses, buildings, or church towers. However, the principle of all is the same, as regards the wheels, although their composition may be different.*

*Rule II.*

*All wheels of clocks move from the center, as was said above.*

The cord is placed for the equalization of the driving force, because in the beginning it pulls more strongly than at the end. However, the fusee of the cord requires greater force in the beginning; Therefore, the driving force is equalized by means of the cord.

Rule III.

This clockwork motion is the resolution of forces inherent in the center, which force expands through the multiplication of wheels and periods into imperceptible parts. However, the prior motion of machines is a restriction, or a gathering, and a union of many wheels, and of parts touching or lightly moving, into a single center.

It is therefore established that the force of clocks is in the beginning, or from the center, and is diffused and expanded. However, the force of the aforementioned machines is at the end, and collected in the axles, as has been said.

happen suddenly and quickly.

# BOOK THREE
## Of motion generated from the natures

### C H A P. I.

*Concerning the nature of formal motion, & concerning certain axioms of the Philosophers,*
*which demonstrate the reason for the diversity of motions arising from elemental*
*bodies.*

#### Rule I.

According to the opinion of all Philosophers, a vacuum is not admitted in the nature of things.

#### Demonstration.

Since all elements are corporeal substances (for they are the matrices of primary qualities), it is necessary that every sublunar place be filled either with elements or with things composed of elements, because elements are dispersed everywhere, and their parts are continuous; Therefore, a vacuum, which is nothing other than the absence of a body, cannot exist in the nature of things.

#### Rule II.

*Air, being a body, does not permit any other body to enter its place, before*
*some part of it or the whole recedes from the aforesaid place. This is demonstrated by the following experiment,*
*commonly not unknown:*

[Diagram of a glass vessel labeled 'A' inverted into a basin labeled 'B' containing water. The opening of the vessel is labeled 'C'.]

*A. a glass vessel filled only with air, whose opening C., if you press it into the water of vessel B.,*
*no part of the water will be able to enter, until some part of the air has exited;*
*For the exit of air is the entrance of water.*

Nnn 3

--- Page 381 ---
470          TRACT. II.  PART. VII.  LIB. III.

*Rule III.*

*Lighter elements naturally yield place to heavier ones; for fire yields to air, air to water,*
*and water to earth: The reason is that heavy things naturally tend downwards, while lighter things*
*are pushed towards the circumference; as will be explained in the following experiments.*

[An illustration showing two scientific apparatuses. On the left, a glass bulb labeled 'A' with a small opening 'B' at the top is partially submerged in a vessel of water. On the right, a similar setup with a tube labeled 'c' and 'd' entering a vessel 'D', and another tube 'E' exiting it.]

It is clear from the preceding experiments that the dense and heavy resists the thin and light;
moreover, the subtle is more volatile and fugitive than the dense. Hence it happens that it recedes
easily, and due to its penetration, it exits through narrower passages. For at the top of the bulb A, there is a certain opening, namely B,
through which the receding air allows water to enter through the mouth of the vessel. But
when that opening is closed, the entry of water is immediately impeded; when it is suddenly
opened, water enters again and rises in the small vessel.
In the second experiment, it is clear that water poured through the opening
of tube c. d. compels the air occupying the region of vessel D to fly out through tube E.

*Rule IV.*

*Sometimes heavy things are pushed out by lighter things enclosed within them; which happens when the path is obstructed*
*by heavier things, so that a light body, pushed by another dense and heavier body to be expelled,*
*cannot exit from its place, unless the less heavy is pushed out first, as appears*
*more clearly in the following example.*

[An illustration showing two more scientific apparatuses. On the left, a cylindrical vessel with a central tube or piston labeled 'H'. On the right, a retort labeled 'H' being heated over a fire 'G', with vapor escaping from the neck at 'K'.]

These

--- Page 382 ---
DE MOTU ELEMENTARI. 471

This rule seems to contradict the previous rule, since the preceding rule states that the heavy displaces the light: But it must be understood that in this place we are not speaking of the simple motion of an element, but of composite motion, namely of the action of one element upon another, and then of that upon a third. For in the previous demonstration, sand poured through opening A. into region B. of the vessel gradually expels the air filling the said region through opening C. which, exiting through C. D. into the upper region D. filled with water, forces that water to give way, and for this to happen, it is necessary for that water to be displaced through tube E. F. Similarly, in the second example, fire in furnace G. acts upon the air mixed with the water of vessel H., both of which rarefy it, and gradually displace it through opening k. until the air has completely filled the vessel.

*Rule V.*

*Fire also expels air by rarefaction, which happens because a container holding some body, after*
*the rarefaction of that body, requires a larger space to better retain that rarefied body, see Num. 1.*

**A.** fire heating region B. filled with air, which, being rarefied, exits
partially into region C. where it seeks a more capacious space.

*Rule VI.*

*Where air enclosed in some place is either evacuated or consumed, it is necessary that some*
*new body fill that place, lest a vacuum be admitted. This is demonstrated by the*
*following examples, Num. 2.*

[Illustration containing two diagrams.
Diagram No. 1 shows a heating apparatus with fire at the top (labeled A), a chamber below (B), and a lower chamber (C) with air or smoke moving between them.
Diagram No. 2 shows a glass flask (labeled A) inverted over a flame in a dish of liquid. A label D is near the base of the flask, and "In." is written in the dish.]

--- Page 383 ---
472          TRACT. II. PART. VII. LIB. III.

In this first demonstration, the exit or evacuation of water through opening D is the cause of the ingress or succession of air through opening A. For the water, leaving the amphora, draws to itself the air existing outside the vessel through opening A, which it leaves as the possessor of the vessel in its place, so that a vacuum may not be admitted.
In the second demonstration, a candle is affixed to the bottom of a vessel filled with water, whose flame, entering through the mouth of the flask, with its mouth depressed at right angles with the candle in the water of the vessel, will draw up so much water as it has consumed of the air enclosed in the flask: For air nourishes fire, and by nourishing is consumed, and so that a vacuum may not be admitted, water, which is the third element, takes the place of the consumed air.

*Rule VII.*

*The substance of the element water is contiguous with air by a tenacious mixture, so that there is no distance between them; From this, therefore, it happens that water is lifted upwards with air. This is demonstrated by the following examples.*

[An engraving depicting a person sitting and using a hollow tube (penna) marked 'A' to draw liquid from a bowl (cyathus) marked 'B'. To the right is a large vessel (amphora) marked 'A' with a siphon-like tube 'C.D.E.' and another opening 'F'.]

In the first demonstration, the contiguity of water with air is shown, because if the end of a hollow tube or quill A, immersed in a cup, has air drawn from it by the mouth, the air enclosed in the concavity of the quill will lift the water with itself.
In the second, a channel inserted through the side of the amphora A, which is c. d. e., will never cease to evacuate the water filling the amphora through its opening e, until the water has fallen to the end of the tube F. For then it will cease to flow: for the water poured into the amphora will expel the air that was in the tube C. E., and water will succeed it: But when the water has descended to mark F, then air is permitted to enter due to the absence of water, so that water no longer flows through E. Certainly, there are infinite examples founded upon the intention of this rule, some of which we recount in our practice.

*Rule VIII.*

*Water does not exit from a pot unless air and a similar body succeed it: From which the wonderful industry of nature in avoiding a vacuum clearly appears to us. This is shown by the following example, No. 1.*
Let there be some vessel or pot, at the top of which there is an opening, and at its bottom many openings, and let that vessel be filled with water, and as long as opening A is stopped by a finger—

--- Page 384 ---
DE MOTU ELEMENTARI. 473
you stop up, no water will flow through the holes in the bottom near B. However, if hole A is opened, it will immediately begin to flow. The reason is that air entering through A will supply the place of the water exiting through B.

*Rule IX.*
*The rarefied element of water requires a larger space, which, if not granted, then*
*in the rarefaction, the place containing it will be broken.*

Let A.B. be a bronze vessel, whose part B must be filled with water, which, made subtle by fire C, seeks a larger space to occupy; for if, during the rarefaction, hole A is stopped up, it is necessary that that bronze vessel be broken with a violent blow like thunder.

*On instrumental motion, that is, on the nature of instruments through*
