*Experiment I.*

So that the base of some machine may be moved on wheels, both forwards and backwards, let a square trunk be erected perpendicularly upon the axle of two wheels, and let it be such that through it two cords, often wound around the axle, orthogonally-

--- Page 385 ---
474          TREATISE II.  PART VII.  BOOK III.
gonally ascend; however, let their arrangement be such that, while one ascends, another always descends. At the top of the trunk, however, let 4 pulleys be affixed; namely, two on its right side and two others on the left, so that the ascending cord may be guided over two of them to one lead counterweight, to which it may be tied by an iron ring; the descending cord also to another weight over the remaining two.

[An illustration of a mechanical device. Two upper rectangular chambers each contain a weight suspended by a cord over a pulley. These cords descend into a lower rectangular box containing a central gear mechanism on a horizontal axis. To the right of the gear is a semi-circular dial or component.]

Let these lead counterweights, however, be equal in every way, which must be supported by a certain heap of sand in different regions of the instrument, and in the bottom of every region it is necessary for a small hole to be made, through which the sand may gradually exit. As the sand of any region decreases, however, the lead weight gradually descends downwards, by whose descent the cord is pulled, and by its tension the axis of both wheels is moved. Hence those wheels move with a third placed in the tail of the instrument, and consequently the entire machine will be perceived to move here and there. But, so that a distinction of the motion of the two weights may be made, it must be understood that the holes of each region, through which the sand exits, must be so subtly plugged, that at the artist's pleasure the instrument may either move or stand fixed. And this must be especially observed, that while one hole is opened, the other must be closed, until all the sand has flowed out from the former region, for then, with subtle ingenuity, the cover of the other must be removed, which in many ways must be accomplished, and especially by the action of the cord moving at that time.

I conclude therefore, that the second weight, by means of the sand of its region, will make as much regression as the first made progression.

*Experimentum III.*

Houses can be burned, altar sacrifices lit, hairy and bearded comets made to
appear, fumigations performed, and many other artifices of this kind accomplished, by
means of the motion of the first experiment, if a candelabrum, an illuminated candle, or a lamp is in
the concavity of the altar secretly held, so that the lit flame touches a copper plate,
blocking a certain hole in the summit of the altar. For by the motion of a
leaden weight or water at a certain given time, that plate will be secretly
removed, and the flame, going out through the hole, will burn whatever combustible
material it finds on the altar. If therefore paper or wooden palaces, or some
fragrant and easily ignitable wood; or fumigations mixed with wood are placed there,
all will blaze. Therefore, for the destruction of *Troy*, the conflagration of *Nero's Rome*,
the burning of *Sardanapalus* with his palace, and the artificial representation of other things of this kind,
this experiment will be very useful.

*A. lamp or candelabrum.*
*B. flame striking the plate.*
*C. Copper plate to be removed.*

*E. small wheel or pulley, over which the cord moves, dislodging the plate at its proper time.*
*F. G. H. I. Altar.*

It is to be noted that this artifice is also performed in many other ways,
namely, either by some illuminated wick, which soldiers use for their cannons,
or by some machines by which, by striking at a given time, fire is produced. Similarly,
the motion of the burning thing happens in many ways. For either at the motion of some
third thing, just as of the plate in the experiment of the preceding experiment,

Images will seem to move circularly, men to dance rhythmically, the position of a theater to be frequently altered, a sphere to be rotated, and many other things of this kind to be performed, if by a counterweight on sand, or by the movement of the sand itself or water, a cord passing around axis A through pulley B is touched at some prescribed time; And this can be done in the same motion, as often as you wish, and with much variety of invention; But it must be observed that in place of an image, a Sphere, a Theater, a crowd of dancing men ought to be placed, similarly a rooster, and other things of this kind. Experiment VI.

Music is made, with certain harmonious sounds, then by the motion of sand, then by the flow of the water itself, both by means of a wheel and without it, and indeed in diverse ways, the first of which concerns sounds produced by a pipe; Here therefore, we will briefly explain by what artifice it can be accomplished.

First, this is certain, that air is very easily expelled from some region of a vessel by a denser body intervening, if only a suitable and convenient exit presents itself, through which it may go out; for otherwise it does not admit another body of whatever element it may be into the place which it possesses, as is sufficiently demonstrated by the second and third rule of this book.

Therefore, this sixth experiment will teach by what artifice a blast is made: For by a blast, organs and pipes will be seen to sound, bottles to cry out, birds to sing, serpents to hiss, lions and bulls to roar and bellow. But this blast is made either by the simple action of sand and water upon the air, expelling it, namely, through an opening from its region, or by a composite action, namely, by the action of fire upon water, and then of that upon air, as is manifest from the following demonstrations.

### Experiment VII.

Music of trumpets, horns, and other pipes is produced from many well-sounding parts by means of the following wheel, with the aid of the device from the preceding experiment. Therefore, let a wheel be made, divided into equal parts, so that each part serves for the musical time called a Semibreve; and let each of these be divided again into 4 equal parts, of which two will observe in their movements the value of a Minim, and each by itself will represent a black note or crotchet; From this it is clear that the length of the wheel will demonstrate the proportion of musical time; and its width will explain the degrees of the musical system: therefore its width is to be divided into as many parts or keys as there are notes in the system, counting in their order; Gamma ut, A re, B mi, etc. Therefore, appendages or keys are to be artificially applied to the width and length of the wheel, so that they may be arranged according to the nature of the song, both by the measure of time and by the true position of the system. Then let the wheel be set in motion; so that it moves according to the principle of the fifth experiment, or according to the inventor's arrangement, so that the keys of the wheel move and depress the keys of the pipes.

Rule XI.
Water contained in one region of a vessel is pushed down, and propelled

and by its relaxation, it is extended at the Artist's pleasure:

but by its relaxation, it is sprinkled everywhere.

Experiment XII.

So that by the heat of a very gentle fire or of the sun, heating some vessel, the air contained in it may be so rarefied, that after the cooling of the vessel, water may be carried upwards against its own nature, and fill the place of the expelled rarefactions of the air. Let there therefore be a leaden ball, or if possible, a glass one, hollow inside, and of moderate capacity, and strong in its construction, so that it may not break. Let this be perforated at its top. Let there also be another sufficiently large vessel, and let that be filled with water; afterwards let these two vessels be so arranged, that one leg of a curved channel or siphon descends almost to the very bottom of the vessel. And similarly let the other leg enter into the opening of the ball, which must be perforated in such a way, that afterwards air may neither enter nor exit it, except through this channel alone. Let the ball therefore be exposed to the sun's rays, or to a fire very similar to the sun. When it has been heated, a part of the enclosed air, now thinned by the fire, exits through the curved siphon, as is demonstrated by rule 5, chapter 1 of this book, into the vessel filled with water, and will mix itself with the water therein, stirring up many bubbles one after another. But when the sun recedes from the ball, or the fire is removed, or the ball itself is placed in the shade, the now rarefied air reclaims its expelled rarefactions because of the condensing coldness which begins to occupy it; which, because they are mixed with water, simultaneously lift the water with them, and together with it ascend into the ball. This water, however, ascends again, and descends into its own vessel, if a second time fire or solar rays touch the ball.

# BOOK FOUR
## On the invention of our entire spiritual machine.

C H A P. I.
*On the figure of the base of our spiritual machine.*

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.8; vertical-align: -0.2em;">S</span>INCE we wish this spiritual machine of ours to revolve around the conditions of the seven Planets, we have therefore arranged its base, according to whose proportion it ought to be raised upwards, into a heptagonal form, so that each side of it may correspond to the nature of any of the Planets. Therefore, let a circle drawn upon some flat surface, namely upon the ground and pavement, be divided into seven equal parts: from any point of division, let a straight line be drawn to the point of division nearest to it, and in this way you will have a regular heptagonal figure. This done, let a straight line be drawn to any angle of the heptagonal surface, which ought to be divided into seven equal parts. And this must be done for every line drawn from the center to an angle. Then, from any point of division, let a straight line be drawn to the point opposite to it, so that many heptagonal surfaces, one proportion smaller than another, may be included within every larger one. But in the center of this surface, let there be a sufficiently large opening, through which a large brass or iron pipe may emerge. Through this, water is to flow upwards, and for that reason, that pipe ought to ascend up to the top of the machine, so that by the revolution of the machine itself, water may very easily flow from one side to another into any region of the machine. And this pipe must also adhere fixedly and immovably to the center of the base, so that the machine may be rotated upon it as if upon an axis. But the divisions of the diameter of this fundamental surface, and consequently of its entire area into heptagons, denote the boundaries of each region of the machine, in which regions the natures of the Planets ought to be expressed, as we will explain more fully below. Here, however, we have thus described the heptagonal surface, ordered and arranged for the base of the machine.

**CH. II.**

***Concerning the construction and arrangement of the shape of this machine upon the aforesaid base.***

The structure, moreover, which is to be built and erected upon this base, ought to follow the shape of the base itself: Let it therefore be divided according to its height into seven regions, and let the distance in height between any region be three feet, and let the width of each region be quite proper and suitable for receiving the actions and movements of images, which can declare the natures and conditions of the planets by their actions. And in this way, it is necessary that from the base of the machine towards its summit, a progression be made in an almost pyramidal form, so that each region, the more it tends upwards, the less its capacity there, and consequently where more actions and a greater number of actors are necessary, there also a larger place and one closer to view may exist. However, on the plane distinguishing the height of each region from the other, certain stories are to be depicted, pertaining to the persona of the Planet, which the ancient Poets described, so that besides the actions of the moving images, the history and life of each Planet on earth may be described: Moreover, the entire substance of this machine, from its summit almost down to its base, through Qqq 3 cen-

melancholy in an *Amphora*, which is proper to *Saturn*, before whom *Athenian* men will
stand: In the fourth, let snow and hail fall upon houses, & cutting down herbs and trees, with
cattle moving, and men kindling fire.

# BOOK ONE.
## On the Species of Time.

### C H A P. I.
*On the difference between time, aeon, and eternity.*

[decorative initial P]OST the history of both natural and artificial motions, order demands that we discuss briefly the nature of Time; since it is defined as the number measuring the motion of mutable things, and that indeed according to before and after. For it is that space derived from the revolution of the heavens and the sun, by which we measure the agitation and change of all mobile things. Whence it becomes manifest that in time there is motion from which to which, by which conditions indeed two of its cognates or relatives are excluded from it, namely Aeon, whose condition is to measure the local motions of those things which indeed have a beginning but no end; and Eternity, which is the infinite measure of that which has neither beginning, nor middle, nor any end. However, this temporal measuring number of motions, if compared to motion as to its efficient cause, as the artificial day to the motion of the sun above the earth, is called the numbered number; but if compared to its mobile subject according to its parts, namely present, past, and future, then it is called the mediating numbering number. Similarly, this number, inasmuch as it measures motion according to the prior, that is, past time, and according to the posterior, that is, future time, cannot occur in the same moment, since a moment is only the minute part of present time; Whence it happens that, just as a number is formed from units, and a line from points, so also time is constituted from minute parts or moments, and therefore a moment is properly so called, since it is the act or substance of time itself, if indeed continuous moments without interval are nothing other than time itself. Time is divided in general into years, months, weeks, days, hours, and minutes, about which we will treat in this book.

### C H A P. II.
*On the Year.*

[decorative initial A] YEAR is that space of time in which the sun, by its natural motion, passes through the 12 signs of the Zodiac, and is said by some (Isidore, etc.) to come from 'An.', which is from 'circum' (around), because in the circular solar motion both extremes of the circle are joined, that is, the Sun returns by its natural motion to the place from which it departed. And from this it also follows that others more correctly believed the name 'Annus' (Year) to be derived from 'annulus' (ring) by the same reasoning; Whence also the Egyptians, before the invention of letters, hieroglyphically signified the year by the sign of a Dragon turning circularly and biting its own tail—

--- Page 416 ---
DE TEMPORIS SPECIEBUS. 505

...represented. This *year*, however, is properly called *solar*, because the sun's motion is measured by this kind of number, namely the space of 12 *months* or 365 days, 5 hours, & 46 minutes; which year is indeed distinguished from the *Lunar year*, inasmuch as the latter is so called in three respects; for it is either taken for that time in which the Moon completes the course of the entire Zodiac in 27 days, 7 hours & 44 minutes, or for the space between one conjunction of the Moon with the Sun and another, or for the space of twelve Moon revolutions, which it completes in a space of 354 days; And this year is smaller than that solar one by 11 days, from which difference or superfluity of days indeed the *Epact* arises, as has been said in our book on Astronomical Arithmetic; Hence every third solar year will consist of 13 Lunations. But the other Planets also have their own years; for the *year of Saturn* consists of 30 solar years, and the *year of Jupiter* of 12 *solar years*.

CHAPTER I.
On the method of constructing a Scioteric rule.

[Large decorative initial R]
THIS rule, which is called Scioteric, contains certain unequal divisions of a straight line,
which are derived from the equal division of two quadrants, so that they may serve for the
expeditious description of sundials. Concerning this matter, the present commentary has been written,
so that from it the method of constructing the said rule, and its use, may be learned. Therefore, the rule is constructed in this manner.
Upon the straight line D. F. in the diagram subject to this chapter, let a quadrant D. G. F. be described from center F.,
which is to be divided into 24 equal parts: Therefore, the sixth part of the quadrant thus divided shall be for an hour, the twelfth for half an hour, and the twenty-fourth part for a quarter of an hour.
Moreover, each of the hours ought to bear a double denomination, as appears in the following figure.
The quadrant being divided in this manner, it is necessary to determine the length of the rule, which may conveniently extend to six digits. Therefore, in the given rule (whether it be brass or wood) A. B. C. D., let the line A. B. be taken of the said length, namely six digits, and according to this distance, let the line I. H. be drawn parallel to the line D. F., the semidiameter of the quadrant D. G. F. just described; which shall cut the semidiameter, extended as needed, at point I. Then from center F., through the fifth or seventh hour assigned on arc D. G., let a straight line F. H. be drawn, which shall intersect line I. H. at point H. From H., let a straight line H. L. be drawn parallel to line F. I., which shall intersect line D. F. at L. Finally, the line F. L. will be the exact width of the rule adapted to the given length. Now, apply the rule to center F. and simultaneously to each of the divisions of arc D. G., and let straight lines be drawn which shall intersect lines L. H. and I. H. into unequal portions as the matter will provide: These small parts ought to be transferred to the rule, and there distinguished by their numbers, as is evident in lines A. B. and B. C. In the following treatise, these parts of an hour and parts of hours are named, and when needed, each is to be taken from the rule, observing the order from A. towards B., and to be described on a given line from a given point, as appears in Horizontal and Mural Sundials on line D. E. After this, upon the line F. E., from center F., let a quadrant E. G. be described, and let it be divided into 90 parts, starting from point G. and ending at point E. From center F., through the 15th degree of quadrant F. G. E., let a straight line F. K. be drawn, cutting line I. K. at K. Let a straight line K. M. be drawn parallel to line F. G., which shall cut D. E. at M. Line F. M. will give the width of the rule and will be found equal to line F. L. Then let straight lines be drawn from center F. to each degree of quadrant G. E.

The lines from G. E., which divide lines M. K. & K. H. into unequal parts as it may be. These small parts are to be transferred to the rule and marked with their numbers, as can be seen in lines C. D. & D. A., and these small parts we now call secants, now tangents. But it should be noted that, when I propose to find the secant of any degree, one leg of the compass should be placed at point B, and the other extended to the assigned degree; and this distance should be marked on the given line. C A P. II.
*On the Use of the Scioteric Rule.*

For a fuller use of the rule, the knowledge of certain propositions necessary for the drawing of Sundials is required; whose geometrical operation, although it may be familiar and known to any beginner, yet since it can be deduced from this rule without knowledge of geometrical elements, I have not considered it irrelevant to the purpose to propose them in this place. Therefore, the Propositions follow.

Proposition I.
*To make a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point, or, which is the same, you will be able to draw a right angle at a given point in this manner:* On the rule, take the semidiameter of the rule from B. to C. and mark it on the given line; then take the tangent of any degree, that is, place one foot of the compass in the letter C. and extend the other to any degree on the line C. D., for example, to the fortieth: With the compass thus extended, place its other foot on point E. of the given line, and describe arc G. H. Proposition II.
*On a straight line at a given point, the method of drawing an angle equal to a given angle.* In this entire treatise, we understand no other angle besides right and acute: Concerning the right angle, it has already been said in the previous proposition, it remains that we treat of the acute angle, which can be described thus.
Let the given line be E. F. and let an angle of 50 degrees be drawn at point F. From F. to E., let the Semidiameter of the rule C. B. be measured. Then take the secant of the complement of the assigned degree, and according to this distance from point F. let arc K. L. be described. Afterwards, take the tangent of the same complement, and from point E. describe arc G. H. which will intersect arc K. L. at P.: Then let a line be drawn from P. to F. and angle P. F. E. will contain 50 degrees, and will be equal to the assigned angle.

C H A P. III.
*On the Horizontal Sundial.*

A Horizontal Sundial is so called because it is parallel to the plane of the Horizon,
and is drawn in this manner. Let a straight line E. F. be drawn from E. towards F. Let the
distances of the hours be measured from the rule, taken on the same line A. B. From point
E. of the given line, let a perpendicular line E. G. be erected; and on the same line from E. to
G. let the secant of the pole's elevation be measured (which in this whole treatise we presuppose
to be 51 and 1/2 degrees). From point G. to each division of line E. F., let straight
lines be drawn, which may be extended as desired. From the same point G., let a straight line be drawn
parallel to E. F. And thus you will have the hours of the Horizontal Sundial described. To construct
the gnomon, however, from E. to A. let the secant of the equinoctial be measured on line E.
F.; and let a line be drawn from point G. to H., which will represent the gnomon. And from
this model, an entire Horizontal Sundial can be transferred to any
assigned surface.

C H A P. IV.
*On the Mural or Vertical Dial.*

A MURAL DIAL is that which is described on a surface parallel to the plane of the vertical circle, from which it is also called a vertical dial: And it is either Southern or Northern: Both can be transferred from the same model, of which this is the delineation: On the straight line E. F. let the hourly distances be measured, as in the previous [chapter]: Then let a perpendicular E. G. be erected. From E towards G, let the secant of the Equator's elevation be measured (which we presuppose to be 38 and 1/2 degrees.) From point G to each of the hourly sections on line E. F., let straight lines be drawn: From the same point G, let a straight line be drawn, parallel to line E. F. And thus the hourly lines will appear, which pertain to the mural dial. To find the gnomon, however, from point E to H on line E. F., let the secant of the pole's elevation be measured, and the straight line, drawn from point G to H, will give the gnomon. 6

[A geometric diagram showing the construction of a sundial. Points are labeled G, E, H, and F. Lines radiate from point G to a horizontal line marked with numbers 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. A diagonal line from G to H is labeled "Stylus."]

It must be noted that the *Southern mural dial* must be entirely transferred from this model, but it is not so in the Northern: For the latter only admits two hours before the sixth, and after the sixth: Those who live closer to the North have more hourly lines; those who approach closer to the South have fewer.
It must also be observed in the *Northern dial*, that the gnomon's apex always points upwards.

**C H A P. VI.**

*On the Declining Sundial.*

**A** declining sundial is that which makes a right angle with the plane of the Horizon, but an oblique angle with the plane of the vertical circle. The quantity of declination is known from the arc, which is contained between the plane of the vertical circle and the assigned surface, which is indeed always less than 90 degrees. A declining sundial has its primary denomination from the south and north, however, with the addition of two other cardinal parts; so that the sundial declines either from the South towards the East, or from the South towards the West, or from the North towards the East, or from the North towards the West: He who knows how to construct one of these, knows all, because they do not differ by any essential reason, but all can be derived from one and the same model, provided the declination is the same. They differ, however, in the denomination and position of the hours, so that, if you describe a sundial on one side of a sheet of paper, which faces from the South to the East, the same lines described on the other side will give a sundial which declines from the South to the West, and with only the denomination of the hours changed, the remaining two sundials will emerge from the same model.

A declining sundial is drawn in this manner: Let us suppose the declination is 40 degrees towards the East: Upon the straight line E. F. let a perpendicular G. H. be erected, which divides the line E. F. at I. Upon the line E. F. at point I. (to the left, if the given surface declines from South to East, or from North to West; but to the right, if it declines from South to West, or from North to East) let an angle equal to the complement of the declination be drawn, and let the angle be E. I. K. On the line I. K. from point I. to K. let the secant of the pole's elevation be measured. From point K. let the line K. L. be erected perpendicular to I. E. at L. From point K. let the line K. M. be drawn perpendicular to I. E. and divide I. E. at M. On the line G. H. from point I. to G. if the declination is Southern, but if Northern, from point I. to H. let the secant of the Equator be measured, from point G. to L. let a straight line be drawn, which represents the sixth hour: from point G. to M. let the substylar line be drawn; From M. let the line M. P. be drawn perpendicular to G. M. and equal to the line M. K. The straight line drawn from G. P. will give the gnomon. From point I. let the line N. I. O. be drawn perpendicular to K. I. which should be extended as far as possible: On this line, on both sides of point I. let the hours translated from the rule be measured; from point K to each of the hour marks let faint lines be drawn, which divide the line E. F. into as many parts as possible: The straight lines drawn from point G. to the intersections of the line E. F. will give the hour lines, which we seek in the proposed declining sundial: The gnomon therefore must be erected upon the line G. M. P.: And from the following model, four declining sundials can be derived.

**C A P. VII.**

*On the Reclining & Inclining Sundial.*

A *reclining* sundial is that whose surface, representing one of the four cardinal points, if extended, forms an obtuse angle with the Horizon: An *inclining* sundial is that which forms an acute angle with the Horizon. Both are fourfold, according to the different orientation of the four cardinal points; for both reclining and inclining are either Oriental, or Occidental, or Septentrional, or Austral. The quantity of reclining and inclining is known from the arc, which is contained between the Horizon and the assigned surface. Reclining and inclining [sundials], which are opposite, essentially agree, and are made by the same art and work, differing only in the denomination of the hours, and in position, as will appear in the following [sections]. First, however, we will discuss the Austral reclining and Septentrional inclining [sundials], which are opposite to each other, and afterwards the Oriental and Occidental.

If the Austral reclining and Septentrional inclining [sundial] is equal to the polar elevation, it is called a Polar Sundial, and is constructed in this manner. Let a straight line E. F. be drawn parallel to the Horizon, in the middle of which let a perpendicular G. H. be erected, which cuts the line E. F. at H. On line E. F., on both sides of point H., let the hours be numbered, taken from a scale; at each point let straight lines be drawn, parallel to line G. H., and thus the hour lines of the polar sundial will appear; Let the style be perpendicular to the surface, and its length be equal to the semidiameter of the scale. But if the distance of the hour lines described here does not fit well to the given surface, it can either be increased or contracted as occasion demands, as we taught before in the description of the Oriental Sundial.

     If the reclining or inclining is less than the elevation of the pole, let the reclining be subtracted from the elevation of the pole, and what remains, let it be for the elevation of the pole, according to which a Horizontal sundial is constructed, as we taught before.      South reclining and inclining sundials have their own proper forms; if the reclining or inclining is equal to the elevation of the Equator, then the sundial has its own character and name, and is called an Equinoctial sundial, because it is constructed on a surface parallel to the plane of the Equator, and is fashioned in this way; Let a straight line E. # BOOK THREE
## Concerning our horological machine.

### C H A P. I.

*Concerning the jar or hollow space containing water, in which the float*
*of the clock ought to move up and down.*

[Decorative initial F] LET a jar be made of lead, in a shape, either round, or pentagonal, or
hexagonal, but it is better to have a lateral shape than a round one
on account of the display of the twelve hours in it, yet in such a way that
that vessel is adapted such that all its sides are equal, and
consequently all its angles similar, and the same dimension of concavity in
all parts, so that the floating cursor can move precisely up and down in it without impediment,
that is, that all angles of the base of the cursor and its sides are aptly accommodated
to the sides and angles of the containing vessel, so that they move without
obstruction, and are raised upwards when water flows into the vessel, and descend
again when it flows out.

Indeed, in the middle of its base, let there be an opening of such a size that almost all the liquid
from the vessel filled with water can exit through it within the space of twelve hours,
and this vessel, so that it can again be filled by a new succession of water, will have a tube
protruding outside the vessel, rising a little above the height of the vessel;
its lower part, however, will enter the lower part of the vessel's side;
whence, the aqueduct, with a key turned by a certain mechanism, as will be demonstrated below,
will gradually and progressively fill that vessel or jar through the tube with water
exiting through the channel's opening. And this done, with the key turned again, the water
will again flow out through the opening in the bottom of the vessel, and in this way,
without manual contact, that clock will always move and demonstrate the hours of day and night.

But since the water gradually decreases from the upper edge of the vessel down to
its bottom within the space of twelve hours, therefore, we will divide one side of the vessel,
counting from its aforementioned upper edge almost down to its foot, into twelve equal parts:
And this division indeed ought to be made with clear lines, always inserting a subdivision
of each part by darker lines into four other parts equal to each other:
For in this way, the cursor's single indication, gradually descending, will, as it were,
point with a finger to the number of hours and its quarters.
We have, moreover, delineated an example of this vessel in this manner.

C H A P. II.
*On the internal part of this machine.*

Let the base of the cursor instrument be prepared from wood, sufficiently solid, but somewhat porous, imitating the angles and sides of the containing vessel, yet so adapted that that base can move up and down without impediment along the angles and sides of the said vessel, also with the condition that it in no way inclines to the right or left, but always performs its movement perpendicularly: Afterwards, according to its form, let a column six feet long be prepared, whose dimension is a quarter of an inch smaller than the base: Its geometrical figure, however, will always be the same as the base. The length of this column ought to be distributed into 40, or 50, or even more parts up to a hundred, which parts in turn ought to be subdivided into four others: These divisions, moreover, will serve for musical times, for a song composed for bells, and sounding at every twelfth hour, which song will indeed last through this ascent of the column from the base of the vessel up to its edges: Similarly from the said intervals not-

C A P. III.

*Concerning the position and situation of the Bells, and concerning the making and arrangement of the hammers striking them.*

As far as the order of the small bells is concerned, it must be known that it is twofold: one, namely, more suitable and fit for the composition of the instrument, the other, however, more accommodating to the arrangements of sounds. And as far as the former is concerned, it is necessary that because of the multitude of small bells, they be placed and arranged in a circular or round order, since that figure is the most capacious of all; or also, if it pleases, according to the order of the form of the column itself or the entire machine, so that the striking keys may more easily touch the hammers of the small bells. According to the order of sounds also let them be constituted in such a way that they present the true series of the Musical system, so that the preceding small bell corresponds to the subsequent one in tone and semitone according to the Monochord's tenor and norm, lest otherwise discords arise instead of harmonies. Therefore, the largest small bell, which represents Γ. ut., should be immediately followed in position by the small bell next to it in size; and so in the others down to the smallest and last of all.
      And since a thing, the more it is removed from the center of a circle, the more space and place it claims for itself, therefore the handles of the hammers, imitating the radius of the circular arrangement, ought to be somewhat oblong, so that a wider interval may be left for the circular position of the small bells; for otherwise the iron keys fixed into the small column will be too close and narrow for the arrangement of the small bells, and consequently, due to lack of space, each iron key will not be able to correspond to its small bell.
      The hammers, however, ought to be made of iron not too heavy, lest the machine be impeded in the elevation of various hammers, to be done at the same instant. The arrangement of the small bells with their hammers is shown in the following illustration.

C A P. IV.
*Of the channel or aqueduct, and similarly of the turning mechanism, by the turning of which to one side water will be emitted through the channel; but by its other part the exit of water will be prevented.*

It now remains for us to explain the method by which this vessel, empty of water after the twelfth hour, may again be filled by itself. Therefore, let an iron projection be made in the upper part of the column, on that side next to the turning mechanism of the channel, which is so adapted that at the time when the water has been completely emptied through the bottom of the vessel, it can meet with the projection protruding from the turning mechanism, and by its contact, turn it. For this having been done, the opening of the channel will immediately be opened; and water will abundantly enter through the tube, and suddenly fill the containing vessel more and more, gradually raising its inner column, which, when it has reached its highest altitude and its highest point, another iron projection, joining itself in its ascent with the turning mechanism's projection, will close the passage of water, and thus the entry of water into the machine of that containing vessel will be stopped, until that water has again flowed out through the lower opening, which will happen, as has been said, in the space of twelve hours. The description of this, moreover, follows here.

C H A P. V.

*How can the movement of the Moon be indicated quite accurately by a clock of this kind?*

Let a round Planisphere be made next to one side of the vessel, containing 12 celestial signs divided into degrees, and let an axis governing a rod pass through its center. On the front of this axis, let the Moon be depicted with a finger or indicator. On the other part of the axis, between the side of the vessel and that Planisphere, let a wheel be made, excavated with as many suitable teeth as there are degrees in the Zodiac. But let that wheel be constructed in such a way that it can be moved by the descent of the column itself, but when it ascends, let it remain fixed. Therefore, small projections descending upon the rod from the top of the column must be adapted so that they strongly press the teeth of that wheel, causing it to move. But during ascent, let them recede easily, and bring no force to the teeth by which the wheel might be disturbed. This can indeed be done if they are so fitted to the joints, which we mentioned above, that they easily recede during ascent, but strongly resist during descent. Therefore, that rod will have seven projections, corresponding to those seven degrees which the Moon, by its natural motion, usually completes and traverses in twelve hours. Thus, by a double repetition of the downward movement of that Rod, about fourteen degrees are counted each day, and fourteen teeth out of the three hundred and sixty existing on the aforesaid wheel are turned each natural day. And in this way, the movement of the Moon for any day of the month, and in any sign, can be demonstrated and observed quite well without great error.

THE END.

# BOOK ONE.
## On Cosmographic Principles.

### CHAPTER I.

*How celestial circles relate to the parts of the earth, and divide it no differently than they do the convex surface itself of the celestial sphere.*

[Decorative initial A] STRONOMERS supposed the convex surface of the universal world to be divided and distributed by circles, both larger and smaller, among which some larger ones are external and immobile, namely the Meridian circle and the Horizon; others are mobile and internal, and these either with latitude or without latitude. The one which has latitude is called the Zodiac or Ecliptic. But all other circles, both larger and smaller, except for two which are called Colures, are parallel to each other, of which only one is larger, dividing the sky into two equal parts according to longitude, and is called the Equator or Equinoctial. But the smaller ones are the two Tropics, namely of Cancer and Capricorn, and the two Polar Circles. The two Colures, just as the Meridian, intersect the poles in their circuit.

CHAPTER II.

*On the use of these Circles on Earth for distinguishing Zones.*

However, sections of this kind on Earth, formed from imaginary celestial circles, cause the distinctions of Zones; For as many intervals as there are of the whole earth from pole to pole, proportioned by the aforementioned parallel circles, so many Zones are also numbered: for counting from the Arctic Pole to its circle, that whole space is counted as one of the frigid Zones: But indeed, that whole interval comprehended between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer is called one of the temperate Zones, namely the northern one: What is measured between the Tropic of Cancer and the Equinoctial Circle, is the more northern part of the torrid Zone, just as

--- Page 444 ---
DE PRINCIP. COSMOGRAPHICIS. 533

...just as that [space] between the Equinoctial [line] and the Tropic of Capricorn is the other part of the Torrid Zone, namely the Southern [part]. So indeed, since that portion of the earth is equally divided by the Equinoctial line, this Torrid Zone therefore appears to be double, and thus two Torrid Zones, namely Northern and Southern, can be counted no less correctly than two Frigid Zones and two Temperate Zones are counted. However, all that space comprehended between the Tropic of Capricorn and the Antarctic Circle is called the Southern Temperate Zone, just as that entire interval extended from the Antarctic Circle to its pole is called the Southern or Meridional Frigid Zone. Here therefore is the principal use of the impression of the celestial Circles on the terrestrial globe. From which it is manifest that the latitude of the frigid zones is 23 degrees and 20 minutes, but the latitude of the temperate Zones is nearly 43 degrees. And both Torrid Zones, which Astronomers count as only a single Zone, have for their latitude 47 degrees. However, all the differences of these are caused by the Sun's closer presence and its more distant absence; For the more the Solar rays incline to right angles, that is, the more perpendicularly they fall upon the earth's surface, the more the heating power is intensified in that region of the earth; But the more acute angles it makes on the earth's surface, the colder it usually renders the region. However, we will not discuss these things further, because authors who have treated Cosmography have described them extensively.

C A P. III.

*On Parallels & Climates.*

We call those circles Parallels which are equidistant from each other. However, we distinguish these into general and particular. The ancients made eight general ones, which extend through the zenith of some region according to longitude: beginning from the Equator and ending with the beginning of the ninetieth degree of elevation or latitude; and each of these parallels differs from each other in latitude by 10 degrees of the Meridian. But particular parallels are certain imaginary lines on a terrestrial map for distinguishing regions, which also approach the poles by progressing from the Equator. There is also another division of these particular parallels, for the space of the earth contained between two parallels, counting from the beginning of one to the end of the other, is called a Climate: Hence, just as every parallel circle at its beginning, the further it is from the Equinoctial and the closer to the pole, always has a longer day than others tending towards the Equator; so a Climate, the more it is distant from the Equinoctial, the more it increases the portion of the longer day of one parallel. Hence, every parallel distant from the Equator towards the pole, counting up to the 14th parallel, has its maximum day, longer than the maximum day of the preceding parallel by a quarter of an hour; but every Climate distant from the Equator will have its longest day exceeding the maximum day of the immediately preceding Climate by half an hour. Here, however, it must be observed that from the 14th parallel up to the 19th, the progression occurs by half an hour, and in the 20th and 21st parallels, the maximum day consists of 20 hours.

As for Climates, Ptolemy described only seven species of them; However, more recent [authors] posited more, namely nine, all of which received their denominations from the more notable places through which they pass. Hence the first, extending from the Equinoctial to the North, is called Diameroe, because it passes through an island of that name surrounded by the Nile. The second is called...

--- Page 445 ---
534	TRACT. II. PART. IX	LIB. I.
is called Dia Sienne, because it passes through a city in Africa situated under the Tropic of Cancer, and so in the others up to the ninth and last, passing over the Maeotian marsh.
	Here, however, it must be diligently observed that the spaces of the earth, enclosed by climates or parallel circles, are not equal, but are so much larger, the closer the parallels or climates are to the Equator or the middle of the world, and so much more contracted and smaller, the further they are from the middle of the world and the closer to the poles.

C A P. IV.
*Concerning the division of parallels, and concerning their division, and concerning their order, as observed by Ptolemy in Book 2 of the Great Construction, Chapter 6.*

Cosmographers observe *three species of parallels*, which they distinguish by reason of shadows, for they call some parallels *Amphiscii*, namely those in which the shadow is cast in both directions, such as all parallels comprehended between the two Tropics, namely the first six; others they call *Heteroscii*, namely those who cast a shadow in only one direction; of which kind the first is the parallel through Syene, namely the Tropic of Cancer, and the last is the thirty-second, and all from the Tropic of Cancer up to the Arctic Circle, numbering twenty-six; they made others *Periscii*, who cast a shadow in all parts of the Horizon in a circle on any given day. The first of these is the thirty-third, in which the days are twenty-four. The remaining Periscii are seven, all from the Arctic Circle up to the Pole, and there the entire Tropic of Cancer is seen above the Horizon; while its opposite Tropic is completely submerged.

C H A P. V.

*On vertical or meridian circles.*

Circular lines, not parallel, passing through the Zenith of any region,
and simultaneously converging at the poles of the world, are called meridian or vertical lines;
whose principal use is to measure the latitude of terrestrial regions, just
as it is the Equator's [use] to determine their longitude, by counting from the
meridian of the Fortunate Isles to that of the proposed region.
The terrestrial globe therefore is usually divided by 24 of these lines, each of
which comprehends the space of one hour. Wherefore it is certain that places situated under
such meridians differ among themselves by the space or interval of one hour, so that
the more eastern of two places, separated by only one meridian,
has its noon, day, midnight, lunar eclipse, and conjunction
and opposition of the luminaries, earlier than the other by one hour;
if it is distinguished from another by two meridians, by two hours; and so in the rest.
And here it will be observed that a single degree of longitude is equal in its
space to 4 minutes of an hour, as will be more easily perceived by arithmetical
calculation.

---

C A P. VII.

*On the division of the Hemisphere by a meridian line, and on the optical adaptation of vertical and parallel lines to it.*

Let a circle of any capacity, namely B. C. D. E., be made, and let it be the outermost meridian circle, which is divided into 360 equal parts, as is declared in the preceding example. Then let two Diameters be drawn intersecting each other at right angles, and let them be B. D. and C. E., of which one will represent the axis of the world, the other the Equator: afterwards let one part of the ruler be placed upon point or pole B., and the other be extended to point F. But where the intersection will occur on the Equator, there will pass the second meridian, or second vertical line: Then

...Then, in this way, with those intersections occurring in the eastern part of the Equator, just as it was done in its western part. And where intersections have been made on line A. D., it will be diligently observed; for the center of that intersection with its endpoint, to which the center must be sought: For example, the center of the first intersection and point O, of the second and point N, of the third and point M, and so on for the others. Then let segment O. P. be drawn through the first intersection, and N. Q. through the second intersection, and M. R. through the third, and so on for the others: And in this way you will recover the general parallels of the entire Hemisphere, and you will have both vertical circles and parallels described optically, as if half of an exactly spherical globe were pressed onto a flat surface. Note, however, that although in optical precepts these two methods of delineating hemispheres are very perfect, they nevertheless suffer a defect in the ratio of parallels to the greatest circle, namely that in the final description all regions situated around the poles of the world always appear smaller than they should.

CHAPTER VIII.

*By what method should any quarter of the world be delineated?*

**IN** the geographical delineation of any quarter of the world, its exact longitude and latitude must be considered. For its latitude, one must observe the distance from the pole most relevant to that part, and measure from the parallel that terminates that part to the parallel that begins it.
      For example, if we wish to depict a Geographical map of Europe, to which Geographers attribute a latitude of 40 degrees, starting from the Southern parallel of 30 degrees latitude, up to the parallel of 70 degrees towards the north.
      Therefore, we draw a straight line A. B., which will represent the central meridian of the given region. From this, you will take a certain length, according to the size of the work to be constructed. Let A. therefore be the pole of the world, and B. the 30-degree parallel (which is below the given parallel). Therefore, you will cut the entire A. B. into 60 equal parts, which will signify degrees of latitude for the given map, starting from the 30-degree parallel and ending at the 70-degree parallel. Thus, the one drawn at 50 degrees will be the middle parallel of the entire map. Now, from the aforesaid pole, as a center, you will draw segments of circles through every ten degrees of latitude, which will give you the principal parallels of

--- Page 452 ---

C A P. IX.

*Concerning the method of displaying regions and islands in the aforesaid world map.*

FOR depicting any region of the world, this will be the chorographic method. Let the region to be described be sought in a larger map or geographical table; having found it, mark its extreme longitude, measured by degrees of the Equator, and similarly its latitude, distinguished by degrees of the meridians. Having found these, determine the region's latitude and longitude as you please, and divide its meridian and the line of longitude into as many parts as the proposed region requires. For example, if it has been our intention to depict Gaul, we find that its greater latitudinal extension is between the city of Marseille in Provence and the city of Antwerp, which spans 12 degrees of the meridian, starting from its southernmost part; namely, counting from the 43rd degree from the Equator up to the 54th degree, progressing towards the north. Let them therefore be arranged in such a way that by means of faint lines a transition is made from one degree of both longitude and latitude to the degree opposite to it. And by the intersection of such lines, many small squares will be produced in the same map of the region, so that all parts of the aforesaid region may be expressed more accurately and more easily and truly delineated in the said map.

# BOOK TWO
## On the composition of our Cosmographical Planisphere.

### C H A P. I.
#### *On the parts of our Planisphere in general.*

[Decorative initial H]IS our Planisphere is divided into two notable or equal parts, each of which represents a hemisphere of the universal world with a detailed delineation of the terrestrial globe. The entire machine of the world thus described is divided in this hemisphere by the Equinoctial, and every superior or celestial portion of the world is joined with the terrestrial one, so that the stars, signs, and houses of the heavens, and every part of them, correspond to the earth and its regions, and govern and rule them: Hence we have feigned the heaven to be extended above the earth onto a flat surface.
Therefore, each hemisphere of our Planisphere is divided into 4 parts, two of which are essential, namely the two lower ones, while the others are demonstrative, namely the hourly sphere, and the index of the total latitude, called the visible rule or meridian, as will appear below.

***

### C H A P. II.
#### *On the lower or northern terrestrial part of the Planisphere, with*
#### *the Zodiac on its margin.*

And in this way, you will have prepared the northern part of the terrestrial hemisphere with its margins, containing the celestial signs and the months of the year, in which every part or region of the Northern land, both according to its true longitude and latitude, and all seas of the same region and more notable rivers, must be depicted.

C A P. III.

*On the composition of the celestial wheel.*

This wheel must be adapted in such a way that its convex surface can move beneath that concave orb of the months, whose width between the convexity of that outer orb of the celestial sphere and its concavity must be the distance between the orb of the months and the convex surface of the Equinoctial line. And upon this orb or space of width, two circles are to be described, the outer of which must not exceed the capacity to receive the numbers of the days of the lunar month, so that its amplitude is not great, but narrow. Another space, moreover, must be composed in the form of the Dragon's tail and head, so that by its bipartite division, the motion of the Moon in its increase and decrease, with its quarters, can be indicated with the greatest ease. Whence half of this sphere, divided eccentrically, must be imbued with blackness; while the other entire part should be adorned with whiteness; Whence a revolving handle or knob of width, containing the Moon's orb at its extremity, will demonstrate the appropriate proportion of the Moon's own light or darkness: as will be said in its proper place. The interior parts of this celestial sphere, however, are entirely empty and transparent, so that through their clarity the terrestrial Hemisphere may be more accurately observed, except that half of the Zodiac, namely the northern part, must be delineated in it, and two diameters of this upper Hemisphere must cross at right angles, to support that celestial mechanism with the semicircle of the Zodiac. Moreover, this half of the Zodiac must be delineated in this upper Hemisphere in such a way that its divided extremities touch the Equinoctial circle, and especially the part of the Ecliptic line itself, with this respect, however, that the middle of that same part of the Ecliptic is contiguous to the Tropic of Cancer expressed in the terrestrial Hemisphere.

Therefore, for this to happen, a suitable center must be found, so that such a semicircular line with its width can be drawn around, and this in some stable part of a meridian. When this is done, this Semizodiac must be divided into six equal parts, assigning to the first part the sign of Aries, to the second Taurus, to the third Gemini, to the fourth Cancer, to the fifth Leo, to the sixth Virgo. Then each space of these signs must be divided into three equal parts, and each of those again is to be subdivided into ten equal parts. And in this way, the northern celestial Hemisphere will be completed, obtaining the second series and order in this our Cosmic instrument. It must be noted, however, that the index of this hemisphere must represent the substance of the Sun; therefore, it must be attached at the end of the diameter of darkness, so that it can, as it were, point out the degrees of the signs and the days of the months with a finger.

C A P. IV.

*On the Horary Wheel.*

Let a small wheel be made, whose radius should have a length of 20 degrees,
and let it be divided into as many parts as the hemisphere is divided by meridians,
namely into 24. And let a Diameter be drawn through every sixth hour, so that these two dia-

CHAPTER V.
*Concerning the rule, both southern and northern.*

Let a small circle be made, whose radius is 10 degrees: Then through its center let a Diameter be drawn, which ought to extend beyond the circumference of the circle, according to the distance from the center of the celestial Hemisphere to its circumference or broad surface, and in that part it ought to contain a small arc of a circle, which arc indeed ought to have the width of the sphere that is equally dark and bright: However, in the middle of this arc, along almost its entire width, directly opposite this extended Diameter, let a small circle be made, whose area ought to be hollowed out, so that the dark and bright part of the underlying orb can be seen through that circle, and this circle will represent the orb of the moon, beyond which the diameter, still further extended, will form an index, whose pointer will be the Diameter itself. Furthermore, it is to be noted here that the interior part of that rule should be divided by the parallels of the terrestrial Hemisphere, and by the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer, on whose flat surface the parallels of the Amphiscii, Heteroscii, and Periscii ought to be laid out, which are so called from the threefold reason of shadows, and similarly the differences of the hours of any part of this Hemisphere: And in this way the northern part of the Cosmographical Hemisphere will be completed.

CHAPTER VI.

*On the Southern part of the Cosmographical instrument.*

The Southern part, or the Southern Hemisphere, starting from its center, will be arranged in all its circles, both meridians and parallels, as was stated for the Northern Hemisphere: Similarly, two circles, namely the Antarctic and the Tropic of Capricorn, are to be delineated at the same distances, counting from the Equinoctial.

*Let also the description of the Southern Hemisphere be chosen, and let the regions be depicted according to the description of Petrus Plancius. And let this Hemisphere have a similar margin, or another one for variety. And let it have an hourly dial of the same kind, with a rule similar in all respects to the aforementioned northern rule, and let them be placed as will be said below.*

*At the center A. of both Hemispheres, both southern and northern, let B. be affixed, the center of the celestial machine with the semizodiac, upon which let the hourly dial be placed at center C. And above the centers of all these, let the handle, or rule, be placed at its center D. So that arc E. is an opening representing the figure of the moon, which must be made with the width of the arc corresponding to the width F. F. F. of both celestial machines, so that by turning the handle D. E. the arc, without passing the limits or margins of the orb F. F. F., may demonstrate various figures and appearances of the moon for a given time.*

As for the Hemisphere or celestial machine, its composition should be proportioned in the manner of the preceding one, except that the surface of its circumference should not be as wide as that of the Northern one, and its width from the center to its convex surface should be the distance between the center of the terrestrial Hemisphere and the convex surface of the Equinoctial circle: In all respects, however, the Semisignifer or Zodiac should be delineated, as in the preceding Northern one, and it should also be divided into six equal parts, of which Libra possesses the first part, Scorpio the second, Sagittarius the third, Capricorn the fourth, Aquarius the fifth, Pisces the sixth. The rule of the Southern Hemisphere must also be divided with similar dimensions marking the climates, as that of the Northern one; At its extremity, an image of the sun must be depicted moving in an eccentric circle, which must be expressed beneath the sun's orb on the celestial surface, so that in it the sun's apogee and its opposite can be most easily delineated: On the outer part of the sun, however, an index or finger can be formed, whose point must pass through the center of the sun, and this must be adapted to explain the contents of the outer orbs. For the outer part of the Hemisphere must be divided into six spheres or orbs, of which the outermost will denote the months with their days, and the sun's degrees in the celestial signs; The second will indicate the twilight of any day of the whole year in hours and minutes; The third, the sunrise; The fourth, the length of day and night; The fifth, the sunset; The sixth will demonstrate the evening, as appears from the preceding demonstration.

C  A  P.	VII.

*Concerning the Horizon of this instrument.*

**W**e have not attached a manifest horizon to this instrument of ours, lest its
bulk or substance render this mirror of ours more obscure. However, a
rule of very narrow width can, if it pleases, be attached and bound to its structure,
namely, so that it is very thin. But rather, to compensate for its absence,
let the Semidiameter of the rule of latitude be placed over the place in question.
Then let some wooden rule be placed transversely over the mirror or
instrument, namely so that it passes through the center like a Diameter, yet with this
condition, that the rule of latitude passing over the given place is as if orthogonally
elevated above the Horizontal rule. The rule of latitude, therefore, will denote the zenith
or meridian of the given town; but the rule incidentally attached
will demonstrate the horizon of the given place. And in this way, we can most easily
delineate the rising of Planets and stars to any given region, and their setting,
and similarly the motion of the Sun itself over the Hemisphere at any hour,
and many other things, to which experience will lead the Artist.

# BOOK THREE
## On the Use of Our Cosmographical Planisphere.

### C H A P. I.
#### *On the general practice of this our Cosmographical instrument.*

[Decorative initial P] WE could indeed with this instrument of ours satisfy many questions, pertaining as much to Astronomy as to the description of the earth, so truly that their number would almost be multiplied to infinity; But truly, indeed, we, having omitted the others, will turn our discourse only to those which are commonly better known, and more daily. And first indeed, beginning from celestial matters, we find the beginning of our discourse in the lunar region, ascending up to the sphere of the fixed stars.

### C H A P. II.
#### *On the method of investigating for how long the Moon illuminates this our Hemisphere, and consequently, when it rises and when it sets.*

FOR knowing those hours in which the Moon offers itself to our sight and illuminates the earth, the day of the moon's age must be sought in the lunar orb, expressed in the northern part of our instrument, that indeed which is found in the penultimate small orb or circle of that machine or instrument, which we have called the moon's motion: For, having found that day therein, under the same division in the outermost small orb, the hours and minutes of the moon's appearance are shown: But it must be observed in this place that the progression and order of days begins from the new moon, proceeding towards the full moon according to the natural succession of the celestial signs; the new moon, however, takes its beginning in the lunar orb from the outer point of thicker blackness, and the full moon exists in the place of broader whiteness, opposite to that point of blackness. For example, if the moon's age is the tenth day, the number 10 occurs in the penultimate small orb. From its region, we find in the outermost small orb eight hours with 0 minutes. Thus, if the moon has reached the twelfth day of its age, we find 9 hours with 36 minutes. And so in the others.
      As for the moon's rising and setting, for the sun's motion, two hours are to be assigned for its transit through any sign: However, having known the sign through which the sun passes, and having observed the moon's own age, it will be very easy, by the distance of one from the other, having observed the time of the sun's rising and setting, to also find the moon's rising and setting.

C H A P.     III.

*On the method of inquiring how much of its part the Moon exhibits to us on any day of its age.*

**L**et the day or index of the Moon be placed upon the degree of the sign in which the Sun exists on the day the question arises; Afterwards, let the pointer of the rule of latitude be turned over the number of days of the Moon's age, which having been done, through the aperture at the end of the Rule of latitude you will see the form or figure of the moon for the day of inquiry. For example, if the sun has been found in the 25th degree of Sagittarius, the index of the lunar volvelle will be turned over the 25th degree of that sign, and then, if the day of the moon's age is the seventh, you will find one half of the lunar body dark and its other half luminous.

**F**irst, it must be sought in which sign and degree of the sign the sun is found on that day when the question is proposed; which having been found, for the hour of the day, which is expressed in the small wheel next to the center of the instrument, let the Hemisphere be divided into as many hours as the sun constitutes on that same day, and with the rule of latitude placed under the hour in which the question is moved, and that sign with its degree turned under that rule, there will appear under that degree, arranged in this manner, the terrestrial region, or the sought-after place on earth.

C H A P.     VI.

**F**or the elucidation of this question, the outer part of the Southern Hemisphere must be inspected, and in the fourth orb, found in its margin, the length of each day, for the entire year, will be demonstrated; Therefore, with the pointer of the handle placed over the degree in which the sun is found at that time, the fourth orb will declare under that degree the length of the day in hours; Which having been known, it will be very easy to also deduce the length of the night.

C A P. VII.

*On the rising and setting of the sun.*

**T**he rising of the sun on any day of the year is known by means of the third orbicule, of the exterior part of the Southern Hemisphere, if indeed the finger of the sun's handle is turned upon the degree of the sign through which the sun passes on the day the question is posed; for below that, in the third orbicule, will appear the hour and minute at which the sun rises on the day the inquiry is made. Its setting, however, is most easily found once the length of the day is known.

C A P. VIII.

*On finding the twilight of any day.*

**T**he twilight of any day is sought by means of the second orbicule of the exterior part of the aforesaid Hemisphere, by turning the finger of the handle upon the degree of the Sun. For below the diameter of the handle in the second orbicule will appear the hour of twilight of that same day; the evening, or night twilight, however, is found by the length of the days.

C A P. IX.

*How it is to be investigated, over which part of the terrestrial globe
fixed stars move at any hour of the day.*

**F**irst, the Sun must be brought to its proper position in the Hemisphere for the requested hour of the day; which being done, the other celestial signs will remain in their proper places over some particular region of the earth. The place of the remaining fixed stars, however, positioned outside the zodiac, will appear in this subscribed table in longitude, always having their references or relation to the signs of the Zodiac.

**L**et the Rule of latitude be revolved over the given part of the earth or nation, and the distances in that rule measuring the latitudes of the Amphiscians, Heteroscians, and Periscians will denote the position of the proposed place under the parallels of each of the aforesaid.

C H A P.  XII.

*On finding the distances of places according to longitude and lati-*
*tude.*

**F**irst, the distance in longitude between two places, or cities, or towns, is sought in this manner. The Rule of the Semidiameter must be placed over one location, and by doing so, the part of the Semidiameter intersecting the Equinoctial will denote the true degree of longitude of that place. Again, let the Semidiameter of the Rule be turned so that it passes through the zenith of another given city or place, and let the degree on the Equinoctial that its semidiameter will intersect be observed. Afterwards, you will count the distance in degrees from one intersection to the other, and you will have the distance between these two places in degrees of longitude. To find the latitudes of two places, the Rule must be turned over one given place, and the degree of latitude of that place perpendicularly above it must be observed. Then let the same Rule be turned over another place, and let the degree above it also be marked. Afterwards, let the distance between the degree of the first and second place be observed, and the quantity of the distance of the said two places in latitude will be denoted. And this latitude is properly called the elevation of the pole for the place where it is found.

C A P. XIII.
*On the method of finding under which zone of the world any region is situated.*

It must be sought on the terrestrial part of our instrument whether the region is situated between the polar circles and the poles themselves; where, if it is found, it is situated in the frigid zone. But if between the polar circles and the Tropics, it is constituted in the temperate zone. But if between the Tropics and the Equinoctial, it is subjected to the torrid zone.

C A P. XIV.
*On the method of finding under which climate the said regions are arranged.*

Let the Rule of latitude be turned over the given place, and the part of the Rule overhanging the region will denote the number of the parallel or parallels under which that region is constituted.

### CH. I.
#### *What Astrology is in general, and how many kinds?*

[Large ornate initial A] STROLOGY, if its hidden nature were rightly and perfectly known (which indeed happens only to very few, and only by the singular benefit and gift of God), it would certainly not be held in such great hatred by almost everyone, nor would it be considered so vile by the common run of men. For the operation of this science is so certain, and so truly concerned with what, or with its object, as it is undoubted that the stars themselves constantly move, and complete their motions by infallible revolutions for a determined end, ordained by the Creator himself. Therefore, the science itself is not to be condemned per se, but rather those ignorant ones, who, engaged in it through their own ignorance, cause that just and

# CHAP. II.

**S**ome astrologers divide this art into six parts, the first of which they call introductory, which indeed deals with its principles, namely concerning the signs of the zodiac, and other fixed stars and the natures of the Planets, about which more extensively in the second book of this work: The second treats of great revolutions, which consider conjunctions and Eclipses: The third denotes the nativities of individuals: The fourth treats of interrogations: The fifth deals with elections, and the sixth teaches the making and operation of images. Others distinguish it into 4 parts, the first of which deals with Crisis and the causes of diseases, about which in our second Volume: The second is occupied with the questions of the Arabs: The third considers elections: The last denotes the changes of the elements: We, however, have more correctly, as it seems to us, gathered all these aforesaid parts into the following distinction.

*to partake of both, namely of the supercelestial nature, and of that sublunary, since it is*
*of the nature of the middle heaven.*

If, therefore, say the Platonists, the Spirit adheres to the mind and flees the pleasures of the flesh, it is beatified and exalted above the celestial nature from which it had its origin, receiving only the good actions of the stars, but sagaciously avoiding the bad ones; and in this way, that prepared Spirit by no means obeys all the actions of the heavens. But when that Spirit, refusing the rays of the mind, adheres to the other extremity, it suddenly turns from a good Daemon into an evil Daemon, and then becomes capable of all celestial actions, and especially evil ones due to the body's proneness to wickedness, because the body and its chief, namely the sensitive soul, inasmuch as they depend on the elements as perpetual receptacles of celestial influences and are most opposed to the mind, are by themselves apt and disposed to choose and eagerly seize all the worst gifts of the heavens, namely voluptuous, wrathful, sad, deadly and cruel, drunken, sluggish, impudent, lustful, and concupiscence-filled influences, along with the reckless affection for every other vice; just as, conversely, the good Spirit of man chooses from the better influences of heaven, by which it renders him desirous of praise, and warlike or strenuous in honest and lawful matters, for example, for the sake of religion, and makes him just and pious, amiable, studious, liberal, and endowed with other virtues from birth, concerning which we will discuss more fully in our second Volume, where we will treat of nativities. We say, therefore, that all these things happen according to God's ordination, and are necessarily carried out by the stars as His ministers, which some philosophers have not inaptly called *fingers of nature*, inasmuch as without them, nature does nothing or operates nothing in these lower regions. But because the human mind is, as it were, a living ray of God Himself, therefore the celestial ministers can no more act upon it than upon the Ordainer Himself, namely God; and consequently, the mind must always be considered immune from all worldly influence or change, and subject to no passion, that is, always acting towards goodness, never suffering the invasions of evil ones; But its vehicle, the Spirit, is sometimes deceived by carnal and worldly allurements, and with the flesh sometimes receives the impressions of evil celestial affections along with the good ones, when indeed the mind is either entirely idle or operates only a little. And hence it is that even the worst men sometimes produce good fruits contrary to their natures, become rich, and are successful in war or other worldly affairs, scarcely, or indeed hardly at all, even with the divine mind assisting. Similarly, an inconstant Spirit, sometimes adhering to this, and sometimes to the other extremity, is sometimes good and pious, neglecting the flesh and the world, sometimes wicked, and prone to all vices. Hence also it is that the Spirits of some men, carnally affected and disobedient to the mind, love slaughter, and engage in robberies; nay, they are even more prompt and eager to commit such evils at one time than at another; for the more powerful Martial stars in the sky arouse a thief, more or less Martial by birth, according to their position and aspect with other stars: This is also what other celestial significators perform according to their agreement with the Lord of the house
