the spirit when the mind is inactive, since those (influences) act upon bodies just as bodies act upon the Spirit itself. From these things, therefore, it is undoubted that, if certain knowledge could be had concerning the virtues of the stars and their mutual operation and qualities in any conjunction or aspect, it would not be difficult, according to the nature of the signifying star combined with the natures of the place in which it is found, and the aspect of other Planets observing it, to boldly pronounce concerning one's stature, bodily disposition, and inclination of the spirit, and to infallibly indicate concerning it, that, with the mind ceasing (to act), which never consents to evil actions, the stars impose upon it the necessity of sinning.
      As for the prognostication of storms and the change of air, it is beyond all controversy that all this lower matter, and every part of it, tends either to generation, or corruption, or to alteration and any other change whatsoever, by the virtue of the inflowing celestial soul, as we have clearly demonstrated in the first treatise of this work. Hence it follows, if a stronger celestial disposition is prone to humidity, that these lower things also receive its nature; if to heat, the elemental things are perceived to be hotter; if to cold, colder; and if more prone to the agitation of winds, then winds and gusts are stirred up in these lower regions, and that indeed by a certain natural necessity, according to the natural position, power, and predominance of the celestial ministers, concerning the truth of which matter even beasts, and indeed inanimate things themselves, offer us ocular testimony, while annual experience teaches us that the parts of the year and the dispositions of vegetables, and all changes, follow the movement of the sun, and that with its approach all things grow green and the air grows warm. Similarly, under the increase of the Moon, waters swell, and all bodies, by an invisible succession, become more and more moist and are filled with humors; and with Saturn reigning in his own house, namely in Capricorn, and inviting the other planets to himself as if to a feast (which happened around the year 1608), frost and most intense cold reign in these elemental parts, and so in other cases.
      We conclude therefore that the heaven has such great virtue and efficacy upon these lower things, and operates with such certain effect, that not undeservedly from this Mercury Trismegistus, in the second chapter of his book, which he names Asclepius, calls heaven a sensible GOD, that is, performing the same thing sensibly and executively, which the intellectual God performs dispositively and by ordination. Hence he also calls it in the same place the administrator of all bodies, whose increases and decreases the Sun and Moon have obtained, and calls it GOD, the governor and effector of all things that are in the world.

C A P. IV.

On the cause of false predictions among almost all Astrologers.

Since in the practice of this science very many errors are committed, by which the practitioner not only deceives himself, but also deceives those consulting him through his false resolutions, it happens from this that some assert Astrology is not a science (since it ought to be founded on certain and true demonstrations), but a frivolous art full of sophistry. To which, so that I may briefly respond, it must be known, not in

--- Page 476 ---
DE ASTROLOGY'S KINDS. 565
that there is any fault in the science itself, but much in the Professor, inasmuch as he, understanding nothing or very little indeed, nevertheless attempts anything. For this age of ours has seen only very few, and perhaps even none, exactly skilled in this science, while in the meantime, nevertheless, *Spurious Professors* are found everywhere in a sufficiently large number, and utterly ignorant in this art, and very far removed from its core, who promise much, and perform little or nothing. The reason for this is that this art is cabalistic, first revealed to the more ancient Jews and Egyptians, from which they drew marvelous things in the divination of future events and the revelation of past ones; as is more broadly declared in Josephus in his history of the Jews, where he teaches that this science, originally discovered by Adam himself, successively flowed to others, which, without doubt, if rightly and perfectly understood, is as certain in its operations as the very motion of the heavens and planetary aspects is certain, and their determined time down to the minutes. However, the ancient wise men concealed the core of this science, so that they might blind the foolish and unworthy, no differently than Philosophers, most skilled in inferior Astronomy, namely, experts in the preparation of the Philosopher's Stone. For just as *Hermes* and the other *Chemical Philosophers* treat the Philosopher's Stone parabolically, allegorically, and sophistically, while one often seems to contradict another, one saying "take this," and another strongly dissuading that, and shouting "take that"; and in this way they deceive students: so also is the situation in this present art, inasmuch as various Astrologers have written various things about its secrets too, so that one seems to contradict another entirely in this study, and in this way, by the uncertainty of the doctrine, they deceive the curious, and compel Artists for the most part to give fallacious and false answers. This, therefore, is the most certain reason for the uncertainty in that science, by which it is indeed uncertain, but relatively, that is, with respect to persons who conceive and treat it not absolutely, and as it is in its nature, but badly. For beyond all doubt, the effects of the stars on these lower things are as certain as it is certain that GOD has ordained all things that occur in this lower world, not only in simple elements, but also in the composite things themselves, both animate and inanimate. Nor is it to be believed that the Devil himself knew future and past events by any other knowledge (since, as scripture testifies, *he partakes nothing of the secrets of the mind*) except insofar as he learned all events from the motion of the stars, as if he had seen them written in golden letters in the ethereal fields. And he (the Devil) is indeed believed to be the most practiced among all Astrologers of the whole world, inasmuch as he has long applied himself to this science, and from the beginning of the world has observed the operations of the stars, through which he constantly perceives the will of GOD in natural things, no differently than a servant hearing the words and voice of his Master understands from their sound what he himself wants, and what his intention is in any matter. But concerning the secret mysteries of GOD, he understands no more, nor concerning His metaphysical operation, than a servant knows his Master's imagination before he declares his intention in words.

From these things, therefore, it is clear that the certainty of this science is supreme (since it is the most sublime among all others, and closest to the Creator Himself), but the truth in the Artists of this age is minimal, because, namely, the truth of this science is hidden under fictitious veils and concealed in the darkness of contradictory words. But I, having left aside the diversities and various ways of the *Egyptians, Jews, Arabs or Chaldeans and Babylonians*, have followed them only at that point where I perceived them to agree most. And although this path of ours is far removed from a true and complete knowledge of the art, nevertheless, because we have experienced that true divinations have for the most part resulted from this kind of operation, therefore we will speak briefly only of it, omitting the ambiguous curiosities of the ancient Sages.

C  A  P.     V.

*Concerning those who forbid the profession of Astrology to men.*

VERY many are found, but very unskilled in this science, and submerged in the darkness
of shadows, nor conceiving anything with the mind beyond sensible things,
who wish that this science, since it is about the ministers of God himself, should not be
practiced, indeed that it is wrong to seek such high things, and to inquire so anxiously and
scrupulously into the secrets of the Creator himself. Others indeed, as has already been said,
are found who assert that Astrology is either no science at all, or at least a frivolous one,
as being in no way certain. And to these latter, indeed, satisfaction has been given, I believe,
in the preceding chapter; But concerning the former, I would wish that they, regarding their
hesitation, diligently read our letter prefixed at the beginning of this Volume, and that
they then consider within themselves whether it is more fitting for a brute than for a man
adorned with the gift of mind to think such things, and to value a thing so noble, such as
man, so cheaply, and to judge so abjectly of it, that his mind, infused into him by the
Creator himself, so that through it he might communicate with Him, and without which
man cannot even be beatified, cannot ascend to heaven by the same steps of speculation
and contemplation by which it descended from heaven into the human body.
      Let us hear, I pray, *Trismegistus'* opinion on this matter, who in the *first discourse of Pimander*
speaks concerning man's wisdom to be understood in Astrology, in these words: *When man
had power over all things in himself, he observed the works of the seven governors: and these,
rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a participant of their own order,
who, after he learned their essence and perceived their own nature, now desired to penetrate
and break through the circuit of the circles, and to comprehend the power of the governor
presiding over fire.* These words of *Trismegistus* are indeed divine, exalting the human
mind to the pinnacle of excellence, inasmuch as by its nobility he teaches man not only
to know the certain essences of the stars and consequently to learn their effects in
Astrological science, but also to contemplate metaphysical actions (and that indeed by
divine permission): Whence also in the same discourse, the same *Trismegistus* speaks thus:
*GOD, creating man in His own image, truly greatly delighted in His own form, and granted
all His works for human use.* It is certain, therefore, that the human mind, being so noble
and divine, naturally tends in every way to the high and sublime, indeed even to GOD Himself,
as a true ray and spark of divine light, and that in these lower things, to which it is unwillingly
committed, and into which it is transported by its vehicle, the Spirit, and as it were delivered,
it is enclosed as in an opaque prison, and restricted and confined from its natural liberty,
and thus contained in a region entirely contrary to its disposition: For just as mind and body
are two extremes in their natural position, so also are their dispositions more contrary to
each other than is the disposition of heat to cold, or humidity to dryness.
      Therefore, we think it not unfitting to conclude that it is not impossible for human
understanding to know the essences and dispositions of the stars and their governors,
nor does this happen against the divine will, since the human mind itself is permitted
to penetrate deeper and to converse with God Himself through divine contemplation,
but the density and darkness of bodies blinds the soul and removes its judgment, no
differently than a cloth drawn over the eyes takes away from them the certainty and
figure of a visible object. Thus, therefore, the first knowledge of the stars was declared
to the human race by revelation, and thereafter continued by Cabalistic tradition.

**BOOK SECOND**
Of signs.

**CHAP. I.**
*Of the zodiac & its parts.*

[Decorative initial S] IT MUST FIRST BE KNOWN that the Zodiac is that unique circle having lati-
tude and obliquity, which divides the roundness of the visible Macrocosm
into two equal parts. Astronomers found its latitude to be 12 degrees,
and to have the same longitude as that Equinoctial circle, namely 360 degrees, inasmuch as it indeed
cuts the entire globe into two equal parts. Hence therefore it is, namely on account of its longi-
tude and latitude, that it is called the zone or girdle of the sky. However, the wise
divided this circle into 12 equal parts, each of which consists of 30 degrees.
And these portions they indeed called *signs*; but the circle itself they named
*signifer* (sign-bearer) from them, as if bearing 12 signs.
A *celestial sign* is taken either for a place attributed to any of the 12 zodiacal signs,
and is taken either for a part of the zodiac consisting of only 30 degrees of longitude and 12 degrees of lati-
tude, and proper to that sign, or for a part of the zodiac containing 30 degrees of longi-
tude with the entire latitude of the world, that is, proportionally
or pyramidally extended from those 30 degrees of longitude (which dimension will occupy the place of both the northern
and southern base) to the very poles of the zodiac.
Or it is taken for a congregation of fixed stars, representing the figure or image
of those things which gave names to the celestial signs found in the zodiac.
Thus *Aries* is so called, because the stars gathered in that place of the zodiac
constitute the form and image of a ram, and so in the others.

**ON THE SIGNS OF THE ZODIAC. 569**

This sign is called Northern, because from the Equator it inclines towards that part of the sky.
It is said to ascend or rise obliquely, because with it the middle part of the Equator does not ascend, for a greater arc of the Zodiac rises than of the Equator.

**Rule I.**
The lower six signs ascending obliquely obey the upper signs ascending directly and opposite to them: Thus Cancer (♋) ascending directly has reverence from Capricorn (♑), its opposite sign ascending obliquely: Leo (♌) also from Aquarius (♒) and Virgo (♍) from Pisces (♓), and so in the others.
Aries is called Oriental by its Triplicity and Cardinal, because according to the natural position of the heavens it claims the Eastern angle for itself: For when the Sun began the first day from its creation, it was found in the beginning of Aries: Whence, with the Sun rising on that day, the dimension of Aries undoubtedly possessed that cardinal point of the heavens. However, four cardinal signs are enumerated, namely Aries (♈), Cancer (♋), Libra (♎), Capricorn (♑).
It is also called Vernal, because from its body the Sun pours down upon these lower regions the spring season, and its equal temperature.
They call it Masculine, because even women born under it are imbued with virile strength.
We also call it Diurnal, because it gives beauty to the native or the signified, and makes him brighter.
Finally, it is called Movable, because it makes the native movable and variable.

     Planets are said to have dignity when, in certain places of the Zodiac, they acquire greater strengths and powers than in others: and indeed, when they enjoy these dignities, they are said to be stronger, which happens because the nature of such a Planet is more congruent with the nature of those stars, and a mutual affinity of their natures occurs: And hence it is that they were called essential dignities by the ancients, of which five principal species are enumerated by Astrologers, namely House, Exaltation, Triplicity, Term, and Face. House is called a sign with which a Planet more fully agrees in the completeness of its qualities, and it is so called because, when a Planet exists in it, it behaves as a man in his own house: And in this way also Aries (♈) is called the house of Mars (♂).

                                   Rule II.

     A Planet possesses five dignities of a house, and it is a more principal place than other dignities, more suitable to the nature and essence of the Planet.

          It is to be noted that *dark* degrees, as well as *Puteal* degrees, affect with misfortune: but *bright* (degrees affect) with fortune; *empty* (degrees), however, are mediocre between good and evil. But *fortune-increasing* degrees are those in which fixed stars assume the natures of fortunate Planets, or occupy the place of elevation of good (things/planets), namely, where they have some dignity.
          *Masculine* degrees are so called for this reason, because they make a masculine Planet existing in them stronger, and so also feminine degrees by the same reason affect feminine Planets according to their nature.
          *Azemena* degrees are degrees of bodily weakness: For *Azemena* is some bodily weakness, such as deafness, blindness, weakness of limbs, and other things of that kind, to which man is subject in this life.
          Therefore, when at the time of birth the Moon is found in any of these degrees, some of these defects befall the native. So if Planets are in bright degrees, they will be stronger in the signification of good things, because these degrees signify beauty, light, fortune; If in dark (degrees), they denote harshness, slowness, and horror, and a dark and evil thing; If in smoky and empty degrees, they signify a thing not a little horrible; if in Puteal degrees, the beauty and appearance of the native will be weakened; if in fortune-increasing degrees, the native's fortune will be greater and he will rule lands, and acquire many riches.
          Note that *Azamen* is the same as incurable, and *Puteus* (well) is the same as wateriness. Hence, wherever a well is found, it signifies rainy air, and if it concerns a man, dropsy.
          A *Planet's exaltation* is a place of the zodiac or a degree of the same sign, in which its power is elevated by a certain natural sublimation. However, the 19th degree of Aries is called the exaltation of the Sun, because the Sun existing there begins to incline towards the north, and to give increase to the days.

                                        *Rule I.*

     *Wherever in the zodiac any Planet is exalted, there in the opposite place of the same zodiac it will find its depression or detriment; as the Sun is exalted in 19 ♈. and depressed in 19. ♎. because there is the elevation of Saturn, who is an enemy to life and the Sun. Similarly, where any of the Planets is depressed, there in its opposite it is exalted.*

          It is to be noted that a Planet, when it is in its exaltation, behaves itself as a man in his kingdom, just as if it exists in its own house it conducts itself as a man in his own house, and if in a Triplicity, as a man in his honor among helpers, as has been said.

                                        *Rule II.*

     *Exaltation claims for itself four dignities, as a house (claims) five, as has been said.*
*Terms or bounds are peculiar parts of the signs and the zodiac, which in each sign for certain reasons are distributed to five Planets, namely, ♄. ♃. ♂. ♀. & ☿.*

                                        *Rule III.*

     *It is to be noted that the two luminaries lack bounds (terms), and in their place usurp two halves of the zodiac, each beginning, of course, from its own house. Thus the Sun takes its beginning in Aries, and ends at the end of Capricorn.*

Rule IV.

Just as a house claims five, Exaltation four, and Triplicity three essential dignities for itself, so a Term retains two.
Moreover, just as it has been said in the preceding (sections) that a Planet behaves in its house as a man behaves in his own dwelling, but in its exaltation as a man in his kingdom, and in its Triplicity as a man in his honor, so also we assert that it, existing in its Term, is aptly compared to a man remaining among his parents and relatives.
For each of the signs, three Decans are counted, namely, the 30 degrees being divided into three equal portions. And each portion will be a face, of which the first portion, consisting of the first ten degrees, is called the First face, the second portion the second face, and the last portion the third face, as appears in the superior distinction.

Generally, it is to be noted here that fixed stars constituting the bodies of celestial animals are not confined to their own intervals, and places or houses, but a part of the body of each sign is contained in its own proper seat, and its remaining members are contained in the place of another sign next to it. Thus a smaller part of Aries is found in the posterior part of the longitude attributed to it, namely towards the end of the 30 degrees measuring its house, that is, its leg, the right horn & half of the neck with a portion of the same head. But its remaining parts extend into the dominion of Taurus, and seem to occupy almost 21 degrees of that longitude.

From the form of each sign, it is easy to know the powers of the individual ones, especially insofar as they can or should be considered in judgments: See the second section of this chapter: Similarly, fixed stars, besides the signs, also have their own signs and figures; Whence, says Ptolemy, appellations are derived from the figures of the constellations, namely terrestrial quadrupeds, etc.

                            Rule II.

    It must be noted that, when the nature of a fixed star is known with the degree found in the cusp, namely, that it is of a simple, or double, or triple Planet, it is necessary to make natural mixtures according to the diversity of natures, as we find that the preceding horn of Aries (♈) participates in the nature of Mars (♂) and Saturn (♄). Therefore, we mix the temperament of Mars with the temperament of Saturn, and in this way, for the matter at hand, we make a description, according to the greater number of testimonies: If its nature is that of a simple Planet, then the nature of the Planet is adapted to it, as its own.


                            Rule III.

    If anyone wishes to know better and more accurately the natures and properties of these celestial images, let him read their fabulous histories.

DE SIGNIS ZODIACI. 581
Therefore, from this, this sign is called *Northern*, as was stated in the first section of the second chapter, in which same section reasons were also given why it is called *obliquely* ascending, why *vernal*, and similarly also words were spoken concerning its *bestial* figure.

It is called *Feminine*, because it effeminates a man and renders him weaker.

It is also called *Nocturnal*, because it confers a more deformed, blacker, and darker face.

We have said why it is called *Tortuous* in chapter 1 of the preceding section and in the immediately preceding table. What *dignity* is, however, was declared in the second section of the preceding chapter, where we similarly discussed the use and power of *house* and *Triplicity*.

As for the *joy of the Planet*, it is to be understood that a Planet possessing two houses has one more familiar than the other, and this Astrologers call *Joy*, because in it the Planet rejoices.

disposition {

			CHAPTER IX.

			On Scorpio.

		SECTION I.

SECTION III.
*Concerning the fixed stars found both in the figure of Scorpio, as well as in its*
*mansion and house.*

The smaller part of the body of Scorpio, namely its posterior part, is found in the house
or interval of Sagittarius; indeed, it extends up to the twenty-fifth
degree of that sign. Its anterior part, however, is found in its own proper place and interval,
with its anterior feet extending to both claws of Libra;
so that the anterior part of Scorpio possesses 23 degrees of its own proper place, and its posterior part
25. Its entire body, however, almost entirely inclines towards the South, except for its
anterior feet, which tend towards the North.

# BOOK THREE
## Of the dispositions &
## natures of the Planets

### C H A P. I.
#### Of planets in general.

[Decorative Initial D]E have spoken above in Treatise 1, Book 5, concerning the composition of the Planets and the reason for that composition; where we declared with the ancient Philosophers that the Sun, standing in the middle or in its ethereal throne, and governing like a king crowned with a shining diadem, gave forms to the other Planetary bodies with its countenance, and that their bodies were formed from the denser matter of the ethereal heaven. We also said in that place that the reason for coldness and humidity in the Moon is this: that the denser part of the aether, by the presence of the Sun exalted into the middle, driven by rarefaction towards its lower limits, becomes colder there, both because of its removal from the ethereal lamp and because of the proximity of elemental fire, inasmuch as that coldness is strengthened by Antiperistasis; but that the Moon is humid because of its proximity to the sphere of elemental humidity, since fire occupies its summit. We also taught that Mercury participates in the nature of the Moon and Venus, and Venus participates in the nature of the Sun (☉) and Mercury (☿). Similarly, we indicated that the cause of coldness and dryness in Saturn is the proximity of its body's substance to the crystalline sphere, and its greater distance from the Sun. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the body of Jupiter is composed of Saturnine cold and solar heat; but that of Mars from the temperament of Saturn, Jupiter, and the Sun, so that it obtains two portions of the fire's heat, and one part of dryness from the Sun, and the other from Saturn. Finally, in the third book of our aforementioned first Treatise, we deduced with sufficiently clear reasoning the goodness and wickedness of the said Planets. It remains therefore at present that we speak in this place of the practical natures of the Planets, namely of those things which contribute to astrological judgment. Wherefore it must be known first of all

the presence of the Planet with some signs of the Zodiac also accomplishes the same;
whence it finds either an exalted nature, or one received in its own house, or its

because of its participation with an alien nature, as will appear in this place.

DE PLANET. DISPOS. E TNATUR.    631

A planet is said to be in Cazimi, that is, in the heart of the sun, when its longitude does not differ from the sun by more than 16 minutes, and then the planet is said to be united with the Sun, that is, to be in the heart of the Sun, and at that time it has the greatest strength and power.

But when any of the planets is more than 16 minutes distant from the Sun, that is, as long as it is covered by the orb and rays of the Sun, so that it does not present itself to our eyes, it is said to be combust; And this kind of combustion occurs until, receding from the Sun's conjunction, it is removed by 15 degrees from it.

But when it is within 12 degrees, then it is especially said to be combust, hidden, and oppressed, except in that case where it is in Cazimi, as we said above.

Planets are called Oriental when they rise at night before the Sun, and set at night after it.

Rule I.

It must be noted, however, that the three superior planets, namely Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars, are Oriental from their conjunction with the Sun (☉—) until their opposition with the Sun (☉—☉): And conversely, they are Occidental from their opposition with the Sun (☉—☉) until their conjunction with the Sun (☉—). But the two inferior planets, such as Venus (♀) and Mercury (☿), are said to be Oriental when they precede the Sun in the morning, that is, when they are seen above the earth before sunrise; And Occidental, when they follow the sun in the evening, that is, when they are seen above the earth after sunset. Finally, the Moon is called Occidental from the new moon to the full moon, because it appears above the earth after sunset: But from the full moon to the new moon, Oriental, because it is seen above the earth before sunrise.

Rule II.

Orientality in the three superior planets gives strength, but occidentality in the two inferior ones, and likewise occidentality in the Moon (☾), that is, when the Moon (☾) is increasing in light.

An Aspect is when two planets communicate maximum power to each other through intervals in the zodiac.

 talis □. This aspect is moderately bad, because two signs distant by such an interval are at odds in sex and nature.
    Opposition is so called because it is a diametrical and opposite aspect. It therefore comprehends half of the zodiacal circle, that is, 6 signs, namely 180 degrees. And its character is of this kind o—o. This aspect is exceedingly bad, not indeed because of the conflict of natures in the signs, but rather by reason of the opposition; for those things which are opposite and most distant from each other, these are most contrary to each other and in every single kind.

From this example, therefore, it is clear how the dexter aspect passes contrary to the succession of the signs, and how the sinister [aspect] passes according to their succession.

Rule VI.

If a dexter radiation occurs to the angles of the sky, then the dexter radiation is stronger than the sinister, for the stars are carried not by their own motion but by the motion of the firmament: But indeed if a relation is made to other stars, then the sinister [aspect] is to be preferred to the dexter, because the stars approach not by an alien, but by their own motion.

Rule VII.

It must also be known that an aspect is divided in yet another way, for one is called Platic, namely when the signs themselves aspect each other, another is called Partile, when from star to star so many parts of the sky are counted as constitute that configuration.

Rule VIII.

Every aspect, however, occurs through the application of the Planet's rays through the middle of the semidiameter of their orbits, or when it adheres to another by six degrees or half the rays of the aspecting planet: However, the orbits of the Planets are varied and diverse, of which some are larger, and others shorter.

Separation, however, is said (to occur) when one Planet leaves another by one degree from a true aspect, and it is always said to be separated until it has escaped the rays of the other.

Rule IX.

Inferior (planets) apply to superior (planets), and are separated from them, but superior (planets) never apply to inferior (planets), nor are they separated from them, since they are slower and heavier in motion than them.
Northernness or the ascent of a Planet is said (to occur) when its latitude from the Ecliptic is Northern, for then it is said to be ascending: Southern, however, is called descending, when its latitude from the Ecliptic is Southern.
A Planet is called direct when it is carried according to the succession of the signs in the direct revolution of its Epicycle, and its motion increases: Retrograde, however, is called when it is carried against the consequence of the signs by the retro-revolution of its Epicycle, and its diurnal motion decreases: Stationary, however, is called when its motion neither increases nor decreases, but remains the same: The station of a Planet is either the first, namely after it begins to retrograde, that is, in the descent of the Planet, or the second, from which the Planet usually moves immediately, that is, in its ascent, and the stations of the Planet are so called, not because they stand still, but because they appear to stand still.
Note, that the Sun does not retrograde, because it does not have an Epicycle. Retrogradation, however, is not observed in the Moon due to its swift motion.
The Moon is said to be slow only in the upper part of its Epicycle, and swift in the lower part.

[Diagram showing an epicycle moving along a deferent circle. Labels include "Direct motion." at the top of the epicycle, "First station" and "Second station" at the sides, and "Retrograde motion." at the bottom. Planetary symbols for the Moon (☾) are shown at the top and bottom of the epicycle.]

Planets

--- Page 546 ---
DE PLANETARY DISPOSITIONS AND NATURES. 635

The point of a planet's orbit carrying its Epicycle furthest from the earth is called *Apogee*: But the point of it most closely approaching the center of the earth, opposite the *Apogee*, is called *Perigee*.
The Sun's *Apogee* is found in Cancer (♋): The opposite of its *Apogee* is in Capricorn (♑).
It must be noted that the Sun and Moon are always *direct* Planets.
A Planet is said to be *swift in motion* when it is carried according to the succession of the signs, and its true motion is swifter than its mean motion: Conversely, its motion is *slow* when it proceeds retrogradely, or when it proceeds more slowly than its mean motion: Finally, a Planet's motion is said to be *equal* when its true and mean motions are equalized.

*Rule X.*

*The strengths of diurnal Planets are increased when they exist above the earth during the daytime, and then the Planet is said to be in its* Hayz: *However, they are diminished if they are found below the earth during the daytime: Conversely, the strengths of nocturnal Planets are increased when they exist below the earth during the daytime, and they are diminished when they pass above the earth during the said time.*

*Rule XI.*

*It must be noted that some regions of the earth are masculine, namely the East and North, while the other two are feminine, namely the West and South: Therefore, masculine Planets are stronger in masculine regions, and weaker in feminine ones; while feminine Planets are stronger in feminine regions, and weaker in masculine ones.*

CHAPTER II. SECTION II. PART IV.

*On the more essential debilities of Planets.*

A Planet's debility is a diminution and weakening of its degrees of strength: Thus, just as in the strength of Planets there is an augmentation of their powers, so in their debility there is a decrease of the same.

The *Fall* of a Planet is a direct place, opposite to its exaltation: Thus, Saturn's exaltation is in the 21st degree of Libra (♎). According to Ptolemy, a certain Planet is attributed to each region of the world, according to the following distinction.

[Marginal note:]
For according to
him.

*   ♄ (Saturn). Has the East, because, since that part of the day is hot by nature, that heat is in a certain way brought to temperateness by the coldness of Saturn.
*   ♃ (Jupiter). Rules the North, from which direction he stirs fertile winds.
*   ♂ (Mars). Has the West and the North, from which directions he excites winds, because he is very similar to the Sun, and has a house in the Trigon.
*   ♀ (Venus). Governs the South, because she is a humid star.

Rule I.

According to PTOLEMY, the two luminaries are first excepted from that distribution, because they are the general origin of winds and atmospheric change; then Mercury, because he is perpetually present with and serves the luminaries.
However, there are others who also attribute a distinct region in the world to the luminaries: Hence they distribute the dominions of the Planets in the regions of the world as follows.

[Marginal note:]
They make, namely, from
the Planets.

    *   the Moon.

    *   similarly in other cases.

Rule II.

These hours always begin from the Sun's rising, which is the first Planetary hour of the day, and the 13th hour begins from the moment of the Sun's setting: Therefore, when the day is shorter, it will have a shorter hour, and conversely, the same reasoning will apply to the nights.

--- Page 550 ---
DE PLANET. DISPOS. ET NATUR. 637

These hours are called Temporal, Unequal, [and] Planetary, because just as in the course of the
year the day is longer or shorter, so also the hour is longer or shorter.
      Unequal [hours] also change for the same reason, according to more or less. For where
nights and days are equal, there also the hours of nights and days
are always equal, which happens at the Equinoxes, but where days are unequal, there the
contrary occurs.
                                Regula III.
      It is also to be noted that every natural day is divided into 4 parts, beginning three hours before
sunrise, and in each of its quarters a peculiar humor holds dominion.
Thus, from the beginning of three hours before the rising of the Sun (☉) to the end of three hours after
its rising, Blood dominates. But from the third hour after Sunrise to the 9th, Choler
predominates; and from the 9th to the 16th, Melancholy; and from the 16th to the 22nd, Phlegm. Therefore, each
Planet has the first hour of the day, to which it gives its name; But note that on its own day,
and in its own hour, it obtains a doubled virtue.

SECTION I.
On Jupiter's complete disposition.

JUPITER is composed of equal parts of coldness and warmth. Whence
he is also humid, since humidity arises from the actions of the warm upon the cold,
as was stated in the first treatise. But truly, because there are two testimonies of warmth,
namely of the Sun and Mars, to that one of Saturn's coldness, therefore he is called warm and
humid. His character (symbol) is such ♃.

C A P. IV.
Of Mars.

S E C T I O N I.
*Of the complete disposition of Mars.*

MARS is a Planet composed of the fiery nature of the *Sun*, and of heat less natural due to the antiperistasis of the watery heaven and the grosser part of the ether, driven into the highest part of the middle heaven by the presence of the Sun, in conflict with the solar body, no differently than the element of fire is born from the conflict of dark vapor rising from chaos with the splendid disposition of the ethereal heaven, as was said above: Hence *Mars* has two testimonies of accidental heat, and as many accepted from the nature of the Sun because of its proximity. By reason of its accidental heat, it is thus malicious and destructive in its nature; however, by its generative property, it regards certain things because of the heat received from the Sun, yet in such a way that they partake of its fiery and destructive nature, although that nature is better the more it is mixed with the rays of the more fortunate [planets]. Hence the origin of bile and bilious people. Thus we perceive iron to be produced from overly burnt and sulfurous material, and so also in many other things: This Planet, however, is more dry than humid, both because of its participation with the nature of Saturn, and also because it is closer to the Sun, whose nature tends towards dryness, and especially tending upwards towards the crystalline heaven. The character of this Planet is thus ♂.

Mars is considered either

1. In its celestial disposition, in which two things are to be noted, namely: its.

   * Nature
     * Proper, and that either
       * Elemental, with respect to which it is said to be
         - Immoderately hot and dry.
         - Nocturnal.
         - Masculine.
         - Western.
         - Friend of the Sun.
         - Enemy of Jupiter.
       * Mobile, by which it completes its natural course in two years.
     * Acquired, concerning which sections 2 & 3 of this [chapter].

   * Density of body, which according to some is 26,308,800 miles.

2. Insofar as it regards lower things, or

   * Generally
     - Malevolent and malicious to the life of creatures.
     - The lesser infortune, that is, not as malevolent to life as Saturn, because of the proximity of the solar body to it.

   * Specifically, concerning which we will treat in the third section of this [chapter].

Why *Mars* is called *Western* was declared in the chapter on *Saturn*.

                    CHAPTER V.

                    On the Sun.

                SECTION I.

            On the complete disposition of the Sun.

THE SUN, contrary to what some who ascribe dryness to it state, will evidently appear to be hot, and more subtly humid, if we have considered its complete and exact composition more diligently; for we have proven by an almost infallible demonstration, that by the intersection of a double pyramid, namely formal and material, that solar mass from equal parts of matter
                                Nunn 3              spir-

--- Page 565 ---
654          TREATISE II. PART X. BOOK III.

composed of spiritual and light portions; Whence we have also called its orb a sphere of equality: But because formal light is an agent, and is manifestly perceived in its action, therefore its quality, namely heat, is said to have dominion in its body, which, entering into the composition of generated things with its luminous substance, is called the innate heat of the living: But because this thing is so formal that it cannot move in a body without a vehicle, therefore this ray of the sun is also present here, in a drop of the spiritual mass of solar substance, which indeed is that very familiar and most friendly humor to the life of animals and plants, and is called the radical humor of life. Hence therefore is the generative power of the Sun, hence its multiplicative virtue and life, consisting not of any dry thing, as that which is entirely contrary to it, but of a humor tempered by such a heat, which beyond the appetite of the solar matter has blessed it with beauty, and effectively acts upon these lower things, and by its actions is accustomed to excite accidental heats, both by reflections, and by reverberations, and finally also by the resistance of dark and less formed matter, by which adventitious actions of heat the Sun is judged to be hot and dry: Its character, moreover, is such ☉.

C H A P. VIII.

On the Moon.

S E C T I O N I.

*On the complete nature of the Moon.*

The Moon is the lowest Planet, formed from the most humid and densest part of the entire ethereal heaven, which received its bright soul from the Sun through Mercury in its first composition. This Planet, because of its extreme rawness and humidity, from which it is also called the mistress of humors, is very undigested, and constantly requires the solar form for its stronger efficacy and fuller perfection: Hence, in its opposition with the Sun, when namely its entire body is illuminated, and similarly also when it is conjoined with the Sun itself, it pours its greatest effects into these lower regions: Hence therefore the splendid disposition of the Sun is to it, as if adventitious, by whose presence it is, as it were, agitated, so that the disposition of that raw matter descends into these lower regions for palpable and manifest things because of its humid nature. And its character is thus ☽.

**C H A P. IX.**

**General Rules of all Planets.**

**Rule. I.**

All the aforesaid Planets signify that disposition of form which we have subjected to each of them in the premises, if they are well disposed. But if they are badly disposed, they lose from their form according to the proportion of their misfortune, and especially in those limbs which are specifically denoted by them, as well as in those which are assigned to the sign in which they are found.

**Rule II. °**

One must diligently observe whether the principal significators are in lucid, smoky, or dark degrees. For lucid degrees greatly aid the beauty and clarity of the face. Smoky degrees make it incline towards darkness and a brown or dusky color. Dark degrees, however, make it dark, deformed, and not dissimilar to the appearances of brutes.

**Rule III.**

When the significators are matutinal, they make bodies large, because they grow.

**Rule IV.**

If the significators are retrograde, they will bring deformity to the body, and there will be no proportion or harmony in it.

*Rule VI.*

C  H  A  P.     X.

*Of the Head & Tail of the Dragon.*

The Head & Tail of the Dragon are not Planets, but certain sections: For the *Dragon's Head*
is the intersection of the Sun's path and the Moon's Eccentric, to which the *Dragon's*
*Tail* is opposite. And these intersections are indeed raised and lowered in certain Zodiacal places like Pla-
nets: Namely, the Dragon's Head is raised 3 degrees in Gemini (♊) and lowered by the same degree in Sagittarius (♐).
Similarly, the detriment of the *Dragon's Tail* is in 3 degrees in Gemini (♊), and its exaltation is in the same degree of the opposite sign,
namely Sagittarius (♐).

*It should be noted, however*, that when the conjunction or opposition of the luminaries
is at the points of intersection constituting the head and tail of the Dragon, or near
them, that is, within 12 degrees, then Eclipses of the luminaries occur, namely of the Sun in their
conjunction, and of the Moon in their opposition.

                          C H A P. IV.

                  Concerning the Lord of any house.

The Lord, called Almuten by the Arabs, is the same as "Victor," because in that
place it has more testimonies of happiness & strength than any other
of the Planets. Therefore, let the celestial figure or scheme be inspected, & let the place,
whose Lord is to be sought, be diligently observed. For example: I wish to investigate the Lord of the first
house or Horoscope, namely the ascendant: I ask therefore, what
sign, & what degree of the sign occupies the beginning of that house? Then I
turn to the head of that sign described in the third book of this [work], in which, first generally,
I seek the more powerful Lords of that sign & of any of its parts, & likewise
the degrees holding the cusp of nature. To that Planet, however, is attributed
                                                                      the rulership.

--- Page 592 ---
DE SCHEMAT. COELEST. ERECT. 681

is chosen, who has there in that place more testimonies of strength and dignities, as if the 10th degree of Gemini
were found on the cusp of the Ascendant, I find Mercury to have
dignities: 5 for its house, as is held in section 1, chapter on Gemini; and three for the Triplicity,
as is shown in the same section; and two for its Term,
as section 2 on Gemini teaches. Nor do I find there any of the Planets equal to it in
dignity; therefore I pronounce it the Lord of that place, and so in
other cases. But if two Planets are found who have had equal
dignities in the same place, then that one which is in the Ascendant: within 3 or 4 degrees near the beginning
of the house will be the Lord, indeed even if it has only two dignities, or if,
of those two thus existing in the same place, only one aspects the Ascendant,
it will be the Lord. But if neither or both aspect the Ascendant equally,
then the stronger in the sky, for example if one is in an angle, the other in a succedent house, or one in a
succedent, and the other in a cadent house, will be the Lord or victor. But if
even in that case they are equal in power, then see which of them is in a degree
more suitable to itself, namely, whether a masculine [planet] is in a masculine [degree/sign], or a feminine [planet] in a
feminine [degree/sign], or exists in a bright, dark, void, well, Azemena, or fortune-
increasing degree; for whoever is stronger, he will be called the Lord. If
finally in all these two Planets are equal, then the dignity of the House is to be preferred.

C H A P. V.

*On the disposition of signs in the houses at meridian time.*

IT must first be understood that two principal times are in use among Astrologers,
namely *Meridian* and *Post-Meridian*. They call *Meridian* that space
in which the sun possesses the point of midday, that is, enters the vertex of the Horizon or the
meridian circle. When therefore you wish to erect a figure for the exact meridian hour,
that is, in which the Sun possesses the point of midday, and to dispose the celestial
signs according to their proper position for that hour in that figure,
then, the figure having been first delineated in the aforesaid manner, let the Sun's place be sought out with all diligence thereafter,
that is, the sign and its degree with minutes, if there are any, in which the
Sun passes on that day and hour. These having been found in an Ephemeris table
serving your year and month, let the Sun be expressed on the cusp or beginning of the tenth house,
together with the sign in which it passes.
Then let it be sought among the tables of houses, under the pole height of the region
or city in which the question is moved, the sign in which the Sun was found, and that
prefixed under the title of the tenth house. Descend therefore downwards from that series of
numbers placed directly under the tenth house, until you find the true degree
in which the Sun was found; which having been found, proceed directly to the right into
the columns of houses 11, 12, 1, 2 & 3, and describe the degrees with minutes which you find there
for the cusps of the houses prefixed to them, namely in 11, 12, 1, 2, 3. These having been thus
produced, the remaining houses opposite to these and their degrees with minutes [are also determined].
And in this way the celestial chart with its signs will be prepared
to receive all the Planets according to their natural positions for that
given meridian hour.

C H A P. VI.
*Concerning the placement of the Planets in the aforesaid figures.*

The placement of the Planets in the figure is very easy, and by no means tedious,
if the day of your question in the given month of the year is sought out: For by proceeding
to the right between two parallel lines from the given day, you will find above each
square the character of both the Planet and also the sign in which it transits. But in the
square itself you will find the degree and minute in which the Planet remains at that
midday hour. Therefore, once the figure has been made for the midday hour, the Planets
are to be set out in it in the same degrees and minutes that are found in the squares: But the matter
is different when the figure is made for some afternoon hour, as will appear in chapter 8.
For example: *A question was posed in London, in the Year 1601, on the 11th day of the month of May,
exactly at the midday hour of that day: I therefore find ☉ (the Sun) to transit in ♉ (Taurus), namely in 20 degrees,
24 minutes of the same: And because the elevation in London is 51 degrees, therefore

CHAPTER VII.

On the erection of a celestial figure for any hour from noon.

Post-meridian time is that which extends from the point of one noon to the
point of the next following noon, that is, which measures the natural day of
24 hours.
But if the time at which the celestial figure is to be erected is post-meridian,
then, having found in the aforesaid manner the sign and degree in which the Sun
is for the proposed year, month, and day, the tables of houses must be consulted
for the altitude of the pole (latitude) of the region or place where the question
is posed, and the small column to which the sign, in which the Sun is found, is
prefixed under the title of the tenth house: For to its left, in the column where
the time from noon is described, the hours and minutes of the post-meridian time
correspond: To these hours and minutes, indeed, must be added the hours and
minutes of the given time: But since the Sun, in any six-hour period, completes
by its own motion 15 minutes of a degree of a sign, to which corresponds a quarter
part of one degree of the Equator, and indeed that quarter part measures one
minute of time, therefore for every six post-meridian hours, one minute of time
must be added to the aforementioned minutes of hours already summed. But if the
aggregated number of hours exceeds 24, in that case 24 must be subtracted from
it, and the remainder with the minutes must be sought in the table of houses
under the column inscribed with this title, "time from noon". But if you do not
find that number exactly, the nearest number smaller than it must be taken;
(for by doing this, no, or at least no great, error will follow) having found this,
one must proceed directly to the right between two parallel lines, through six
houses, namely 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3, as in the preceding chapter, adorning them
with their proper signs, along with their degrees and minutes, which are to be
expressed at the cusp of the house, and the other six houses opposite to these
must also be decorated with their signs and degrees, opposite to those already
expressed. And in this way, the celestial figure will be prepared for the time
given from noon, for aptly delineating the planets then predominant in the sky.
Let the given year therefore be 1615. The tenth day of the month of June of the
same, according to the Roman Calendar.

                    CHAPTER VIII.

*On the placement of the Planets in the celestial figure for the afternoon time, with the finding of their true mean motion for any afternoon hour.*

When the time of the question is afternoon, the mean motion of the Planet is not
found exactly in the Ephemeris: Therefore, let the day of the month be sought in the Ephemeris,
and in its square (or table) you will see the mean motion of the Planet for the meridian hour
of that day, but in the square immediately placed below it, you will perceive its motion
for the following day at noon. Therefore, take the difference between one and the other,
and reduce it to minutes, and similarly also reduce the hours to minutes:
This done, multiply the minutes of one by the minutes of the other, and divide the product
by 24. and divide that quotient number again by 60. and the quotient will de-
clare the true time of the mean motion of the same Planet. For example; the mean motion
of the Sun is 59 minutes. and the given hour from noon will be 20 hours and 30 minutes. Therefore,
reduce 20 hours to minutes, by multiplying them by 60, in this manner.

Rule I.

*Where the mean motion of a Planet does not extend to minutes, there one must deal with seconds and thirds, in the preceding manner, as appears in the motion of Saturn.*

Rule II.

*Always in a retrograde Planet subtract as many minutes and seconds as there were between noon and the given hour; but in direct ones, add.*

But also in another, better way, without great error, the preceding operation is performed: namely, let the mean motion of all Planets be taken from noon of your day to noon of the following day, and let it be divided into minutes or seconds or thirds according to the nature of the motion of the slower or faster Planet. Divide this number by 24 and you will find the value of one hour of the day, which, multiplied by the hours elapsed from noon, will show the value of the Planet's motion in hours or minutes: Or divide the aggregate number by the given number, which is done more quickly: For example; The difference in the Sun's motion between noon of the 15th day of January in the year 1615 and noon of the same [day, i.e., the next day] was 61 minutes, that is, 1 degree and 1 minute. *On the change of the air throughout the entire year & through its quarters and months.*

### CHAPTER II.
*Concerning the change of air throughout the whole year and through its quarters and months.*

**S**ince there are various times in which the constitution of the heavens must be considered for a perfect change of air, we shall discuss each of them briefly and concisely, beginning with the more general and thus successively descending to the more special. Therefore, to begin with the year itself, as it is the space within which all other things are comprehended, it will not be difficult, by preparing a single celestial figure erected in the direct Ascendant of the year, to judge its nature and disposition pertaining both to the change of air and to the disturbance of lower things. So that this may be more easily accomplished, when you desire to know what will happen to the world regarding rains, winds, heat, dryness, or cold, establish the ascendant of the year, and at the same time place the Planets in the figure, and diligently observe which of them...

688          TREATISE II. PART X. BOOK V.
...presides over and rules them; For if the Lord is fortunate, a fortunate time will follow; but if unfortunate, the world will likewise be hindered and corrupted. Concerning the discovery of the stronger Planet in the figure, we have already spoken in previous books, namely that he is the Lord who has more testimonies or dignities in the figure at the time it is erected.

From these things, therefore, it is manifest that if the cold Planets are more powerful, and in colder signs, they universally constitute a cold time of the year: And indeed, the year will also be drier or more humid, the more eminent testimonies the Planet has with its sign, either of dryness over humidity, such as Saturn (♄) in Capricorn (♑), or of humidity over dryness, such as the Moon (☾) in Cancer (♋), or in any other watery sign.

Similarly, also, if the Lord is hot, and in some hot sign, it will have intense heat, either with dryness, if Mars (♂) is in Aries (♈), Leo (♌), or Sagittarius (♐), or with humidity, if Jupiter (♃) or Venus (♀) are in signs

for I observed, and I saw that this would happen on Thursday in the morning around the ninth hour: I therefore predicted that at that time this stubborn frost would undergo dissolution, and the beginning of its dissolution would be from snow mixed with rain, because neither could Mars act so vigorously on the lunar body due to its sluggishness, nor could the Moon so suddenly receive or suffer Mars' actions, due to its congealed humidity; so indeed that in this dissolution Saturn would have dominion in part, and on the other part, Martian heat, with Mars certainly initiating the dissolution, and the Saturnian forces leaving something of their congelative nature in the air, not yet entirely yielding to Martian power, yet so that with Mars ultimately prevailing, all that snowy matter would be converted into pure water.       Therefore, in making judgment concerning the change of air, many rules must be observed; among which this one is not to be held in the last place: that the effect of the predictions will be stronger, the more significators there are, and weaker, the fewer there are.

C A P. IV.

*On the change of air by reason of the region's location.*

It is certain and proven by experience that some nations are more subject to warm changes in the air, while others are more subject to cold ones, and this for reasons both manifest and hidden: Indeed, for manifest reasons, we see that regions nearer to the poles of the world are more rigid with cold and frost; whereas towards the equinoctial circle, fiery meteors disturb the air more: But for hidden reasons, we see that some places are more burdened by a multitude of storms than others; Thus, for example, the Bermudas, a Western Island, are afflicted by thunder and sea storms, Dalmatia by winds and earthquakes, and all islands everywhere by rains, as experience testifies: And furthermore, regions subject to hot stars are more affected by hot and aerial disturbances than others, just as those which are subject to cold stars are affected by colder ones. Which regions are subject to any given Planet is best recognized by the Climates under which they are found: But certain regions are also subject to fixed stars, and according to their nature, they change their own natures in diverse ways; for these, see the following tables.

C H A P. V.

*On the particular operations of stars, both wandering and fixed,
in producing Meteors.*

Among the signs of the Zodiac, some exist which produce especially the principal
atmospheric changes, namely Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces; although other signs also,
each indeed united with the nature of any Planet, produce various and diverse effects in any
region of the air, as we shall soon declare, when we have made mention
of the Planets. Among the wandering stars, however, the inferior Planets especially
induce atmospheric changes, and particularly Mercury.
   What each of the Planets, however, operates in the air to induce Meteors
will be clear from the following account. If Saturn alone is the disposer or Lord
of the figure, it produces dryness, and so much greater, the more it agrees with
the nature of the sign. But, if the Moon, after a conjunction or aspect of the Sun, seeks
an aspect of Saturn, dark clouds will be produced, which will very often dissolve
into rains.
   Jupiter, however, alone as disposer will produce moderation and serenity, which
nevertheless, if the Moon, after a conjunction or aspect with the Sun, applies itself to this Planet, will not be
without white clouds having a reddish tint mixed in; these indeed, which also, if
a testimony of humidity or dryness has been added to those Planets, as for example, if
the Moon obtains a humid or dry mansion, will resolve into rain or
wind. And therefore this change will also be the greatest of all, if after the application
of the Moon and Jupiter, the Moon seeks a conjunction of Mercury or Venus. And these
same things also happen, if after a conjunction or application of the Moon and Jupiter,
the Moon increases or applies to Venus or Mercury.
   Mars alone as disposer will increase heat in summer, but in winter
time will diminish cold, and at other times will always increase heat. And if after
a conjunction or aspect of the Sun, the Moon seeks an application of Mars, the air will be filled
with saffron-colored clouds and emitting thunder, lightning, and storms; these
indeed, which will be so much greater, if the Moon, after separation from Mars, seeks Mercury.
   Venus alone, Lady of the figure, will increase humidity in winter and spring, but
in summer or autumn will make a dry time humid. To which if the Moon applies itself after the Sun's
separation, it will generate a minute or light rain, and long-lasting,
which will afterwards become greatest, if the Moon, after this application of hers, seeks Mercury.
   Mercury alone as disposer will generate huge and rapid winds, which
indeed will be associated with showers and copious rains, if the Moon, after separation from the Sun.
                                       Or [unclear]        itself

--- Page 605 ---
694          TRACT. II.  PART. X.  LIB. V.
...if it has sought Mars itself; and these things will happen so much more if Mercury has aspected Jupiter with any aspect: And indeed it will produce these effects in all seasons of the year, the winter alone excepted, in which it will generate an accumulation of clouds.
     The Moon alone, Lady and disposer, if after the application of the Sun, it has been void of course, will induce very great changes, and these indeed will last for so long, until it itself again applies to some planet; for then the weather will be changed or intensified according to the quality of the planet, with which the application is made.

                          C H A P. VI.
                    On the Eclipse of the Sun & Moon.

Planetary conjunctions are properly so called, when two planets are found in the same degree of a sign, for there they are then said to be conjoined. It must be observed, however, concerning them, that some of the conjunctions of the luminaries occur at the points of their intersections, which are called the Head and Tail of the Dragon, about which we have spoken above; And indeed in those very conjunctions occur solar Eclipses, inasmuch as they happen

--- Page 608 ---
DE PROGNOST. TEMPEST. 697

Regula III.

Note, for how many hours a Solar Eclipse lasts, because for so many years its effect will endure; And similarly, observe the hours of a Lunar Eclipse, because for as many hours as it lasts, for so many months the effect denoted by it will remain in its vigor.

C A P. VII.

On the conjunctions of the other Planets

As for the conjunction of the other Planets, great things arise from it, and that because of the slowness of their motion, especially when those three superior planets are conjoined in one term and face, and the Sun has aspected them; For this is the greatest conjunction, which signifies the destruction of certain Climates, kingdoms and regions, and their change, and other difficult and very important matters according to the quality both of the stronger or conquering Planet, and also of the figure itself, especially if the Sun or some other of the inferior Planets has helped them, where however it must always be kept in mind that the stronger among the others is the significator, and indicates, if indeed it is fortunate, good, but if evil, evil.

Similarly, if these Planets have been conjoined in their exaltations, they portend a good constitution of the time, and a multitude of movements and warlike commotions; if in their falls and detriments, they denote drought and sterility of the earth, and famine, unless they have been fortunate: But if they have been conjoined in a fiery sign, they signify sterility of the earth; if in a watery, a multitude of rains; if in an airy, winds; if in an earthy, excessive cold, snows and damages; if in a masculine, harm to animals of that sex; if in a feminine, harm to the feminine sex.

But it must be noted in this place that there are three species of conjunction among the superior planets; namely, one between Jupiter and Saturn, which is called the greatest; a second between Saturn and Mars, which is called the middle; and a third between Jupiter and Mars, which is named the minor conjunction.

In the major or greatest conjunction, if Saturn is in detriment, it signifies tribulations; if in dry signs, sterility of the earth; if in earthy signs, famine and destruction of seeds; if in watery signs, a multitude of waters and plague.

Furthermore, the middle conjunction denotes occurrences of wars and contentions, and that indeed better, if the Lord of the figure, that is, of the ascendant, has been good, but worse if evil.

Finally, the lowest or minor conjunction signifies cold, snows, rains, corruptions of the air and war, unless good fortune prevails in it at the hour of the conjunction; but if otherwise, the opposite. But if this conjunction has been in the ascendant of the year, or in one of the four angles, it indicates the stirring up of kings and rich men, unless good fortune has aspected it.

Regula I.

When a fortunate (planet) has been conjoined with an evil (planet), it will appear of the nature of the stronger; and when an evil (planet) (is conjoined) with an evil (planet), evil superabounds, unless the one who presided over the conjunction has been fortunate: And this is a secret not common among Astrologers.

*Rule II.*

*In every conjunction, look to the ascendant and who is the Lord of the figure: For if*
*he is good, he will indicate good; if bad, he will indicate bad: For the fortunate (benefic planets) signify an increase of good*
*things in all matters, while the malefic (planets) signify a diminution.*

*Rule III.*

*When a conjunction occurs in any of the angles, and especially in the Midheaven, it signifies a kingdom*
*on the part of that same sign: And if the same sign is good and its Lord is fortunate (benefic), they denote triumph,*
*and stability or firmness; but if they are afflicted, (they signify) the death*
*and downfall of the king.*

*Rule IV.*

*Any conjunction in human signs, as was said above concerning the medium conjunction,*
*signifies a multitude of infirmities.*

*Rule V.*

*A conjunction in any of the angles of the year signifies adversity for the rich and for kings,*
*and a multitude of wars, which will last until another conjunction occurs.*

*Rule VI.*

*Let it be noted as a general rule, that conjunctions indicate in fiery signs, sterility*
*and dryness of the earth; in airy signs, strong winds; in watery signs, great rains; in earthy signs,*
*frost and snow.*


C A P. VIII.

*General Rules.*

*Rule I.*

*Concerning the change of air for every time and hour.*

**T**herefore, considering how many testimonies and dignities a Planet has, and what quality
more abounds in the active and passive (principles), to this Planet the time is attributed.
For example, the Sun at 23° Aries has 4 dignities by exaltation, and 3 by Triplicity,
and is, as far as we are concerned, moderately hot and dry. Venus in her own house
has five dignities, and is hot and humid; And so in all other cases.
   It must be noted, however, that for prognosticating about the disposition of the air,
testimonies from minor dignities, namely, from Triplicities, Terms, and Faces, do not
indicate anything based on a single planetary position, but only testimonies from
Houses and Exaltations, and from their aspect to each other.

--- Page 610 ---
DE PROGNOST. TEMPEST. 699

each other: For Ptolemy says that, if a Planet is in minor dignities, namely in Triplicity, Term, or Face, it should be considered as nothing, unless it has two testimonies, namely either Term and Face, or Term and Triplicity. Likewise, as a sign is the whole sign of a Planet, as the whole of Aries (♈) is the sign of Mars (♂), and the whole of Aries (♈) is the exaltation of the Sun, and the whole of Aries (♈) is the Triplicity of the Sun, and the first ten degrees of Aries are the first Face of Mars, and the first six degrees of Aries (♈) are the Term of Jupiter (♃).
     Therefore, with these things considered, to make a prognostication about the change of weather for every hour will not be laborious or difficult.

Rule II.

*On the prognostication of heat.*

     When the Sun is in Leo (♌) and Mars is in the first Face of Aries (♈), or in a Trine aspect, it will give excessive heat. However, Saturn in a Square (□) aspect with the Sun diminishes the heat somewhat.

Rule III.

*On the prognostication of cold.*

     Observe the testimonies of the cold Planets: For Saturn in Capricorn (♑), that is, in its own house, and in Aquarius (♒), disposes winter according to its nature, and greatly mitigates the heats of summer through an aspect opposite to the Sun: However, it will be harmful to the autumn and spring seasons; for the ripening of fruits will be hindered and the dying of flowers will occur; Whence a scarcity of grain is to be feared, and especially of wine, unless Mars or Jupiter contradict.

Rule IV.

*On the abundance of rain.*

     Humid Planets abundant in testimonies, especially if dry Planets have aspected them in Trine in watery signs, generate an abundance of rain.
     There are also certain changes of air to be diligently observed, which are called by Astrologers "Openings of the Gates," and are caused by the following constellations, namely, if the Moon, after an aspect or conjunction (☌) with the Sun, seeks Saturn (♄) or Jupiter (♃), then Mercury (☿), or seeks Mars (♂) and then Venus (♀), for then great rains and storms will occur. And the same is also to be understood if the Moon (☾), after an aspect with the Sun, seeks Mercury (☿) or Venus (♀), then Jupiter (♃), Saturn (♄), or Mars (♂).
     In a similar manner, great changes occur, while two Planets having opposite houses arrive at a conjunction or aspect, such as the Sun (☉) and Saturn (♄). Likewise the Moon (☾) and Saturn (♄). Likewise Venus (♀) and Mars (♂). Likewise Jupiter (♃) and Mercury (☿).

Rule V.

BOOK SIX.
On the Thief & the Indication of Theft.

C H A P. I.
On the Truth of this Branch of Astrology.

[Decorative initial 'H' containing a figure] The truth of this art is confirmed not only by the practice and experience of others but also by my own.
But why the stars in a certain way impose the necessity of evil deeds upon the thief and other criminals, we have declared the reason for this matter in the first book of this part, namely, because the mind (which otherwise has dominion over the stars, so much so that it is not inappropriately said from this, that the wise man rules the stars) is either absent in them, or indeed, as Trismegistus would have it, is not present in them at all, since all men, as he says, are indeed speaking, but only a few of them are endowed with mind, namely, those who have sought it in the treasuries of wisdom.
But as for this practice, omitting a long circumlocution of words, I will briefly recount only certain histories of experiments proven by me, which are also not unknown to others. For after I had assumed the degree of Bachelor at Oxford, at which time I was immersed in the very core of mathematical study, among other arts, I strove with all my might to scrutinize the depth of this astrological science as well, and I devoted no small effort to the investigation of nativities and theft. It happened therefore around that time, that my tutor, from whose guardianship I had recently departed, named Perinus, Doctor of Sacred Theology, entering my room unexpectedly, told me that a certain laundress of his had lost all her linen the previous night: He therefore asked me, if my Astrology had anything in that matter, by which I might be able to detect the thief for him, that I would oblige him in that respect for the sake of our friendship: Therefore, for the hour of this request, I erected a figure or celestial theme, and diligently sought out the Lord of the Western angle, which is always attributed to the thief, whom I found to be Mars, and I found him in a watery sign, namely in Cancer, and similarly I also saw the Moon conjoined with him: From which I boldly declared that the thief could not have come into the laundress's house unless he had passed through water: And thus also the outcome showed the matter to be; for he had crossed up to his navel through a ditch filled with river water, before he reached the place from which he had snatched those things. Similarly, according to the doctrine of Guido and Sconer, I described the disposition of the thief's body, namely, that he had a medium stature, yellowish eyebrow hairs, reddish hair, and I declared many other things in observing the constitution of the other parts of the body: Likewise I also added, that the thief had not yet departed outside the parish, nor had the goods been sold or dispersed; I also noted that the Eastern part of the Parish, according to the regions of the world, was the thief's statio-
Tttt 3 nem

--- Page 613 ---
702          TRACT. II. PART. X. LIB. VI.

...dwelling place, and the door of the house where he lived had a certain mark or hole made by fire and repaired with a new plank. When these things were told, she immediately suspected the described place, and said that from my words she saw with her eyes, as if present, the house in which that thief was hiding, and that she herself had indeed also suspected it before. Therefore, she, going there with an officer, whom they call a Constable, immediately at the very entrance of the house encountered that man described by me in form, whom she immediately recognized by the color of his hair and eyebrows. Therefore, the aforesaid officer, inspecting the pockets of his breeches, found therein two collars, and several other smaller linen items of that kind, and thus in this way, little by little, what had been lost was recovered.

It also happened not long after, while I was so anxiously occupied in my studies concerning a treatise on Music that I scarcely left my room for an entire week, that on a certain Thursday, a rather noble youth came to me for a visit. He was also engaged in more humane sciences in Magdalen College, which was situated directly more to the East from our college, designated by the name of St. John. He dined with me on that day in my room. However, on the following Sunday, I was invited to dinner by a certain friend of mine, an inhabitant of the city. Preparing myself for this feast, I saw that my belt with the hanging sword-strap was missing, the price of which indeed amounted to 10 French gold coins. I asked everyone in our college who came by during that period of time whether they knew anything about this lost item of mine, or if anything had become known, but I could not learn anything from anyone. Therefore, I was compelled by this reason to erect a certain celestial figure for that time when I first discovered the absence of the belt. This done, I perceived Mercury to be the Lord of the seventh house, whom I found quite well-disposed in the tenth house. From this, therefore, I concluded that some youth, and to some extent still a boy, was the thief, and that he was endowed with excellent speech and a faculty for reasoning. Similarly, I saw Mercury itself, with other testimonies, to be more Oriental, and from that, I understood that the item snatched or taken away had been carried towards the South.

These things, therefore, having been diligently considered, and the person of the thief quite well described, suddenly there came to my mind the presence of that guest of mine who had been with me on the preceding Thursday, since his dwelling was, as said above, in Magdalen College, which was to the East with respect to the place where the theft was committed. Wherefore I sent my servant without delay to him, that he might address him in this matter with gentle and humane words. But he, adding oaths, denied that he had ever touched those goods. I, however, since I had perceived that the lost item had been carried towards the South, sent my servant a second time, not only to him, but also at the same time to a certain youth or boy who was with him at the time when my things were stolen. Therefore, my servant vigorously attacked this youth with sharper words and even threats, affirming that he had the lost items, and had hidden them in a place towards Christ Church, well known to me, and indeed there, where he had sometimes heard music, and had been intimately acquainted with certain women: (This, moreover, I ordered my servant to signify to him, because the lost item was shown to be hidden towards the South, and furthermore, because Mercury was found in the house of Venus; for from that I concluded that the thief was mostly occupied and delighted with music and the company of women.) When the accused heard this, he was suddenly cast down before his companion, and striking the floor of the room with his foot, he swore that he himself had committed the deed, and had not dared to look at my face from that time, and begged my servant not to say anything further about this matter, adding the promise that on the next day he would return the stolen belt with the hanging sword-strap to me through his companion; that indeed, which also...
