C A P. II.
*Concerning questions pertaining to the thief and the theft.*

QUÆST. I.
*Whether the item is lost or not?*

IF the Lord of the hour or the Lord of the ascendant itself is in the ascendant, or if the Lord of the hour and the Lord of the ascendant are conjoined, or also, if the Lord of the Moon's house is corporally conjoined with the Moon or with the Lord of the ascendant, it is probable that the item is neither lost nor stolen, but lies hidden somewhere within the querent's house.

QUÆST. II.
*Whether there is one thief or more?*

      See if the Moon is in an angle of the chart, and in a sign of two faces or two bodies: if this is so, there are several thieves, provided the ascendant is of that condition: But if the ascendant is fixed, there is only one thief, and not more: But if the Lord of the ascendant is Masculine, and the Lord of the hour is Feminine, or vice versa, there are two thieves, one male, the other female.

QUÆST. III.
*Is the thief male or female?*

      If the Lord of the ascendant and likewise also the Lord of the hour is masculine, the thief is male, but if both are feminine, the thief is female: But if indeed one of them is masculine, and the other feminine, then, as was said in the preceding question, there are two thieves, one male, the other female.

QUÆST. IV.
*Is the thief a familiar person?*

      Look at the Lord of the sixth house, who, if found in the second house, or with

--- Page 615 ---
704          TREATISE II.  PART X.  BOOK VI.
...with the Lord of the second house, the thief is of your family, or kindred, such as a brother, sister, etc. And the same is also signified if the Lord of the sixth house is found in the first or third house. Bacon.
     If the Sun & Moon simultaneously and at the same time aspect the ascendant, the thief is a familiar (household member). Alkindus.
     Look at the Lord of the sixth house, and if he is found in the ascendant, or in the second house, or with the Lord of the second house, the thief is a servant, and a familiar (household member) of your house.

QUESTION V.
*Is the thief noble?*
     If the significator is benevolent, and especially Jupiter, the thief is free-born and noble; otherwise, the contrary.

QUESTION VI.
*Of what age is the thief?*
     If the significator planet is Oriental or in the Eastern quarter of the sky, or if the Moon is in its first age, it shows a young person: Mercury always denotes a boy or a young person, especially if it is Oriental and in the ascendant.
     Thus every significator (except Saturn ♄) indicates a boy or a young person.
     If the significator is joined with Mercury ☿. or Venus ♀. it suggests a youthful age.

QUESTION VII.
*Concerning the form of the thief.*
     The form of the thief is sought both from the Significator Planet itself, and also from the Planets & fixed stars with which it is joined in both longitude and latitude. Fixed stars give a similar form to that planet whose nature they are. Thus Martial stars give the form that Mars does: But if the significator is joined with the South Node ☋. it renders the thief deformed, especially if there is a bad aspect of Saturn; and this deformity will especially be in that member which is ruled by that sign in which the significator exists. Furthermore, the sign of the seventh house & the planet or stars on its cusp are to be considered, and by mixing these with the aforesaid, you may pronounce concerning the form of the thief. Moreover, if the significator is Apogean, it makes the thief tall; if Perigean, the opposite: It must also be seen how the significator behaves from its own nature or from the conjunction of the nature of others; for if it is humid by its own nature, or is configured with humid Planets & stars, it designates a very corpulent body habit, but if it is of a dry quality, it will denote the contrary.
     Read our descriptions of the form of man, which the fixed stars confer upon him, given above in the book treating of celestial signs, and similarly also those which we proposed in the book immediately following it, concerning the form attributed to man by a Planet. For most often in my practice, I have exactly derived the figure & description of a person not only from the sign of the seventh house, but also from its Lord & also from the sign in which that lord was found.

# BOOK SEVENTH.
## Concerning Elections.

### C H A P. I.
#### What election is & concerning its species.

Astrologers call election the observation of days or hours, that is, that part of time in which the sky is so disposed that what someone intends to do can be done happily.

Election, moreover, in general is either
*   Superstitious, namely that which is corrupted by the trifles of Astrological doctrine and the depraved commentaries of the Arabs and Chaldeans, specifically by the inventions of Necromantic incantations, and apparitions of Spirits, and compositions of characters, and many other things of that kind ascending beyond natural limits.
*   Physical, depending on the most constant motion of the sky and celestial bodies, which is either
    *   Universal, under which are contained
        *   The initiation of works concerning livestock.
        *   The beginning of agriculture.
        *   The construction of buildings.
    *   Particular, which is either
        *   Medicinal, under which are contained
            *   Bloodletting.
            *   The administration of medicines.
            *   The healing of a certain limb.
            *   The weaning of infants.
            *   The use of baths.
            *   Haircutting.
        *   Non-medicinal, pertaining to
            *   Auspicious beginnings of dignities and offices.
            *   Journeys,
            *   Navigations.
            *   Legations.
            *   Migrations.
            *   Marriages.

The time to be observed in elections is twofold: For one election is { [the observation] of the day alone, in which the Moon is joined to the Planet, the ruler of those affairs for which the election is made, or in which the ruler of the affair, established in its dignities, comes to a fortunate aspect. { [The other involves] not only the day, but also the hour, so indeed, that with the theme of the entire sky established, significations may be found fortunately in the angles or cardines.


C A P.	II.

*On the utility and necessity of knowing the nativity of certain persons concerning them in elections.*

REGARDING the necessity of knowing the time of birth of that person, about whom the matter in elections revolves, he will judge most easily who has rightly observed the outcomes of things: For indeed we sometimes see someone undertake a certain work under a good constellation, from which, however, he reports nothing but detriment and misfortune, because, namely, the ascendant in the election, although generally good, is nevertheless unfortunate for this or that individual or person, inasmuch as it is contrary to the ascendant of their radical nativity. Hence, therefore, I strongly affirm, against the opinion of those who contend that elections can be given directly without knowledge of the time of birth, that no elections, except for a few in medicine, can be made unless the appropriate time of nativity is first known: For indeed we see, among several merchants embarking on one and the same ship at the same hour, some return home with profit, happy and enriched, while others are in danger, and return to their homes with loss and misfortune: This, indeed, happens from no other cause than from the diversity of the radical charts in their nativities. Therefore, it is not undeservedly held as an axiom among Astrologers that a good election cannot avert the evil of planets being diminished in the radical nativity.


*Rule I.*

*An election is beneficial when the significators of the radical chart aid the goodness of the election.*

C H A P. IV.

*Concerning another Canon of signs; and similarly concerning the principal elections of Planets in this work.*

**H**aving known the nativity (which indeed ought to be investigated before all else, if possible), or even, where knowledge of it cannot be had, having considered the hour of the begun matter, the nature and quality of the ascending sign must be observed; which ought to agree with the nature and quality of the matter itself to be performed. Similarly, also, the Planet naturally signifying the matter must be well adapted. For example.

[bracketed list]
It must be observed concerning the signs and Planets naturally
signifying matters, that we ought to choose in

War & quarrels from { Martial Signs.
                     { The Planet Mars.

Marriages from { Venereal Signs.
               { The Planet Venus.

Substance & riches from { Jovial Signs.
                       { The Planet Jupiter.

*Rule I.*

After the knowledge of the nativity, the matter to be signified must always be referred to the Lord of the house of the celestial chart: And similarly, also, the Planet of the nativity, which ought to render a happy outcome, in the proposed question, must be fortified in the Ascendant or 10th house: For example: If someone has decided to make a journey to a king, the ninth house and its Lord must be adapted; and the tenth house ought to ascend in the nativity, and its Lord ought to be either in the Ascendant or the 10th house, and indeed strong and fortunate therein: Similarly, also, the Lord of the Ascendant and the Lord of the sign in which he is, must be diligently and accurately adapted.

*Rule II.*

The place of the conjunction and opposition of the luminaries immediately preceding, as well as their Lord, must be adapted.

*Rule III.*

The Moon ought not to ascend in your election because it is afflicted by misfortune in the Ascendant.

*Rule IV.*

The Sun must be placed in the Ascendant or the house signifying the matter, or in Aries (♈) or Leo (♌), for otherwise it is considered to be evil.

*Rule V.*

The Lord of the fourth house notes the end of the matter, if only it is found in it, or aspects it; for otherwise, that office will be performed by the Lord of the Moon's house, if it aspects the Moon, or by the planet to which the Moon is first conjoined, etc.

                                                                  Rule

--- Page 624 ---
DE ELECTIONIBUS. 713

Rule VI.

In every Election, observe that the ray (conjunction $\sigma-\sigma$, square $\square$, or opposition $\sigma-$) of any planet operating a contrary effect does not strike the significator. For indeed, the significator must be removed from all such configurations, and strengthened by position in the midheaven or in the eastern angle, to which the Moon is conjoined either in a sextile ($\ast$) or a trine ($\triangle$), and both Jupiter (♃) and Venus (♀) ought to aspect it.

Rule VII.

But in giving medicines, it is necessary to do the opposite; for example, if the physician's intention is to purge the head, he ought not to strengthen Mars (♂), but rather render him entirely unfortunate and unfavorable. For otherwise, the strength of the head resists the medicines, so that it can be purged either little or even not at all. But concerning complete medical Elections, we will treat more extensively in the second volume concerning the Microcosm.

Rule VIII.

The Moon ought to be strong in elections, and free from all impediments, and be found in a sign suitable for the proposed matter, whether movable or fixed, inasmuch as the latter will bring stability, while the former will bring speed to affairs.
The exact knowledge of the Moon's mansions will also be of no small profit, inasmuch as by suddenly observing their dispositions, when the opportunity for erecting a celestial figure is denied, it will not be difficult to adapt the hour. And the table of those (mansions) is as follows.

788          THE PRINTER'S EPISTLE

[Decorative headpiece ornament]

THE PRINTER TO THE READER.

[Large decorative initial E] Here for you, friendly Reader, is the essence of the second volume, reduced into a concise table, the entire substance of which I could not append to this work, because it is not yet entirely completed by the author. But I hope that its knowledge and contemplation are not only to be compared with the doctrine of this volume, but also to be superior to it in many respects, since it deals not only with the divine contemplation of the Microcosm itself, or the inner man, in a wonderful and by no means common way, but also some paradoxes are proven by the author in it, both by authority and by philosophical reason, and also, which is the most certain demonstration of all, by ocular experiment drawn from spiritual things. Moreover, in it, the arts pertaining to the composition of the Microcosm's nature are dissected by true anatomy, and things by no means common are freely revealed; and at the same time, chemical preparations of medicines, not yet known by many, and proven by the author himself at no small expense, are explained. Among all these things, indeed, nor is that to be held in the last place, that the secrets of the corporeal nature and disposition of man, insofar as it pertains to the preservation of his health, are clearly and plainly described in it, so indeed that I do not doubt at all that that work will bring not only the highest delight and divine contemplation of human structure, but also no small utility to the world. Therefore, you, Candid Reader, be sparing in judging, and consider the author's labors, performed in this first volume, as good and fair, lest otherwise, by your importunity, he be deterred in his second labor, still imperfect and less complete, and thus leave it unfinished in the middle without publication. Farewell.

A MOST LUCID EXPLANATION OF THE EMBLEM AT THE BEGINNING OF THIS VOLUME.

[Large decorative initial 'A' containing a triangle with the Tetragrammaton in Hebrew and an eye in the center]

[Marginal note in French cursive]:
the seraphim are loving
persons
the cherubim perceive
the sciences

BEFORE the creation of things, the incomprehensible and omnipotent maker of the Macrocosm, by his immense power, divided the entire mass into three parts differing in purity; from the purest of which he ordained Cherubim, Seraphim, Archangels, and all other orders of Angels to be created; from the less pure, heaven and the ethereal regions; and from the most impure, the elements and all sublunar things, saying; let them be made, and they were made. The first division of matter, however, because of the simple purity of its substance, he placed beyond the comprehension of natural things, for it is metaphysical and supernatural, which modern writers on Philosophy confirm to be circumscribed by the Empyrean heaven, that is, by the fiery and burning [heaven]: The remaining parts of the more impure mass, however, namely the ethereal and the elementary, since they are subject to Nature (the governess of the Microcosm under God), are deservedly called natural.

Two efficient causes of these parts contained in this fabric of the Macrocosm are enumerated: namely Nature, and its Ape, which we call Art. The Father and Lord of Nature is God, the Best and Greatest; to whom she herself is closest, and from whom we know all her virtues and effects to be derived: She is, as it were, the knot and bond of the elements, and has the power to rightly temper the mixture of elements with due proportions, and aptly to mix them in every compound, and to impress a suitable form on each species. Nature is also a certain infinite force creating like from like, since she is the fertile mother of all qualities and things, which she increases and nourishes: And to describe her in a single word according to the opinions of Zoroaster and Heraclitus, she is an invisible fire; which they themselves call the soul of the world. We, however, have depicted her visibly in almost the same way as some modern Philosophers; which we did with the intention that her power might be better understood by the reader's mind. We have therefore fashioned a naked virgin, tender and blooming in age, with starry and most beautifully gilded hair, praiseworthy for the clearest keenness of her eyes, and most lovable for the blushing color of her cheeks; and the virgin was so remarkable for the complete whiteness of her body, and so sweetly adorned with all the gifts of the greatest maker, that Poets could not prefer Pallas, nor Venus, nor Juno, nor any other however beautiful Goddess to her beauty. By her singular prudence the prime mo-

--- Page 641 ---
8

the mobile is governed, and the eighth sphere adorned with stars is handled and turned by her hands, and by the influence of the same sphere, the generations of elementary things are daily prepared and arranged by her fingers; the bodies of the Planets also serve as instruments for the works of Nature; they are also like hammers, by which metals are produced in terrestrial mines; the region of the heart and breast of this virgin is the true seat and matrix of the celestial Sun, and her belly is filled with a lunar body; from her breasts, to all creatures of the elements, she perpetually instills and nurses the innate heat and radical moisture, from which their life and vegetation arise; also, by a certain golden splendor of her heart, the stars, both fixed and wandering, are illuminated, and as it were, they borrow their souls, lives, and beauties from it; whose imperceptible influences, infused into her matrix by the Mercurial Spirit (which Philosophers call the Spirit of the Moon), are carried downwards to the earth, penetrating even to its center; by whose impressions diverse generations, differing both in place and species, are constantly produced. By the actions of this nature, the Planets come together simultaneously, and by coming together, they produce various things differing in species in the animal, vegetable, and mineral realms; from her lower parts, beginning from the loins, the four Elements are comprehended; for her right foot occupies the earth, and her left foot the water, signifying the conjunction of the sulphurous and mercurial nature of the same: by which it is argued that nothing can be generated and grow without the union of both. This Nature, I say, is not a GODDESS, but the closest minister of GOD; she has beneath her a handmaid or attendant, who, by imitating her Mistress and impressing upon herself, through consent, the likenesses of things produced by her, wonderfully follows and imitates her footsteps and delineations: And hence it is that we have depicted her in the form and habit of an Ape beneath the feet of Nature; whom we also call by the more dignified name of Art. This beast (I mean Art), originating from human ingenuity, just as from diligent observation of her Mistress, she learns many beautiful and notable secrets, by which she is accustomed to enrich humans in every kind of knowledge; so also, conversely, she brings no small utility and advantage to her same teacher and Mistress. For unless Art, produced by human ingenuity, sometimes assists in certain things, Nature herself will soon fall short of the perfection of her operation: For Art sometimes corrects Nature, supplements it, indeed, in the realm of mineral things, it even seems to surpass her, if only we give some credence to those Chymical Philosophers; especially since in the animal kingdom, eggs hatch more quickly, silkworms multiply, and by their growth transform into diverse forms like Proteus, bees are generated from a bull's head; in the vegetable kingdom, crops by the art of the plow, by which fields are cultivated and harrowed, trees by grafting, herbs and other vegetables by planting, both grow and multiply; and in the mineral kingdom, metallic bodies and lesser minerals are prepared both for medicine and for other uses, and are purified from their dregs, and also the Philosopher's Stone, concerning whose praises Philosophers have so much proclaimed, is certainly produced and proven by experience. Therefore, it is our purpose in this volume to discuss these two efficient causes of the Macrocosm both clearly and copiously.

P R O E M,
IN WHICH IT IS DEMONSTRATED,
HOW CAUSES ARE INVESTIGATED THROUGH THEIR EFFECTS,
THAT IS, BY DEMONSTRATION
*a posteriori*.

[Decorative initial Q] SINCE to demonstrate or know God Himself, the author of the fabric of the Macrocosm, *a priori* is impossible even for the wisest or most ingenious person, inasmuch as to define Him essentially has never been granted to anyone, nor indeed even to the divine leader Moses himself, nor will it ever be granted in any age (so omnipotent indeed and incomprehensible is He in His being!), therefore it is necessary for Him to be investigated *a posteriori*, so that our knowledge may approach Him through His most excellent effects. But the Psalmist teaches us (Psalm 19:4) to behold His nobler effects in the heavens and His glory in the firmament, as in a most polished mirror, with universal eyes. To the knowledge of these, since they are placed above us, it will also be necessary to ascend through elementary steps, as if from more composite things, by resolution, to simpler ones; nor is any rest to be granted in this ascent until those first principles are reached, which, because of their simplicity, cannot undergo further resolution. Therefore, this journey is immense, very thorny and perilous; and indeed, by what ladders we may be able to reach the summit of this invisible height, it is not easy to discover without the aid of divine light and the illumination of the Spirit.

Therefore, may it not displease Your dignity, Most Merciful GOD, creator of creatures and my helper, I humbly pray and implore, that I, an unworthy sinner, beg Your mercy; deign to enlighten me in the knowledge of created things, so that, although You are unknown *a priori*, You may at least be known *a posteriori* through Your glorious effects; since You have promised to open the door to those who diligently knock, nor have You forbidden anyone to eagerly search the fount of goodness; especially since that Spirit of life, whom You inspired into our father Adam, no less warns and urges us at every moment to strive towards the clear fount of beatitude and towards the ultimate goal of divine knowledge, than the heat of some raw and unripe fruit, inspired into it by Your noblest creature the Sun, is perceived to constantly move it towards mature perfection: indeed, by this very breath of Yours, adorned with a divine mind, daily of men

C H A P T E R I.
*On the infinite nature and the maker of all things.*

[Large decorative initial N] NFINITE Nature, which is the immense, ineffable, unintelligible Spirit, beyond all imagination, above all essence, unnameable, to be proclaimed by the heart alone, most wise, most merciful, FATHER, WORD, HOLY SPIRIT, the supreme and sole good, incomprehensible depth, the unity of all creatures, which is stronger than all power, greater than all excellence, more worthy of all praise, the indivisible TRINITY, most splendid and inexpressible light, finally, the divine mind, free and separated from all mortal concretion, the glory of all, divine nature, necessity, end and renewal; This one, I say, [Marginal note: *Hermes, sacred discourse.*] GOD, supreme and greatest of all, whose name be blessed forever, most skillfully founded the admirable machine of the entire Macrocosm, and most beautifully adorned its structure: Which also all philosophers, both ancient and more recent, except for the Peripatetics, who wish the world to be from eternity, assert with almost unanimous consent, naming this most divine founder of the universe with many appellations, suitable to each property of his action. Among whom *Hermes* calls him *eternal*, *Thales* *most ancient*, *Plato* *the unbegotten principle of the world*; others *the infinite cause*, and *as if outside all things*, and *yet in* *all things*, and *everywhere*; others *the Being of beings*, *the first cause*, inasmuch as other causes and effects depend on him, *the maker of all*, *the author*, and according to Plato *the creative intellect*. Hence some others called him the Prince of worldly things, governor, ordainer, the first mover and the first moving, and the immobile principle; because all things are moved by him remaining immobile, and subject to no passion, since he is always stable, fixed, and permanent; *Trismegistus* calls him *the principle of the universe*, by which he seems to understand only the maker of the creation; Finally, Plato and Mercurius Trismegistus call him Father, inasmuch as he is the author of all fruitfulness and the begetter of all things; Finally, the greater chorus of Philosophers (among whom I name Orpheus and Democritus) concludes that GOD *has every name*, because *all things are in him and* *he in all things*; no otherwise than all straight lines drawn from the center to the circumference are said to be in the center, or just as number is said to be in unity, which is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers, and contains every number uniquely joined in itself; Hence the Pythagoreans, most skilled in numerical science, applied the monad or unity to God the maker; both because before all things he was alone and unique, and also because he was the first agent and sole mover for perfecting the vast structure of creation; his

God can be compared to this incomprehensible Triangle, because comprehending all things in Himself, and extending Himself everywhere by His power, He actualizes all things, and outside of Him is nothing; and furthermore, each vertex of the angle corresponds to each third part of the world, and yet all joined together in unity of nature, constitute one single regular, equal, and most perfect Triangle; so indeed that it is also declared simultaneously by this demonstration, that, just as all the angles of the aforesaid Triangle, emerging from the spherical surface of the world, in all their dimension, figure, and capacity are found to be similar and equal, so also are the three persons in the unity of the divine essence co-equal in every aspect of perfection. C H A P T E R II.

*In how many ways* is GOD *said to be in a place, how is He everywhere present*
*and fills all things? And concerning His principal seat*
*in this world?*

[Decorative initial P] EFORE we discuss the proper seat or dwelling of the 'naturing Nature' (Natura naturans), it must be asked whether it can be in any place, since it is infinite in its essence? To this doubt, the entire School of Theologians responds by distinguishing, that He is in a place, *not definitively*, like intelligences or spiritual creatures, nor *circumscriptively*, like corporeal things, *but only by presence*; although according to *Gregory*, God is said to be in all things in three ways; namely, *either by presence*, as He reveals good to them, or *by potentiality*, that is, through influence, or *by essence*, namely, through intimate essence. But God is said to be everywhere, inasmuch as His divine power permeates all beings, through which He defines the relation of the potentiality of the entire universe to Himself: Thus He is also said to fill all things, not so that He is contained by them, but rather so that they are contained by Him. *For it is*, says *Ambrose, the property of the Godhead to be everywhere and in all things*. It is therefore manifest that God is not in all things, for example, so that any thing can grasp Him according to the measure of its portion, just as greater things [contain] less [than themselves]; but He is said to fill all things in such a way that there is nothing where He is not. We understand therefore that God is within all things, but not enclosed, because He is infinite and immeasurable; and outside all things, but not excluded, inasmuch as by His uncircumscribed magnitude He encompasses all created things. And hence it is that all things created by God are said to be good by Him, participatively, that is, through His presence, or according to the degrees of essence, by which angels are preferred to souls, and souls to animals; and yet, inasmuch as any creature has obtained more or less dignity according to the beauty of its form proceeding from the first nature or Being, to that extent, as *Iamblichus* testifies, in the goodness acquired through participation, it will possess a higher or lower seat. But indeed, as good is understood absolutely, simply, etc., to use *Iamblichus'* words, 'above essence', to that extent it is taken as the cause of good, that is, as the principle of essential good; concerning which *Mercurius Trismegistus* speaks there, where he admonishes us to beware lest we call anything good except God alone. Therefore, all the works of the Creator are found to be participations of goodness, not 'above essence' (which is proper to God alone), but according to essence, namely, inasmuch as they receive essence, form, and substantial light from the fiery benevolence of the Creator, by whose gifts they are illuminated, informed, and led from potentiality into act, and consequently are called good participatively. And indeed, this essentializing goodness the world and the creatures of the world received from the Creator Himself not by compulsion of necessity, as philosophical tradition holds, but from His free and most abundant will, desiring to perfect all His creatures, according to the mind of the Royal Psalmist; *Whatever the Lord pleased, He did in heaven and on earth*. Finally, the ancient philosophers placed the dwelling of this 'naturing nature' in heaven, because of the beauty and clarity of that place. Hence *Plato* asserted that God dwells in fiery substance, that is, in the aether. To this, even more recent philosophers (among whom I name *Isidore, Bede, and Basil* as true worshipers of this Nature) seem to assent, calling the *Empyrean Heaven* the dwelling place of God. For although God is said to be everywhere, (as above) yet properly and principally, that is, with

--- Page 654 ---
DE MACROCOSMI PRINCIPIIS. 23

with His greater presence He is said to be in this heaven, where the works of His power shine more brightly, as if in a more worthy place and situation, in which divine power operates more fittingly; as Damascene testifies. For God is not said to be above all things and outside all things by local distance, but by excellence of nature, as is held in Theological Resolutions, tract 1, p. 1, quest. 4. And hence it is that this heaven is called intellectual, because God, whose seat it is, is called an intellectual Spirit. Some others attributed this supercelestial region to angels and blessed souls, and therefore established another dwelling outside of this very one, which they called the heaven of the Trinity, fitting for the Trinity alone, namely the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They say this is God Himself in reality; but differs in concept. For according to Albert, this heaven is the excellence of divine power, which contains and circumscribes all created things. Hence, to be in this heaven is to be in the equality of God's power, creating, containing, and saving all things. Through Ezekiel's vision, all these things are clearly explained, where, although these two regions, namely that of Intelligences and that of the Trinity, seem to differ only in purity and exaltation of essence, nevertheless the Prophet indicates that they are contained in one Empyrean heaven, so called from its perfect illumination, no differently than air and fire are contained in the ethereal heaven. For the single heaven, encompassing the convexity of the firmament, resembled the likeness of a man, whose upper part, from the loins of the image upwards, shone with fire of an amber-like form, that is, most subtle and most spiritual; while the lower part, from the loins downwards, gleamed with fire somewhat denser and thicker: through which partition of this place it seems to indicate two regions differing in dignity, namely, the precœlestial heaven proper to spiritual creatures, and that supercœlestial one.

CAPUT III.

On the origin of prime matter, whether it is created or uncreated?

<span style="font-size: 3em; float: left; margin-right: 0.2em; line-height: 0.8em;">I</span>NGENS disagreement arises among more recent Philosophers concerning the origin of prime matter's creation; the larger chorus of whom assertively says that it was created; among whom Artefius uses nearly these words: The Creator of all things in the beginning, without uttering a word, said; Let such a creature be made, and afterwards that nature itself or prime matter was created by God. But another, smaller chorus, of which Paracelsus partakes with the rest of his school, calls this matter a great mystery, which had no likeness to anything created, nor was it even created, but only prepared by the most high artificer God. Both these schools, however, try to prove their reasons from the Holy Scripture brought forth by Moses, interpreting the nature and sense of the word "Beginning" in various ways. For Artefius, with others of his opinion, explains the beginning of the narrative of Genesis handed down to us by Moses, namely, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, etc." in this way: "Firstly or primarily God created the heaven and the earth." And indeed, the followers of Paracelsus, striving to refute this exposition of the word "Beginning," propose these three doubts to us: Whether, namely, by "in primis" or "primò" the interpreter intended to refer the name of the Beginning to some time, or to order and time simultaneously, or whether by it he intended to designate the first place. To these questions, indeed, they respond by absolutely and confidently denying them: To the first, that time did not yet exist, since it had its origin only from evening and morning; hence they admit that interpretation of "beginning" in no way. To the second, that it is absurd to place the world in time and order before its matter.

--- Page 655 ---
24          TREATISE I. BOOK I.

first matter; because, obviously, things in potential are not placed after things in actuality, nor the principle after that which is principled; therefore, they completely reject this interpretation. Finally, they contend that the name "Principle" cannot be adapted to "place" by a reason drawn from these words in chapter 1 of the Gospel of Saint John, "The Word was in the beginning"; for to wish to include the Word of God in a place is believed to be an impiety by all pious people, since it is incomprehensible; and moreover, even before the creation of the world, there was no place, because there was nothing located. With these, I say, and similar arguments, Paracelsus, with some of his disciples, attempts to refute the aforesaid opinion of the opposing sect, who takes the primordial words of Moses in this sense: "In a great uncreated mystery God created heaven and earth," that is, "in the first unformed, dark, and potential matter God created heaven and earth." And this Paracelsian opinion does not seem to differ from that of the Peripatetics, who, considering the world to be eternal, also established that the first matter was co-eternal with the World itself. Some philosophers also rise up against the creation of Hyle with an argument of this kind: "That which is unformed is not created: But hyle is unformed: Therefore hyle is not created." The major premise is clearly demonstrated by the fact that creation is an actualization, and to make something out of nothing: But hyle in its nature is nothing in actuality, wherefore it is certain that it lacks all form. But all these ambiguous and controversial disputes of these philosophers I refer to my superiors in Philosophy, and to those far more learned than myself in these matters, at least I will descend to the description of that matter.

CHAPTER IV.

Description of the First Matter or the Subject of the Universal Work.

MATTER or the subject, in whose bosom that greatest architect of our Macrocosm arranged its structure, is that Philosophical *hyle*; which physicists have called absolutely first matter: and indeed, just as nothing is more common than it, so also nothing is found more unknown than it. Therefore, concerning its investigation, two among other ancient philosophers especially devoted diligent effort: the former of whom, namely Thales (with whom Heraclitus and Hesiod agreed), after long study and many nocturnal labors, constantly affirmed that water is the first matter of things, and he confirms the reason for his opinion, because, he says, "the seed and nourishment of all things is moisture." Both pagan and sacred writers also seem to approve of this opinion. For the former consecrated Neptune, Oceanus, and Tethys for this reason; the latter, among whom I name that divine high priest of Philosophy, Moses, called this matter "abyss" and "water"; and St. Peter (2.3) indicated to us that heaven and earth were from water and through water. The other diligent investigator of this matter was Anaxagoras, who, after many labors endured in this study, was of the opinion that the first matter of things was a rude and undigested mass, called Chaos, to which the Poet in Metamorphoses also seems to assent: Other philosophers wrote differently about this matter: For Anaximander established infinite principles as the material origin, Anaximenes infinite air, Diogenes air endowed with divine reason, Plato an invisible and unformed species, Zeno the Stoic the substance of fire converted into water through air, the Epicureans atoms, Empedocles the four elements; who almost all, because of the hidden and secret disposition of this mystery, which without doubt is truly and essentially known only to God alone, wrote uncertainly and indeterminately, contradicting each other, and whatever

--- Page 656 ---
**ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THE MACROCOSM.** 25
whatever they conceived vigorously and probably in their minds, this they immediately set forth in their books: This Plato also seems sufficiently to confirm in his *Timaeus*, while he describes this matter as *being a thing perceptible without sense, and scarcely credible by spurious reasoning;* for indeed from these words it is clear that his knowledge in this matter is like a dream, and mere imagination. To whom also in this part Augustine, as is clear from the following discourse, seems in a way to agree: *“When,” he says, “I conceive something formless, I understand nothing more than I understood; just as by seeing nothing, darkness is seen, by hearing nothing, silence is heard.”* The difficulty of knowing this thing is admitted even by Aristotle himself, who asserts that this matter cannot be known or described by itself, except by analogy, that is, by examples taken from accidents. Hence he, with other Greek Philosophers, assimilated it to *hyle*, that is, to an immense forest, whose wood is suitable for constructing any house, machine, or other thing. Hence also that divine Moses compared it sometimes to empty and void earth, sometimes to waters and the abyss; Hermes Trismegistus in his *Poimandres*, to a certain horrible shadow migrating into a humid nature; Plato to the mother, nurse, and seat of generated things, because it contains and fosters all things: Augustine to darkness and silence, as has been said: Pythagoras to duality: Some to a mirror, in which the soul of the world is seen: others to wax and clay, which are suitable for receiving any impression; *There are also those who wish to compare it to an ointment, which is ready to receive and retain any scent.* And hence it is that Plato called it infinite; namely, because of its inclination towards infinite forms: Although this matter can also be called infinite as far as we are concerned; for GOD alone knows how widely this potential extends beyond the convexity of the world. And Aristotle seems to understand this same thing in his *book On the Heavens and the World;* where he says, *that outside the heaven there is neither place, nor body, nor dimension, nor repletion, nor time, nor number, nor measure of moving,* and consequently nothing exists outside the heaven except this formless matter, to which the aforesaid properties alone are proper. Hence also it is that Hermes Trismegistus in his sacred discourse speaks these words; *“Shadow,” he says, “infinite to the abyss, etc.”*

We conclude therefore from all the writings of both ancient and more recent Philosophers, that this first matter is a primordial Being, infinite, formless, in potentiality both for something and for nothing; of no quantity or dimension, since it can be called neither small nor great; of no quality, since it is neither subtle, nor dense, nor perceptible; of no property, nor inclination, neither moving, nor resting, without any color or elementary quality; Yet the first passive recipient of all actions, and capable of things: Hence it is called the mother of the world, in whose bosom the ethereal orbs adorned with gleaming fires, and the four elements suspended below near the center, are contained as in a maternal womb. Moreover, we have depicted here an imaginary effigy of this formless matter, imitating the description of Hermes Trismegistus and the truthful Moses, in the form of the blackest smoke, or vapor, or a horrible shadow, or a dark abyss, or finally a certain rude, undigested, and imperceptible mass.

CHAPTER V.
On darkness & privation.

AUGUSTINE against the Manichaeans asserts that privation is nothing other than darkness, which is defined as the absence of light. But if the meaning of darkness is rightly considered, we will perceive that it extends more broadly than the term privation. For, as Moses testifies, darkness was upon the face of the deep, before light or form was created; but privation cannot be named except with respect to a certain position, that is, where there is the absence of some preceding form. Therefore, so that I may agree with Augustine, every privation is darkness, that is, of luminous
                                                                                                        form

--- Page 658 ---
DE MACROCOSMI PRINCIPIIS. 27

absence of a lucid form, but not vice versa: Hence it is manifest that darkness, or privation, occurs only from the creation of the world to things subject to corruption, such as the elements and things composed of elements in the lower heaven: for since the form of the elements is not sufficient to satisfy the appetite of matter (whence their volatility and imperfection), it is necessary that their matter itself always desires a new form: and since this appetite cannot be satisfied without the absence of the preceding form, it is necessary that corruption or putrefaction precedes that new form, the old form having been first extinguished and cast off, the signs of which are darkness, which is nothing other than blackness and obscurity signifying the absence of light and form, from which the beauty and essence of the putrefied thing was previously derived and known. However, the Chemical Philosophers have called this blackness by many names: among which they often called this sign of putrefaction the "raven's head," by which they understood a purely accidental principle, and a medium associating matter and form, joining the bridegroom with the bride, which dark color indeed perishes immediately after generation. Here, therefore, it must be considered that the matter of a thing, while submerged in darkness, is in a state of privation, just as the prime matter of the macrocosm before the production of light, for it has the potential for the presence and beauty of a certain light, without which it can never be brought into actuality: It must be understood, however, that the word "darkness" has a twofold meaning among philosophers; for sometimes it is taken for some dark substance, namely, as for dark and black air, or for the shadow of some opaque body, and sometimes it is taken for a mere accident, namely, for the color of blackness: In the former sense, it is said by Moses to be "upon the face of the deep"; in the latter, it is considered as the privation of light; however it may be taken, darkness is always entirely contrary to light. For darkness makes a thing hidden and secret, induces fear and sadness, removes shame, promotes sleep, and is most friendly to rest; hence, darkness is a companion to matter: But light renders a thing known and manifest, removes fear, brings confidence, courage, and joy, makes people modest, drives away sluggishness and idleness, and does not allow an animal to rest, since it excites life and motion in its blood: for it is, as was said above, the origin of forms and actions.

CHAPTER VI.
Concerning the universal essence, by which the Creator of the universal work informed matter.

[Large decorative initial S] APIENTISSIMUS Creator of the world, who said, "I am the light of the world," the true fire, and father of lights, decreed to make this unformed matter, this foundation of nature, or subject of the universal machine, the dwelling place of forms, and, to speak with Plato, their nurse; so that by their presence the whole mass of the abyss, overwhelmed by darkness, might be rendered visible and perceptible and brought into actuality, which, to be easily perfected, He first most freely communicated the clarity of His fire to the Empyrean heaven (for the spirit of His mouth, which Mercurius Trismegistus calls the GOD of fire and the deity of spirit, was carried upon the waters), and then secondarily to the ethereal heaven and to the sun and the other spherical creatures of the same kind, so that through their virtue, as through instruments, the ethereal heaven might be adorned, and form and life might be imparted to the lower creatures: This fiery creature, created on the first day in the likeness of the divine idea, and given as the first and most excellent gift by GOD for the perfection of His remaining structure, Moses called "light," Artefius "clarity," Plato "idea," and Aristotle "the divine and best principle:" For he himself, in his book "On the Sacred Substance," acknowledges that light gives form, beauty, and being to all things, since without it no matter can be manifested or known, but remains hidden and, as it were, in potential: This very light Mercurius Trismegistus

--- Page 659 ---
28 TREATISE, BOOK 1, CHAPTER 1.

Trismegistus in his sacred discourse called it holy splendor, which he asserts flourished in the beginning and brought forth the elements from sand and moist nature; by which holy splendor Marsilio Ficino, in his commentary on that discourse, wished the formless bosom of matter to be illuminated by forms. Finally, almost all with unanimous consent are accustomed to call it the first act, form, species, and essence. This light, therefore, is a unique substance, and it is corporeal, existing simply in itself, the simplest, most worthy, and most noble of all; indeed, it is of such nobility, as Augustine testifies in his commentary on Genesis, that even corporeal things, the more they partake of light, the more perfect and noble they are considered; whence he confidently states that light holds the first place among bodies. And this substance of light, the same Augustine and Dionysius define, because of its sweet heat, to be pure fire, incombustible, immeasurable, and indivisible, growing and multiplying itself infinitely, extending itself everywhere and present to all in one moment, comprehending all things, yet not comprehended, always shining in itself, but invisible and unknown to others by itself: because it never illuminates visibly unless some body, whose matter is apt to be illuminated, intervenes. And hence it is that the substance of the middle heaven, although it is very luminous in itself, and on account of the abundance of its light holds the first place among composite bodies, nevertheless does not illuminate during the nighttime. From this super-celestial source of light, therefore, that invisible fire of Zoroaster and Heraclitus is undoubtedly derived, from which they teach all things were generated; whose power, though invisible, all animals, and all other sublunar creatures, indeed, even the sea itself in its ebb and flow, day and night, seem to recognize and perceive. Finally, philosophers call this fire a simple act because of its vivacity; than which nothing is more mobile, and in its movement swifter and more powerful, nothing more subtle, and because of its subtlety more penetrating, nothing more useful or full of virtue, nothing more beautiful, or more uniform in its essence, nothing more perfecting and exalting beings to a greater or lesser degree, nothing dissolving them more quickly, and more easily removing their bonds, as Calcidius testifies in his commentary on Timaeus. From which it is manifest, against Damascenus and Aristotle, who in this respect somewhat contradicts himself, that light is not an accident, which in itself is nothing, whence to render the substance to which it adheres more noble does not seem probable, because that is the office of the essential form, from which both the name of any body and its being are derived. We conclude, therefore, that light is either uncreated, namely, GOD, who gives nature to all things; (for in God the Father himself is true light, then in His Son is illuminating and abundant splendor, and in the Holy Spirit is burning brilliance surpassing all understanding) or created from that uncreated [light], which is either the simplest quasi-soul of any of the three heavens, and the true essential form, informing the most limpid spirit, as its receptacle and vehicle. Hence Iamblichus, because of the luminosity of the aether, thought it was nothing other than light itself, or in any of their composite creatures: For in angels there is a certain infused shining intelligence, diffused beyond all bounds of reason, yet received in different degrees according to the nature of the recipient; It then descends to celestial things, where in them it produces a vivifying power, whence life and effective propagation with vivifying splendor are imparted to lower things: In humans there is a lucid discourse of reason, in other animals there is a hidden fire manifestly governing the actions of life and sense; in plants there is a certain lucid soul, lying hidden around their centers, causing vegetation and multiplication infinitely: in minerals there is also a spark of splendor promoting them towards the goal of perfection. From the supernatural light, therefore, created on the first day, arise the differences of the macrocosms of the heavens, and of the bodies existing in them (for they are distinguished by purity, simplicity, and dignity): For according to the degrees of excess or defect of this essence, the highest heaven differs from the lowest, and the lowest from the middle, and

--- Page 660 ---
ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THE MACROCOSM. 29
and every element of each heaven is found to be depressed or exalted by its presence or absence: for the more matter differs from the nobility of form, the grosser, more impure, darker, and more unworthy it is. Hence also the diversity of created things and substances, hence their perfection and imperfection, rawness and maturity, volatility and fixation, density and subtlety, darkness and splendor, gravity and levity, and every proportion of things distinguishing one from another, according to Hermes Trismegistus, asserting in his sacred discourse that distinct and balanced things are carried by a fiery spirit: for prime matter before the production of this light was not capable of the aforesaid qualities, because, equally dark and empty, it always retained the same state of imperfection, as if utterly destitute of all action by which it might move from one state to another. From which it is manifest that, if clarity from light were removed from the world, matter would return to its first state and disposition, and no particle of it should be believed to be superior to the others in dignity, place, or any other quality or quantity. *Demonstrations by which it becomes manifest that, with the cessation of the action of the luminous form, and its complete absence, it is necessary for the world and its matter to return to the first abyss and*
*to dark matter, according to the reasons expressed by us above.*

      Since the presence of solar light is the closest and most similar of all to the luminous creature created on the first day, inasmuch as, according to the Fathers of Theology, the solar body was made on the fourth day as the receptacle of all its rays; therefore, we shall begin this demonstration of ours from its power and effect, by which we shall prove that the presence of light itself has caused this formal alteration in matter; and that in its absence, that very matter, once formed, will return to its pristine, that is, unformed, state.
      Let therefore a ball be made of lead, of sufficiently ample capacity, so that the thickness of its material is neither too thin, lest it break easily, nor too porous, lest air penetrate through it: In the summit of this, let a hole be made, into which a curved tube, descending almost to its bottom, made of the same material, is inserted, in such a way that no air can enter or exit by any other way than through the concavity of that channel. The other end of the same channel or curved tube should extend almost to the bottom of another vessel filled with water: Let the ball therefore be A, the channel or tube B, and the vessel filled with water C. We conclude therefore that the sun's rays, heating the ball A, will expel the thick and sooty air contained in ball A, through channel B, into vessel C, to the bottom of the water contained in that vessel C; which thick air, expelled by the power of heat, will mix with the water of vessel C, and will make many bubbles, one after another; But as soon as the sun has withdrawn, or some other object has been interposed between the sun itself and the ball, or the ball itself has been placed in shadow, the former state will return into the concavity of the ball in the absence of the sun and the cooling of the ball, namely, the same portion of thick and dark air that was there before. The proof is thus: since it cannot find the air in the same nature in the vessel filled with water, it draws to itself the water itself, which is still coarser, in place of the air, of which necessity compels such a proportion to descend into the ball as the solar rays first expelled from it by the subtilization and purification of the air; by which experiment, it is demonstrated as if with a finger, that all purification in this world and all inequality or diversity in thickness or thinness arises from the act of the essential light itself, and that by its presence such a difference is retained until the end of the world: But when light fails, all things will return to their pristine state, this is infallibly proven by this very experiment, the truth of which is also declared to common eyes by the two experiments written below, which derive their effects from elementary fire. We have thus depicted the demonstration of this first experiment.

CHAPTER. VII.

*On the two simple & primary qualities, derived from the two first sub-
stances: likewise on the two qualities arising from
those simple ones.*

[Large decorative initial E]
FROM each of the two aforementioned parts of the constitution arises a certain simple nature, which bears the disposition of its source: For when the fiery spirit was carried upon the waters (which we called above the fount of light and the origin of forms), it produced a certain essential quality accompanying its actions: Hence the Philosophers called it an agent, as it were, an effect of the most vibrant form or light, which they also called heat, whose nature it is to penetrate even to the center of density, and by penetrating to open dense and solid things, and by dilating them to resolve them, and to make them loose, and after their resolution to dissipate and separate the gross from the subtle, and by rarefaction or attenuation to cleanse them, and to make them volatile and light; whence by nature they are elevated and carried upwards: Finally, it gathers, digests, matures, fixes, and perfects homogeneous things; but heterogeneous things it cuts, disaggregates, expels, and reverberates: all of which it accomplishes, inasmuch as it is immediately derived from the noblest and most subtle of all bodies, and accompanies its most tenuous and noblest substance. Therefore, with the origin of this active nature declared, it remains that the quality or simple nature of the other constitutive part, namely the passive one, now be revealed, since no action can occur without a disposed passion. Hence it is necessary,

--- Page 665 ---
54 TRACTATUS I. LIB. I.

it is necessary that such a disposition be derived from hyle, or the prime matter of the macrocosm, overwhelmed by darkness before the origin of heat. For at the first appearance of light, shadows began to move, and, just as heat was induced by the motion of light, so also by the motion of the substance of the abyss, another quality, tolerating the actions of heat, and therefore called passive (inasmuch as it suffers more than it acts), is produced; which accompanies the grosser substance of matter no differently, and is intensified and remitted according to its grossness, than heat [accompanies] that essence of light, which is also perceived as more intense or more remiss according to its abundance or scarcity. Therefore, the nature of coldness, now manifested by the origin of heat, is entirely opposed to and adverse to heat, which it resisted as it pursued it with its subtle penetration, and by resisting, by simultaneously gathering, restricting, and condensing the more impure, grosser, and darker parts of the substance of the abyss, it contracted them towards the center of the cosmos, since coldness naturally flees there, as if to a place more remote from the periphery of the world, in which a greater and purer essence of the luminous Spirit exists, enclosed within it from the origin: And hence the grossness of the lower celestial elements, hence the density, opacity, and darkness of the earth: Hence also it is, that no heavy thing could pass beyond the center point, even if some hole were bored directly through the entire mass of the earth, namely, because the central point of the earth itself is a part more remote from the circumference of the world, and consequently, the seat in which coldness naturally desires to rest, as if free and immune from the enmity of heat and its contrary action. We conclude therefore, that the hot embraces forms more, and provides to each thing the functions of life, and is the companion of its soul: but the cold possesses material bodies, and loves them, and naturally inheres in them. Therefore, from the mutual action and passion of these, some parts of the macrocosm are made more or less subtle according to the recession of coldness and the accession of heat, namely, the superior ones, and some are made grosser according to the absence of heat and the presence of coldness, namely, the inferior ones. Thus therefore was the world made and its regions distinct, and if these natures fail, it is necessary that all things return to their pristine state, and be reduced from something in act to something in potency. From these simple natures or qualities, however, two other dispositions arise, which Artefius called "simple from simples," namely, humidity and dryness: of which the former arises from the mixture and temperament of the two simples: For if heat is joined with an equal part of coldness, the nature of humidity arises: But we call that quality dryness when it is joined with heat or coldness where humidity is entirely absent. It is therefore clear that dryness is nothing other than the absence of humidity, and hence these two qualities are called contrary to each other; yet they are passive with respect to the primary simples, as we shall explain below in its proper place.

a spiritual receptacle and container for the fiery, clear, and lucid soul descending from the Empyrean heaven: therefore, in this spirit, or fifth essence, all generative and seminal virtue resides. Finally, the supreme part of this spiritual matter is so purified and made spiritual by the newly created light and its so inexplicable splendor, and as if intoxicated by the lucid and illuminated nectar of the same, that almost its entire substance is nothing other than mere essential form, especially with respect to lower things, by which the other dark hyle parts are reduced from potential to act. If some spark from this formal mass descends into its middle region, it is immediately received by the middle spirit, namely the ethereal one, and enveloped in its subtle corpuscle; and then both, namely, the vehicle and that which is carried, descending downwards, are enclosed in the body of the lower region in such a way as the soul itself descended in the middle spirit, as will be more fully explained at the end of the second book of this treatise. From these things, therefore, it is manifest that darkness relates to matter in potential as light relates to it in act, and that matter not brought into act is, as it were, a certain substance overshadowed and hidden by the gloom of darkness: This is, between something and nothing, and a being scarcely imaginable, because unformed and unknown a priori, which indeed is clarified, informed, manifested by the presence of light, and is known a posteriori to exist in the form of subtle waters, along with Thales, Hesiod, Moses, and Peter the Apostle, whose lower region is called air, containing water, which is called dense air, and the spheres of the superior sublunary elements; the middle is called aether and the middle spirit; and the supreme is called the dwelling place of light and fiery love, as we will demonstrate more extensively below in its proper place.

CHAPTER IX.

*That the entire substance of the heavens, both spiritual and corporeal,*
*is either an element or composed of elements.*

THEREFORE, after the completion of this divine work, every portion of the
substance of any of its regions has been found to be either an element or ele-
mentated; of which, that which is called an element is the first, smallest,
and simplest part, from which the elementated (substance) of any heaven is
immediately constituted. And because the substance of any heaven is considered
coarser, more impure, and more imperfect due to a greater or lesser presence
of light, therefore the simplicity of the element is understood either absolutely,
only of the elements of the spiritual heaven, or is considered relatively:
For if they are compared to those of an inferior heaven, E 3 simpler

--- Page 669 ---
58          TREATISE I. BOOK I.
are called simple and pure; but in respect to the superior, the elements are judged dense and material, and consequently less pure. For the elements of the spiritual heaven, on account of their inexplicable simplicity, spiritual purity, and ineffable virtues, sacred writers confess to exist not only in the blessed intelligences and angels frequenting that abode, but also in God himself, the ordainer and patron of the entire structure. For in angels there is stability of essence, and an earthly power, by which they are the firm seats of God; there is also in angels clemency and piety, which is a watery and purifying virtue; moreover, there is in them a subtle and airy Spirit, whence in sacred Scripture they are called the wings or feathers of the winds; finally, there is in them love, which is the most splendid fire. And hence it is that the Royal Psalmist speaks: *Who makes your angels spirits, and your ministers a flaming fire.* Moreover, Seraphim, Virtues, and Powers are fiery: Cherubim are earthly, Thrones and Archangels are watery; Dominions and Principalities, however, are airy. Finally, concerning the Archetype itself, it is said: *Let the earth open and bring forth a Savior.* Likewise, it is called *a fountain of living water*, which purifies and regenerates. It is also called *the Spirit of life, a breathing spirit*, and finally, according to Moses and Saint Paul, it is *a consuming fire*. Similarly, the sphere of the Trinity, without doubt, is the more luminous and subtle part of that spiritual heaven, since it is the abode of the Trinity, to which the Seraphim are closest. Its throne or foundation, however, is the firmament or crystalline sphere, which Saint John called the glassy sea, by which he denoted something earthly, subtle, and watery; by diligently considering these extremes, the intermediate natures are easily understood. Elements are also found everywhere in the ethereal heaven, whose mass is called the fifth essence, because they are exalted above those four of the lower heaven both in dignity, subtlety, and place. For in this region there is the solidity of earth without the grossness of water, and the agility of air far from efflux, and the heat of fire is incombustible, incorruptible, preservative, luminous, and vivifies all bodies of the lower heaven with its heat, since it is immediately derived from the spiritual heaven. The creatures of this region also partake of its elements, since its stars, both fixed and wandering, claim more eminent dispositions from them. Thus, among the Planets, *Mars & Sol*, among the fixed stars *Aries & Leo* are called fiery constellations from their heat combined with dryness: *Jupiter & Venus, Gemini & Libra* are airy, because they retain hot and humid natures: *Saturn & Capricorn* are called earthly, from their melancholic disposition: finally, *the Moon* is known to have a watery faculty, since it is called the mistress of humors by Philosophers: And so also among the images of the Zodiac, *Cancer & Pisces*. Hence it is also that Astrologers have especially observed the triplicity of this heaven, without whose observation they can accomplish nothing in their art. Through the qualities of these elements, too, each Planet produces various effects in these lower regions, as we shall declare below in its proper place. Finally, that the elements, along with the elementates, occupy the lowest space of the world, no one, not even the ignorant, can be unaware: but these are more impure, grosser, more subject to our senses, and more prone to corruption, as being far less worthy and simpler than the other, more sublime ones. And by the same reasoning, creatures formed from the composition of these are known to obtain their complexions from their temperament. For the faculties of herbs and minerals are described and distinguished by heat, cold, humidity, and dryness, according to the dominance of the elements within them. Therefore, no one can deny that elements are found everywhere and in all regions of the world, but in a diverse manner according to the defect or abundance of the universal form; namely, in the lower region they are dreggy and gross, in the middle part purer and cleaner, in the summit or supercelestial part most spiritual and blessed in every respect. From which it is understood that elements in the Archetype are ideas of things to be produced, in intelligences they are distributed powers, in the ethereal heaven
                                                                                                              virtues

--- Page 670 ---
DE MACROCOSMI PRINCIPIIS. 39

powers, and in the lowest region, denser bodies imbued with coarser forms. Therefore, according to our intention, we conclude that the matter of an element is nothing other than each simple portion of prime matter embraced by the superior orb, and now brought into actuality by the presence of clarity; which portions are indeed distinguished from each other all the more, the richer they are found to be in essential form. For, as we said above, the nature of light is to purify, to subtilize, and to sublimate to the apex of the superior heaven, if it is possible, since it naturally tends upwards, and intends to carry upwards with itself, as much as it can, the substance it inhabits, that is, to make it more worthy, until it has led it to the summit of perfection. For then this nature is said to rest. Of these portions, I say, in each heaven there are four kinds and no more; for that portion of matter of any heaven which has more essential form, that is, light, and less matter, is called fire; but that which has less form and more matter is called earth; from the mixture of which portions intermediate elements are produced; of which one participates more in earth, namely water, since both are cold, because they have less form, but more matter; but the other participates in fire, namely air, since both are hot; and therefore have more form, but less matter. Whence it is manifest that elements are made from the varied action and passion of simple natures, since from them each portion of matter, called an element, is derived and distinguished.

C A P U T X.

*Concerning Chaos, and the principles of creatures of the lowest heaven.*

**M**ANIFOLD is the prime matter of things, as is manifest both from what precedes and from what follows; of which that which we called *Hyle* above is most remote from the composition of all things: The second is the matter of the elements, distinguished in itself by reason of predominant coldness or heat, and called by various names on account of its various positions and operations: The third is Chaos, or a confused and undigested mass of matter, in which all things, namely, the four elements, were confused and commingled, because from them earth and water, which are heavier than the others, rose upwards even to the orb of the moon; but fire and air, as lighter, descended even to the center of the earth. And this, according to some, was that formless mass of the matter of heaven and earth, gaping from the beginning, from which afterwards all things emerged individually through various species and proper forms; for without doubt this formless mass was, on the first day of creation, in both lower heavens, under a veil of blackness, reverberated by the light acting within it, and on the second day compressed into the lowest heaven, which we can more rightly define as a formless mass of darkness, or of waters lying hidden in darkness, supplying matter to the whole work, with a tiny portion of the luminous rays of each heaven retained in a dark prison by the viscosity of the said waters; which portions of light, however, without the aid of the perennial luminous fount (which they received gradually on the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth day, that is, more and more from the divine will of the Creator) could inform nothing; nor indeed did anything yet hold its proper place; for the portion of light due to the darkness of the Empyrean heaven possessed the center of the dark mass against its nature, and that other portion, which was proper to the middle heaven, was more upwards, that is, above the incarcerated light of the Empyrean heaven, towards the concave

--- Page 671 ---
40          T R E A T I S E  I.  B O O K  I.
the concave surface of its region was retained in that undigested mass, so that, contrary to the order of nature, a denser and heavier portion of light occupied a higher place, while the more subtle and lighter occupied the lowest parts; and for this reason, because of this inverted position and arrangement, growing things could not yet be informed by the light of the middle heaven. This, finally, is that matter about which philosophers, both ancient and chemists and more recent ones, as well as poets, sang and wrote in their books, and from which they necessarily wished diverse natures to be drawn forth, both for the perfection of the macrocosm and also for the completion of the Philosophical Work. But the philosophers called that the fourth and ultimate first matter which is closer to bodies, and from which the compounds of the lowest heaven are immediately generated and multiplied; of which kind in animals is recognized as sperm, in growing things, seeds, and in minerals, sulfur and quicksilver: Concerning these, we will treat more extensively below. But we thus describe the Philosophical Chaos according to their common intention, where hot things fought with cold, and moist with dry.

Although we ourselves are eyewitnesses, we can delineate a better demonstration of this thing in the anatomization of any part of that mass (for according to *Aegidius de Vadis* only some part of that matter, sufficiently known to all, remained in the world). For in the outer part of the same mass, I clearly observed at first glance, at a friend's place, a foul, very black, and ponderous substance of earth, by whose blackness and horrid veil all the other elements, indeed even the substance of the Sun itself and the heavens, were so covered that no natural order could be found in them. For I discovered everything therein placed against the laws of nature; since what was light was pressed down towards the center, while what was heavy, I perceived to dwell around the periphery of the mass; for by anatomizing this deformed body with nature's most fervent knife, namely fire, I saw fluid water to be contiguous to this deformed, most black, and earthy crust appearing in the outer part of the mass, so that that middle part of the water, more interacting and conjoined with this earthy nature, flowed out first of all, according to that earthy coldness which it clearly and crudely had within itself; but another part of this element, nearer to the fire and the center of the mass, tinctured and mixed on all sides with airy spirit, I perceived to distill after that crude nature; so that I observed air to be equally mixed with water in the lower part of the watery sphere, that is, tending more towards the center of the mass; nor yet was the humidity of such air free from the rebellious dryness of the black earth; which earth indeed not only in the periphery of the mass, where it held its chief and more royal seat in confusion, but also diffused its power throughout the entire mass, and dispersed the vapors of its nature through it, so that no part of the entire mass existed pure and free from that most black defilement. After the airy water, fire emerged from the abyss of that chaos, foul and ill-smelling because of the earthy pollution. From which it is certain that this fire had continuous war and conflict with that part of the watery substance which was imbued with air; for while that fire naturally sought and attempted to be nourished by its airy food, it continually experienced the constant injuries of that hostile water mixed with the said air. But from the middle and innermost center of the entire formless mass, as if from the very point of the entire abyss, I observed the solar substance of the mass miserably and as if from purgatory, as if rising from the dead and still laboring with the impurity of the mass and appearing as if sick, and by a wonderful operation of ingenuity and philosophical industry, to be sublimated: And indeed, some Philosophers have called this obscure part of the mass the Central Sun. By whose operation, indeed, we are taught in what manner in the beginning of the world, this our celestial Sun, after a purification first made in this lower place, was exalted to its incorruptible place, that is, into the heart of the ethereal heaven, as we shall more clearly demonstrate *in the 4th book of this treatise, in the chapter on the rising of the Sun*. But these precious gems having been extracted from that most black mass, and as if snatched by violence, I found a certain foul and very black matter left at the bottom, whose blackness was manifest, but whose redness was hidden, having a quasi-metallic nature; This, like Lucifer, having fallen from heaven, was cast down to the lowest abyss, because it strove to preside over and predominate even celestial matter.
