C H A P T E R I.

*Of the world and its division*

[Large decorative initial M] MARTIANUS accepts the term 'world' in three ways, namely, either for that which is called the Archetype; whose substance is incorporeal, invisible, intellectual, and eternal, according to whose example and divine image the real beauty and form of the world was fashioned, as Boethius testifies: And this world is permanent in the divine mind. Or for the corporeal heaven, which is that greater world, which is bounded and contained by the concave surface of the *primum mobile*; and this world also is eternal by the will of God. Or finally for man, who is called the lesser world, and is said to be perpetual with respect to form, but corruptible with respect to matter. We, however, not differing much from Martianus' opinion, will treat of a twofold world; namely, of the Macrocosm and the Microcosm, distinguishing the former from man or the Microcosm, considering that whole space of prime matter as the world, cosmos, or macrocosm, which the spiritual light or spirit of the Lord, encompassing the waters, comprehends in its circular embrace. This circular portion of the substance of the abyss, from the varied confluence of light and darkness, by disposition, that is, by distinction into degrees of temperaments through purity and impurity, is distributed into three parts differing in formal nature: Of which the superior is that space of the world, in which the fiery spirit was carried, and the primary substance of light is contained, extending itself from the concave extremity of the sphere of the Trinity up to the convex surface of the starry heaven. And indeed the substance of this part of the world, because of the abundance of its form, is so subtle and pure, that with respect to us it is considered insensible and entirely imperceptible: Hence the Philosophers called it intellectual, and in the highest degree spiritual. The middle part, however, is adorned with fixed and wandering stars; for it possesses that whole concavity of the universe, which is comprised between the convex surface of the lunar orb and the concave surface of the *primum mobile*; and the substance of this region is corporeal with respect to the superior. Finally, the inferior part of the world is that whole space, which the concave surface of the lunar orb embraces: Hence it becomes clear that the mass of the world is distinguished into two principal parts; one of which is incorporeal, spiritual, purest, and most subtle, namely the superior; while the other is corporeal. And this corporeal part is again subdivided into two parts; one of which is subtle, tenuous, and incorruptible, namely the middle part; while the other is impure, gross, and subject to corruption; and this is the lowest portion of the world, which we shall hereafter call sublunary and elemental. These regions of the Macrocosm, however, both ancient Philosophers and sacred Writers have called Heavens. For they named the superior, the Empyrean heaven, and as it were fiery, because it is everywhere filled with spiritual fire or the substance of light. And this was that third heaven into which Saint Paul confessed himself to have been caught up by the Spirit, which he himself called Paradise;

--- Page 677 ---
48          TREATISE I. BOOK II.
...called Paradise: But the middle (part) all writers generally called the ethereal and as it were luminous heaven, and heaven *par excellence*. Finally, the Apostle *Matthew* seems to call that whole aerial mass between the ether and the earth heaven, speaking in these words: "The birds of the air build their nests, etc." But since the subtle part of earth is water, and the subtle part of water is air, and the subtle part of air is fire (for there is a rotation of one element into another), it is necessary that this whole region also be called heaven. For Saint *Peter* confesses that the matter of the firmament and the earth is the same. Ezekiel also describes the natures and positions of these three heavens, expressed in his vision, chapter 1. For there a great cloud surrounded by fire describes two heavens, namely, one above the firmament, the other below. But the lower heaven is that whole space delineated below the cloud. From these things, therefore, it is clearly evident that the entire substance of the world is nothing other than these three heavens, differing in subtlety and density, that is, in purity and impurity.

CHAPTER II.

*That GOD shone only to Himself before the creation of the world: Concerning the loving gift that GOD gave to the hyle, the part forming the world: Whence the spherical shape of the world?*

MONAD, according to Hermes Trismegistus (who is the light of the world), before the ages, fire gave birth to the monad, that is, GOD, and reflected its ardor within itself: For this father of lights shone only within Himself before the creation of the world, nor did He wish to reveal His clarity until He thought about the creation of the world. (Psalm 18, v. 11. He made darkness His secret place, and His tabernacle He made with dark waters, and covered it with thick clouds. Hence a portion of the hyle outside the world is signified: Darkness and clouds are around Him. Psalm 97, v. 2.) For then, says Mercurius Trismegistus, He changed His form, that is, He manifested His hidden essence, by which He suddenly revealed all things. (Psalm 18, v. 12. at the splendor of His presence, clouds and dark waters fled) Therefore, this omnipotent GOD freely and uncoerced decided in His ineffable wisdom to create the Macrocosm, and before its structure, to mystically determine its matter, essence, figure, dimension, and the concatenation of its parts: He chose matter from the bosom of infinite hyle for this structure, suitable to be adorned with diverse virtues and essential forms; He wished to freely bestow upon it a holy and loving gift, proceeding immediately from Himself: For actually, before creation, GOD breathed, and the Spirit of His mouth, that is, a passive breathing, proceeding from Him by way of bestowable love, was carried upon the waters, that is, the watery sphere, or rather, it moved around and upon all the matter of the corporeal world, namely, upon the two lower heavens still unformed, whose primordial matter was water, as Saint Peter testifies (2. 3).

It was carried, I say, doubtless by a circular motion in the world, effected by the spiritual presence of that very Spirit upon the convex surface of the material world, as by the noblest of all motions, by which the corporeal matter of the world, and its simplest spiritual substance, are distinguished from that infinite hyle or unformed mass of conglomeration pushed out beyond both worlds, and the corporeal world received its convex boundaries or edges, and the most capacious and noblest of all shapes, namely, the spherical. Indeed, this is that exalted gift of GOD, of the divine essence, which GOD gave to it, having the fullest aptitude by the power of its procession, so that it might be given, and proceeding only by way of bestowable love, in which all other gifts are given: because all gifts are called common by reason of the love of that Holy Spirit, who is infinite love proceeding from the Father and the Word; therefore, from His simple act, all virtues and essences, by divine will, are distributed to each part of the world as gifts, according to the saying of the royal Psalmist: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of His mouth all their power." Saint Paul also seems to confirm this same thing: "Through the Holy Spirit," he says, "all things are explored and individual things are distinguished by individual degrees." Therefore, this Spirit of the Lord, who is fiery love, was carried upon the waters, imparting fiery vigor to them, the divine will thus commanding: Whence the first creature of the world, the most subtle, simplest, noblest, and most active of all, first shone forth in the world. Therefore, even the pagans recognized this Spirit: For the oracles of the Chaldeans said that He was fiery love proceeding from the Father and the Word.

--- Page 679 ---
48 TREATISE I. BOOK II.
proceeding, as Iamblichus testifies; Hermes Trismegistus [called it] the GOD of fire and the deity of Spirit; Gentiles, as is read in Plutarch, described it as the intellectual and fiery Spirit itself, having no form, but transforming itself into whatever it wished and making itself equal to all things: Concerning which also Zoroaster and Heraclitus, speaking, wished all things to have been generated from a single fire: Hence also Orpheus, saying that the middle heaven was illuminated by the light of this fiery Spirit, called it aether, as if *aethaërem*, that is, a burning spirit, and *pyripnon*, that is, a fiery breath, as was said before: The Platonists called it the soul of the world, to which, as next in nobility, they acknowledged only light, saying that there is nothing in the circle of the firmament itself, besides the soul, that bears a greater likeness to GOD than light itself; indeed, some more recent Philosophers wish any thing to claim for itself as much Divinity as it is capable of light. Nor is it surprising, since GOD Himself, as is handed down in the sacred scriptures, calls Himself the light of the world and the father of lights, by whose holy gift or fiery spirit, which appeared to the Apostles in the form of fire, the mundane light, that is, the fiery vigor of the waters, was honored on the first day of creation, and from whose essential substance the heaven, in which the spirit moved, and both the lower heavens, and their creatures and their beauties divinely and metaphysically received their own. And hence it was that Democritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans, because they perceived the virtue of this divine nature to be present in all inferior creatures in greater or lesser degree, believed that all things were full of Gods, to whom they established divine honors, dedicating prayers and sacrifices to them, and venerating them with divine worship. Moreover, they reduced all these Gods to one JUPITER; by which they most clearly signified that all streams of heat, clarity, life, and essential forms emanate from a single supernatural luminous source, and from its perennial and spiritual water they obtain their increase and multiplication.

CHAPTER. III.
*Of the three prior days of creation.*

[T]HE knowledge of the arrangement of the days made before the creation of the Sun seems difficult, since even among the Theologian Fathers themselves, no small difference arises concerning the nature of those days. For Basil, Damascene, and other Greeks hold that that light made on the first day caused day through the emission of light, and night through its retraction, made by divine will. But the Doctors
Latin

--- Page 681 ---
30 TRACTATUS I. LIB. II.
The Latins probably say that that light made a circulation, similar to that which is now made by the Sun; and illuminated the hemisphere in which it was, and thus darkness was induced in the opposite hemisphere because of the obstruction of grosser, denser, and blacker matter; which existed in the midst of all unformed matter. But we will put forward a twofold interpretation of those days, neither of which, perhaps, when considered a little more accurately, will seem to deviate much from the boundary of truth; the first of which is, that the day before the creation of the Sun can be considered as primary, secondary, or tertiary light, extending itself through the entire transparent (medium), so indeed, that night is understood as the dominion of darkness, in that part where no light had yet shone forth. And thus the first day is taken for clarity generally dispersed throughout the entire Empyrean heaven, after it had, namely, driven darkness downwards from its region, and had purified and refined the spiritual matter of its heaven according to the proportion of its action. The morning of this day was the first penetration of divine light into its darkness, and the beginning of the action of light in the higher darkness; no differently than that time is called morning among us, when the Sun's rays begin to penetrate into the obscure and dark mass of night. Similarly, evening is the lowest surface of this heaven, in which still dark vapors exist as if on the surface of the middle region, and there they still revolve in an oblique revolution, and terminate the action of the first day, and so in the others. Nor certainly is this explanation to be entirely rejected, since both day and night must be considered with respect to the subject, to which the aforesaid dispositions of the two times ought to be applied. But indeed the Empyrean heaven after its creation was entirely luminous and clear: Whence it also received its name from fire, and for that reason neither night nor darkness was tolerated in it in any way immediately after its creation. And the same can be said about the substance of the ethereal heaven. Our second interpretation, however, which seems to us closer to the truth, inasmuch as it also directly agrees with the Latin Theologians, will elucidate itself from the following declaration. For it is probable that the divine Spirit, sent forth and carried upon the waters before any creation, encompassed them with a threefold circumvolution, and each of its courses produced a spiritual or supernatural day: Whence by its first circuit it constituted the first day, in which it perfected the Empyrean heaven, and drove darkness downwards by one degree. But by the second revolution it brought forth the second day, in which, by the twofold presence of divine power, darkness was pressed down by a second degree; and in this way divine light and power shone forth in the middle and ethereal region of the world. Finally, by its third and last revolution, through the third degree, and to the ultimate boundary from the circumference, the darkness of the third impression was dispersed by divine power. And thus the tabernacle of the entire world was completed, and by the power of the divine Spirit all the virtues and essences of its regions were produced. Here therefore those three spiritual days were finished, measured in no other way by the act of the divine Spirit, and related to the number of persons of the Trinity, all of whom acted for the creation of the world. For GOD the Father said; and by His Word the heavens were established, and by the Spirit from His mouth all their power. Therefore, in the space of these days, and after their completion, the heavens were produced and brought into being by divine operation, in which the universal Spirit of the macrocosm received form and being. Soon thereafter, the solar days, which are concerned with the more corporeal things of the world, received their origin; for producing the kinds of these creatures, the first three of these solar days arose, just as for fabricating the mansions of the three heavens, the three spiritual (days) first shone forth. For on the first solar day, which is the fourth from the origin of creation, the stars or wandering celestial bodies, and the creatures of heaven, on the second, all irrational animals, and on the last day, the lesser world or Microcosm were created and completed; no differently than the Macrocosm was brought to its perfection on the last spiritual day. Who therefore can almost doubt, but that

--- Page 682 ---

that such is the motion of the Sun after the completion of the world, as was the motion of the Spirit
before its perfection, since GOD after the end of the three spiritual days established his tabernacle
in the Sun itself? Therefore, through the Sun itself, as through the only demonstration from effect to cause (a posteriori) to the true motion of that divine Spirit, by which it moved, as said, each day for the composition of the world, we can arrive; nor indeed will anyone hesitate in this, that the subsequent days in creation were equal in dimension to the preceding ones, and consequently, that the divine Spirit moved in its revolution for the same time as the Sun moves in its own: Indeed, the solar body itself seems to be, as it were, a mirror and heart of the world, into which the supernatural rays of the Spirit itself, shining forth from the Trinity, are infused; by whose radiant power, beyond all human reason, that solar body is rendered visible, and it always exhibits a constant and immutable motion by divine will, producing days of the same quantity at all times, by which creation was completed: It seems therefore that that Holy Spirit, who appeared to the Apostles in the form of a radiant and shining dove, spiritually circled the waters, illuminating their darkness with its motion, and infusing its rays into them, and leaving them (the rays) to the waters after its departure, so that the waters might be informed by them, that it (the Spirit) clarified and illuminated all things spiritually in an ineffable way by its presence, no differently than the Sun does by its presence, corporally. And that (to pass on to the opinion of Latin Theologians) that uncreated light, by infusing light into created things, made the same circulation in the first three days of creation as the Sun thereafter completes each day with its motion; and that it illuminated its sphere, in which it was, no differently than the Sun illuminates its own; and similarly also that darkness was made in the opposite Hemisphere because of the interposition of grosser, denser, and more opaque matter in the middle of the whole formless mass or horrendous shadow. However, we have spoken of the motion of the divine Spirit upon the waters in the preceding chapter, at the end of which we also depicted, for human understanding, its motion made on the first day of creation; the reason for which emblem we explained near the end of this fifth chapter.

CAPUT IV.
*On the creation and nature of light, and on its operation and the constitution of the Empyrean heaven or the first region of the world.*

<span style="font-size: 3em; line-height: 0.5em; float: left; margin-right: 0.1em;">D</span>IXIT DOMINUS; *Let there be Light, and there was Light* on the first day the supreme heaven, most full of light. For the content of this heaven is nothing else than the most essential and most spiritual substance of light, formed from a large portion of soul and a small amount of the most subtle Spirit; which is therefore called the fiery Spirit and the Empyrean heaven, that is, fiery and burning, as *Isidore* says; not that it burns, like elemental fire, but because it is everywhere suffused with the splendor and clarity of light. Hence I do not agree with the opinions of those who thought this heaven to be immobile and at rest; because these properties are entirely contrary to the substance of light from which this heaven is formed; since light is the first and simple act; than which nothing is swifter in its motion. (*His lightning enlightened the world, and the earth, that is, the darkness, seeing it, was afraid and fled: Psalm 97, v. 4.*) Therefore, by the presence of this creature or fiery vigor, the darkness and gloom of that upper part, still formless and obscure, are driven downwards through an oblique revolution; and this for two reasons, the first of which is, because the hidden and potential quality of shadow is now revealed by the fiery activity of light and assumes the name of frigidity; whose disposition, since it is in every way contrary to the quality of luminous heat, is to flee and shun the operations of light and its object. It therefore happened from this, that the cruder and coarser part of matter because of
G 2 predo-

--- Page 683 ---
32 TREATISE I. BOOK II.
...predominant coldness in it, moved towards the center of the universal globe; which, being more distant from the dwelling place of the primary light, withdrew itself more and more. The second reason is; because the same relation exists between light and darkness, which exists between form and privation: wherefore darkness, avoiding the sight of light like a horrible shadow, to use the words of *Hermes Trismegistus*, glided away with an oblique revolution, and sought the center of the Periphery; and hence it is that this heaven is purified and cleansed in the highest degree, by separating the subtle from the dense; and is illuminated and made to shine beyond measure by driving all darkness from its margin towards the center. This heaven, therefore, or the supreme and supernatural region of the world, is the dwelling place of the luminous fount and, as it were, the homeland and native soil, in which the beginning of things, light, was first created and placed; whence it is called the foundation of the world, by whose formal presence the desire of the matter of this entire heaven is fulfilled in the highest degree. For it is certain that the matter of this heaven is very thin and subtle, since its entire substance is formal: For according to *Aristotle, Metaphysics Book 4*, where there is more form, there is less matter, and consequently, the density of matter argues for a scarcity of form; for the multitude of luminous form, by its actions, continually rarefies the purer part of the abyss of matter, retained in this heaven by divine will, and by rarefaction extends its mass more widely, just as is perceived in the art of chemistry; where if a dense substance in a sufficiently ample glass, hermetically sealed, is subtilized by a more vehement fire, its rarefied parts naturally seek a larger space; whence the glass ruptures, so that the attenuated vapors may find space more freely; So also the very clear matter of this heaven extends itself very widely, rarefied by the amiable heat of this heaven. And hence it is that this heaven, according to *Basil, Book 2 of Hexameron*, extends itself more widely than all heavens. We conclude, therefore, that this heaven is the noblest of all forms, and beyond all spiritual and simple imagination, the greatest of all in quantity on account of the attenuation of matter, most luminous in quality, and most filled with fiery vigor, most active in action, and most swift in the motion of its luminous substance, most pleasant in heat derived from motion, most temperate, amiable, not burning nor destroying, but connecting all lower things with harmonious peace by proportional bonds, and preserving them in its own spirit, which scarcely on account of its subtlety can be perceived by imagination, moving and living by itself, and existing in its connatural seat without contact with any heterogeneous thing, or any impediment of coldness, spherical in shape, which it received from the motion of the Spirit, which moved over the waters; and from the luminous virtue proceeding from it by divine will; By name it is called Empyrean, as if fiery, as above. It is also called Olympus from its clarity. It is also called supernatural, because beyond the laws of nature, spiritual against corporeality, and intellectual, because not visible to us, but only intelligible, and perceptible only by a posteriori demonstration, or because it is most filled with angels and intelligences.

CHAPTER VI.

*Concerning the middle heaven & concerning its various appellations and*
*the reason for them.*

[Large decorative initial M] THE middle region of the world, completed on the second day of creation, due to the downward-tending operations of the light matter, has various appellations; for as it is taken by itself; that is, with respect to its own proper matter, it is called the middle spirit after the dispersion of darkness; but with respect to the superior heaven, that is, the lucid substance, and its mixture with this spirit, it is called aether; however, insofar as it is referred to the four lower elements appearing and distinct on the third day, it is called the Fifth essence.

Therefore, by itself, that is, in its own substance revealed on the second day, and purified from its darkness, it presents the form of most subtle waters, and a certain vaporous and never-resting smoke. Hence among the Platonists it is called the middle spirit of the world, which we called the receptacle, retainer, and vehicle of essential light and the soul of the world above in chapter 5, book 1; where we also demonstrated the reason for the same appellation.

But insofar as this spirit is a retainer of light descending from a spiritual source, by whose action a vivifying and natural heat is excited; to that extent it is called aether, that is, shining, according to Isidore; because there is perpetual limpidity and clarity there; or fiery according to Anaxagoras, who affirms that everything that burns is called aether, since aether is nothing other than inflamed air, whence, according to Greek grammar, it is derived from αἴθω, which means 'I burn'; air spirit, as if 'athaer', that is, 'burning spirit': Wherefore Orpheus calls it Pyripnon, that is, fiery breath, and Porphyry with the other Platonists placed the soul of the world in the midst of this spirit; And hence it is that, according to Marianus, in the aether there is perpetual day, because darkness never approaches there; although its simple substance, separated from stellar bodies, is invisible, that is, not perceptible to mortal eyes, as we shall explain more fully in the following chapter.

Finally, it is considered a unique element, as Aristotle holds in his book Meteorologica, where he asserts that aether is nothing other than a unique element: Hence it is necessary that this unique element be outside the number of the four lower essences soon to be produced in the lowest region: and hence it is also called the fifth essence by Philosophers, in which nothing of corruption is found, because two contraries inducing putrefaction are not found in the same element.

From the reasons for these names, therefore, it is manifest that the matter of this region, formerly primary, but now secondary through its reduction to act, is nothing other than a most pure vapor, or a certain most subtle mist, generally called spirit; and its form, by whose presence it is brought into act, is that light or clarity essentially gushing forth from the perennial source of the divine and supercelestial spirit, and totally fulfilling the appetite of this middle spiritual matter, as will be declared below.

CHAPTER VII.

*The composition of the middle heaven, why it is called the sphere of equality? And why is this region, in respect to the superior, called the corporeal heaven?*

[Decorative initial V] Just as the Empyrean heaven was created on the first day from a single thing, namely from the substance of light, which is composed of three-quarters of the finest fire and one-quarter of the most subtle spirit; whence, in respect to inferior things, it is entirely formal, and on account of the predominance of fire in it, it is named fiery: So the matter of this second heaven, since it is more corporeal than that of the first and superior, corresponds to its luminous form, by that due proportion by which matter is accustomed to be weighed against its form with equal scales: whence it is composed of one part of fiery and most subtle light descending outside the source of the Empyrean heaven through the diaphragm of the crystalline sphere, and an equal quantity of primary matter already informed and having acquired the name of spirit, which Pythagoras also seems to assert, writing that the sun, moon, and other stars are formed from fire and air: Hence it is also that Artefius, with the support of the ancient Philosophers, named this region the heaven of equality, in whose center the wise placed the sphere of the soul; From which, it seems probable that the constitution of this heaven consists of two quarters of middle spirit, and an equal number of parts of most beautiful substance, well suited to the luminous soul for fulfilling the spiritual appetite of the same matter and preserving it from corruptible changes.

Now, that this region is more corporeal than that supreme one, we can prove by many reasons; one of which is, because, where there is less form, there is more matter; but in this second heaven there is less form than in the Empyrean heaven, whose entire substance is completely formal; Therefore, in this heaven there is more matter than in the Empyrean heaven. The major premise is drawn from the fourth book of Metaphysics. Another reason is, because the mass of primary matter, before the appearance of light, always retained a single and the same state, for it lacked an agent by whose actions it might be reduced from one disposition to another; Hence it could be called neither thinner nor thicker, since all its potential and imaginable parts are to be considered of the same condition both in one region of the potential world and in another. But since the disposition of light is such that nothing exists subtler than it, and nothing more penetrating and opening bodies, it is necessary that it always seeks to attenuate the parts of coarser matter, so that it may act and move more readily in them without impediment; whence, the more formal a thing is, the more subtle its substance must necessarily be; The reason for this, certainly, is purely philosophical, because formal light moves by its own act, and by its own motion excites heat; whose nature is to attenuate, to dilate, to dissipate: Hence, therefore, it is that that perennial fount of light, created on the first day in the superior region of the world, soon revealing its hidden matter and reducing it to act, formed the thin and most subtle part according to its own disposition, thrusting its coarser portion downwards towards the center into the middle region, so that it might govern the most simple substance of spirit, which it reduced as it were to a universal form, and transfer it with itself through all the hidden places of the world, without any impediment. And hence it is that the corporeal nature of half of this informed region, reflected into the middle, made the middle more corporeal...

C A P U T. VIII.

*Concerning the repercussion of the darkness of the twofold middle heaven into the lowest region of the world, and concerning the disposition and effect of its light, that is, concerning the heat originating from it, and that light shines invisibly through itself and in itself.*

[Large decorative initial V] IRTUE or clarity of the supernatural heaven, descending by the Creator's ordinance through the openings of the watery sieve, or rather, its breasts, and pouring itself downwards, as if from its perennial fount, into the middle heaven, which was still potential and unformed, by its presence dispersed the gloom and darkness of this part of matter, and drove them towards the lowest region, still invisible and hidden, thereby making its substance visible and formed, pure, subtle, thin, and far more excellent in perfection and beauty than the mass of the lower heaven. Indeed, this is that luminous essence gushing forth from the first supercelestial fount through infinite streams into every part of the celestial sea, which the ancients called aether; but we call it Secondary light, because it is immediately derived from the first root. Thus also, we shall call the rays of the Sun and stars penetrating into the lowest region of the world tertiary light.

This light, therefore, although secondary, is so active and filled with most vibrant power, that it frees this entire heaven from its primordial impurity, and drives away its darkness, and causes it to glide away into the lowest part of the world by an oblique revolution, like a dreadful shadow; it thrusts its imperfect and coarser parts, along with the darkness, down to the nether regions, separating the subtle from the dense, it illuminates its substance and makes it ethereal; it fills its material spirit with its perfection and satisfies the entire appetite of matter, whence it is not subjected to corruption or putrefaction and is minimally afflicted by contraries, because all its parts are homogeneous.

Finally, this was that secondary essence which, acting as a substitute for the Sun for three days from the creation of the world, on the fourth day, as Dionysius holds, passed into the substance of the Sun; indeed, this is that simple act by whose operation this ethereal heaven is most skillfully adorned with glowing fires, and its motions, differing in various ways, namely, oriental, occidental, and according to latitude (which they call trepidation), arise, and finally, a benevolent heat, most friendly to the life of creatures, and exceedingly necessary, is kindled, which, due to the denser substance of this heaven, is more intense and more perceptible in this place than that of the superior heaven; for the denser the matter, the more vehemently it resists the agent, and consequently, the agent acts more strongly upon the patient; But the matter of this heaven, as has been said, is coarser than that of the Empyrean heaven: Therefore, light acts more strongly upon it, and it likewise resists, and consequently produces hotter effects to repel the injuries of cold, formerly hidden, but now manifest due to the presence of heat, whose nature it is to always accompany coarser matter. This heat, therefore, as it is more intense than the supreme, so in respect to the inferior, it is far more temperate, subtle, and simple; because it follows the disposition of the form, from whose action it immediately proceeds. We conclude, therefore, that just as the substance of the form of this heaven is born from an immortal parent, and is in no way corruptible, and exalted in dignity due to its origin and most noble, inspiring life and soul into worldly creatures, and nurturing them with its light; so also its heat from the
H 2 action

--- Page 691 ---
60          TREATISE I. BOOK I.
derived from its action and motion, it becomes life-giving, natural, amiable, sweet, temperate, and incorruptible; from whose source the innate heat of animals, and of vegetables, and of minerals is drawn, and by whose apparent benignity all lower bodies are generated, vivified, multiplied, and fixed unto perfection. But as for the light of this region, although it is constantly clear, lucid, and transparent with respect to the substance of the same place, yet, insofar as it is compared to lower things, it sometimes exists invisibly, the reason is at hand; For, according to Dionysius, light is a substance existing in itself, and from which the clarity, splendor, and brilliance of bodies proceeds: Light, therefore, shines by itself, only in itself, but to others by accident; communicating light and splendor to those bodies, namely, which are found aptly disposed for illumination; of which kind are more opaque bodies, and those endowed with no or not excellent transparency. Augustine also seems to affirm this, asserting that the substance of heaven is most lucid, and holds the first place among bodies because of its lucidity, and yet it does not shine visibly to us at night, but is invisibly present; insofar as it shines in itself; and in this way light is said to be everywhere, that is, in any place and located thing, namely, invisibly in opaque and transparent bodies, and visibly on the surface of opaque bodies, just as it appears in stars and in lower opaque bodies receiving the reflections of stars: indeed, it is necessary for the continuation of animated bodies that light somehow shine upon them at night. For according to Hippocrates' doctrine, if the life of the stars did not temper the thickness of the air during the nighttime, bodies and their spirits would be suffocated, and yet this impression of the stars is not perceived at night; indeed, their splendor, dispersed everywhere, is barely or with difficulty distinguished, except in lights.

CHAPTER. IX.

*That the poles and circles of this heaven are merely imaginary, artificial,*
*and in no way naturally suited to it.*

MANY things have been discovered by those more skilled in Astronomy that are more useful to the cosmographical art than true; which, although they are fictitious and artificial, nevertheless, because they more readily guide students in the art, are to be esteemed as true and natural; among which they have placed two poles in the periphery of this heaven, opposite to each other, which they have called the ends of a certain imaginary axis or diameter passing through the center of the world, and the vertices of the world; around which they feigned its globe to revolve; they also described circles in them, *greater and lesser*; of which they made the *greater* ones partly *immobile*; partly *mobile*: they established only two *immobile* ones, which they called *external*; of which they called *one the Meridian*, drawn through the poles of the world and the Horizon, and *the other the Horizon*, dividing the upper hemisphere from the lower, and terminating our sight; and they made this more direct or more oblique according to the depression or elevation of the pole. Moreover, the *mobile* circles, which they feigned to be *internal*, they called either *greater* or *lesser*. All the *greater* ones, however, except one, lack latitude, and they distinguished them into *parallels* or *non-parallels*; The *greater parallel Equinoctial*, because of its division of the world into two parts (for equally

--- Page 692 ---
DE MACROCOSMI FABRICA. 61

...for it is equally distant from both poles) they called a mobile girdle. They established four Lesser parallels (which are called lesser for this reason, because they divide the world into unequal parts); namely two greater and as many lesser: They called the greater ones *Tropics*, one of *Cancer*, namely the northern, and the other of *Capricorn*, which they placed in the southern part of the world. But the lesser circles, one of which they imagined as *Arctic* and the other as *Antarctic*, they called polar. Finally, the greater of the non-parallels, which has latitude, is called the *Zodiac*, which they also call the *Sign-bearer*, because twelve signs are depicted in it. But this circle among the other internal ones is the only oblique one: For it is imagined to extend obliquely from the Tropic of Cancer to that of Capricorn. But the remaining two lacking latitude are called *Colures*, passing through the world's vertices, and intersecting the Equinoctial circle into four equal parts. These circles, I say, with the two world vertices, are merely fictitious and conceived only by imagination, as terms of art, and in no way connected to the nature of this heaven from its origin. Nevertheless, by Astronomers and Cosmographers, they are intentionally delineated upon the convex surface of the firmament and its center for an easier explanation of their arts; for to each of the aforementioned circles they attributed a certain property suitable for the art of Cosmography: Hence, *in the meridian circle* the Sun makes midday and midnight: The *Horizon* separates the visible part of the world from the invisible; The function of the *Equinoctial* is, that with the Sun passing through its intersections, which the *Zodiac* makes in Aries and Libra, an equinox occurs throughout the entire terrestrial globe; whence it is called the *Equator* of day and night; Both *Tropics* encompass the extreme motions of the Sun according to latitude, and separate the temperate zone from the torrid; To the *polar circles* is given the task to terminate the frigid zones, and separate them from the temperate ones; The *Zodiac* demonstrates the path of the seven planets; Finally, to the two *Colures* a twofold function is attributed; namely, both to mark for us the solstices, namely summer and winter; and also to demonstrate the equinoxes, namely vernal and autumnal. All these things, because they pertain more to technical history than to Physics, we will reserve for a treatise on Astronomy.

CAPUT X.

*Concerning the third heaven, and its various names; Why this lowest*
*region is called heaven?*

[Decorative Initial A] N TE the action of light into the third and lowest region of the world, its content was like a shadow or a very thick and foul smoke, endowed with no visible form, but in a certain way distinguished by the density of its substance: For downwards it was thicker because of the presence of light and heat; Afterwards, however, on the third day, with the operation of light tending downwards to create the earth around the mathematical center, this heaven, I say, being completed, as will be said below, Philosophers, both more recent and ancient, attributed various appellations to it; for some, wishing to signify its dimension, called it the *sublunar region of the world*, denoting all that space which is measured between the concave surface of the middle heaven or the sphere of the Moon and the physical center or the convexity of the earth: Others, considering *its elementary orbs*, by the bodies of which the capacity of this heaven is filled, called it the *elementary region*; although we have declared above that the higher elements also in some way fill the heavens: Not a few

--- Page 693 ---
62 TREATISE I. BOOK II.

none called it corruptible, because its matter is prone and disposed to seeking new forms and abandoning old ones. But that it is heaven is demonstrated by two reasons: namely, first, because it is a portion of heaven taken in the general sense, that is, by which heaven is distinguished from earth; then also, because in many places of Sacred Scripture birds are called "volatiles of heaven" [birds of the sky]; where the word "heaven" is taken not broadly but strictly. Therefore, from its second appellation, it is certain that there are four degrees of difference in this heaven, which the luminous form of the third order, distinguished by its greater or lesser presence, rendered them, that is, thinner, more active, more vibrant, and lighter, or coarser, slower, more immobile, or heavier; for the more remote matter is from the nobility of form, the coarser, more impure, more unworthy, and darker it is, as Aristotle testifies in his book *On Substances*. Hence therefore arise the four elements,

--- Page 694 ---
DE MACROCOSMI FABRICA. 63

Through its presence, its convex surface, and all the substance around it, is ignited by an invisible flame; Hence the power of cold is entirely expelled from that sphere, and consequently it is impregnated by no portion of humidity, but incidentally, that is, through the absence of humidity (which arises from the conjunction of some cold part with a hot one), it must necessarily be very dry. This heat, however, although naturally inherent in this part, yet, because it is not of the true essence of light, but as it were the ultimate effect of its action, flowing immediately from the motion of matter, therefore it does nothing for the function of life, except insofar as it relates to the constitution of the body, which is the seat of life. Nor is it that invisible fire of the Philosophers, from which they say all things are generated; but only that, by the dominion of whose preternatural heat all things are led to putrefaction, while the radical humidity or the spirit of humidities is absorbed by its preternatural ardor, the viscous and watery humidity is converted into poison, and the substance of the universal composite is ignited by a feverish heat and dried out. However, as long as a natural proportion of humidity remains in it, with innate heat proportional to it, which we call vital, the forces of that adventitious quality are suppressed, so that they are prevented from passing beyond the laws of nature in the physical body. Therefore, this fervor and its entire substance, that is, the disturbed spirit, the Philosophers called the element of fire; which occupies the highest seat of the lowest heaven; whose nature all, with unanimous consent, made hot and dry for the aforesaid reasons. It must not be denied, however, that celestial light is present in this element, since it cannot descend to lower regions unless it penetrates the sphere of fire. The position of the element of fire is expressed in this way.

CAPUT. XII.

*De elemento terræ.*

DUAbus igitur viribus unitis, naturali scilicet & adventitia, fortiter ab iis reverberatur materia ob frigiditatem suam rebellis; Ea quæ naturali quodam instinctu illos à peripheria emissos, & frigidam suam naturam persequentes, tam primarios, quàm secundarios lucis effectus usque ad locū ab ejusdem istius lucis circumferentia remotioris sedem fugiens; sese in forma horrendæ & obliqua revolutione subterlabentis umbræ circa universi machinæ sphæricæ centrum seu medium punctum, in durum solidum, & opacum globum restrinxit. In hoc enim loco ab adversarii sui, caliditatis nempe, actionibus multò est securior, & à lucis domicilio, utpote à cujus actu caliditas illa inimica oritur, longè remotior; qui quidem materiæ motus non per se, sed prædicta illa duplici lucis actione concitatus est. Sicut enim absque lucis manifestatione materia tenebrarum fuit tantummodò aliquid potentiale; sic etiam sine caloris præsentia, quæ essentialis est lucis qualitas, naturalis illa materiæ dispositio, nempe frigiditas, nihil quidem actu erat; & per consequens nullas per se mutationes producit. Deorsum igitur materiæ frigiditas pellitur, tam lucis primariæ, quàm elementi ignis virtute activa à materiarum motu producta; sine his enim nihil quicquam agitur. Frigiditas autem illa caliditatis repercussiones patiendo resistere quodammodò, & resistendo reagere videtur. Quibus actionibus & passionibus alii in hoc cœlo infimo gradus producuntur, & regiones intermediæ dispositione differentes, quas elementa inferiora vocant Philosophi, constituuntur. Ex his igitur ratio illa præcipua explicatur, cur gravia ultra mundi centrum decidere nequeant, & quamobrem in eo perpetuò conquiescant; quod scilicet gravitas materiæ densioris & compactioris existat comes; cujus crassitiei causa frigiditas erat, materiam dissipatam & tenuem ad mundi centrum à caliditatis penetrantis rabie contrahens, eamque ibi loci constringens, & contra radiorum lucis invasiones defendens. Cùm autem frigus in qualibet rei crassæ parte, & præcipuè circa centrum magis dispersum ex omni sui corporis mole caloris actio persequatur, lucisque radii, quorum est, corpora facillimè penetrare, ipsum ubique veluti obsideant & circumcingant, fit inde, ut gravia ultra illud centrum versus naturale lucis habitaculum nulla ratione queant procedere, nisi caloris violentia frigus illud in gravibus à natura conclusum opprimatur & violetur. Atque hinc est, quod grave aliquod sursum violenter emissum, naturaliter & sua sponte deorsum ad centrum seu frigiditatis sedem revertatur. Manifestum igitur est, omnem tenebrarum substantiam, cujus præsentia totius mundi materia spiritualis occultata erat & informis, jam tandem virtute lucis, in molem densam & opacam circa mundi centrum collectam redigi & conglobari, quæ quidem elementum terræ appellatur. Reliqua vera totius materiæ jam informatæ massa spiritualis, diaphana & mirificè transparens à terræ marginibus usque ad convexam mundi spiritualis superficiem extensa cœlum generali nomine audit. Hoc inter sacros scriptores Moyses divinissimus in ipso Geneseos limine confirmat; In principio, inquit, creavit DEUS cœlum & terram, hoc est, lucem à tenebris separavit; cœlum enim perspicuum lucidumque fecit; terram verò opacam, hoc est, mundi centrum tenebris immergebat. CHAPTER. XII.

*Concerning the element of earth.*

Therefore, with two forces united, namely natural and adventitious, matter, rebellious because of its coldness, is strongly repelled by them; That [matter], which, by a certain natural instinct, fleeing those effects (both primary and secondary effects of light) emitted from the periphery and following its cold nature, even to a place more remote from the circumference of that very light, restricted itself into a hard, solid, and opaque globe, taking the form of a horrible and oblique revolution of a slipping shadow around the center or middle point of the spherical machine of the universe. For in this place it is much safer from the actions of its adversary, namely heat, and much more remote from the dwelling place of light, inasmuch as from whose action that inimical heat arises; indeed, this motion of matter was not excited by itself, but by that aforesaid twofold action of light. For just as without the manifestation of light, the matter of darkness was merely something potential; so also without the presence of heat, which is an essential quality of light, that natural disposition of matter, namely coldness, was indeed nothing in actuality; and consequently produces no changes by itself. Therefore, the coldness of matter is driven downwards by the active power of both primary light and the element of fire, produced by the motion of matter; for without these, nothing whatsoever is done. That coldness, however, by suffering the repercussions of heat, seems in a way to resist, and by resisting, to react. By these actions and passions, other degrees are produced in this lowest heaven, and intermediate regions differing in disposition, which philosophers call the lower elements, are constituted. From these, therefore, that principal reason is explained why heavy things cannot fall beyond the center of the world, and why they perpetually rest there; namely, that gravity is the companion of denser and more compact matter; the cause of whose thickness was coldness, contracting dispersed and thin matter to the center of the world from the rage of penetrating heat, and constricting it in that place, and defending it against the invasions of light rays. But since the action of heat pursues coldness in every part of a thick thing, and especially when it is more dispersed around the center from every mass of its body, and the rays of light, whose nature it is to penetrate bodies most easily, as it were, besiege and surround it everywhere, it follows from this that heavy things can by no means proceed beyond that center towards the natural dwelling place of light, unless that coldness enclosed by nature in heavy things is overcome and violated by the violence of heat. And hence it is that something heavy violently thrown upwards naturally and spontaneously returns downwards to the center or seat of coldness. It is therefore manifest that all the substance of darkness, by whose presence the spiritual matter of the whole world was hidden and formless, is now at last, by the power of light, reduced and conglobated into a dense and opaque mass collected around the center of the world, which indeed is called the element of earth. The remaining true spiritual mass of all matter now informed, diaphanous and wonderfully transparent, extended from the margins of the earth up to the convex surface of the spiritual world, is generally known by the name of heaven. This the most divine Moses confirms among the sacred writers at the very threshold of Genesis; "In the beginning," he says, "God created heaven and earth," that is, He separated light from darkness; for He made heaven clear and luminous; but the earth opaque, that is, He immersed the center of the world in darkness. Therefore, its positive part, the origin of days

--- Page 696 ---
ON THE FABRIC OF THE MACROCOSM. 65

...made the origin [of days]; and constituted the privative part as the cause of nights. For if the Creator had not placed the earth in the center of the world, nor would the world be defiled by any filth or impurity, all things would also be luminous, and a perpetual day would shine forth. Therefore, it is least to be wondered at that so many and so great corruptions and changes of things occur in this lower world; seeing that in its center or heart lies hidden that most corrupt mother of ruin and privation, that mournful and obscure seal of the separation of forms and essences from composite creatures, and a truthful witness and messenger of the preternatural tyranny of the element is perpetually placed therein in physical things once formed. Hence the most holy Job (says); *'And the dark earth is covered with the darkness of Death;'* and elsewhere; *'the earth is said to be of misery and darkness;'* indeed, this is, as it were, the place of perdition, in which Adam, expelled with Eve from the joys of Paradise, received for himself the sign of inevitable death, and left it to his heirs. C H A P T E R. XIII.

*Concerning the middle sphere, which is called the sphere of humidity, and concerning*
*the element of water and air.*

THE sphere of humidity, situated in the middle between the center of the earth and the convex surface of fire, is called the *sphere of equality*, because it is formed from an equal part of both extreme elements; for neither the coldness of the earth by itself, nor indeed the heat of fire alone, is able to produce humidity, but the conjunction of both, and, as it were, the coitus of male with female, constitutes it. For just as the coldness of the earth alone constricts the middle spirit, to which it is present, so it is the property of the heat supervening upon it to resolve that icy spirit, to liquefy it, and to render it fluid. Similarly also heat by itself, that is, annexed to its own dryness, absorbs—

--- Page 698 ---
DE MACROCOSMI FABRICA. 67
absorbs, or certainly by its quality dissipates it into insensible parts; hence it deserves to be called a separator of humidity rather than a producer. Therefore, the violence of heat is more or less blunted by a greater or lesser concurrence of coldness; hence the intense operations of both are hindered; and the spirit is by no means permitted to coagulate from cold due to the presence of heat. Nor is it possible for heat, according to the property of its nature, to dissipate and scatter the parts of the moistening spirit, which happens due to the resistance of present coldness; hence the spirit is dissolved by the assistance of heat; but being dissolved, it is not dispersed, nor is it almost subtilized to nothing, which is entirely accomplished by the presence of cold; but it remains in the middle, naturally flowing, and through its fluid nature and liquidity, it moistens all intermediate things, either more corporally and visibly, namely if it adheres to a larger portion of cold, or more spiritually and insensibly, namely if it embraces a larger part of heat. And it is from this disposition of humidity that two intermediate elements are derived, as we shall immediately demonstrate.

Therefore, dense matter, as was said before, driven from above to the center, and retained there due to the immense coldness with which it is endowed, desires to rest there; But indeed, because it is the nature of heat always to attack coldness hostilely, and to pursue it with a certain natural antipathy; and likewise, it is also the nature of any subtle thing to penetrate, therefore this active quality, driving that passive one downwards, pursues it there, and constantly attempts to penetrate its mass. And because the end of anything is its opposite, and not only rest but also motion is opposed to motion, therefore another motion succeeded that motion directed downwards to the center or middle, namely from below upwards towards the element of fire, excited by the resistance and opposition of coldness opposing itself to the injuries of heat, and by this reverberation of light rays. Hence two parts of terrestrial coldness ascending upwards to repel the injuries of heat met an equal number of parts of heat descending to expel that coldness, in the middle way between the center and the sphere of fire. And by the union of these parts, the sphere of humidity is constituted, whose middle part is simply and equally humid: For the forces of heat in its middle are proportional to those of coldness, so that they are weighed as if by an equal balance not inclining more to either side, and possess the same strength and power of action on both sides; that is, they tend neither more downwards nor more sideways, and consequently, while they move, it is necessary that they are carried circularly.

Moreover, the dimension of this middle sphere, tending downwards towards its concavity, is called the element of water, which, because of its proximity to the element of earth, and its greater distance from the sphere of fire, appears more terrestrial, dense, visible, and sensibly moistening. For its temperament is composed of three-quarters of terrestrial coldness (for it is much more contiguous to the earth) and one-quarter of the heat of fire; in which temperament, although a very small portion of heat is present, it is nevertheless sufficient to prevent the congelative disposition of cold, and to preserve this part of the sphere of humidity in its fluid quality. And this is the same reason we brought forth above; so that it may be most clearly evident that coldness exists much more intensely not in water, but in earth, because water, by the absence or diminution of that one-quarter part of heat, is frozen and reduced to ice, that is, to a more terrestrial and non-fluid substance.

But the other half of the aforesaid sphere, protruding upwards towards the concave surface of fire, because it is further from the earth, and due to its proximity to the element of fire, it is greatly partaker of heat, and contains very little coldness in itself by which its fiery heat might be tempered, therefore it is much more subtle, spiritual, and invisible than the lower part of the same, and because of its subtlety, it penetrates more and moistens more profoundly. From which it is to be gathered
I 2

--- Page 699 ---

it is to be gathered that its temperament coalesces from three parts of fiery heat and only one part of terrestrial cold. Moreover, Philosophers have called this portion of the sphere of humidity the element of air. We conclude, therefore, that by the action and passion of the two primary qualities naturally inherent in the extreme elements, several intermediate motions are generated; one of which is, from each extreme to the middle, by which the middle sphere of humidity is produced; another tends to the middle point, descending thence even to the universal center, whence the sphere of water arises, and a third proceeds by ascending from the aforesaid middle point to the sphere of fire; and thence the element of air is generated. From which it is manifest that the lowest heaven is divided into three parts, namely into the sphere of fire, into the sphere of humidity, and into the center of the universe. But the elements of air and water are produced, as it were, accidentally, namely on account of the proximity of the extreme elements, which impart varied force and virtue to each part of the sphere of humidity. Therefore, these things having been more exactly considered, it is evidently clear that coldness can operate nothing at all, unless insofar as it is provoked by the action of heat, and consequently light, whose effect is heat, is the cause of every difference both in the lower heaven and also in the higher ones, and also of the variety of those very places. And here also it must be observed that that transparent substance between the two extreme elements is spirit; concerning which, what may be sufficient, we have mentioned in the first book; whose substance is matter, in which simple qualities, opposite to each other in place and nature, produce their various effects. The entire humid sphere is here described with its twofold partition.

CHAPTER. XIV.
Concerning the form of the elements.

THE form of this heaven is weaker than that of the higher ones, because of its remoteness from its origin; This, moreover, is very easily proven by its effect. For indeed, our terrestrial fire, receiving its power of heating from the action of light, the further it is distant from its passive (object), the more weakly it usually heats; and consequently it is certain that the matter of this heaven, the more it approaches the center, the grosser, more impure, and more unworthy it is; according to that (saying) of Aristotle in his Metaphysics, "where there is more matter, there is less form, and vice versa." Hence it is clearly evident that the matter of this heaven, because of the weakening of its form, predominates, and consequently constantly seeks a new form daily, for neither is enough form supplied to this region so that the appetite of its matter can thereby be fulfilled and satisfied. Hence therefore constant changes of things arise in it; hence any corruptions...

And in this way, the admirable operation of nature in the selection, purification, and ordering of the elements of matter is clearly explained. We conclude, therefore, that Earth is the dregs of the spirits of every heaven, and an accumulation of substantial darkness; Water is that coarser spirit of darkness of the lowest heaven, almost devoid of light; for the spirits of that heaven embracing light are converted into various metals according to the greater or lesser proportion of light contained in them; whence their radical moisture is found by Philosophers to be thick and viscous water. Air is that spirit of the fertile heaven, having escaped from the earth by subtiliation, whose denser part, embracing secondary light, produces hotter or colder plants according to the suitable proportion of light and that rich spirit; and finally, Fire is the spirit of darkness of the Empyrean heaven, whose coarser substance, filled with primary light, constituted the solar body; as will be declared below.

*An experiment concerning wine, from which the nature of each of the elements*
*can be gathered.*

From the most excellent wine itself, we made an experiment, clearly indicating to us the substances of the elements and of the Quinta Essentia itself, as if by a finger and a rule of trust. For, the spirit having been extracted from the wine, by no new operation, I extracted oil from it, floating upon the spirit. Then from the dregs of the wine, I extracted oil, and brought it to the highest purification by various rectification. Afterwards, I frequently rectified the phlegm also distilled after the extraction of the spirit. Finally, I purified the dregs of the whole wine from their muddy filth by many washings: Therefore, I put all these into a round glass in equal proportion; which I sealed hermetically, as they call it, and with this vessel resting for an entire night, in the morning I found 5 regions; the lowest black and veiled in darkness; upon this resided a portion of phlegm; Next, oil extracted from the dregs covered that, upon which, in the fourth place, the spirit of wine ascended; But the oil extracted from it covered it in the fifth order.

CHAPTER. XVI.

*Concerning certain experiments of waters demonstrating various dispositions in the constitution of the aforesaid heavens through the operation of light.*

IT IS CERTAIN that fire is understood under the name of light, and originated from light itself; since nowhere in the universal description of creation did our divine Leader Moses make mention of that noblest creature, fire, except when speaking of light: This is also more clearly declared in the sixth book, chapter 8. No one will doubt that air and water also came from that mass, namely, the substance of the universal waters, since the sacred Scriptures testify that all things consist of it. Now indeed, because undoubtedly the aforesaid operations are suspect to some who rely more on sense than on reason, it remains to represent these operations also to their eyes through effects derived from those two primary causes, namely water and light, which indeed they will most easily perceive visibly, if they diligently observe the following experiments.

*First Experiment concerning fire and air or subtle water.*

Fire being kindled in the upper part of a concave and very well-closed instrument, at the bottom of which, opposite the fire, a small hole or tube is placed, the air inside, the more it approaches the place of the fire, the more it is attenuated, and the thicker part of the attenuated air, which is colder, tends from the operating fire towards the lower part of the vessel, as being further removed from its enemy, which indeed is visibly evident, because the form of moist vapor is gradually perceived to exit through the tube or hole of that region.

Experiment II.

Therefore, let a certain glass or copper globe be made with three distinct regions, so that one embraces the entire concavity of another; and let these regions have certain openings or tubes protruding in the manner depicted below, and let the outermost surface of the globe be surrounded on all sides by a very lively fire. CHAPTER I.

*On the theory of mundane proportions.*

[Large decorative initial 'E'] From the preceding it is evident that just as the Empyrean heaven is the dwelling and seat of supernatural fire and light, from which natural fire immediately, and that other more accidental fire mediately, proceeds, so also its opposite place, terminating and ending the movements of its rays, is the receptacle of matter and darkness. But since the relation of contraries is the same, it is necessary, for the continuation of the world, that the disposition of humid nature's darkness should relate to that fiery nature of light by the same degrees and in the same proportion. Hence, just as we declared above that the physical center is naturally cold in the fourth degree, most dense, most opaque, and most ponderous, and naturally desiring rest by itself; so also the outermost region of the machine is undoubtedly opposed to it in all respects, not only in place, but also in condition, so that all intermediate bodies are constituted by the equal action of the one and the proportional passion of the other, and according to the nature of the subject—that is, according to the abundance or lack of light predominating in it—they either resist privation longer, or yield and submit to it more quickly. Who then will doubt that the supreme region of the Empyrean heaven is free and immune from every invasion of coldness, whose property it is to thicken? Since it is most subtle, most pure, most light, translucent to the highest degree of clarity, and as it were nothing else than fire sublimated to the ultimate peak of loving and most sweet heat. Without doubt, therefore, those proportions of things introduce a most noble mundane harmony, through which, with the virtue of primeval light operating on intermediate matter, an indissoluble concord of things is reconciled, and the ears of the intellect are soothed by a certain inexplicable music. For the instrument of this melody, namely the world-machine, is like a monochord, whose string, through which the consensus of parts is introduced, is the intermediate matter of the whole world. But the author in this music is the soul of the world or the essential light; no differently than in that instrumental music of man, in which Γ, that is, Gamma, takes its beginning from the lower part of the system, ascending with grave, excellent, and superexcellent voices; Such indeed is also the progress in the mundane monochord, namely from the earth proportionally to its *ee la*, ascending, which is the terminus of the ultimate periphery: And just as in Γ the sound is graver and deeper because of its extreme distance from *ee la*, from which ascending the percussion of the voice becomes more intense; so also the higher one ascends from the earth towards the Empyrean heaven, the stronger the effect of light and heat is found, and the more subtle the mundane spirit is rendered by its virtue; just as also for the elevation of the human voice greater force, and therefore greater virtue of the luminous soul, is required, while in its depression, less is entirely desired;

is desired; so also a greater proportion of the mundane soul is found in the higher and more subtle spirit of the world, and consequently renders the harmony sharper and more excellent; whereas in the lower and denser [spirit], it is less; whence it is known to produce more grave and profound harmonic effects. From these things, therefore, the consonances of this harmony, consisting of due proportions of numbers, are very easily gathered, which it is not difficult to prove are derived and proceed from the embrace of simple principles, namely from the mutual commingling of the material and formal pyramid: for each of these has a pyramidal dimension in this Macrocosm, by which it is accustomed to operate no differently (though more in one place and less in another) than one portion of a corporeal pyramid gradually requires a larger concavity for itself, in which the other may be contained: But the base of the formal pyramid is contiguous to the heaven of the Trinity itself, and its cone extends down to the earth; just as, conversely, the base of the material pyramid is in the earth, and its cone ascends up to the summit of the Empyrean heaven, that is, into the concave surface of the heaven. Moreover, we have delineated these formal dimensions of the world at the end of the fifth book, where this pyramidal dimension is to be understood in physical things. Here, however, we have briefly delineated the proportional embrace of one pyramid by the other, so that we may better induce students to a more sensible demonstration of proportions for a more perfect explanation of this our mundane music; in which light it is indeed more manifest that three parts of the material pyramid occupy the lowest region of the world, with which one part of the formal pyramid mixes, namely that which is near the cone; that which gave essential form to that whole mass of matter; and two parts of the same [material pyramid] fill the middle region, which are informed there by as many portions of the formal pyramid; and its single portion gives substance to the Empyrean heaven, which three portions of the formal pyramid supernaturally inform. From which it clearly appears that the material pyramid attributes substance to each part of the world, and that the reciprocal reception of the luminous pyramid transmutes it from prime matter into secondary and formed matter, and consequently all things between the edges of the earth and the highest periphery of the Empyrean heaven have received their proportions from the action and passion of these two pyramids; from which also all the proportions and consonances of the Macrocosm constituting the mundane harmony are derived. Moreover, the demonstration of this matter is as follows.

Therefore, these principles being known, it will not be difficult to elicit proportions from them, by whose consonance we say the mundane music arises.

But because the downward-tending rays of natural light with the cone of its pyramid have not yet penetrated to the inner parts of the earth itself, therefore it is necessary that the inner parts of the earth, since every thing is composed of four quarters, retain and possess four testimonies of coldness due to the complete absence of light: But indeed the diaphanous region floating above it, since it is limpid, transparent, and clear, denotes by this very fact that a single portion of light has been granted to it, by which it obtains its diaphanous and mobile nature of this kind: From this it appears that the proportion between the earth and that lowest region is clear, since the earth has four testimonies of density, while the elementary diaphanous region has only three; so indeed, that they stand in a sesquitertian proportion, inasmuch as the earth stands to that transparent elementary region as 4 to 3. Then three transparent parts of this lowest region to those two parts of the ethereal region, in the middle of which the sun is exalted, are found in a sesquialtera proportion, and stand to each other as 3 to 2. just as also further two parts of that intermediate region constituting corpulence,

CHAPTER. III.

*On the worldly monochord and the discovery of its consonances,*
*both simple and compound, from which the worldly harmony is formed.*

**S**INCE all these proportions in each aforesaid pyramid are worth nothing by themselves for producing musical consonances without the commixture of both (for neither a lyre without a musician, nor a musician without a lyre, suffices for making musical consonances), therefore both pyramids must necessarily concur to constitute worldly harmony: namely, the material one, which stands in place of a musical instrument, or a monochord string, or an instrument and a singing spirit; and also the formal one, which performs the office of a striking or singing soul and of producing a voice. Therefore, an increase of the formal substance produces sharper and more subtle air, and consequently emits rarer and more excellent worldly symphonies; no differently than a more intense human spirit or instrument string will produce sharper voices and more subtle air through more violent vibrations. But its decrease makes grosser air, and consequently a graver worldly harmony, no differently than a relaxed human voice or a loosened monochord string renders softer sounds; and this happens because of the excessive density of the air. Therefore, light acts upon worldly matter by the same means by which the human spirit acts upon air. From which it is manifest that one nature, whether material or formal, is worth nothing without the other, and therefore that worldly Music arises from both pyramids mixed in the smallest parts. For without the presence of light, humid matter would not have a pyramidal form, nor would created form have its own without humid matter. Whence it is certain that they are mixed more or less with each other according to the nature of the portions of each pyramid moving oppositely in the Macrocosm and concurring with each other.

Therefore, these things being known, let us take our beginning from the matter of the world, which we have likened to the string of a monochord, whose great instrument is the Macrocosm itself, so that we may aptly compare every degree, by which some difference of places between the center of the worldly instrument and its periphery is discerned, to musical intervals, both simple and compound. Wherefore it must be known that just as the string of an instrument is usually divided by metric proportions into intervals by reason of ascent from Γ, so also both matter and its form are distributed by quantitative degrees and distinguished by similar proportions, constituting musical consonances. For if a monochord were imaginatively extended from the summit of the Empyrean heaven to the base of the earth itself, constituting the radius of any pyramid, we would perceive it to be divided into parts constituting consonances; of which, if half were pressed, it would produce the consonance of a Diapason, just as experience teaches that the same thing happens in an instrumental monochord.

It must be considered, however, that in such a worldly monochord, consonances both simple and compound, and similarly the proper intervals measuring them, can be delineated no differently than when we divide an instrumental monochord into proportional parts. For the effect of coldness in the earth, and consequently the very matter of the earth in thickness and weight, is so naturally related to the coldness and matter of the lowest region, in which there is only a single

And to those diligently observing the matter in this place, a divine mystery will reveal itself: that, just as the formal Diapason is more excellent than the material, so also its foundation is more excellent and far nobler, both in the proportion of harmony and also in its every basis; Therefore, just as the earth is far less noble than the solar body, so also the material Diapason and the consonances comprised in it are far to be ranked after the spiritual ones. For the earth is the basis of the material Diatessaron and Diapente consonances, constituting the material Diapason: But the solar orb itself is the foundation upon which the spiritual Diapente, Diatessaron, and Diapason are raised. Moreover, the fundamental consonance of the material Diapason is the Diatessaron, more imperfect than all concordances; but the fundamental concordance of the formal Diapason is the Diapente, a concordance, namely, perfect: Hence therefore the degrees of all material things are seen as in a mirror; and thence also to the eyes of the intellect the spiritual scale and order are manifested. Therefore all generations happen under the sun and receive their power from the inferior minor semitone of the sun's sphere, which we called material above; But all regenerations have their origin from the superior semitone of the solar orb, from which a sublimation to the summit of spirituality occurs. Therefore those things which have not reached the summit of the solar orb cannot acquire the perfection of regeneration, nor become spiritual from corporeal. Blessed therefore are the bodies to which it is permitted to attain such height and dignity. But, to return to our purpose, those three parts of light informing a single most subtle matter, related to those four purely formal ones, and constituting an integral form, in which there is absolutely no matter (of which nature is uncreated light), agree in a sesquitertia proportion, which constitute the spiritual Diatessaron consonance; whose most subtle spirit also, as if transformed and freed from corporeal substance, is further divided into three intervals, which are attributed to the three Hierarchies; of which the two lower orbs are assimilated to whole tones, but the superior one to a Semitone, inasmuch as the orders of Epiphany, and especially the Seraphim, are said to administer as if to GOD himself, extending themselves beyond the limits of matter—

Let therefore a musical instrument be constructed pyramidally, and from one point of one side of the same (instrument) let a bronze string be stretched to a point of the other side diametrically opposite to it. Then also from another point let a second string be stretched likewise to its opposite, and then a third and a fourth, proceeding thus also in the others, until the entire pyramidal thickness of the instrument is filled with strings proportionally differing from each other. We say therefore that the same strings, stretched with equal force, retain the intervals of Tones and Semitones, so that from the base of the pyramid towards its cone, through those musical scales, which we more correctly call intervals, we shall always ascend from lower sounds to higher ones, until the cone is reached; beyond which it will be no less impossible to ascend higher than to penetrate further by progressing beyond an arithmetical unit or a geometrical point. This instrument, moreover, is delineated in this manner.

*How is all the aforesaid more clearly demonstrated through a pipe, an instrument invented for Music?*

[Large decorative initial E] BEHOLD before our eyes a notable demonstration, not perceived by the inventor himself; through which it clearly appears that great and immense secrets often lie hidden in common things, whose reason and root, however, common eyes by no means perceive, looking at things more superficially than fundamentally.
