For from this musical instrument, called a pipe, the true proportion of the whole world is gathered. But it is divided into three regions; of which the two lower ones have three holes denoting the beginning, middle, and end of each region; the uppermost region, however, consisting of only one large hole, designates the nature of the supracelestial heaven, whose every part is of the same condition as being most full of divine unity: But just as this instrument in its nature and by itself without a moving soul does not sound, is not moved, or has any power; so also neither the world nor parts of the world can move or act by themselves without the stirring of an immense mind: Therefore, just as the supreme mind, GOD, at the apex of the whole machine, and as it were outside the outermost surface of the world, makes the structures of the world exhibit their music, heavier in the lower part, and more acute and clearer, the more and nearer they approach to that very summit; so also, with the musician blowing life and motion outside the pipe's body and at its summit, the more the holes are distant from his blowing power, the heavier sounds they produce; but the higher one ascends towards the bellows of his spirit, the more excellent the sounds are rendered; and just as that single hole, A, gives, as it were, life and soul to the other lower ones; since without it they do not produce sounds; so also the Empyrean heaven to all lower spheres: Oh, how great and how celestial would this contemplation be in such a trivial matter, if it were considered diligently and somewhat more deeply by an intelligent mind!

CAPUT. V.

*On elementary music.*

[Decorative initial I] N the elementary part of the world, it is also established that there is a certain harmony; whose consonances, because they proceed more from proportions derived from the heat of celestial fire, which is not of the true essence of light, but rather from forced and adventitious ones, than from that essential one, therefore also produce symphonic compositions, whose harmony, due to the smallness of true luminous form in them, is not indeed permanent, but transitory and vanishes with a certain sudden swiftness. But that each element is arranged by musical proportions, both in its own heaven and in any composite of heaven, by natural consent, we will perceive more clearly than light itself, if we examine their natures and positions more accurately and deeply: For it is certain that their matter or corpulence is thicker, and consequently heavier and harder; or thinner, and therefore lighter and softer; which happens according to the greater predominance of earthly coldness or fiery heat in it: Since therefore coldness alone has dominion in the earth, (whence, because of the absolute absence of fiery heat, those four quarters of coldness are present, which is, as it were, the entire nature of the earth; but indeed the element of water possesses no more than three quarters of coldness, combined with a single quarter of fire, (which happens to it because of its participation with the middle sphere of humidity; similarly the middle sphere of humidity contains only two portions of coldness, and as many of heat, and finally the element of air has obtained only a single portion of humidity, while it embraces three quarters of the quality of the neighboring element of fire; it is necessary that earth be denser, heavier, harder than water, and water than the spurious sphere of equality, and that finally than air, which is the upper part of that humid sphere;

From which it is manifest that in the mere natures of the elements no consonance is found except that imperfect one: Indeed, the reason for finding these intervals is this, that in every degree, the more one ascends from the terrestrial towards the fiery nature, the more, on account of the greater operation of fire gradually increasing, matter is more altered by ascending; and since it is certain that these operations are found perceptibly in three places of the said elements, therefore from these degrees of alteration we have derived the intervals of the consonances of our Music. Therefore, in order that all these consonances of the Diatessaron may act naturally and peacefully towards each other, it is necessary that two of them, the corporeal ones (which indeed are of the visible elements), be chained together with those two of the invisible elements. And we will clearly demonstrate that this connection arises from the sphere of spurious equality, to which sphere we have assigned the interval of a whole tone, indeed, the most perfect interval; which indeed, if joined with the Diatessaron of the watery sphere, produces by such a connection and coupling a less perfect consonance, which, united with the terrestrial Diatessaron, generates that most perfect corporeal consonance, called Diapason. Similarly, ascending upwards to the invisible elementary regions, if the Diatessaron of the aerial sphere is joined with the perfect interval of the sphere of spurious equality, immediately a less perfect aerial consonance will be produced, which, joined with the fiery Diatessaron, will constitute an incorporeal, that is, invisible Diapason. Therefore, by this means, fire will communicate with air in a Diapason, composed of [a] Diatessaron, and an aerial Diatessaron, and the interval of the middle sphere. And fire in air will communicate with water in a Diapason, composed of the Diatessaron of air with fire (animated by the preceding Diapason), and the tone of the middle sphere, and the Diatessaron of water, since these constitute another Diapason. And fire in air and air in water, as if in vehicles of the invisible elements, will communicate with earth through a third and lowest Diapason, composed of the tone or interval of the middle sphere, and the Diatessaron of the watery sphere, and the terrestrial Diatessaron, inasmuch as all these joined together produce a Diapason. And by this way it is most clearly demonstrated by what bonds the elements are chained together, and why fire is more in air, and less in water, but least of all, or in the most minute portion, in earth. Hence it is also declared how one element is, as it were, a matrix, vehicle, and receptacle for another, namely, for each of its nearest superiors, as air for fire, water for air, and earth for water, which for this reason is the recipient of all elements; from which also, by Philosophers, earth is not undeservedly called the mother of all elements. This therefore is that elementary harmony, by the virtue of whose consonances the parts in the mixture of composition are most exactly and by weight connected, and are peacefully preserved therein.

We conclude therefore that the true mode connecting together in composition the proportions of contrary elements is the sphere of equality, and that its entire interval, filling it, is that natural bond of the superior and invisible elements with the inferior and visible elements, without which the four elements can in no way concur for any natural composition.

CAPUT VII.

*On the practice and action of worldly music and its consonances,
infused from the spheres of the ethereal heaven into these elemental ones.*

[Decorative initial Q]UEMADMODUM in vocal or instrumental Music, speculation is not suf-
ficient, unless it is transferred to practice, and its use is recognized by practical experience;
so also in this worldly harmony, our present discourse will perhaps be considered fictitious, unless
we extend it, to the best of our abilities, to a practice familiar not only to the intellect, but also to the sense itself.
Therefore, we will first discuss by what proportions and consonances each sphere of the world infuses its harmony into another, and then, in the second place, we will declare the reason for worldly discords.

Since therefore the clear space of the lowest region is related to the earth in a sesquitertian proportion,
it follows that accidental fire corresponds to it, but with an imperfect consonance;
for with respect to dryness alone, which is an accidental quality proper to both fire and earth, it exists in such harmony with the earth: But
the reason why this region agrees in the genus of earth is in the multitude of corporeality,
which it originally received from the earth; Hence the intervals of the clear region lead
to connecting this more material region to its foundation with an imperfect consonance (according to the nature of the place, namely)
so that a symphony may arise from the apt concatenation of its spheres.

But if we ascend to the first degree of the ethereal region, we will find that the sphere of the Moon has a reference to the earth in a sesquialtera proportion, and with
respect to this proportion, the earth tastes of the Fifth essence, and by this same
proportion, worldly melody is infused into the earth, blended with it from a less
perfect consonance. For inasmuch as between the earth and the sphere of the Moon, four are found,
namely water, air, and the sphere of the Moon, which carry tones, and the sphere of fire,
which is held in the place of a semitone, to that extent it will consonant a Diapente with the earth, and a Dia-
tessaron with water; consisting, as has been said, of two tones, namely air and the sphere
of the Moon, and one semitone, namely fire: And this is the reason why the Moon constantly
acts so strongly and vigorously on these lower regions, and especially on the earth, through its influences.
Similarly, the *sphere of Mercury* will resonate a Diapente into the sphere of water: Hence there-
fore floods of waters, and disturbances of the seas, because of the subtle and airy Mercurial spirit hidden in them,
and likewise also by its operation with the aid of the Moon, the ebb and flow of the sea occurs. Furthermore,
*Venus* is also related by a similar consonance to the sphere of air, which has a gentle and sweet symphony
in the air, because of the exact concord of its proportions: Hence the air
retains in itself the same qualities that Venus has, namely warmth and hu-
midity, which are always propitious to animal life; indeed, they even serve plants in place of radical
moisture with their own spirit. Finally, the lowest part of the *sphere of the Sun* spreads its influences
into the sphere of fire, which are simultaneously carried down into these lower regions, and contribute
to the multiplication and perfection of plants by virtue of the consonance of a Diapente.
But, so that we may arrive at the powers and faculties of a more perfect consonance,
which is found between the earth and the sphere of equality, it is certain that all perfections
of the life of every terrestrial animal arise from the intervals of this consonance,
namely the increase of corporeal matter and of that vital form.

**CHAPTER VIII.**

*On the practice of elementary melody and its effect both in simple
as well as composite bodies, and on its discord
and strife.*

[V] Just as the more subtle dispositions and natures of higher things are infused into lower bodies; so also it is necessary for bodies to be composed from the region of the pyramid of material substance, which is divided into elements, in order to aptly receive such influences: And this material composition indeed has its essential form not from the elements, but from heaven itself; as I myself have experienced by seeing such things with my own eyes: for from a living thing I separated four distinct elements; then, in the last place, I perceived and with wide-open eyes saw the life of the thing, which I knew to be from heaven, the Quintessence and solar nature, since I had separated the four lower elements to one side. Our intention here, therefore, is to treat of proportions and of those consonances by which, in the mixture and composition of mundane bodies, a suitable connection of one element with another is made. Thus, in Elementary Music, earth relates to the sphere of water as 4 to 3, since there are in earth four fourths of coldness, related to those three of water; for that single part of the element of fire, together with the cone of the luminous pyramid, is present in the sphere of water, which, if more parts of heat existed in it, would be of a thinner substance, and thus would even be converted into air, and for that reason neither would its sphere remain closest to the earth, nor would it be burdened with such heaviness or weight: But that it has something of heat, that is, of igneous form, in itself, is attested by its transparency and fluidity, as has been said before in its proper place: Therefore, because of this sesquitertian proportion, earth agrees with water; but this combination of the said elements is imperfect and less absolute; because the humid parts of one are contrary to the dry parts of the other; nevertheless, they consonant with each other through the consonance of a Diatessaron; because they agree in the active qualities predominant in them. Thus also, to the sphere of spurious equality, in which there are two material parts and as many of fire, earth relates in a double proportion, namely, as 4 parts of earth to two of the same sphere; for terrestrial nature produced these humid parts by the power of light conjoined with it, dissolved and subtilized. Similarly, water relates to that sphere of equality as 3 to 2, whence the sesquialtera proportion arose; And thus we have obtained the Diatessaron, Diapente, and Diapason of the terrestrial pyramid. Similarly, the sphere of equality relates to that of air, comparing two igneous parts of the sphere of equality to those three portions of air; whence the igneous Diapente arises; and the three igneous parts of air to those four of the sphere of fire produce the consonance of a Diapason. Therefore, earth agrees with water in a Diatessaron, with the sphere of equality in a Diapason; And water agrees with the sphere of spurious equality in a Diapente, and the sphere of spurious equality with air in a Diapason, namely, because they are held in a double proportion. Thus also, fire agrees with air in a Diatessaron, and with the sphere of equality in a Diapason, and air agrees with the sphere of equality in a Diapente, and the sphere of equality with water in a double proportion or Diapason. Therefore, two visible elements concur optimally for composition through the bond of the Diatessaron consonance, and two invisible elements mix themselves with them by virtue of the embrace they have with corporeal proportions. For fire is referred to air

air through the consonance of Diatessaron, and air to the sphere of equality through Diapente, and the spheres of equality of both fire and air are joined in the proportion of Diapason. But the sphere of equality connects these invisible elements, simultaneously chained by formal consonances, with the visible elements through corporeal bonds or consonances. Similarly, air is joined to earth by a quadruple proportion, and consequently, fire, also glued to air by the bond of Diatessaron, is accustomed to unite with earth and water; but nevertheless they are joined to each other in such a way that the proper seats of consonances and their legitimate order are observed, lest discord and strife arise among them; Hence, corporeal consonances ought to regard the more corporeal elements, and fiery consonances the fiery ones. The reason for this is that the region, both more terrestrial and visible, as well as fiery and invisible, is terminated and perfected by the most perfect consonance; Hence the boundary of the corporeal or visible pyramid is within the corporeal Diapason, and likewise that fiery one within its less corporeal Diapason: But inasmuch as both Diapasons are joined by the virtue of the spurious sphere, to that extent the corporeal elements are joined and chained to those invisible ones; Hence, one proportion ought not to regard another outside its own region; for otherwise, discords would arise instead of concordances; For example, fire consists of 4 parts of heat, and water of three of coldness; although therefore here is a sesquitertian proportion, nevertheless it exists badly arranged between bodies, by reason of qualities, and a progression occurs from the fiery realm to that corporeal one, whose natures are entirely opposite. Similarly, earth relates to air as 4 to 3, but for the same reason they can in no way agree; Hence fire is enclosed in air, by means of which, through the sphere of equality (which is to be regarded as a medium for joining fiery and aerial forms with watery and terrestrial bodies, no differently than the ethereal spirit is considered such in the conjunction of the soul with the lower body), air passes, and with its fiery soul is comprehended by water, which water, by virtue of the consonance of Diatessaron, is most easily and naturally joined with earth: And this is that harmony by which the composition of sublunary mixed bodies occurs. However, bonds of this kind are dissolved by strife and discord; For the Martial fire, its proportion increased beyond the due nature of its consonance, most swiftly absorbs the humidity of its aerial vehicle, and from its prison, with the Diatessaron consonance of the fiery proportion violated, it bursts into the watery region and causes war out of peace in the composite; Hence desperate and incurable diseases arise, and that fiery nature, violently penetrating through water and earth, and bursting forth from them, snatches away with itself the celestial soul, to which it is closest in composition due to the familiarity and kinship of the ethereal heaven with the sphere of fire, and in this way the composite is dissolved, and suffers corruption, and is gradually reduced to its primary matter. The same thing happens when Saturnine earth, with its coldness and dryness, destroys aerial heat and humidity, so that it may find a way with water to extinguish fire and suffocate the life of the thing: But concerning this mundane strife, we will say more in the following chapter.

ON MUNDANE MUSIC. 105

CHAPTER IX.
*On Mundane Discords.*

[Large decorative initial P] AFTER we have discussed mundane harmony, it follows that we should begin a discourse on its discords and the reason for them: From the foregoing, therefore, it has been clearly demonstrated that chaos before the completion of the world was formed from contentious proportions, and that there was nothing of harmony in that crude mass, according to that of the Poet: *Cold things fought with hot, moist with dry.* From these causes, therefore, of the Macrocosm's hostile incursions and its peaceful friendship, effects are produced. For in the beginning of generated heat, its opposite, cold, also arose; between these, waging war against each other, humidity intervenes as a third element, as something formed from those two primary ones, yet not in any way totally conforming to either of the said extremities, inasmuch as it participates in those two extremes, whence it also holds a middle place between them. Hence, therefore, dryness, never departing from either extreme, has perpetual war with its opposite, humidity, so that one unending enmity follows another. Interrupting therefore these hostile concurrences in the nature of the Macrocosm, infinite nature made distinct and balanced things from indistinct things: this done, light things flew up into higher regions, while heavy things settled beneath the moist earth, so that each of them, to speak with the mouth of Trismegistus, is carried by a fiery spirit into its proper and proportional place.

These things thus disposed in the ethereal heaven, each Planet was found in its proper exaltation, inasmuch as they were so situated in the celestial Zodiac that those which were of contrary conditions were further distant from each other: Hence the *Sun* found its exaltation in the first instant of its creation in *Aries*; to which the *Moon* had the nearest exaltation, because the former bestowed upon the latter, as it were, of its own substance, and this one is like a wife or woman, and ruled *Taurus*: Similarly, *Jupiter*, most friendly to the Sun and Moon, was exalted in *Cancer*, *Mercury* in *Virgo*; but *Saturn*, most malicious to the Sun, was distant from it by the entire semidiameter of the whole heaven, exalted in *Libra*: Finally, *Mars*, exalted in *Capricorn*, was equally distant from both the Sun and Saturn. And thus all these creatures of heaven were disposed, so that there was no manifest strife among their qualities.

But indeed, after they fell by their natural motion into a malevolent aspect, which commonly happens annually from their origin, they produce rebellious effects in these lower regions, by which these lower compositions are either utterly destroyed and eradicated, or wonderfully afflicted and debilitated, and this because of the malevolent influences of the Planets in malevolent aspect to each other, which are the more corrupt, the more corrupt among the Planets in aspect to each other is that one which at the time of that aspect is stronger and more powerful than another: Now they call *Saturn* and *Mars* the corrupt Planets; inasmuch as they naturally extend their double proportions tending downwards into spheres incongruous and contrary to their natures: Whence they make harmony corrupt, and produce effects in these lower regions, and especially in living things, that are accidental rather than natural, as was said before: for all Planets are good in themselves, but their influences, although they too are good in themselves, and especially those of these two for the reasons already alleged, work evil effects in bodies not aptly disposed to receive their influences and natures, so truly, that the fault is not in the giver, but in the receiver: This also Iamblichus seems to confirm with these words: *Celestial things are not evil, although they are received as evil here; for all the powers of celestial things descend thence

which had hitherto reached from above; Indeed, the explanation for which is confirmed by the effect in our Philosophy. For first, generally speaking, the sphere of water received the influences of Mars through the consonance of the Diapason, but a sphere whose nature is contrary to its own received them; Whence fire invisibly fights with water, and water, by resisting, is preternaturally disturbed: Similarly, Saturn, in the same proportion, sends forth its influences into fire, which, in receiving them, similarly both acts and suffers in more particular cases. We see that any Saturnine influence is constrictive and frequently causes harm accidentally, namely when it is received by colder matter: for then it harms, because it is received, for the most part, by way of congelation. Similarly, we know the force of Mars to be motive, and we see its influences cause harm, namely when it is received by hotter matter; and then it harms, because it is received through heat: which harms indeed do not occur because of an evil operation of the influences, but because of a bad disposition of the matter.

C H A P T E R I.

*On the difference of the spiritual creatures of the Empyrean heaven, both*
*according to the ancient Philosophers and the Fathers of Theology.*

[Large decorative initial D] THE word DAEMON is taken not for the Devil alone, but
for a spirit, so called from the property of the word, as if
knowing, intelligent, and wise; who is therefore called by the name of
intelligence, because it is an intelligent substance, free from all
gross and corruption-prone bodily mass, immortal, insensible,
assisting all, and influencing all; It is sometimes called *Angel*,
that is, messenger, because it is commanded by GOD to reveal His
mandates to men; And thus the name Daemon seems to be a general
term pertaining to all spiritual creatures, with the soul alone
excepted; although it is known to me that some have existed who distinguished Daemons from other
creatures of the highest heaven. Iamblichus, making mention of four orders of celestial
spirits, namely, the first, *Gods*, the second *Daemons*, the third *Heroes*;
and the last *souls*, called these latter three the attendants of the GODS,
and demonstrates that one of these orders is more powerful than another, and that
according to their dignity, they each possess the more excellent places or regions of this heaven,
which we named elements a little earlier, as he declared quite extensively
in their descriptions and differences of properties; And the same
author elsewhere divided the choir of celestial spirits into eight species or differences,
namely into GODS, *Archangels, Angels, Daemons, Heroes, Principalities, Princes & souls*;
although the tradition of the Magi seems to comprehend all these species, except the outermost,
or rather, with the last one excepted, under the name of Daemon (taking the word Daemon for
a knowing, intelligent, and wise spirit); Hence they named spirits, both pre-celestial and celestial,
as well as the repeatedly inferior ministers, Daemons. The *Theologians* (among whom I name
*Dionysius*) wished to contract these species of Daemons into three hierarchies;
each of which they distinguished into three orders differing in degree and property,
which they called choirs: *Therefore, in the superior hierarchy, which Dionysius calls Epiphany, the first order is Seraphin, the second Cherubin, & the third Thrones; in the middle, called Epiphonomy by him, are Dominions, Virtues, Powers; in the lowest (called Ephionia by him) are Principalities, Archangels, & Angels.*
Finally, all who wrote about divine matters were accustomed to divide Daemons
into good and evil: those who are good are called celestial by Iamblichus;
who likewise asserts that such are benevolent, and strive for and work nothing but good itself:
*Proclus* calls evil Daemons material and terrestrial; and says that
good Daemons are more exposed to the mind; but that evil and terrestrial ones are
to be repelled with the utmost caution we can. Therefore, so that we may agree with the ancient
Philosophers, and the modern Theologians of this age, celestial or spiritual

...tual creatures created on the first day in, and with the spiritual heaven, we divide into two species: These, moreover, are Daemons and souls: Daemons, whom Theologians call angels, we again subdivide into good and bad; whom others name beneficent and malevolent, and John in the Apocalypse names favoring and harming Angels: The good ones they themselves arranged into three hierarchies; The bad ones, moreover, whom Plato calls Cacodæmons, angels of destruction, worshippers of crimes and impiety, they named Lucifer with his companions, of whom there are infinite legions: The good ones are again called angels of light, the bad ones indeed angels of darkness. The soul, moreover, is the lowest species of intelligences; which indeed is proven by the fact that it naturally tends to mix itself with inferior bodies, so that it may adorn them with essential form.

C A P U T II.

*On the composition of Daemons and Angels; How are they said to be incorporeal? Some arguments proving the composition of Daemonic substances.*

<big>A</big>UGUSTINE, on Genesis, says Daemons are aerial and fiery animals: By aerial he denotes pure spiritual matter; by fiery, indeed, he understands form. Damascenus, in book 2, chapter 3, calls Angels intellectual lights, which Pythagoras believed to be made from fire alone, and which are said to be more luminous than the Sun, Moon, and other Stars, because these drew their origin from the finest fire enclosed in the most subtle spirit; those, however, received their origin from thick fire participating in air or ethereal humidity; wherefore it is manifest that Angels are by no means participants in the matter of the lower heavens, as is held in the third book on the soul, but certainly of formal spirit, whose matter, with respect to inferior substance, is entirely form, and as if composed of a single essence; Hence Dionysius calls Angels Agalmata, that is, most brilliant mirrors, reflecting the light of GOD, representing His image, and revealing hidden things, as he testifies in the book on divine names: Moreover, that these spirits differ from each other in degree, dignity, and splendor, Iamblichus attempts to prove to priests by their apparitions in this manner; He says, "Most brilliant spectacles of the GODS appear to us, shining to the highest degree, and wonderfully distinct in splendor:" Archangels have around them, both before and behind, a very great multitude of fire, and light precedes them, divided within itself; The light of Angels is brilliant, but less than that of Archangels, and it is divided; Daemons appear as if they were turbid fire; Heroes have a mixed light from several sources; Principalities, however, have a purer light; Princes possess a light confused from dissimilar and contrary elements; Souls render a fire full of many generations and admixtures, and divided; which differences indeed they have according to their position: for the closer they are to GOD, the more brilliant they are, and the more remote, the darker they are. From these, therefore, it can be gathered that Daemons are composed of the matter of the most subtle elements of the spiritual heaven, which matter, with respect to inferior things, is most simple and aerial, and from divine form, emanating from the most splendid beatitude of GOD; whose composition, if compared with the creatures of the lower heavens, is called incorporeal; but when compared to the simplicity of the luminous substance of the Empyrean heaven, in which, with which, and from whose elements they were created on the first day, they are to be regarded as a body composed of spiritual elements, just as plants, herbs, and their seeds were made on the third day with the earth, which is opposed to the Empyrean heaven.

--- Page 741 ---
110 T R E A T I S E I. B O O K IV.

will be considered as a body formed from spiritual elements. And hence it is that *Augustine* asserts that they had aerial bodies from the beginning of their creation; that is, they were formed from the upper part of the air, suitable for acting, and not for suffering; and *Basil* moreover affirms this same thing: But what can more clearly denote the composition of Daemons than their actions and passions: And that they act and suffer, (*Resolut. Theolog. tract. 2. cap. 2.*) since they both receive and in turn give illuminations, and produce the act of understanding, and also receive it, I certainly think no one is so grossly blind and deluded as to deny this. It is certain, therefore, that there is in them one thing that acts, and another that suffers; nor indeed can that, according to which they act, be anything other than act, which is called form; nor is that, according to which they suffer, anything other than potency; and this is called matter. Moreover, it must be especially observed here that the composition of matter and form, according to the diversity of the three heavens, likewise has a threefold aspect. For in lower bodies, matter is subject to the quantity and contrariety of form; but in celestial bodies, it is subject to form and quantity, but not to contrariety; while in spiritual creatures, it is subject to form, but in no way to corporeal quantity and contrariety. We conclude, therefore, that Daemons are of the most subtle composition among all creatures, and more brilliant and clearer than all, because they are more replete with formal essence, and consequently more spiritual, nobler, and as it were incorporeal, always mobile, free, and, as *Damascenus* says, partakers of immortality. For their essence, from which they exist, is most simple, and as it were immaterial, lucid, pure, distinct, and discrete; their virtue, from which they have power, is free, intelligent, amiable, and everlasting; finally, their operation, by which they are exercised, is voluntary, sudden, useful, and honorable; for they operate without delay or impediment, and serve us entirely without cessation, as is found in *Resolut. Theolog. tract. 2. part. 2.*

C H A P T E R. III.

*How are angels said to be in a place?*

[Large decorative initial A] WE declared in the second chapter of the first book that God is in a place differently from Angels, and Angels differently from corporeal creatures; since GOD is said to be here and everywhere only according to His presence, namely in the Empyrean heaven, as His blessed tabernacle, and in every part of the world, as a part of His empire; but Angels, without the assumption of bodies, are judged to be in some part of the world not only presentially, but also definitively; and having assumed corporeal substances, they are judged to be presentially, definitively, and circumscriptively in some concave surface: Hence, *Angels, according to the resolution of Theologians, are said to be formally in a place*, that is, by their presences; yet they cannot be everywhere at the same moment in time; because they are said to be definitively in a place; nor indeed are they necessarily in a place, because they can be carried even if no containing body exists: for they can be outside all corporeal nature. And hence it is that they are said to be potentially in a place; for they have the power of existing in some containing body, but not in act, because they neither make the sides of the container separate, nor do they actually form any containing surface. From these things, therefore, it is clear that Angels, because of their composition, in a certain way

--- Page 742 ---
CONCERNING THE CREATURES OF THE EMPYREAN HEAVEN. 115
...to be in a place: But here it must be observed; that Angels, insofar as they have assumed coarser bodies for themselves, are in a place circumscriptively; For it is certain that Angels, both good and evil, have very often assumed accidental bodies of any kind; which they soon again put off; as is found from various places of sacred Scripture, and confirmed by the apparitions of witches and conjurers.

CHAPTER IV.

*Concerning the differences of Demons, and their offices, both according to the tradition of ancient, and more recent Magi.*

[Large decorative woodcut initial M] AGI, establishing three kinds of Demons and intelligences (for some, according to them, are pre-celestial, others celestial, and the rest ministers of inferior things), called the pre-celestial ones minds, entirely separated from the body, and as it were intellectual spheres, worshipping the one GOD as their most stable point and center; indeed, they assert that these are full of GOD, and as it were intoxicated with divine nectar, and believe that they revolve around GOD alone, nor do they think that they undertake any care whatsoever of worldly bodies, nor do they judge them to serve the administration of inferior things in any way; They conclude, however, that their office is to immediately infuse the light received from GOD into the lower orders, and to distribute individual offices to each. And this species of Demons is, without doubt, that which Iamblichus calls GODS following the first GOD who gives all things to all, who bestow certain things upon all. This is also the first and superior Hierarchy of Angels, comprising the orders of Cherubim, Seraphim, and Thrones, whose office is to contemplate the order of divine wisdom; For the Angels of the first order look into the goodness of GOD, those of the second into the essence of GOD as a form, and those of the third into His wisdom. These, finally, are the Angels closest to GOD, whom they magnify with continuous hymns and everlasting praise, and pray to GOD for our salvation, as Athanasius says. The wise call the celestial intelligences worldly Demons; because beyond divine worship they are accommodated to the spheres of the world, and preside over each of the heavens and stars; Whence it happens that they are distributed into as many orders as there are orbs in the world and stars counted in the orbs: And hence it is that some are called Jovial, others Saturnian, etc. Mercurius Trismegistus, in his sacred discourse, calls such Demons GODS, who, after heaven had shone forth in seven circles, were seen in the ideas of the stars with their signs, and he says that the stars were numbered according to those who inhabit them, the GODS. These, however, are without doubt those Demons of Iamblichus, whom he calls ministers of the Gods, as architects in the worldly work, who express those things which are ineffable and hidden in the Gods. These are also those Angels who are placed in the middle hierarchy, as having dominion in the middle region of the world; And they are called by Abbot Trithemius, second intelligences, who, by the ordination of the first intellect, that is, GOD, are said to govern the aethers and the orbs of the Planets. The Magi call Demons of the lower order ministers, who are referred to those things which are to be disposed in the lower regions: Origen calls these certain invisible virtues, through whom all earthly things are disposed, and he asserts that they are conspicuous to no one and accomplish our affairs, and direct our journeys, and avert the dangers of battles when present, and prevent the outcomes of clandestine ambushes, wish-

CHAPTER VII.

*Which region of the lower heaven Lucifer most frequently inhabits with his Angels?*

[Decorative initial D] THE DEVIL, Prince of rebellion, formerly called *Lucifer*, but now *Lucifugous* (light-fleeing), with his legions closest to him in gravity of sin, dwells more in the Northern parts of the earth, so that we may agree with sacred Scripture, by which we are taught that Satan holds his seat in that part of the world;
which, indeed, it would by no means be difficult to confirm both by clear reason and by vivid examples. For if we accurately consider the nature of that extreme part, we shall see its location perfectly agree with the disposition of the Lucifugous Demons: For *Olaus Magnus* says that the region of *Biarmiæ* has the North Arctic pole for its Zenith; and the Equinoctial for its horizon: Furthermore, he says that in its outer parts (namely, those which face the *Tropic of Cancer*) only a single natural day shines in the solar year: For them, the year is divided into two equal parts; namely, into a single artificial day, and then also into a single night: Day emerges when the Sun enters *Aries*; night, however, begins when the same leaves *Libra*: But in the parts of this region more remote from the Tropic, and more under the Pole, and beyond it, an immense part of the earth is found, where the Sun never casts its rays, but which is obscured by perpetual darkness and gloom: which *Freigius* also asserts in his *Geography*, who states that the part of the frigid zone nearer the pole is never illuminated or warmed, but shudders and stiffens with cold and gloom: Hence, therefore, it is demonstrated by clear reason that these Lucifugous Demons delight in this region of the earth with greater pleasure, because they naturally hate the presence of light, as an image of GOD, and so, to avoid it, they retreat into such dark places.
[Marginal note: *Apuleius, Book 2 of Metamorphoses.*] And the ceremonies of the ancients seem to confirm this, for it was their custom to place very large lamps with sufficient oil for light next to the bodies of the deceased, so that Demons serving such *Cacomagi* (evil magicians), deterred by the extraordinary brilliance of the light, might be restrained from their usual slaughter; But indeed, in this place, since they always find the absence of light, it is wonderful how they gather there in crowds; which, since it has been so ordained by Almighty GOD, cannot be avoided by any means. Moreover, here also the misery of these Demons,
&

--- Page 748 ---

& the greatest unhappiness can be observed; who, although in their creation, they were formed from an airy and fiery substance, afterwards, however, when they had committed horrendous crimes, their fiery soul was suffocated by a vapor as if dark and extremely cold; their airy bodies were frozen by earthly dryness, and deprived of the liberty of their spiritual humidity: wherefore they are afflicted in every way by contrary actions, punished, and tormented in a quasi-perpetual abyss of Gehenna. Indeed, very many authors supply us with examples that prove the frequency of these Demons in the aforementioned places: Among whom *Olaus Magnus* in the outer parts of *Biarmiæ*, especially in *Sweden*; and similarly, though not so frequently, in *Denmark, Finland, Iceland*, declared that lares or specters dance at night; that lemures appear in the form of beasts, and the spirits of the dead terrify the inhabitants: Fauns also and Satyrs, and Pans, and Striges (witches/vampires), and infinite species of such Demons visibly wandering about in the tempest of the night, strike the natives with the gravest terror. This species, however, secretly contains within itself a certain fiery glow as if suffocated by darkness; nor indeed are the parts of their composition so contracted and constricted by cold and earthly dryness, as happens to those Lucifugi; because, namely, they are ardent due to an internal fire somewhat blunting the operations of cold: And this hidden sulphurous glow prevents the dark and liquid vapors of their substance from freezing. The Divine will, therefore, wishing to inflict a lighter punishment upon them according to the degree of their sin, thrust this second order of the worst Demons as exiles into this part of the world, where the sky neither rages so stubbornly with cold, nor are heterogeneous things so easily gathered by earthly dryness, due to the proximity of the Sun existing in its perigee, which there approaches the center of the world more closely, just as in its opposite, namely in its apogee, it is elevated and, according to astronomers, is farther from the earth: Hence in the Northern region, indissoluble snows and perpetual ice, giving their name to that part of the sea, and violent and earthly blasts with their congealing spirit, bringing hail, frost, snow, and ice; all of which often happens to be stirred up by the breath of the Lucifugus Spirits to the great detriment of men and beasts: And these indeed are the most true and wonderful operations of Satan, the Prince of this region. The rest, which seem marvelous to the Cacomagi themselves, are to be considered as fictitious and fantastic imaginations, and to be strongly rejected as Diabolical illusions. But another part, not so abundant in snow, nor so hardened by ice (whence its seas are furrowed in any season of the year), although it is covered with a veil of darkness equal to the opposite seat, nevertheless everywhere erupts flames and fiery meteors; Whence it is called *Terra del fuoco* (Land of Fire) by Cosmographers. C H A P T E R V I I I.
*Concerning the soul by various appellations, and the uncertain opinions of ancient Philosophers
about its essence.*

[Large decorative initial I] HE lowest species of spiritual creatures is called Soul, insofar
as it bestows life on all; Whence some of the Gentiles called it wind
and spirit; It is also called mind, insofar as it has some will;
Reason, insofar as it judges directly; Spirit likewise, with respect to
breathing; Finally, Sense, while it senses, as Isidore testifies in book 15, chapter 14.
But so that it may be more fully understood by all what this ultimate species of intelligences is,
since ancient Philosophers, both Greeks, and Arabs, and Latins, who toiled in the exploration
of its nature, brought forth not so much certain as diverse and wavering opinions about it,
therefore we deem it worthwhile to explain their opinions first in this place. For some here,
some there, and all drawn into diverse opinions, brought forth a varied judgment about it.
Plato therefore defines the soul as an essence living in itself; Aristotle (defines it as) the act
of a physical organic body, having life in potentiality; Zeno (defines it as) a number moving
itself; Xenocrates (defines it as) a number moving in itself; Aristoxenus (defines it as) the
principle of number; Pythagoras (defines it as) harmony and the concord of melody, with
whom Dinarchus (agrees), (defining it as) the principle of the four elements, bringing to the
body with which it is joined their most beautiful temperament and harmony; Hipparchus
(defines it as) fire or fiery force; Heraclitus Ponticus (defines it as) light; Another of the same
name (defines it as) the substance of a star

...the spark of some star's substance; Posidonius calls it an idea, inasmuch as it is the form of an animated species; Asclepiades imagines it as a kind of string, providing the five senses with the faculty of performing their functions; Hippocrates considers it a subtle spirit, dispersed through all the passages of the body; Democritus deems it an indeterminate subtle spirit, composed of the smallest and indivisible particles, which he calls atoms, converging and cohering within itself: Tertullian and Avicenna assert that the soul is born from the soul in the same way that the body is begotten from seed, and that it multiplies in the same way that the light of many candles is kindled from a single flame; Thales of Miletus calls it the motive power of everything; and from this is derived his opinion that the magnet is animated because it attracts iron plates to itself; Alcmaeon compared it to celestial bodies, because it is a most mobile thing, indeed always mobile; from which disposition, he says, its eternity can most easily be discerned; Parmenides holds that it is made from earth and fire; Epicurus, from fire and air; Empedocles and Ericrates say it is the most powerful thing in the body; Finally, some consider it the brain, others blood, like Critias; others believe it to be vapor and humor; some utterly deny it to be a substance. However, the assertions of these ancient philosophers, although they seem for the most part to differ very greatly among themselves, nevertheless some approach closer to the truth than others, indeed we will clearly declare from what is written below that some even agree with the truth itself.

CAPUT IX.

What is the Soul? And concerning its properties.

[Decorative initial S] ACCORDING to the opinions of Augustine, Damascene, Isidore, Bernard, Remigius, Calcidius, and almost all philosophers, both Gentile and Christian, we gather that the nature and disposition of the soul are explained in a twofold manner; either, namely, it is considered by itself, that is, separated from the body, or inasmuch as it is joined to the body and informs it. Therefore, as it is understood in its own proper and free disposition, it is described: I. To be a certain divine light created in the image of the first exemplar, that is, of uncreated light, and adorned with a beauty as if angelic. [Marginal note: Agrippa lib. 3. c. 37.] II. A spiritual substance, emanating from divine sources, simple, indissoluble, immortal, free, incorporeal, and invisible, lacking quantity, figure, weight, and color. [Marginal note: Damaſcen. homil. & Bernard.] III. Rational intellect. IV. An intellectual spirit, [Marginal note: Damaſcen. ibid. Senec. Auguſtin.] partaking of reason, always moving and tending towards blessedness by itself. V. Finally, a divine mind, understanding all things, and assimilating itself to all things. And in this description, its properties are accurately delineated. One of these is to illuminate cognition: Hence in *Resolutiones Theologicae*, tract. 2, part 2, por. 3, quest. 2, the intellect is called the light and reason of knowing, because it is the active principle of cognition: Another is to lead back the Microcosm to GOD by its presence, as is held in the first book of Genesis; Hence we have defined the soul as a light created in the image of uncreated light: Its third property is that, since it is a most pure, most simple, most spiritual, invisible, and incorporeal substance, it has communication with intelligences, and, to speak with Iamblichus, sometimes reconciles itself to divine beings through the harmonies of its essence and actions: The fourth is that, while it is enclosed in the body, it never permits the body to die; because it is life itself, nor is it ever destroyed by the violence of death (as Porphyry most excellently says). Hence we, with the Sages, call it immortal and indissoluble: But it is also distinguished by yet another property,

--- Page 751 ---
120 TREATISE I. BOOK IV.

...it is distinguished, namely, that it may always remember itself and never fail to understand itself. For it knows nothing so well as that which is present to itself, nor is anything more present to the mind than itself to itself; as Aurelius testifies, book 10. and 14. chapter 10. And hence it is that we have defined it as rational intellect and intellectual spirit, because all things are understood by the mind; which by Augustine, because it assimilates itself to all things, is called the likeness of all things, in the book *De Anima et Spiritu*; or because it retains in itself the likenesses of all things which it intends to understand; since all knowledge occurs through the way of assimilation: Hence by its essence it is assimilated to earth; by imagination, to water; by reason, to air; by intellect, to the firmament: Its sixth property follows, which is, according to Bernard, that it be a companion of reason: The seventh is, that it tends by itself to beatitude, which Porphyry calls divine life itself; the contemplation of which thing melts the contemplator with that which is contemplated into one, as can be seen in the aforementioned author; hence it is that Bernard called the human soul a partaker of beatitude and an heir of salvation: Its ninth and last property, which we observed from the aforementioned definition, is, that it is always and indefinitely moved; Wherefore it is certain that it is a most vital form, and a primary act; Hence by Plato in the Phaedrus it is called a number moving itself, and by Xenocrates a number acting in itself; for the soul is moved in its spirit. From these things, therefore, it clearly appears that the first of the aforementioned properties concurs with the opinions of Hipparchus, both Heraclituses, and Epicurus: Through the third, the wisdom of Plato and the profundity of Alcmaeon shine most clearly: Finally, with the ninth, the opinions of Thales of Miletus, Aristoxenus, and Xenocrates agree.

Furthermore, insofar as the soul is joined to the body, to that extent we have also described it in two ways; either with respect to the Microcosm alone, or insofar as it refers to beasts and plants: But when it is joined with the body of the Microcosm alone, the soul with its vehicle is defined as an incorporeal principle, a proportional number,
[Marginal notes:]

and a primary act accommodated to our bodies, by whose presence we live, feel, move according to place, are endowed with reason, understand primarily, and are capable of good or evil will. From which description of it we have observed certain of its properties concerning the disposition of the human body: The first of which is, that it is a principle, connecting the four elements in composition so aptly and congruently that it imparts to them a most beautiful temperament and a sweet harmony: The second is, that insofar as it is a proportional number, it has the power, by a certain harmonious consent, to rightly dispose the parts of the body for the reasons of life, sense, motion, and action: And such a proportion in the human body produces human Music, which is nothing other than harmony; through which the soul loves the body and the parts of the body; Hence Pythagoras' opinion was not unsound, who considered the soul to be the harmony of a melody: The third, that it is necessary that the body, where this soul is found, live, feel, move, and reason: The fourth, that in its motion it is always capable of good or evil will; For, although, free and separated from the body, it never ceases to remember itself and never fails to understand itself, as has been said, nevertheless, insofar as it is involved in earthly things, which it draws in through the senses, it sometimes does not usually perform that so exactly. And here indeed we think the opinion of Iamblichus should by no means be rejected, by which we are taught that whatever passions of animals are certainly not inherent in their soul, but in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul, by which it acts and suffers: Its last property is, that it universally rules and governs the body, according to Remigius' opinion, no differently than a sailor a ship, or according to Chalcidius, just as a spider remaining in the center of its web is perceived to move the entire web by its motion, so also, hiding itself in the heart, which is the center of the body, it usually moves the entire mass of the body. Moreover, insofar as this spiritual creature refers to beasts, its definition

--- Page 752 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI EMPYREI. 121

its [definition], applies equally to all these [creatures] as to humans; except that it does not impart intellect and rea-
son to them; since this is the specific difference distinguishing humans from brutes,
which [brutes] are called irrational due to their lack [of intellect and reason]; Hence, through the presence of this
soul, they live, feel, and move locally in the same way as humans; but they understand
nothing, only sensually distinguish and recognize certain things. Similarly, the soul
in plants is defined in the same way as in brutes, except that it does not supply sense
to them. Therefore, just as the soul does not make beasts partakers of reason, so it leaves
plants devoid of sense. This description of the soul, therefore, applies to every species
of animals; namely, that it is a certain sensible power, or a spirit vivifying the animated
body, and imparting sense to it, by which it recognizes and discerns material sensibles,
that is, the corporeal forms of corporeal things, both present and absent, externally and
internally. However, as it applies to animals in general, as well as to plants, it is defined
by Damascenus *homil. 26.* and Aristotle himself, as being a certain power imparting
to the body the heart of life, vegetation, and generation, that is, a certain virtue or first
act in a living physical organic body, converting nourishment into the substance of the
nourished, so that it may preserve itself in its being, promote it to its due quantity, and
enable it to generate a like being in species; in which description indeed three powers
of the vegetative faculty are expressed, namely, *to nourish, to grow, and to generate*.
From this description of the soul, therefore, we can gather many other properties; about
which, since they readily become known to philosophers without elaboration, we shall
refrain from speaking in this place.

CAPUT X.

*Of the soul of the world, or the divine power dispersed everywhere in the world,*
*and especially in its midst; whence it is called the middle soul*
*of nature.*

MUNDUM not only did all Platonists, Pythagoreans, Orpheus, Trismegistus,
Aristotle, Theophrastus, Avicenna affirm that the world has a soul and spirit;
but they also judged it in some way to be a partaker of the divine mind,
with whom Marcus Manilius, and Virgil, likewise Boethius and Augurellus,
poets both Gentile and Christian, seem to agree; The former of whom in

122 TRACTATUS I. LIB. IV.

*The world, however, and the parts of the world, also consist of body;*
*A spirit becomes a medium among these, which they say is neither body*
*Nor soul, but a god who alone, participating in both,*
*At the same time brings these extremes back to the same thing.*

Therefore, the world has, the heavens have, the stars have, the elements have a soul, with which they generate soul in the lower and mixed things themselves; because, to use Augurellus's argument, bodies are perfect; whose perfection must come from a certain soul. What doubt then is there that the world, as it were, lives and moves with a natural motion, since it is the noblest body, and consequently has the most vital soul, suggesting life and motion to it with a certain most pure spirit, which is the vehicle and medium by which the soul is transferred to lower things.

But what kind of soul of the world this is, although we have already spoken sufficiently long ago in the chapters on the universal form and the description of the Empyrean heaven, nevertheless, what some others think about it, with a slight touch of our own opinion, we will briefly examine in this place. This soul of the world is therefore, according to some, a certain essence filling all things, penetrating all things even to the center, binding and connecting all things, so that it renders the entire machine of the world as one, and is like a single monochord resonating with three kinds of creatures with only one breath and one life: In the particulars of this definition, both the aforementioned opinions of ancient philosophers and those of more recent ones are best depicted; as is more widely declared in the aforementioned chapters on the soul.

According to others, the soul of the world is described as the virtue of God, and as it were, God of nature itself, or the middle soul of nature, through which God is said to be everywhere in the world, to fill it, to moderate it, and to constantly preserve it. And this is that divine virtue which God continually pours liberally into created things from the perennial fount of His Spirit, by which all things live, are sustained, grow, and multiply; and this soul of the world they believed to be placed especially in the Sun. For very many philosophers assert that the solar body received its exceptional splendor and beauty from there; nor do they report anything in heaven that bears a greater resemblance to God in light and clarity; indeed, they believe that any thing, in as much as it is capable of light, claims that much of God for itself.

We conclude therefore that this soul of the world is, as it were, the act and essence of light created on the first day, submitting itself from the Empyrean heaven through the sieve of the Crystalline heaven into lower things, and on the fourth day gathering itself in the Sun, as in the center and heart of the ethereal heaven, and from there circularly ejecting and extending itself everywhere: and this formal nature of light Augustine, in his book *On Free Will*, seems to argue is the form of every thing, and the soul by this reasoning. For he says that light holds the first place in bodies, which indeed is a disposition of the soul itself. Furthermore, in the book *On Genesis, literally*; and elsewhere it is said that light is of such nobility that even corporeal things, the more they participate in light, the nobler and more perfect they are judged; as is perfectly observed in the elements. For there is nothing in the whole world more worthy than it, since it is a certain simple act, converting all things to itself with life-giving heat, permeating all beings, leading their qualities and virtues through all things, and finally dispelling all darkness and gloom: And hence it is that the Sun, because of the excellence of its clarity, as an ethereal King, and Emperor of the corporeal world holding the scepter and helm, is placed in its midst, illuminated by an exceptional splendor above the other creatures of the world, inspiring and infusing life, sensation, motion, and vegetation into lower things through its rays.

CHAPTER XI.

*That the intellectual soul, although composed, like many Angels, nevertheless differs from them in certain respects, and concerning the immortality of the soul.*

<span style="font-size: 200%; line-height: 0.5; vertical-align: -0.2em;">A</span>LMOST all philosophers, both ancient and modern, testify that the soul is composed of matter and form: But this kind of composition does not occur from pre-existing matter, as is the case with generable and corruptible things, but from nothing, that is, from non-pre-existing matter, and produced by creation, from which the Empyrean heaven and its creatures, among which souls are numbered, are derived, as is more fully declared in *resol. Theolog. tract. 2. part. 2. port. 3. quæst. 3.* And although the composition of souls and angels is the same, it is nevertheless found that these two supercelestial creatures differ in species for many reasons, both by philosophers and by theologians themselves, as is stated in the aforementioned treatise; the first of which is, because the nobler a created form is, the more specific degrees it multiplies; which Iamblichus also confirms, distinguishing intelligences into four degrees: But the intellectual creature is the noblest: Therefore it has more species; and consequently, an angel and a soul are not of the same species: The second is, because the mode of understanding is different; greater in angels, lesser in souls: The third, because the soul is sometimes discursive, namely inasmuch as it is in the human body; an Angel, however, is always intuitive and without discourse: The last, because the soul is the perfecter of the body; an Angel, however, brings nothing to the perfection of the body. From these points it is clear that the soul is a lower species of intelligences and closest to humans, and most apt for governing their bodies, yet immortal and perpetually surviving after the corruption of its body.

For although the power of composite matter is naturally corruptible and grows old with time; the operation of the rational soul and mind is nevertheless not at all consumed by the passage of time, nor does it become older; indeed, it seems rather to grow younger and to flourish anew in a wonderful way. For in old people wisdom thrives, and prudence increases with the passage of time. Furthermore, since understanding is a rational operation of the soul, not dependent on the body, because no bodily organ determines it, it is certain that it is incorruptible. It is also incorruptible, inasmuch as it naturally desires beatitude, as was said before; which natural appetite is not in vain, since the soul can have beatitude; And wherever there is beatitude, there is security; where there is security, there is immortality and incorruptibility, as is stated in *resol. Theol. tract. 2. port. 3 q. 2.* In these reasons, authors certainly seem sometimes to mean the mind, sometimes the rational spirit, inasmuch as it desires beatitude; not infrequently also the mind together with the spirit, from which the composition of the rational soul is made.

Therefore, in addition to the aforementioned reasons, we conclude that the soul is incorruptible because of the nature of its composition; because no contraries concur in its composition, since the spirit, which is as it were the matter of the soul, is airy; while the mind is fiery, which is the form of the composite; for it is of the spiritual substance of light: And since air and fire are most friendly, and one is, as it were, the nourishment of the other, and the other, as it were, life and soul to its nourishment, they are joined together by a natural marriage, as if by perpetual bonds, and they act upon and suffer from each other without the destruction of one or the other, just as a man and woman coming together [do so without destruction]: Furthermore, the multitude of luminous form has so satisfied the appetite of spiritual matter that it desires no new form at all; but it is so formal in its substance that the Sages have written that it divinely informed even the crude corpuscle of the microcosm, made from earth and mud.

CHAPTER I.

*Concerning the substance, nature, and disposition of the stellar body.*

[Large decorative initial O] ALMOST all Philosophers agree on this, that stellar bodies are
from the proper substance of the middle heaven: And Aristotle also in his book
on the heavens holds that stars are of the matter of the heaven in which they are placed:
But we, not entirely agreeing with them, say that the solar body
is derived from a dark mass expelled from the upper heaven,
as we will declare below in its proper place. As for the constitution
of the nature of the other stars, it is necessary that some density and opacity
be inherent in the stellar body, by whose presence it is rendered visible; which, however,
can by no means be found in the thin substance of the heaven. And this is what
those more skilled in Optical science have maintained. For, says Algazel concerning the nature of a mirror, that no part of the stellar
orb is visible

before they were affected by that decay, they could in no way manifest. Simi-
larly, the scales of certain fish do the same; for, because of their moisture, easily decaying by the heat of the air, they make invisible light manifest by a certain magnetic force. There are also other bodies which, because of the complete perfection of their substance, naturally, and indeed gradually, draw solar rays to themselves, and firmly retain those which have been drawn. For, according to the merit of the matter, as Plato says, form is given, since form acts according to the disposition of the matter. Therefore, of this kind are gold and the Carbuncle. There are also still some other bodies which, although they are not perfect, nevertheless have a certain spirit within them, so akin to the body of the Fifth Essence, because of the purity of their disposition, that they are perceived to shine at night; of which kind is that glow-worm, rendering its whole worm-like body visible in the darkness. the aforementioned would be entirely invisible with them. Similarly, if this white way were as dense as the bodies of the fixed stars placed near it, without a doubt it would shine forth through its entire substance no less than any of the aforementioned stars. It is therefore manifest that this Galaxy has a medium dimension and opacity between the body of the crystalline heaven itself and the stars fixed on its concave surface; whence it is quite visible, colored, and moderately luminous. And hence it must be observed that, the more a stellar body tends towards transparency, the darker it is, and less luminous, which is manifest in fixed stars of the fifth magnitude, which therefore, on account of their obscurity arising from excessive transparency, are called nebulae; for they are not much denser than the Galaxy; wherefore they do not much excel in brightness. From these things, therefore, the reason is at hand why some fixed stars are more luminous than others. We conclude therefore that the matter of a falling star (in appearance) is the same as that of a Comet, and that of a Comet is the same as that of the Galaxy, and that of the Galaxy is the same as that of stars, both fixed and wandering, and that all their difference is derived from a greater or lesser density, transparency, and purity; which varieties of matter, we have above and often inculcated, flowed from a greater or lesser portion of form.

CHAPTER II.

That stellar bodies are not corruptible.

[Decorative initial Q] ALTHOUGH every substance of this world, both visible and invisible, originates from prime matter already brought into act, which in its nature is apt to desire form, and for this reason is always mutable and corruptible, where that form is found to be weaker; if however it should ever arrive at some place where it finds a form sufficient to satisfy its desire, then certainly it rests, that is, it no longer desires. For every natural thing has an inclination towards perfection, in which its desire is its end and completion. But indeed, since the measure of all perfection consists in the essence of formal light, matter rejoices in its embrace, and is, as it were, carried into heaven; for unless matter is in heaven, desire is by no means completed. Hence, I say, it is that although the bodies of the stars, and indeed the substance of the entire heaven, are to be considered corruptible in themselves, because they were formed from the universal dark substance of hyle, and were reduced to act by the presence of light; nevertheless, on account of the presence of proportional form, since there are two parts of light, and as many of matter, it is necessary that the density of that substance be completed in its desire and rendered perfect. Just as also, where the proportion of form exceeds matter, it is said to be more-than-perfection and spirituality; a substance of which kind is found beyond the convex surface of the ethereal heaven. Hence therefore it is manifest that both the form of the middle heaven, called secondary light, and that of the spiritual heaven, vindicate whatever substances are found in their regions from decay and the injuries of corruption, preserving them always in the same state, and rendering them perpetual according to the laws of nature; although it is necessary that the continuation of every thing depends on the eternal will of GOD, inasmuch as all things are subject to His sole command and disposition.

CHAPTER III.
That it is probable that the fixed stars were made on the second day of creation;
Concerning their origin, place, & diversity, both in magnitude
as in splendor.

[Large decorative initial 'I' containing a landscape scene with a sun and clouds]
IN the foregoing, it has been demonstrated that light was created on the first day, which filled the entire concave surface of the supreme heaven; And in this way, the light inhabiting the supreme region, which we called primary, was separated from the darkness which that light thickened in the lower parts, namely, by its presence and action driving away that darkness of the upper region towards the lower parts, and towards the center of the whole; Hence the first day, that is, the primary light, now occupied the Empyrean heaven, and night, that is, darkness, occupied all that space lying between the base of this heaven and the center of the whole. Then, when the light, already established in its spiritual heaven, was most active and never resting, by its force acting in opposition, namely, dark matter

--- Page 760 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI ÆTHEREI. 129

day after the purification of that region from its dark filth, no such bodies, except those of the stars, are found, on account of the thinness of the other parts. It is necessary that some stellar bodies be those organs and instruments, through which that secondary light, luminous only to itself, may visibly show itself for illuminating the other substances of the world as well. Therefore it does not seem alien from the truth that the fixed stars were made on the second day before the complete creation of the ethereal heaven, since without them it does not seem reasonable for a visible day to appear in this heaven. For they are like udders, through which divine Nectar, supercelestial Ambrosia, or luminous milk, as if from a nipple most full of light, is poured down into the lower regions, and the son of the world, whom they call Sol or Phoebus, is nourished and suckled after his birth; For such celestial milk is prepared in the nipples of the upper heaven, and its udders swell before the birth of the Sun, no differently than the breasts of women before they give birth.

   *But here someone might object that it was not so necessary for light to appear visibly on the second and third day, if indeed sensible things had not yet been created?* To this, we can respond in a threefold way; *Firstly,* that day could not be distinguished from night, nor light from darkness, without a visible manifestation of light; *Secondly,* because celestial light visibly and perceptibly descended towards the center for the expulsion of darkness, and for the vegetation of plants emerging from the earth, since three things are required for their essence: light, heat, and influence; *Thirdly and lastly,* that the Sun appeared visibly in the heaven even before the production of animals, and consequently it is not necessary to require any sense for the visibility of a thing. From which it is manifest that light was manifest and visible before the creation of seeing animals. Nor indeed will it suffice for such unbelievers to assert that the sacred Scriptures of Moses are contrary to this opinion, in which it is found that GOD *made two great luminaries on the fourth day, and that the other stars were also made on the same day?* For here it is probable that that Sacred Prelate understood the other Planets or wandering stars, since immediately before he made mention of the two principal ones. This also *Trismegistus* seems to verify in his sacred discourse, where he says, *that, when all things were disturbed, the light things were carried by fiery spirit to the upper regions, and immediately the heaven shone forth in seven circles;* From which it was manifest that the seven Planets were made immediately after the ascent of fire into the supreme region; but he makes no mention of the other stars. Moreover, the order would be irregular if on the very day of the creation of the Empyrean heaven its creatures were also created, and similarly in the creation of the earth, some of its creatures also came forth, if in the creation of the middle heaven no creatures were assigned to inhabit it on the same day.

   But perhaps someone might doubt concerning the method of forming such a mass of stars; *namely, by what way or from what subject their bodies could be produced, and be elevated to that place which is called the firmament on the second day, and there, as it were, adhere fixedly; Similarly, by what reason they are so distinguished by diversity of light and magnitude of body?* To which, so that I may respond probably and philosophically in all respects, it must be known that immediately after the penetration of light through the diaphragm of the crystalline sphere, as if through a sieve, a very great conflict arose between the rays of light and the dark matter of shadow found there, both on account of the actions of the one substance, and the sluggishness and forced movement of the other, and also because of their contrary qualities; for the rays of light vigorously acted upon the passive substance of darkness, driving it downwards and pursuing it so eagerly and vivaciously, that sometimes some part of them would be submerged in the depths of the shadow, and, as it were, captured in the snares of a certain viscous Spirit, which is the true matter of shadow; which the contiguous rays, attempting to redeem and, as it were, free their brother from prison, eagerly lifted high with this help, then by the rebound of the invading rays, and the reverberation

the reason from the resisting matter, then by its attractive faculty of heat; which part of the
imprisoned light, although it might be freed from the entire mass of darkness by the magnetic virtue of light,
yet it was so imbued with that thick and viscous Spirit that it could never
be freed from it; since matter naturally seeks its form and retains what is attracted;

adheres to the substance of that sphere like ice; because of its dark density,
rays of light, passing through the sieve of that sphere, striking against such icy
and crystalline globules in their passage, are presented as if in a mirror to the
visual faculty.

Similarly, formal light is attracted from every part of the middle heaven for the fulfillment of its appetite;
Hence, what the nature of the middle heaven is, such also is its luminous form,
because the composition of this heaven is formed from an equal proportion of material
heaven and spiritual heaven; therefore, if the matter of heaven is invisible, it is necessary
that its light also be invisible; since being visible proceeds from the visibility
and appearance of light, and the visibility of light arises from a colored material
object: but, because every part of the middle heaven is formed from an equal substance
of matter and light, it is necessary that, where matter is invisible due to its subtlety,
there also light shines invisibly and secretly; since such matter is too diaphanous
and lucid, and consequently not colored; moreover, the thicker the matter is, the more
visible its light will be. For every dimension of this heaven never ceases to desire,
until its appetite is satisfied by an equal part of light. Therefore, every part of it,
even the denser parts, has a similar portion of light for itself, by which it is led
to the goal of perfection and freed from the gate of corruption. If, therefore, matter
is visible due to its dimension, it is necessary, I say, that its formal light also
appears to the eyes. And hence it is that those stellar bodies are more or less
luminous because of their greater or lesser density, and due to their brightness,
are more subject to the visual faculty than other parts of the ethereal heaven.
The probability of this matter is shown by a common demonstration; For thin air
is invisible by itself due to its subtlety; but if it is condensed into a cloud or mist
by the force of cold, it will assume a visible form, sometimes luminous and glittering
with splendor, sometimes whiter, and sometimes fiery, or tending towards blackness
or lividity, according to the greater or lesser predominance of light in it.
But that the body of one star is larger and denser than another, this happens
according to the quantity of viscous matter enclosing the light; just as we see in this
lower heaven larger or smaller vapors or exhalations elevated, according to the more
effective virtue of the light or soul enclosed in them, suitable for sublimating upwards
a greater or lesser dimension of weight. But why the substance of one star is less
luminous than another, we have explained the reason above, for we said that due
to its greater or lesser opacity, according to the nature and disposition of the celestial
matter, it is more luminous or darker. The position of the fixed stars on the concave
surface of the crystalline heaven is described in this way.
