CHAPTER IV.

*Concerning the bodies of the Planets, their positions, and how they are always sustained in the same place; that is, why they do not tend more downwards at any time, since, due to the density of their matter, they are in a certain way heavy?*

[Large decorative initial V] To follow up on what was said before, it is certain that not only the fixed stars, but also the wandering stars themselves, which they call Planets, are formed from a certain condensed spirit, containing some spark of light, although by a different method and dissimilar action. For we recall that the fixed stars above are formed from the conflict of light pursuing dark shadow, with the thicker, colder, and in a certain way dark matter of the same shadow, and that their position and location are in the lower part of the crystalline heaven, where we declared them to be fixed, and as it were frozen, due to the terrestrial disposition of that sphere, namely cold and dry, firmly gluing their moist bodies, like ice, towards the concave surface of their sphere; from which these stars are perceived to move with the motion of the aqueous sphere, and to always observe the same distance in their motion; for which reason...
R 2

--- Page 763 ---
132 TRACTATUS I. LIB. V.

for which reason they are called fixed. But indeed, the composition of the bodies of the three superior Planets, and likewise of the three inferior ones, originated immediately from the creation shining forth from the radiant diadem of their King. For after the purer part of the Spirit of darkness, driven around the center—that is, the most splendid substance of the Spirit of darkness of the upper world region, flowing downwards on the first day—had been impregnated and made pregnant by a portion of the light of the same region, and had given birth to and produced a quasi-animated offspring with the help of supercelestial and celestial rays, that earthly opacity, born of rays of light invisibly dispersed in the spirit of the world, as well as those visible rays of the fixed stars, which as yet shone only dimly due to the density of the Spirit of the middle heaven, is drawn upwards, and partly also by the sparkling power of its own soul, or essential light, whose nature it is to naturally seek its native soil, it is elevated up to the royal throne in the midst of the middle heaven, and there, by dignity, splendor, and clarity, on account of the multitude of invisible rays gathered to it, it is exalted through the manifested presence of its dense and corporeal spirit to the world, and is held to be the most beautiful creature of the whole world; inasmuch as without its benevolent operations, no life, no sense or motion, no increase or multiplication exists in creatures. By the presence, I say, of this royal Planet, and by its light and the operation of its light, the spherical bodies of the other Planets are formed from the denser spirit of the middle heaven; and gradually, one above another, in a position and situation in no way to be altered, they are sustained in this middle heaven, and according to the variety of their position and situation—that is, according to their proximity to or distance from the solar body—their natures vary. Hence, therefore, the limpidity and transparency of the celestial spheres; hence the density of the astral bodies, and the collection of the denser matter of each of the aforesaid spheres into one round mass, as we shall explain more fully in its proper place.

**But here a very great controversy can arise, namely, why these spherical bodies, since they are dense, and consequently heavy, do not tend downwards, but always remain in the same state and position?** To which it must be answered, first, that the body of every star hangs in its own proper place, and is sustained by the divine power of GOD; For thus the divine will desired that the matter and spirit of each sphere should be united in such proportions, that each was destined to occupy its natural place; Hence, if the aforesaid bodies were lighter and more subtle, they would tend more upwards; but if they were too ponderous, they would fall more downwards. Therefore, each of these bodies has within itself a luminous soul, by whose immortal and never-decreasing power the body is exalted, elevated, and, because of the permanence of the luminous soul inherent in it, will never be depressed or corrupted, except in the very period of the world. Thus we also see in that artificial fire, which they call a rocket, by the force of a certain fiery spirit, by which it is moved upwards, that it is fixedly sustained in the same place in the air, until its artificial and quickly perishing soul fails; for then its body returns downwards. This same thing is also observed in a cannonball, whose upward motion is perceived to be longer or shorter according to the greater or lesser force of the artificial fire propelling it; indeed, if its motive power were not transitory, but fixed, it would never return from the goal towards which it is moved and emitted upwards, but by the force of its moving soul, it would remain firmly and constantly on high; but that failing, the metallic matter, elevated upwards against its nature, naturally tends towards the center of the whole. From these things, therefore, it can be directly concluded that there are two natural causes for the elevation or depression of a Planet's body, made in the ethereal heaven on the fourth day of creation, namely, the proportion or weight of the spiritual matter, and the abundance or defect of the luminous form. For a small amount of light will not elevate and keep elevated fixedly, unless it is a small amount of matter; but a multitude of form will sublimate a large quantity of matter as if with fiery wings; But if the matter

--- Page 764 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI EMPYREI. 133
ria in aliquo gradu proportionem sui agentis excedat, then that agent is not able to elevate its vehicle so high, but will place it in a lower position: But where the body is smaller, and the form of light contained within it is greater, there that body is carried more upwards, and is retained there according to the proportion of its power, that is, at the same distance from the center of the whole machine.

CHAPTER V.

*That every Spirit of darkness carries with it a small portion of the luminous essence of its region; On the generation of minerals and vegetables; That the work of the third day is, as it were, a prelude to that of the following day.*

[Decorative initial P]
ON the first day of creation, immediately after the production of essential light in the upper heaven, it was necessary that the darkness of that same region should yield place to the substance of that light, which was contrary to them, and by its life-giving activity be driven downwards into the depths of the second and third regions; yet in such a way that some part of the aforesaid light, because of its too deep penetration into the spiritual matter of those darknesses, in its

--- Page 765 ---
134          T R A C T A T U S  I.  L I B.  V.
its separation from fire without the destruction of its species; Hence it is necessary that air be exalted from the earth immediately after fire; For the same reason, water, being contiguous to air, is elevated after air. Since finally earth, to which water is naturally chained, is very heavy and adverse to motion, it is necessary that it be the principal impediment that detains the plant's soul, preventing it from ascending higher towards its natural seat: although the density of the other elements also seems to contribute to this in some way. Finally, with all these elements converging for the plant's composition, a certain impurity of earth is conjoined, infecting the entire body of the plant more or less, by which it is rendered dense and opaque; which happens because the quantity of secondary light enclosed within it was not sufficient to remove those impurities of the constituent elements; which if it had accomplished, it would have ascended higher like a solar spirit. This, therefore, was the end of the work of the third day, and as it were, a preparation for the work of the following day.

C A P U T  VI.

*Concerning the Rising and Origin of the Sun, and the Spiritual Purification of its Body in the Undigested Earth, and its Ascent or Elevation into the Heart and Middle of the Middle Heaven.*

<span style="font-size: 2em; float: left; margin-right: 0.1em;">L</span>That immortal Light, which we said above, veiled in darkness with the superfluous and coarser spirit of the Empyrean heaven, was snatched to the center of the universal machine, (when indeed the rude and undigested chaos, formed from a threefold mass of darkness with a threefold species of light, had been collected at the center of the machine) depositing every form of corruptibility in its own receptacle and vehicle, is exalted into the heart of the middle heaven, according to the opinion of Hippocrates, who in his *book on principles* speaks in almost these words: "The greater part of that immortal [thing], which we call hot, when all things were disturbed, retreated to that supreme region, which the ancients seem to call aether." And certainly it was necessary that such deformed spirits descend to the center, since they could deposit their obscurities and impurities in no other place than in that sole seat of corruptibility and darkness, namely, the undigested mass which we have named earth. Likewise, it was necessary that the luminous soul be contained in such a spirit, since without its action, that spirit or body could not have been purified and regenerated from its horrible filth, or exalted to its ethereal seat; since nothing whatsoever is rendered pure, or sublimated to the pinnacle of perfection, to which portions of light are either entirely lacking, or present in too small a quantity; and hence it is that *Trismegistus in his sacred discourse* thus writes: "When all things were undigested, all things began to be distinguished and weighed, and the lighter ones were carried by fiery spirit, and flew forth into the exalted region, and immediately the heaven shone forth in seven circles." For these reasons and others of this kind, it is probable that by the will of infinite nature, the denser part of each heaven, overwhelmed by darkness, with some particles of its own light enclosed within the recesses of its darkness, fell headlong downwards to the center of the universal structure, with the rays of primary light operating, and was condensed into an earthy mass by the constrictive faculty of cold; in which the lighter spirit of the ultimate heaven's darkness, both because of the excellence of the place from which it gushed downwards, and also because of the nobility of the fire or light which it includes, is considered purer and simpler than all the rest. But indeed this light, although most noble in itself, yet because of the perpetual night in the belly of the earth's presence—

--- Page 766 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI ÆTHEREI. 135

...its presence and governance was greatly weakened before the fourth day. For still the coldness of the earth, repelling the action and heat of the luminous rays of each heaven, and resisting their penetrative faculty, vehemently constricted the pores of its body; yet this resistance of coldness around the fourth day, partly because of the multitude of descending rays, which daily more and more exert their operations, partly also because of the heating of the sphere of fire, which was gradually inflamed daily by the rotation of the middle heaven, and consequently more effectively propelled the earthly coldness towards the center of the body, and finally because of the stronger resistance of the condensed earth, by which the descending rays are more vehemently reflected, and by whose strenuous reflection a greater effect of heat is excited, the earthly mass is repressed, perforated, and its pores are opened and dilated, rays are joined to rays, and force is united to forces, by which that supercelestial light, once captivated and made weak, now freely emerges from the bosom of the earth; and is liberated from its dark prison, endowed with its pristine powers, and freely tends towards its homeland. But since such a receptacle of the luminous soul is, as it were, a medium, through which it was carried both upwards (after it had been purified, that is) and downwards (when it was burdened by the impurity of darkness, to be sure), it was necessary that that vehicle also be elevated upwards with its ray; since it was to the light as the matter to its form; and indeed this exaltation of it could not be perfected before it had deposited the foul impurity of darkness, since no unclean thing can communicate with the purest substance of the middle heaven. Nor could this mass be impeded in its ascent by the substances of the lower elements, as was that fifth essence, from which vegetables originate, whose substance is naturally contiguous to the sphere of fire, and consequently has a relation to all other elements, which are concatenated with each other, as we said above; but it is exalted to the aether without impediment from the nature of the lower heaven, because its spiritual substance was a denser part of the Empyrean heaven, between which and these lower things the ethereal spirit or fifth essence is interposed; from whose denser part, attracted to the center with its own darkness, vegetables are formed, if it includes any sparks of light, and air, if it possesses nothing of the substance of light. And hence it is that, just as in vegetables the gross ethereal spirit is bound to fire in its ascent; so also that denser supercelestial mass must be connected by the bonds of nature to the denser part of the ethereal mass in its elevation; with which mass also the elements more or less mix themselves, and especially Air. The reasons, however, why these substances of each heaven thus gradually cohere with each other, is the extremity of appetite, by which the matter of one heaven, ascending upwards, desires to seize and retain the form of another; since every spirit, of whatever density, naturally tends towards the goal of perfection. Therefore, this entire supercelestial mass, by means of its soul, was carried upwards on the fourth day, distributing all the more impure dregs of its now purified mass, if any there be, to the sphere of fire as it ascended, and is elevated up to the middle of the ethereal heaven in the form of a most polished body, attracting the ethereal body from every side by magnetic force, by which it appears more splendid, as is clearly explained in the experiment written below, where it holds the scepter and governance of the entire visible world, comprehends its action within itself, and acts therein as the universal Emperor, claiming for itself the names of Phoebus, Apollo, Titan, and Sol.

For this mass, triumphing in the heart of the middle heaven because of the purity of its substance and the simplicity of its nature, since it is of the same condition as that spirit of the luminous fount, eagerly attracts to itself the rays distilling from the luminous fount through the openings of its diaphragm and dispersed throughout the entire middle heaven, by that magnetic power by which matter seeks form for its perfection; indeed, these primary rays of light are also attracted to the center of the spiritual mass, in which their brother holds his dwelling; since like naturally rejoices in its like, where they congratulate its brotherly liberty and its return from the Tartarean realms with a fiery, as it were, love. Therefore, a quantity of such light having been gathered from the fount of the supreme heaven into the center of the matter of that heaven, which is similar in substance, so that in equal measure that portion of light is weighed against the other spirit, it is necessary that that mass, now completely illuminated and visibly looking upon the world with a diurnal and placid countenance, should be perpetually moved because of the active quality of its form and the passive quality of its matter. But many objections can indeed be raised against this opinion of ours; among which someone might begin by asking, if the substance of this spiritual mass were originally from the supreme heaven, why does it not return again to that heaven, since it is of the same nature and condition? But to this a reply will very easily be given, namely, both because the substance of the superior heaven cannot become denser on account of the immense predominance of light in it, and also, because the accumulation of the aforesaid spiritual matter is too dense to ascend higher, but too thin and spiritual to descend. For this solar mass is sustained in the middle of heaven, both with respect to its matter, which it received from the earth, and indeed principally by reason of its form; For the spiritual matter of each heaven, of which we made mention before, ascends pyramidally, as it were, from the earth into heaven; (we are not speaking of a mathematical pyramid having a cone and a base, but we understand a certain physical body ascending circularly from a thick central base, always more acutely and thinly towards the circumference) pyramidally, I say, it ascends in a physical manner, like a tree, from whose root, ascending upwards, the dimension of its mass always decreases, since the lower part of the trunk is thicker than the upper, and the branches moreover, the higher they are, the smaller they are; finally, the leaves and flowers are the thinnest of all its parts. And so also the spiritual tree of the heavens is structured; for the earth is the thickest of all, which water succeeds, and air succeeds this, and fire is compared to its branches and leaves; But the planets surrounding the Sun correspond to the flowers, and in the solar body the true seeds of this tree are gathered, through which all natural things thrive and multiply. And certainly if we examine the anatomy of a tree more correctly, we find that a certain earthy disposition is the only impediment which obstructs its other parts from returning to their proper seats; since all elements are found distinct in a tree; Moreover, we will even find a part of the Fifth Essence with its soul there, inasmuch as by its motion the plant is elevated upwards. CHAPTER VII.

*Reasons, both Physical & Chemical, as well as Theological,*
*defending the probability of the preceding opinion.*

ALTHOUGH this opinion of ours concerning the origin of the solar body may
perhaps seem new and unheard of to the Philosophers of this age,
nevertheless we shall endeavor to demonstrate that it rests upon probable
arguments, using several reasons, both Philosophical and Chemical,
as well as Theological. For what is to be thought of the density of the bodies
of the Planets, since by the apposition of many spirits it has an obscure and
somewhat opaque form, so that it may be more capable of visible light, no
differently than invisible air, when condensed, produces a visible shining cloud.
Since therefore, according to the said Philosophers, the matter of a hailstorm
cloud evaporates from the bosom of the earth, and in its density is entirely
assimilated to subtle earth, why then should not that solar body be formed
from the most subtle matter of its womb, seeing that the earth is said to be
the parent of all things which are created after it? Do not meteors or corruptible
Suns, not much different from the figure of that incorruptible Sun, appear
in the upper region of the air from the exhalations of the earth, whose bodies
could not ascend higher into the ethereal region on account of their spurious
impurity? Are not also, by the authority of almost all the aforesaid Philosophers,
fire into air, air into water, water into earth converted by a certain thickening?
Through which it is also very easily seen that earth, conversely, is transmuted
into water, water into air, and air into fire by subtilization; and that fire has
something in common with aether. Furthermore, since all things are from water,
what is the difference between gross water and that subtle water, except that
the latter is from the part of the most subtle spirit, the former from the part
of the earth? Whence it is certain that the density of the Sun is from the part
of the earth.

Indeed, this assertion of ours relies upon and is supported by the very
words of certain Philosophers; since it is found in Hippocrates: *'A part of that
immortal [thing], which he called hot, when all things were disturbed, departed
into the highest periphery, which the ancients called aether.'* That is, when the
threefold portion of darkness of the threefold heaven, enclosing bright rays and
constituting a rude and undigested chaos, had been gathered into the lowest
heaven, the light, which they call *Immortal Heat*, ascended, etc. Which certainly
*Hermes Trismegistus in his sacred discourse* seems to confirm, where he speaks
thus: *'There was infinite shadow in the abyss, water moreover and a subtle
intellectual spirit were in the chaos by divine power; and when all things had
been indistinct, the light things afterwards flew forth into the exalted region,
the heavy things settled beneath the moist sand, and with things distinguished
and balanced, which were carried by fiery spirit, the heaven shone forth in
seven circles.'* For what else would that Sage mean by these sayings, than that
light and essential spirits were in the chaos of the lowest heaven by the word
of GOD, and that then the light things, that is, the spiritual things enclosed in
the chaos, were carried up into the celestial region by fiery spirit, that is, by
the bright rays enclosed in the chaos? This having been done, the Sun and the
other Planets shone forth. From those words of Trismegistus it also evidently
appears that chaos is a congeries of the darkness of all heavens compacted into
the lowest, along with captive rays. For he says; *'light things are carried by fiery
spirit into the exalted region, that is, into heaven.'* This also in almost the same
S 2 sense

--- Page 771 ---
140          TREATISE I. BOOK V.
In this sense, he himself emphasizes in his Pimander, where he says, *that a certain horrible shadow had slipped down with a slanting revolution, and had migrated into the humid nature, and from the depths of the humid nature a pure and light fire immediately flying out had sought the heights*, etc.

But setting these things aside, what is to be thought of the constant communication of the Sun with the earth? Since the Sun daily cohabits with the earth, as with its female, or at least with some humid spirit retained in the earth, as a disposed recipient, which acts as the female or the same womb; by whose annual copulation or coitus infinite things differing in species are produced, and each species multiplies itself; this indeed could not be accomplished unless there were a great affinity between the spirit of the terrestrial and solar body; which, beyond doubt, is on the part of matter, whose source is the earth, and not from form, since its origin is found in the opposite part, namely in the Empyrean heaven. Finally, since the solar body is visible, and therefore material according to half its part, it is necessary that its more corporeal part be derived from the source of matter, which we have demonstrated above to be the earth. What else did the Chemical Philosophers mean, who all, with almost unanimous consent, said that that most noble offspring of the Sun, which they called *Son of the Sun and Terrestrial Sun*, received its substance from the earth and other elements, but its form from heaven? Did not Mehumius also call the earth, in the Lamentation of Nature, the mother and nurse of all things, which she conceived in her womb from fire, that is, from light? Finally, that we may approach the reasons of Sacred Scripture, if we consider more diligently the time of the creation of the earth and the solar body, we shall perceive a very great mystery in the order of creation.

For on the third day of creation the earth was made, and its merely vegetable creatures, and after the creation of the earth, on the fourth day, the spherical body of the Sun is produced; into whose dimension the rays dispersed everywhere in heaven are gathered on the same day. Since, therefore, the Sun is a body to be preferred to the earth by infinite degrees, why would not infinite nature have made it before the creation of the earth, since it had begun its creation from the most perfect creature, namely light, and since it had perfected the ethereal heaven before the creation of the earth, in which the Sun is a far more excellent creature, unless because it had preferred to choose the mass of its body from the earth to receive such a most noble form, and one most suitable for rendering the invisible and hidden rays of the middle heaven manifest and visible? Indeed, this creation of the Sun is very mystical and an evident sign of the future uncreated good, which is to come to men. For just as the created supercelestial light descended from heaven to earth, that is, into shadow by means of spirit, and there, from the creation of the Empyrean heaven, for three days, like a vegetable body, it was buried in the abyss of darkness and earth, and then, by the assistance of the superior rays, shedding the corruptible impurity of the earth, it itself, glorified with its body, and as it were regenerated, on the third day after its enclosure in shadow, ascended into the ethereal heaven, from which, endowed annually with a shining scepter and diadem, it pours life, form, and the power of growth upon all vegetable bodies: So that uncreated light, the true and sole offspring of the uncreated Father, by divine will descended to earth, took on the nature of a human body, and according to corruptible flesh died, but by its divine and uncreated essence rose on the third day after death, its body now purified from all mortal corruption, and glorified beyond human understanding; Whence it ascended into the Empyrean heaven with inexpressible splendor, where, exalted at the right hand of its Father, brighter than all clarity, it daily and liberally pours spiritual gifts upon human souls, illuminating them with its divine light, and defending them from the rage of evil spirits; indeed, washing perishing men with the water of the fountain of life, and regenerating them with spiritual ablution, and redeeming and saving them from the corruption of sin. Therefore, no one ought to consider it an impossible thing, that this created solar essence descended to earth, so that there it might lay aside the opacity and impurity of its vehicle or body, into which it descended.

CHAPTER VIII.

*That the entire substance of the middle heaven was thicker and darker before the production of the Sun than after its appearance.*

[A large decorative woodcut initial 'L' depicting a figure in a landscape]
That first light, a creature, although before the production of the luminaries it performed the role of the Sun for three days, as *Dionysius* testifies, yet it was more imperfect than the Sun, as is affirmed in *resolut. Theolog. tract. 2. part. 2. port. 2. quæst. 1.* For it was dispersed and dissipated in a greater quantity of matter; whence, because of the multitude of matter, it could not manifest its effects, namely light and heat, so powerfully to the world, since the disposition of matter always opposed the actions of form. Hence therefore it was that it did not have such an effective power, flowing from heat, to subtilize and dissipate condensed matter before the creation of the Sun, since a united and simultaneously gathered force is always stronger; Whence this matter of the heaven was thicker before the fourth day than after. Wherefore it is manifest that the day, which the divine Philosophers held before the rising of the Sun to be for quality alone, that is, for mere light, and not for quantity or time, inasmuch as it finally received its origin from the fourth day, as *Theolog. Resolut.* testifies in the previously cited place, was far more shadowy and darker because of the thickness of the aether before the creation of the Sun than after its production; For after the third day, that entire mass of secondary light, diffused throughout the vast capacity of the middle heaven, contracted into the solar body. Indeed, according to *Dionysius, On the Divine Names, chapter 4*, this light is asserted to have been the substance of the Sun, but not yet fully formed; whatever that may be, it is certainly probable that this light, dispersed everywhere, was gathered into that purified and exalted solar mass, for the reasons declared in the penultimate preceding chapter, and produced more vehement effects in that part of the world through which it passed than when its light was dispersed everywhere: whence it heats more, thins, disperses, and illuminates: And by such actions of it, the thicker parts of this heaven, equally diffused before the rising of the Sun, are now, after its manifestation, reverberated more or less, both downwards and upwards in the same region, by whose resistance, and by the action of this solar body, diverse spherical bodies of the Planets are produced, as we shall declare below.

CAPUT IX.

*Concerning the production of the other Planets.*

[Large decorative initial I] N the chapter concerning the constitution of the Sun, we delineated that the Spirit of darkness of the supreme region of the world, retaining a portion of that light, having been reverberated with the darkness of the lower heavens to the cosmic center, had cast off its foul and black impurity, and had been exalted by the power of celestial light into the heart of the aether; and that the rays dispersed on the second day through the vast capacity of the ethereal heaven, both by the magnetic power of the solar matter, which desires form, and especially because of the luminous soul retained in that place, and soliciting its quasi-brothers surrounding it for its aid, are gathered and collected into its substance, no differently than some very cunning fowler, to deceive passing birds, encloses a small bird in a cage, by whose presence and songs others of that species are enticed into the same snares.

Therefore, with a multitude of luminous rays collected, and equally occupying the mass of the same Spirit, the thicker parts of this heaven are dispersed by the power of these united rays, whose nature it is to rarefy, and gradually, that is, according to more and less, are pushed towards the outer parts of this heaven; Whence the parts of that heaven more remote from its middle, in which the solar body is suspended, are colder, and consequently coarser and denser, and especially that extremity which tends more downwards, that is, towards the center; And hence it is that the Planets situated in those extremities produce cold effects, due to the dense disposition of the place. Therefore, into the lowest concavity of the middle heaven, the thicker part of the aether, reverberated by the power of the Sun's essential rays, because of its vicinity to the sphere of humidity, is very humid, and because of its contiguity with the sphere of fire, beyond which it cannot descend due to the purity of its substance, its coldness is strengthened by antiperistasis. This lower sphere of the middle heaven therefore relates to that middle sphere of the same, in which the solar body moves, as the element of water of the lower heaven relates to that of fire of the same; Whence the coldness of the thick aether of this sphere, by resisting the actions of the solar rays, excites an upward motion up to the midway point between this sphere and that of the Sun; for another motion meets that motion, namely that of the descending solar rays, and because these descending solar rays are equal to the ascending vaporous matter, and consequently the struggle of both natures is proportional; therefore the power of light is not sufficient to impede the ascent of the vaporous Spirit all the way to the midway point; nor are the forces of that ascending exhalation strong enough to repel the actions of the luminous rays, descending to that middle point, further upwards; whence they mutually contend with proportional forces at the same point, and in contending, they move with a double circular motion, namely, from west to east according to the appetite of matter, and from east to west for the progression of primary light. And hence it is that, with the motion of one nature seizing against the slow, though very resistant, motion of the other, the thicker substance of that sphere is gathered, applied, and assimilated into one globe, no differently than two opposing winds blowing together, by thickening the air, create a cloud. And this same thing happens in every sphere of this heaven immediately before the rising of its Planet. Therefore, by the action of the descending rays and the resistance of the ascending vaporous Spirit, a double circular motion occurs in the midway point between the lowest sphere of this heaven and that of the Sun; and from this, a globe is born.

--- Page 775 ---
144          TREATISE I. BOOK V.
That luminous globe, which we call the planet Mercury, into which solar light is visibly gathered by a certain magnetic force, by whose presence its body appears to our eyes. Similarly, by the constant rebounding of rays from this spherical Mercurial body, certain thinner vapors agitated from its body are excited upwards up to the halfway point between the solar body and that Mercurial one; to whose motion also in the same point another motion occurs to prevent the higher ascent of the aforesaid vaporous Spirit, namely, that of the rays descending from the solar body. Therefore, the equality of the Sun's nature with the equality of Mercury's nature generates a middle orb between them; by whose double circular motion its denser matter is gathered into one spherical mass, which Astrologers have called Venus. And this is the cause (namely, the proximity of the nature of the matter of these two Planets with the essence of the Sun) why their natural motion differs less from the solar motion than that of the other Planets, as we shall explain more fully below.
Also, another motion occurs from that lowest sphere upwards, towards the globe of Mercury, and another from the body of Mercury downwards towards that sphere, so that in the middle way the motion of one is opposed to the motion of the other: And by the equal struggle of these, a double motion is excited in that middle orb, by whose apposition that spherical mass is conglomerated from the equal nature of the Mercurial body, and the humid disposition of the innermost sphere, which is called the lunar body, Luna, Phoebe, Diana, Cynthia, Lucina, etc. Whose body, because of the vicinity of that region of corruption, and also because it receives only a tiny bit of luminous form from its nearest Mercury, desires the solar form more and more; by which, although it is adorned equally, that is, in the same proportion, as far as itself is concerned, nevertheless, according to its distance from and proximity to the solar body, the illumination of its body appears more or less visibly to us; by which it is manifest that its greater part is in a certain way opaque, and consequently, a certain opacity is required for the visibility of stellar bodies. Similarly, it is certain that this body is formed from the denser substance of this heaven, because it cannot be totally penetrated by solar rays. And in this way we have three Planets moving in their own orbs, arranged proportionally by distance and order from each other between the convex surface of the lowest heaven, whose bodies are to be considered thicker and denser, the further they are from the solar body.

Since also as many Planets are found above the solar body, namely, between the place of the fixed stars and the orb of the Sun, how, or by what reason, they can be produced there in their distinct orbs, must be diligently investigated: We have said, therefore, that one part of this heaven, thicker and lower, is driven downwards from its heart by the presence of the Sun, and the other, namely, drier, upwards, towards the concave surface of the watery, or crystalline sphere, in which we declared above that the fixed stars are congealed; in which limits coldness also, as in its opposite place, abounds by antiperistasis, that is, because of the gentle warmth of the most spiritual heaven supereminent, and contiguous to the crystalline sphere, and the lively heating of the solar body, by whose operation it is dispersed from the solar orb to those margins, and its dryness from the congelative disposition of the crystalline sphere, which all for this reason have called the glacial heaven, the crystalline [nature] comes from the multitude of congealed waters. Therefore, the action of solar rays on this supereminent subject is the sole reason and origin of the Planets gradually suspended above the Sun. For, just as we demonstrated concerning the production of the sphere of humidity of the lowest heaven, in the origin of the elements, that the constrictive nature of earth, with that of fire, in equal proportion, as it were, meet and concur in the middle way; so also by the motion of solar rays up

In a part of the heaven, a conflict arises from equal parts of diverse natures: by whose varied motion, namely from east to west, and from west to east, a spherical mass is conglomerated, which they call the *Jovian body* or *Jupiter*, formed from two portions of solar nature, and as many parts of this colder and drier heaven: However, from the reverberation or reflection of the Sun's rays rebounding downwards from the Jovian body, a subtler vapor is excited, and accompanies those reflecting rays; and these, in the middle way between the Jovian and solar bodies, meet new rays of the Sun ascending upwards: from whose double opposite motion, a new double circular motion arises; from which the density of that entire place is rolled up and reduced into one globe, which they name the *Martian body* or *Mars*, formed from an equal disposition of *Jupiter* and the *Sun*. Similarly, towards the upper motion, a motion occurs from the luminous nature of *Jupiter*, which is applied to a motion contrary to itself in the middle way between *Jupiter* itself and the convex surface of this heaven; from whose conflict a double circular motion also arises; from which the coarser portion of that interstice is gathered into one round body, which we call *Saturn*. And in this way we have the bodies of the seven Planets exalted to their proper seats, having various qualities and dispositions according to their position and composition, as we will clearly explain in the following chapter. The production of the Planets, moreover, is thus described.

CHAPTER X.

*On the natures of the Planets, and their dispositions, by which they operate in these lower things.*

[Decorative initial Q] ALTHOUGH from the preceding it is sufficiently clear that the bodies of the three inferior Planets, and as many superior ones, proceeded from the virtue of the Sun; nevertheless, here we shall produce another reason, by which we will declare, both that the creation of the solar body was prior in order to the bodies of the other wandering stars, and also that it received the formal disposition of light first. For almost all Philosophers have agreed on this, that light is in the Sun, as in something luminous in itself, but in other Planets participatively; and since the light of a star is its essential form, without which a star cannot exist or be named, and the other Planets received it from the Sun itself as from their informing principle, it is necessary that the Sun precede the other Planets in the order of creation, no differently than a principle precedes what is principled by it. Light, therefore, emitted downwards from the highest heaven through its common diaphragm, is received into the Solar body on the fourth day, and is kept there, as Basil testifies. The Sun imparted a certain portion of this to each Planet, both above and below, making it either greater or smaller, both according to the proximity or remoteness of its body from the Sun's seat, and also according to the disposition of that Planetary body to which it gives. And hence it is, that according to Iamblichus all celestial virtues are in the Sun, and, as Proclus testifies, at the sight of the Sun the powers of all celestial bodies are gathered into one, which we finally believe to be disseminated into this lower world through its fiery spiracles. Whence the Platonists believed the soul of the world to be enclosed in the Sun. Therefore, Phoebus sits in the middle, shining with golden hair, holding a scepter and rudder, like a King and Emperor, most replete with the light of all stars, which he received from the intelligible world above all other stars, because his intelligible soul is more capable of splendor, as some Platonists hold. The primary royal disposition, both by reason of its composition and by its effect, will clearly reveal itself: For it is composed of an equal part of spiritual matter ascending from the earth, and of essential luminous form descending from the Empyrean heaven: Whence by Artefius its orb is called the sphere of soul and equality. From which it is clear that its temperament is warm in a most gentle degree, which it received from the disposition of secondary light, and imperceptibly humid, this coming from the nature of its spiritual body. But because the multitude of its form completely satisfied the appetite of its matter, therefore warmth certainly predominates in its body; by the benefit of which not only the Planets received their natural dispositions, but also all lower things. Hence it is, therefore, that Mercury, receiving one part of its nature from the Sun, and another from the humid and cold mass spherically dispersed downwards, has three parts of frigidity and humidity, and as many of the Sun's temperament; Whence Mercury is much more humid and cold than warm, because in the disposition of the Solar body, we said one part of the body concurs with one part of the luminous soul. And hence it is, that Mercury is so variable in its nature, and so inconstant, that it sometimes joins itself to good Planets, sometimes to evil ones, and their natures

--- Page 778 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI ÆTHEREI. 147

tures as good as they are bad. For since it has much cold matter in its composition, and only a little form with respect to its substance, it desires to assume the natures of other Planets, and those it encounters, and whose aspect it has had, it readily receives their impressions. Hence in its nature it is very fluid, and more humid than hot. \*Luna\*, however, since it is composed partly of the nature of \*Mercurius\*, and partly of the cold and humid mass of the same heaven, is extremely cold and humid with respect to celestial bodies, since it has only one part of warmth from \*Mercurius\*, with one of coldness and humidity, and two from the cold and humid sphere itself; Hence it constantly seeks and receives help and light from the solar body through participation. The nature of \*Veneris\*, however, because it consists of an equal part of that of the Sun and \*Mercurius\*, has three parts of the Solar disposition, but one part of the inferior cold and humid sphere, which it received from \*Mercurius\*: hence it is beneficent and life-giving in its nature and fortunate for living things; for it moistens more than the \*Sol\*, and warms more than \*Mercurius\*; Hence it is hot in the second degree of pleasantness and humid in the first. \*Jupiter\*, however, differs from \*Veneris\* in this, that in its nature it is hotter and more virile because of the proximity of \*Mars\*, to which it is contiguous; for it participates in its nature in a certain way, since it was joined with the Sun for its composition; similarly it is drier than \*Veneris\* due to the proximity of the sphere of \*Saturn\* in the upper part, and \*Mars\* in the lower part; Hence its nature is plainly hot and humid, formed from an equal disposition of the \*Sol\*, and from a part of the thicker ether driven towards the concave surface of the supreme heaven or the crystalline sphere; because the substance of its sphere, frozen by the power of the glacial heaven and agitated by the power of the solar rays, and its power of resistance, meeting those rays descending into the middle way, produces the same effect in this heaven which the nature of the earth with the heat of the element of fire descending into the middle way produces in the inferior heaven, namely humidity. But because heat exerts greater forces in ascending, that is, it heats more strongly, therefore \*Jupiter\* heats a little more than it moistens; \*Mars\*, however, is produced from the simple action and passion of \*Jupiter\* and the \*Sol\*: Hence its nature consists of three parts of the Sun's nature, namely one of Jupiter's and two of the Sun's; it also has a portion of the cold and dry sphere, which it immediately received from Jupiter's disposition; hence, because of the warmth of \*Jupiter\* and the \*Sol\*, it has three indications of warmth. Indeed it is very hot and dry, that is, it has an entirely fiery nature, because the nature of the \*Sol\* heats more by ascending than by descending; which is also proven by the nature of artificial fire placed on the grate of some wind furnace; for downwards, that is, below the grate, it heats only a little; but upwards vehemently; For fiery nature is always carried upwards with great violence, imitating the disposition of its origin, from where it was first derived. But because the malignity of the sphere of \*Saturn\* on the other side relates to the nature of \*Mars\*, it both makes it drier by its dryness, and also by antiperistasis from that part, it inflames the nature of \*Mars\*, and drives and reverberates its forces downwards, and attributes to it a malignity fatal to human nature, no differently than a cloud enclosing lightning multiplies the fury of that lightning by its contrary disposition, and renews the exhalation enclosed in its belly by illuminating the contrariety of natures, and bringing its destructive qualities into action. \*Saturnus\* has a nature participating in that ethereal cold and dry mass driven to those margins by the force of the Sun's rays, and in the constitution of \*Jupiter\*: Hence it has three quarters of styptic coldness, and only one of solar heat, which it received from the nature of \*Jupiter\*; and hence its constitution is very fixed, cold, and dry, greatly resembling an earthly disposition, and drawing its congealing coldness from the crystalline heaven: Wherefore this Planet is strongly opposed to \*Jupiter\*, \*Mars\*, the \*Sol\*, and \*Veneris\*, and is a vehement adversary of the generation of inferior things, the radical humid

radical moisture, absorbing by its dryness, and blunting innate heat by its immense coldness. Here, however, it must be observed in passing that even the fixed stars induce the natures of these Planets, or rather, have had similar dispositions from their creation, which differ from each other according to the mass of vaporous matter and the proportion of luminous form from which they are composed. Similarly, because of the proximity of one star with another of the same or contrary condition: Hence, a Planet, passing under a fixed star or stars, which they call signs, of its own condition, is found by experience to have a stronger effect on these lower things; and then it is said to be in the house of exaltation or joy; and if it moves under signs of a contrary condition, its powers and influence in the lower things are weakened; and then Astrologers said it was in its fall or detriment. Therefore, the fixed stars act upon the bodies of the Planets, either to impede their virtues and natural influences, or to strengthen them and render them more effective.

CHAPTER XI.
*That it is necessary for two extremes to be produced before any
middle can be assigned.*

[Ornate initial Q] UONIAM in the preceding chapters we have discussed many middles, which cannot exist without extremes, it is necessary that the extremes first be produced in the order of creation, before the middle can be reached; For nothing can be called a middle that is not placed between two extremes; nor was the middle heaven called such before the lowest heaven was created; just as GOD also created the Empyrean heaven and the earth before He suspended His gleaming and glorious fire in the middle space between both extremes; nor did He produce the sphere of humidity in the middle of the lowest heaven, unless fire and earth were first made manifest, between which it might move. Thus also Mercury in the middle of the lowest part depends on the virtue of two extremes, namely, the sphere of ethereal coldness and humidity, and the solar body. Similarly it was necessary that the Sun, and the sphere of coldness and dryness, precede the rising of Jupiter, to which a middle place between them is assigned. Finally, since the origin of the aforementioned middles arises from the mutual action and passion of the extremes, it is necessary that the extremes first be produced in the order of nature, before the middles, which are composed from them.

CHAPTER XII.
*Concerning the influences of the Planets, and how through them they
act upon these lower things?*

[Ornate initial P] HILOSOPHORUM opinion is that the stars act upon these lower things by motion, light, and influence; among which operations they consider influence to be more subtle and effective, which they assert penetrates without any impediment even to the very depths of the earth. Nor indeed do they stray at all from the truth, since by constant experience we are compelled to recognize the admirable operations of influences. What kind and how manifold, therefore, this influx of the stars may be, we will briefly discuss in this place. Therefore, we call the influence of any Planet when a spark of its luminous soul

--- Page 780 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI ÆTHEREI. 149
luminous, led in its most subtle and imperceptible spiritual vehicle, its penetration by no means to be repressed, is accustomed to enter any thing and produce new effects, whether manifest or hidden, in it, either for generation and conservation, or for corruption and ruin. Hence, therefore, the difference of influences arises, which nevertheless do not differ in themselves, but with respect to the subject into which they descend: For if a Planet has an influence on matter naturally disposed to it, namely where the matter in the lower regions is of the same composition as it (the planet) in the higher regions, then certainly such an influence brings fuel and nourishment to bodies; but if it finds matter of a contrary condition, it undoubtedly operates destructively upon it. For either the stubbornness of the receiving subject receives it perversely, or its weakness can hardly tolerate the influence. For example; Saturn's power is indeed restrictive; but Mars' is motive; and the former frequently harms by accident, when it is received by colder matter; while the latter when by hotter; Likewise, the former harms when it is received; for it is received by way of congelation; the latter when by heat: This (Mars' influence) is also the cause of many fevers, when, namely, a large mass of crude humors accumulates around the heart/diaphragm. The influence of the Martial Planet entering such a body stirs up the conflict of contraries, from which putrefaction arises, and the cause of fever is excited. Similarly, the influence of the Sun, and its light and heat, although they seem to offend the languid, are nevertheless exceedingly necessary for life and generation. But so that we may discuss the disposition of congruent influences, and those agreeing with the nature of the subject, we will first approach the dispositions of the influences of the two luminaries. For it is certain that the Sun diffuses and disseminates its influences into well-disposed bodies, such as plants of every species, as if through fiery breaths, and from this, they become green, mature, flourish, blossom, and the Sun, as it were, inspires life and heat into such lower things with its light. Similarly, at the full moon, due to the multitude of solar rays occupying the lower part of the Moon's body, a thicker portion of its sphere flows downwards each month by virtue of the light acting upon it (which is demonstrated by the experiment of the altar), and not only does it penetrate the immense substance of the sea and make it swell, but it is also accustomed to secretly enter plants themselves, increasing their sap, and it is accustomed to invisibly scrutinize the interiors of animals, multiplying their phlegmatic humor. Indeed, this increase of the said humors could in no way come from the air, since it is known that air itself is not subtle enough to accomplish such a work. For experience itself has taught us that air or wind enclosed in a bladder, a box, or any unperforated vessel, or in the stomach, or the head of an animal, is accustomed to exit in no way, unless the aforesaid vessels or places are opened. From which it is manifest that this augmentation of humidity flows from the sphere of the Moon, whose substance is much more subtle than that of air, so that it is accustomed to flow insensibly and without resistance at the time of the full moon into the aforesaid bodies, which are of a similar condition to its sphere, but when the Moon's splendor wanes, that infused humidity always gradually decreases, insensibly exhales from bodies, and gradually, with the retreat of clarity from the lower parts of the Moon, returns into the concavity of its sphere. This, however, is demonstrated more clearly by the effect of the experiment of a leaden globe placed against the Sun, which, while the Sun's rays touch it, thicker vapors around its circumference are driven downwards; but when the rays are removed, that thick air returns to its original place.

CHAPTER XIII.

*That although the heavens and Stars are governed by intelligences, as is the opinion of the ancients, it is nevertheless not probable that they are moved by these intelligences themselves, but that a faculty was naturally infused into them from the beginning by divine will.*

[Decorative initial P] IT is the opinion of all Peripatetics that the Stars are not moved by their own motion, but by the circuit of their sphere; and that the sphere is moved by an intelligence, or its own daemon; and they teach that daemons received their motion from GOD, the prime mover. But, as it seems to me, in naturally moving things, the cause of their motion must always be said to be natural, and not supernatural. For GOD, from the beginning of heaven and earth, bestowed upon all creatures the first act, as a most beautiful gift, by which they might be brought into their being, and actually be led from one state to another, or from one place to another, according to the nature of the creature, by themselves. For since light, which we have called above the first and principal creature of GOD, is the first act, most swift in its motion, bestowing form, life, and greater or lesser motion by its presence upon every creature, who will doubt that some light and ethereal body, whose appetite for formal light has been satisfied by its presence, has the power to move by itself and from its own form; since we have experienced that lower natural bodies, in which a smaller portion of that luminous form resides, perform this very same thing before our eyes?

For we see animals move hither and thither by the action and agitation of their internal light: Indeed, since a twofold motion is perceived in animals (for sometimes they are led by the desire and appetite of their body, and sometimes by the will of the moving soul), why would it be impossible for the stars, in which the quantity of light is a thousand times greater than in animals, and from which that light of animals descends, to be led both from west to east according to the appetite of their matter, and also to be carried from east to west by a contrary path according to the disposition of their luminous form? Far be it, however, that we should therefore try to prove, with the Platonists and Astrologers, both of the Arabs and Egyptians, and of the Chaldeans, that the heavens and stars are animals, since they are to be preferred to these by infinite degrees of perfection. What also is to be thought of a subject far viler than an animal, namely a plant or a tree, in whose vegetation motion from one point to another is found, and according to the three dimensions of its body without any aid from intelligences?

But, to descend to yet viler things, what shall be said of artificial things, when images, immobile by themselves, are immediately moved by the action of some light or a lit candle, and are turned around by the effect of that light, as has been demonstrated in the experiment below? Therefore, since our artificial and elemental fire, which is derived from the effect of light, can accomplish such things, who will be so dull of intellect as to deny that a stronger virtue lies hidden in the efficient cause of fire? For according to that old axiom of the philosophers, *That which makes something such, is more such itself.* All these things, since they can be performed, both by nature and by art, without the incitement of any intelligence in these lower things; doubtless in the ethereal heaven, they are performed better and more exactly because of the multitude of light

cap. 4.
The tradition of the Magi called them celestial and mundane; thus we exclude them from the bodies of the stars, as if they have no office or dominion within them. For we confess, according to the opinion of the ancients, that they are accommodated to the spheres of the world beyond divine worship, and preside over each of the heavens and stars, and that they are distributed into as many orders as there are heavens in the world, and stars in the heavens. Wherefore the wiser Magi made some Saturnine, others Jovial, etc. Nor indeed was that opinion of the Platonists far from reason, affirming that infinite Daemons inhabit the spherical substances of the stars, no differently than animals inhabit the earth, whom they divide into legions, to whom they say kings, or princes, or governors are appointed. And this is the same thing that Abbot Trithemius seems to approve, saying that seven spirits were appointed to the seven Planets from the beginning of heaven and earth: Of whom the spirit governing the kingdom of Saturn is called Orifiel, of Jupiter Zachariel, of Mars Samaël, of the Sun Michael, of Venus Ana

it usually bears a resemblance to its cause; then also, because such a figure is the noblest, most useful, most perfect, and most convenient of all others, since it is far more capacious than the rest. Immediately therefore after the action of this Spirit, that first creature shone forth, proceeding from motion as if from the splendor of uncreated light; and it is indeed probable that it moved in the same way and with the same kind of motion, imitating the actions of its first cause. Moreover, the effect seems to declare to us the path of this circular motion, that is, the terminus from which to which, namely, that it was from the east to the west, or rather from the right hand to the left, looking towards the North Pole; (for East and West received their names from the creation of the Sun) and this for two principal reasons; the first of which is, because human nature, in which that divine light especially predominates among all other animals, is accustomed, as it were, to move the right hand by the divine appetite of its light, and to exercise it in every manual operation, as being more excellent and nobler; by which it is manifest that the natural appetites of the primary light move from the right side of the heaven: The second reason, which indeed seems infallible, is, because the swift and very rapid motion of the heavens is perceived to tend from that part towards the west. But since essential created light proceeding from the uncreated light is said to be most mobile, according to most Philosophers, and indeed even by those most skilled in Theology, among whom I name Augustine on Genesis literally, because nothing is more mobile or subtle; and so also by him in the same place it is called the foundation and principle of supreme natural motion, it is necessary that the swifter and more rapid motion of the entire heaven be derived from its source; and consequently, that the diurnal motion, by which the entire material world revolves from East (contrary to Copernicus's opinion) to West, in the space of twenty-four hours, by virtue of that luminous spiritual source, flows from it; which Trismegistus also seems to confirm in his first discourse with these words. "The creating Mind, indeed, containing the circles together with the Word, and turning its machine towards itself with swift rapidity, commanded it to revolve from beginning to end without end:" by "beginning" he seems to understand the East, and by "end" the West. Do we not also see that Holy Scripture in almost every place always places the name of the East before the West, Genesis 13:14, Psalm 50, and countless other places? Moreover, in all adoration, worshippers turn themselves towards the East, as in Ezekiel 8:16, Matthew 11, Luke 13:29, and many other places. Similarly, that star declaring the advent of Christ appeared in the East. And so also the coming of the Lord will be from the east towards the west, Matthew 24:27. By the foregoing, it is demonstrated that that uncreated Light moved from East to West. For what is clearer than this? especially since the effect of that thing also falls under the senses. Are we not certain that there is a soul in man or any other animal, although invisible, while we perceive its body moving itself hither and thither? Do we not recognize an invisible act to be contained in a plant, while we see it growing strong and germinating? Are we not also certain that an intellectual soul exists above the surface of the corporeal world, while experience testifies that it gathers itself and revolves in a natural day? Which motion, indeed, the matter of this world, since it is inefficacious for motion by itself, could in no way accomplish, except through the motion of the luminous source, which is the foundation, source, and origin of every natural motion. And consequently, it is certain that the motion of that first luminous creature was circular, and from east to west, which was primary among all, and swifter, nobler, and more powerful than the others, since it arose from the source of universal action. How, however, that spherical matter, inept for motion by itself, is moved by that fiery soul, placed upon the surface of its periphery, is declared by the following experiment; where B. C. A. is a wheel, on whose circumference that artificial fire, called A. Fusum, is attached. Therefore, by virtue of this ignited spindle, the whole wheel is violently carried along, completing its circular motion as swiftly as possible.

We say therefore that the preceding experiments clearly demonstrate that the outer parts of the globe, that is, those tending more towards the circumference, are by nature more apt for motion than the more central parts; because they are moved around with less effort than those at the center. Wherefore it is more probable that the diurnal motion of the mundane machine originates rather from the circumference than from the center; and this is clearly proven by two reasons; namely, first, because a hundredth part of the force proportionally moving the center will move the circumference; as clearly appears in those artificial machines described above, and conversely, as is clearly evident in the outcome; whose motion, although produced by art, is nevertheless certain to have a natural reason; secondly, also, because we have declared above that in the beginning of the world the origin of actions proceeded from the supreme fount of forms; from which source the smallest part could descend to the earth, both because of its remoteness from the Empyrean heaven (for the center is further distant from its circumference) and because of the immense coldness of the earth; indeed, in which there are four quarters of coldness, and no warmth, unless it comes to it accidentally, namely either from light enclosed in darkness at creation, or from the influences of the stars flowing into the earth's depths, as we said above. Hence certainly Gilbert's reasons are ridiculous, believing it impossible for the heavens to be revolved in the space of 24 hours due to their infinite magnitude; for if he had considered with more exact judgment, both the infinite nature of the agent and also the disposition of the patient, he would most easily have found that the matter stands far otherwise than he supposed. sulfur and mercury of the alchemists: from whose coition the solar infant, the glory
of the world, and its true soul, was born; Whence it is most truly called the sphere of the soul.
This, therefore, is the reason for the sun's position and location and sustenance in the middle
of the heavens; Indeed, this intersection of the Triangles is the most true seat of the heart
of the Macrocosm, in which all things are tempered in due measure; for matter does not
predominate, nor does form excessively assert itself, except in that which splendidly
and completely and perfectly satisfies the appetite of matter: This is the true mundane
unity forged from duality; in whose composition Divinity itself is seen as if in a mirror;
Indeed, this is that true marriage between heaven and earth, by which earthly things
taste of heavenly things, and rejoice in them, and are blessed and informed by them;
Thus we have the Philosophical Sun and Moon contained in a single body, by whose
amiable aspect the entire world rejoices, grows green, thrives, and every species
multiplies in its like.

CHAPTER II.

*How vegetative souls are daily infused from heaven into the lower regions*
*after the completion of creation; and concerning the magnetic*
*and attractive property*
*of matter.*

CUM Since the life of lower creatures is from the luminous soul itself, and that soul arises from a celestial source, it will be diligently investigated by what path, or by what vehicle, this soul is transferred through the aethers to these lower regions, contrary to the appetite of its own nature; and infused into terrestrial bodies, since such bodies are entirely contrary to the nature of the soul; both inasmuch as they are derived from the dark mass opposed to light, and also because they are entirely ineffectual for motion, and therefore most opposed to the mobile faculty of the soul. It is therefore manifest that, just as the spiritual substance of the middle heaven is interposed between the lowest heaven and the luminous source; so also no spark from that source can descend downwards into the lowest region of the world, unless it first passes through the Spirit of the middle region. Moreover, just as every matter is always eager to attain the goal of its perfection, and since the mover towards that goal is the essence of light, it is necessary that every material portion of the Spirit of the middle heaven receive any spark of the passing rays as its form, and carry it, enveloped in its viscous and tenacious substance, downwards to the lower regions, both because of the great communication that exists between the substance of the middle heaven and that of the lower heaven, and also because matter, by a certain magnetic virtue, draws the soul and form to itself. And since the substance of the aether is more subtle than corporeal air, therefore it very easily penetrates the spermatic body, which is optimally disposed to receive it, without any impediment; so that that soul is enclosed in a double vessel, namely first in the aerial spirit and finally in some terrestrial body; Thus also that ethereal spirit, serving as a vehicle for the soul, is enclosed in the aforesaid body in the same way as the soul in the spirit; and just as the soul moves in the whole and in every part of its spirit; so also the spirit is dispersed in the whole body and in every part with its soul, generating motion towards the goal of perfection or maturation. And in this way, spirits are added and joined to spirits annually, and their souls to the souls of others daily and liberally into bodies well-disposed to receive them; From which the multiplications and generations of things occur assiduously in every part of the terrestrial globe. Hence, therefore, the increase of one grain into a multitude, hence the infinite growth of one animal, hence finally the hastening of minerals towards the perfection of gold, that is, the inclination towards fixation. And certainly it is wonderful to consider how or by what reason this luminous nature, after the completion of creation, can descend from its place with an ethereal and spiritual vehicle to the lower regions, since light and every fiery thing naturally and eagerly seek the higher regions

--- Page 802 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI ELEMENTARIS. 171

it is perceived. Hence it is likely that this happens from the appetite of matter, and not from form, since every thing naturally tends to its own proper place. And without a doubt, a great and strong magnetic virtue is inherent in these lower composite things, attributed to them by God from the beginning, for attracting and retaining for themselves such a quantity of form as the species requires; by which, according to the proportion and species of the desiring matter, form is attracted to it. Indeed, we find a virtue of this kind in the stomach of animals, by which prepared food is attracted through the esophagus to its cavity; and also in the lower limbs, a power of attracting animal spirits downwards is observed, through which touch usually occurs with judgment. There is, I say, a similar magnetic virtue and property in matter, by which superior virtues are attracted to lower things in the proportion that is said to be inherent in the attracting species for attracting from its creation; for the matter of the earth does not desire the form of heaven differently than a woman desires a man, nor does it otherwise allure the form with its spirit, which it desires, by its flatteries and attractions, than a harlot allures passing men with the wanton property and disposition of her flattering eyes; indeed, it always desires a luminous form, and never fails to attract it to itself as much as it can. And although both the animal and vegetable kingdoms are richer in multiplication than the mineral kingdom, nevertheless, they cannot approach the goal of perfection any more than a man most corrupted by avarice and rich in much money can approach the pinnacle of immortality. For in every apposition and union of a new form with the seed of the same species, new corruptible parts of the elements are also added and applied, because of the porosity of its species; which indeed cannot happen in the mineral kingdom, because of the hardness and fixation of that substance, or the constriction of its parts; Hence its treasure, acquired by the sun and the rays of the planets through the magnetic property of its matter, is continually stored up and reserved for the perfection of its body; wherefore it appears annually more luminous and more and more similar to the solar rays themselves, and in perfection and fixation, though imperceptibly, it grows and multiplies, that is, it is more fully adorned with formal beauty, as will be more clearly explained in the following chapters.

CAPUT III.

*That the earth is the mother of all bodies, both simple and composite, and that the influences of the stars are like seeds of heaven cast into the womb of the earth; On the difference of composite bodies.*

MORIENUS ROMANUS calls the earth the mother of all elements. For he strongly contends that they proceed from the earth and return to the earth; Mehunnius, in his "Lamentation of Nature," demonstrated clearly enough that the earth is the mother and nurse of all things which she conceives in her womb from fire, that is, from heaven; and almost all authorities of the Philosophers conclude that heaven is the father of composite things, but the earth is their mother, bearing them in her own bowels. Ptolemy and Calcidius give the reason for this, asserting that all celestial influences flow into the depths of the earth, which, like the seeds of things, there as if in

Y 2 a womb

--- Page 803 ---
172	TREATISE I. BOOK VI.
common matrix, are included; Hence, because of the varieties in the proportions of these descending (influences), diverse generations of diverse things occur on earth, and diverse impressions arise. These things, therefore, being known, it remains evident that the earth is the mother of bodies, both simple and composite, bearing them in its womb at the beginning before their production, no differently than a woman bears her fetus. Concerning the simple elemental bodies, we have already treated sufficiently in the preceding (sections). Here, therefore, we will briefly discuss the differences of composite bodies, into which, when well-disposed, certain sparks of essential light are continually infused. The ancients, therefore, generally divided composite and mixed bodies into five species of composition; of which the two former embrace inanimate bodies; for mixed bodies of the first composition are Meteors, formed from smokes, vapors, and exhalations. And of the second composition are metals and other minerals. Furthermore, the later species are animate; for mixed bodies of the third composition are plants and vegetables; of the fourth are irrational animals; and of the fifth or last, the rational body, man, the noblest of all creatures. Whence, because of his greater similarity with the Macrocosm, he is called Microcosm. Of these species of composite bodies, some are perfectly mixed, such as minerals themselves and all animate beings; but only one is imperfectly mixed; namely, that which comprises all genera of meteors of the first composition. It must be diligently observed, moreover, that celestial light abounds more in perfectly mixed bodies and is retained more firmly in them than in imperfectly mixed ones; similarly, that it is more abundant in animate beings than in perfectly mixed inanimate ones; and that purely sensitive animate beings are richer in that celestial gift than purely vegetative or irrational ones. And this is what the Philosophers seem to hint at, asserting that in intellectual beings fire predominates, in sensitive beings fire is equal to air, in vegetative beings water is weighed with air in similar scales; in which, however, the dignity of air is diminished because of the cold disposition of water; and finally, they hold that minerals are composed chiefly of earth and water. From which, indeed, it is manifest that in humans that celestial fire prevails more, inasmuch as they are intellectual; then in other sensitive beings, inasmuch as air and fire predominate in them; afterwards, that is, in a still more diminished degree, in vegetables, inasmuch as their airy parts are tempered by the coldness of water; and finally, the smallest part of the luminous form is found in minerals; because earth and water have dominion in them, and consequently admit a smaller portion of fire into their composition.

Others, however, hold that they live occultly and secretly, and have the power of multiplying and taking on increase, and they say that that life-giving Spirit is hindered by the excessive dullness and grossness of the matter; whence they contend that it (the matter) does not exercise that power and natural virtue with which it is naturally endowed. through that motion, which some portion of light produces, therefore that light

the vigor of the mineral soul grows, and according to the degrees of its increase,
that body also becomes more perfect, more brilliant, and more fixed. From which
it is manifest that minerals secretly live, essentially flourish, and, although slowly,
hasten and are sublimated to the pinnacle of perfection, contrary to the assertion
of the aforesaid Philosophers, who wished to deny them life and growth.
Therefore, the Chymical Philosophers did not imprudently make a twofold
mineral matter, of which they called *one masculine, simple and pure, sulphur,
tincture, fire, Sun, and agent*, and *the other feminine, quicksilver, water, spittle
of the moon, moon, and patient:* by the former they understood its soul with the
element of fire, by the latter, the vaporous spirit, which, according to the
augmentation of its fiery soul, they called in Hermetic and natural operation *the
waxing Moon.* Therefore, from the mutual conjunction of these, a metallic body
of any species is formed; and the difference of mineral species arises from a greater
or lesser proportion of sulphur and quicksilver. For if a smaller portion of
sulphur and a larger portion of water concur in the composition of a mineral,
from that composition is generated some metallic body from those, of which
seven species are enumerated, namely, *Gold, or silver, or lead, or tin, or copper,
or iron, or quicksilver,* which they commonly call *Mercury*. But if the quantity
of sulphur in the composition exceeds the quantity of water, from such a mixture
arise those mineral bodies which are not among the number of the seven aforesaid
metals, for example, salts, and other friable substances. It must be observed here,
and indeed most diligently, that the freer the sulphur and Mercury of each species
of minerals are from the pollution of darkness and the irregularity of heterogeneity,
the purer, more perfect, and more precious the mineral of either species is produced.
We conclude therefore, that if the passive matter is gross, sooty, and thick, and its
active form, on the contrary, is small and weak, such a composition as is found
in the bowels of the earth, then that species of compounds arises which is called
mineral and metallic by the Arabs: that indeed, which is formed from earth and
water; but because the earth itself predominates in its composition, therefore its
life or soul is chained in a most opaque and dense prison; whence it is not perceived
to move sensibly, or to act openly. Concerning the particular nature of each
mineral and its medicinal property, both hidden and manifest, we will treat more
fully in the fourth treatise of the following volume.
