CHAPTER V.

On the origin of the insensate or vegetable animated body, and that it grew on the third day immediately after the existence of minerals.

__________________________________________________________________

[Decorative initial Q containing a landscape scene with trees and hills] ALTHOUGH the matter of vegetables is softer and more pliable than that of minerals, and their heat more efficacious and freer for carrying out its operations; nevertheless, because it was necessary that the earth be firmed up and optimally founded before things could grow from it; and since the more solid part of the earth, such as the shadow of the lowest heaven, would fall to the center more quickly due to its gravity than those parts that are lighter and more subtle, necessarily, after its natural rest, sparks of that same light, though at first small and weak, acted according to the ordination and appetite of nature, and then sparks of the parts of the earth which are next to this in gravity; for these were firmed up immediately after the former and came to rest in their destined place; such is the matter of the darkness of the second heaven. For it is certain that created things had their origin sooner, the less heat they had in their origin. For a greater quantity of enclosed light makes the spirit of the shadow enclosing it lighter; Hence minerals existed before vegetables, and both were made on the same day; because the presence of the sun was not required for their creation; then animals after the sublimation of the Sun in the heart of the ethereal heaven; because a greater virtue of light and heat was necessary for sensitive beings.

Therefore, the vegetative body, although it consists of four elements, nevertheless water and air predominate in it; but the dignity of the air is diminished due to the presence of water. It acquired its Soul and Spirit in this manner at its origin: namely, when the secondary light of the second heaven reverberated the shadows, and sparks of that same light were captured by the bonds of their more tenacious spirits, the shadow or darkness of the second region, joined with the last ones, gradually coalesced into the substance of the earth, according to the gravity and weight of both. Therefore, with this spiritual subject of vegetables established and confirmed near the outer part of the earth, the sparks of the soul or enclosed light begin to act within it, and by their action they try to ascend with their vehicle upwards towards the origin of their source: but, because there is great proximity between the substance of the aether and that higher substance of the lower heaven, therefore the element of fire accompanies the aforementioned ethereal Spirit with its soul, and rises and is sublimated from the earth with it; and since the nature of one element always embraces and concatenates the nature of the element nearest to it, therefore the heat of air is annexed to the heat of fire, and the humidity of water to the humidity of air, and the coldness of earth to the coldness of water (which is clearly demonstrated by experiment below), and consequently the subtle and more volatile part of the earth mixes with the parts of water and ascends in them. The soul, therefore, enclosed in the spirit of plants, naturally desires to ascend upwards: and it had help for its exaltation before the creation of the Sun from the wandering stars, and from rays of light emitted from the higher heavens, and after the creation of the Sun from the Sun itself, which on the fourth day contracted to itself both visible and invisible rays dispersed through the concavity of the middle heaven. For the rays emanating from it penetrated the dense surface of the earth, and with their heat opened its pores, which had been constricted by cold; and they provide a way for vegetables to emerge. Hence, the stronger and more perpendicular the solar rays are, the better and faster things emerge from the earth, and the more easily and higher they extend above the earth. It is therefore from this that in springtime
time

--- Page 807 ---
176          T R E A T I S E I. B O O K V I.
and in summer, plants and herbs rise above the earth, grow and multiply;
and the reason for this kind of vegetation is this: namely, solar rays extended from the east

air, since it is contiguous to fire and is bound to it by ties of friendship, immediately after
fire ascends; similarly water after air, and earth after water. But, since
earth cannot naturally ascend from its place because of the gravity of its substance,
it is necessary that the plant's base and foundation be fixed in the earth as in its

own proper seat, is hindered by the gravity of its root, fixed in the earth, and
cannot tend higher than is customary for its species. The rising sun therefore,
beholding the bright spark of the plant itself, is perceived gradually and indeed daily
to extend and augment the plant; whence things are said to grow and vegetate.

joined to that water, it is likely that the subtle part of the earth itself, ascending
with the parts of water and mixing with them, constitutes the visible body of the plant's
seed or egg, in whose center the soul with its Spirit is contained. Similarly the
other two invisible elements are hidden in the aforesaid visible ones, namely fire
in earth and air in water. There is also the vigor of this soul dispersed throughout the
entire vegetable body, just as that of an animal; for it is virtually in the whole and
in every part of it; through which every part of the plant grows and increases
equally and proportionally with every other part. But why the multiplication of the plant's egg or seed
occurs infinitely, the reason is certainly at hand; for since all multiplication
proceeds from the vigor of the soul, it is necessary that there also be an increase
of the soul itself, since a single soul of an individual cannot inform many individuals. But
since this soul is nothing else than a spark, as it were, of the essential light of the middle heaven, it is ne-
cessary that such a spark be augmented and strengthened by the apposition and conjunction of other
sparks from the same source, proportional to its species, by which infinite
bodies of the same species are accustomed to be informed, which indeed is effected by means of
solar rays; for rays are accustomed to be joined to rays, and spirits to spirits, no differently
than sparks of fire to sparks, and drops of water to drops. Hence therefore it is that from one
grain infinite things, and from one seed innumerable things proceed; and thence also it happens that
seeds buried in the matrix of the earth are wonderfully affected and delighted by the solar
approach, through which they become enriched, grow and multiply. Indeed, this is that nature which
generates all things, and nourishes that bond of the elements, and the power of mixing;
which in every thing of this sublunar world perfects the mixtures of the elements,
and impresses a form congruent and proportional to its species, by which every
thing is distinguished and separated from every other. We conclude therefore that, where the
material is thinner and softer than that of minerals, and the heat of light is stronger, there that
composition will elevate itself upwards above the surface of the earth, and will have a root as its
foot and base, which we call a plant and a vegetable; because of the
softness of its composition, the light and ethereal heat enclosed within it is more agile, free, and
lively than that of mineral composition. For the thinness and subtlety of the body
is the cause of greater freedom, liveliness, and agility of the soul. Concerning the individuals of ve-
getables, their virtue both hidden and manifest, and concerning their chemical

CAPUT VI.
*De corporis animati sensibilis origine.*

[Decorative initial A] N animal also is formed from a simple ethereal nature, namely, and an elementary composition, no differently than that vegetable body; but a larger portion of celestial heat was required for the creation of sentient beings than for vegetables, since the action of the senses is derived from a stronger power of heat, and their defect proceeds from excessive cold torpor and stupor. And hence it was that in the days of creation, animals were not created before the rising of the Sun; for the heat dispersed everywhere through the regions of the world, and especially through the firmament, before the fourth day was weak, so that it did not have the power to communicate sensation to creatures, whose actions proceed from an abundance of heat, whence it bestowed upon them vegetative life and imperceptible motion, through which all vegetables were created on the third day, that is, before the production of the Sun, and yet under the same species they perpetually receive from the Sun a multiplicative and generative power, not having more heat than GOD attributed to them in the first creation; Whence according to

--- Page 809 ---
178 TRACTATE I. BOOK VI.

...from a small quantity, perhaps illness and bodily disturbance arise from this. Therefore, so that the proportion of each of the aforesaid qualities may be maintained in weight or at least in balance, a twofold nourishment is required for the preservation of the whole composite, namely *spiritual or ethereal and corporal or elementary:* That spiritual food enters the body, either through a thin and invisible body, namely air, or through a thick and visible body; of which kind is that common nourishment, namely animal and vegetable: That invisible nourishment retains within itself some portion of solar light and ethereal spirit, by which the vital spirits, hidden in the arterial veins of the animal, are wonderfully and at every moment refreshed; Therefore, such food, namely air, is drawn in respiration to the innermost chamber of the heart, and its more essential parts are received for the refreshment of the vital spirits: while the remaining parts, as if excremental and superfluous, namely the more aquatic substance of the air itself, are exhaled.

Also in its visible and corporal nourishment, which is usually either animal or vegetable, a twofold subject is found, suitable for feeding both equalities; one of which is of the nature of heaven, which is called the essential or ethereal part of the nourishing thing, namely radical moisture with its innate heat; the other is of the nature of the elements, namely its more corporal part, from which a portion of the element of fire is drawn out and separated for the proper nourishment of the choleric humor in the thing to be nourished; similarly, by the substance of the element of air, by which animal blood is nourished, and that of the element of water, by the addition of which the substance of natural phlegm is preserved; finally, the coarser parts of nourishment strengthen melancholy: and since the composition of the entire animal body is made from these elements, it is necessary that its more solid parts be extracted from the more subtle parts of the body's nourishment for its conservation in the state and vigor of a natural and optimally disposed body, and that the coarser and more dreggy portion of the same, as useless, be expelled either through the viscera or through the urine.

Hence it is that from the lack of such elementary nourishment the animal body withers, indeed it is rendered weak, and with its strength utterly cast down, it falls into decay, just as it happens to those who are afflicted by the most acute hunger. From these things, therefore, it becomes manifest that that old axiom of the Philosophers is most true: *namely, that like rejoices in like, and nature is not improved except in its own proper nature.* Finally, we conclude that if the matter of a creature is purer and more subtle than that of plants, and its essential light more powerful, a far more beautiful and nobler work is produced than that vegetable one, which is called an animal, in which air and fire wonderfully operate. We will treat of the particular virtues of animals, both hidden and manifest, in volume 2, Tractate 4.

CHAPTER VII.
*Whence the difference of species of creatures, and why some are hotter than others,*
*colder, wetter, and drier?*

[Large decorated initial V] NIVERSALLY, the difference of all things undoubtedly flows from their souls or essential forms, which we have called above substantial sparks of light enclosed in spirit, since matter by itself is only in potentiality, and is not brought into actuality unless it is informed by light; Some Philosophers call these forms influences, which, descending through the element of earth, penetrate even to its center, in such varied ways and by such diverse reasoning, that they produce diverse generations in the bowels of the earth through diverse impressions. Such a luminous soul, I say, does everything, without which no action is found in the body. Therefore, it draws fire from the earth of the creature, and from water that light and airy spirit which we call air, so that if there is a large quantity of earth in the creature, and a small quantity of water, with a strong portion of essential heat effecting the mixtures, then the element of fire will manifest itself in that composition and will have dominance: But if the heat in the aforesaid measure of earth is small, and water is scarce, earth will have domi-

--- Page 810 ---
DE CREATURIS COELI ELEMENTARIS. 179
dominion: Conversely also, if a sufficiently strong operating heat is found upon a small quantity of earth and a larger quantity of water, the composition will be crude and aquatic; but if in the same composition a stronger and more potent heat is still found, the compound will be drier, and from such a mixture a fatty body will arise. Therefore, when the soul descends upon such matter, clothed in a spiritual garment most familiar to the ether (without whose dryness that soul and the composite body would never agree, be familiar, or be joined to each other), with its most temperate heat, it moves that matter, and variously and diversely alters it, producing various states and species of things, differing according to the greater or lesser proportion of the same light, and the obedience of the material subject into which it enters. For a multitude of form brings greater perfection, activity, subtlety, and purity to the body, if the matter is well prepared to receive it; and in this way, vegetables and animals are born: But if the body is rebellious, gross, and disobedient to the quantity of its form, in that case the soul's vigor is impeded in its actions, and it produces a mineral species; But where in the threefold division of the aforesaid things, some individual species has its difference, as in the animal kingdom man from a lion, and a lion from a bear, and again that from a mouse; in the vegetable species an oak from a hazel, and a hazel from a bilberry, and vervain from betony, and sage from thyme and others; and in the mineral, gold from lead, lead from antimony, and so on with similar things, there it happens because of the infinite proportions and degrees by which matter differs from its form. For in some, the form is exalted to such a degree in this creature above that of another, because of the obedience of that material nature and the disobedience of this one. Now, the disobedience of a species can occur in two ways, namely, where that essential light enclosed is very small, so that, although the matter is sufficiently rare, thin, and tractable, its form is nevertheless not powerful enough to govern it and promote it towards the goal of perfection: Thus phlegmatic and melancholic creatures move more slowly than sanguine or choleric ones; Thus houseleek and hemlock come to maturity more slowly than warmer vegetables, or where the matter is very disobedient, gross, hard, minimally porous, and as if binding its soul, though not small in quantity, with chains, and entirely impeding and prohibiting its power and vigorous actions. We conclude, therefore, that the softer and more obedient the substance of the body, the more proportionally noble the composition is rendered by the invisible light enclosed within it. But just as the proportion of any material thing to its form was in the first creation; so also its generation from the origin of the world to its destruction continues in the same proportion of mixture, and under the same species, by the divine will of the creator: for sparks of light are continually rained down from above.

C A P U T VIII.
What is artificial or common fire? How does it participate in celestial fire?

[Large decorative initial Q] THAT this lower fire of ours, which we call common and artificial, derives its origin from that celestial light, is sufficiently proven both by the reasoning of ancient Philosophers and by their own examples, whose opinions we also, diligently pursuing our intention, do not hesitate to confirm very easily. For that immense, uncreated light, and the head of the world, created the primary light, from whose supercelestial source rays are sent down into that solar body and those of the other stars: for with these bodies, without doubt, the splendor of the Empyrean heaven continually communicates, from which luminous rays are infused into this artificial fire of ours. Whence it is manifest that this fire not only has participation with supercelestial light, but also a certain likeness and presence of that uncreated light itself, Z 2 since

--- Page 811 ---
**180 TREATISE I. BOOK VI.**

since the Cacodæmons themselves are weakened and put to flight by the kindling of fire, just as
[Marginal note: Barthol. book 11.] good Daemons are refreshed and made stronger by its sight. For this reason, the ancients placed lit candles and lamps next to the bodies of the dead, nor did they permit them to be removed until the sacred purifications were finished and the bodies were laid in their tombs, so that they might drive away the Lucifuges (light-fleeing spirits) and evil Spirits serving Cacomagi (evil magicians), or impede their access, as is found in Apuleius' Golden Ass. Similarly, the Vestal Priests, according to Roman rites, always had fires burning next to their altars. Hence finally, true worshippers of GOD, as is found in the sacred scriptures, are commanded according to the old law of GOD to offer sacrifices with fire, and that fire should burn continuously upon the altar; indeed, even to this very day among the worshippers of the Roman Christian religion, diligently observing that anagram of Pythagoras, it is perceived to burn unceasingly in temples. But what this burning light is, which they call common and artificial fire, or how by its action it destructively acts upon the subject it occupies, we will briefly declare here. Pythagoras posited only one fire penetrating all things, which Pliny called a great portion of natural things; this we have called that essential light. But this fire, in its action, is found to be stronger or weaker in any given subject, according to the greater or lesser resistance of its actions, whence in the Empyrean heaven, due to the subtlety of the substance of that place and its slight resistance, it is immensely diffused, and most gently and sweetly warms, and is exalted to the highest degree of spirituality and perfection, because there it is freer. In the middle heaven, due to the denser consistency of the ethereal parts, it is more intense and hotter, because the composition of that body resists more the actions of the supercelestial fire emitted downwards; yet it does not heat so much as to tend to the ruin and destruction of creatures; but due to the moderation of its temperament, it is constantly occupied with the conservation and multiplication of inferior creatures themselves. However, the more this fire tends downwards, and hastens towards the center, the more its operative virtue is resisted and its rays are constricted and compressed, due to the corpulence of the substance of the lowest heaven, gradually thickening towards the center, and being compressed, they act more violently, since united force is stronger. Thus also we see that in a narrower riverbed or torrent channel, waters move more swiftly and rapidly. And hence it is that among Theologians, that infernal and accursed fire, due to
[Marginal note: Barthol. book 11.] the excessive constriction of the descending rays, and the compression and condensation of the descending light's substance, is said to be destructive beyond all imagination, burning with immense pain and horror, and tormenting with never-ending suffering, and wondrously dark, horrendous, and sad due to the narrowness of the accursed matter containing it: The intermediate fire, however, participates both in that celestial fire and also in that of hell, according to the disposition of the denser parts of the lowest heaven which it occupies; whence it happens that this fire of the lower heaven both conserves and causes to sprout, but by different means. From which it is certain that that single fire extending through all things, since it is hidden and unknown by itself, as Dionysius holds, differs in operation, and reveals itself more or less according to the disposition of the intervening matter which it occupies, inasmuch as by its resistance the nature of fire, both conservative and destructive, is manifested; for it separates heterogeneous things, and those differing from the nature of their radical moisture, so that it may find its true nourishment and, as it were, food; no differently than animals seeking the central substance of a nut separate its husks and skins, so that they may choose the kernel for their food, by which they are nourished. Therefore, just as that celestial light, clothed with an airy body, air, and what is called spirit, not only moves by its heat and performs its operations, but also requires pure and subtle fatness of the aether for its nourishment (for nothing can subsist without food), so innumerable rays of celestial light or fire, as if for the sake of hunting, descend into the lowest region of the world

region descend, and being constrained, desire coarser foods; wherefore they invisibly seek those subjects
which are softer and easier to penetrate, and in which
a larger part of that ethereal fatness, which they seek, is accustomed to lie hidden; and especially

rays, it is condensed, in the manner of the fire acting previously, and is rendered

rays, provided that the quantity of food and fuel is sufficient for the satisfaction of their
appetites. But if the passive matter fails, the parts of that fire gradually
are dissipated and vanish through the spirit of the vast air; and the subject being destroyed, and

natural place. And certainly here a great mystery seems to lie hidden, and a huge
doubt arises; namely, whether these gathered rays constituting common fire devour these lower bodies so rapaciously
because of the great enmity that exists between the opacity of matter and its coldness, or so that they, being hungry,
may be refreshed by that ethereal nourishment contained in the patient, or at least, so that they may redeem
and free their imprisoned brethren with their ethereal vehicles, so that, because this cannot be done
without the destruction of the elemental body, they seem primarily to perform that work by the dissipation of the parts themselves?
And certainly, as it seems to me, that invisible and attenuated fire can be content with its natural food,
since it is dispersed so widely through the ethereal sea, whose substance is very simple, and as it were the radical
humidity of the whole world; to which the substance of the air most closely approaches, by which also the fiery nature

But truly, when an infinite number of scattered sparks contract together into one flame, there a coarser food is required;
which is most easily demonstrated in animal life; for because of the mediocre
disposition of its celestial fire, the attracted air is not sufficient for its food,
but also more solid foods are required for its preservation,
without which it cannot long subsist.

C H A P T E R I.

*That imperfect mixtures or Meteors are not according to the nature of the Macrocosm*
*but are preternatural, and as if passions*

[Large decorative initial 'U' with a landscape scene inside]
UST as we have demonstrated above that perfectly mixed things exist naturally in the Macrocosm; so we shall declare that its Meteors, which are called imperfectly mixed, happen to it not according to, but beyond the nature of the world; indeed, these are, as it were, accidental impediments and affections of that elemental mass, which we otherwise call diseases in animals.

For what has the world or the nature of the world to do with Comets; flashes, lightning, thunder, leaping goats, burning lances, halo, parhelion, ignis fatuus (will-o'-the-wisp)? What has it to do with dry or wet clouds, hail, snow, mists, dew, frost, or with the eruption and inundation of springs? Likewise, what has it to do with winds and blasts, wet or dry, hot or cold? What with earthquake or its chasm? Do all these things usually happen necessarily to the Macrocosm, or rather, can they, in the manner of an accident, be present and absent without the destruction of the lower world and its parts?

It is certainly and undoubtedly true that the elemental region of the world and its creatures suffer and are afflicted greatly by the presence of these things. For how many calamities Comets have brought upon the air and earth, countless experiments prove, since histories also testify more than sufficiently that at their appearance the temperament of the air migrated into a pestilential constitution, and great changes occurred on earth, and indeed even entire cities and regions were as it were destroyed by famine; and likewise by lightning temples and palaces have been consumed by fire, and crops, herbs, and trees have been scorched and withered; by thunder cities, towers, and tall trees have been leveled to the ground, and even the serene face of the air has been veiled as if by darkness by the presence of clouds, and these lower regions look upon with a sad, as it were, countenance; and an excessive abundance of rains and snows has brought about floods and inundations, which have been followed not only by the ruin of houses and cities, but also by the slaughter of all kinds of animals, and even the corruption of the earth itself; Furthermore, by hail trees and fruits are corrupted, and many other evils are inflicted; Winds are accompanied by the overthrow of towns, temples, and houses, and the agitation of the swollen waves of the sea to the destruction and ruin both of ships and also of the men sailing in them; By whirlwind tall trees are thrown to the ground; By earthquake the terrestrial mass is shaken, and as it were wounded by a chasm, cities are swallowed up either in part or entirely, and trees are uprooted, and innumerable other evils are brought about.

Therefore, not in vain or inappropriately do we say that the meteors of the greater world are preternatural, and bring the greatest harm to its creatures, and for that reason are not undeservedly held to be diseases in it; no less than we shall clearly demonstrate in the second volume that all the meteors of the Microcosm are its morbid affections.

**CHAPTER II.**
*On imperfectly mixed bodies in general.*

[Decorative initial C] MPERFECTLY mixed bodies are those of the first composition, which are called Meteors; those which ancient Philosophers said were formed from vapor or exhalation; although we will prove that some of them originate elsewhere, as we will discuss below in the description of clouds. Moreover, Philosophers distinguished this type of composition into fiery, watery, and intermediate; of each of which there are various subdivisions, distinct from one another both by the type of appearance and by the place of generation. For in the uppermost region of the air they place perpendicular fire, a burning spear or beam, a lit candle, flying sparks, leaping goats, a Comet, etc. In the middle (region), lightning, flash, thunder; In the lowest (region), that ignis fatuus (will-o'-the-wisp), etc. Meteors, which they call intermediate, contain wind, earthquake, whirlwind; Watery (meteors) truly contain cloud, small cloud, mist, rain, dew, frost, snow, and hail; to which also fountains, hot springs, rivers and the sea with its saltiness and tide are annexed due to their affinity. We do not intend to discuss all these things in this place, because almost all Philosophers have dealt with them, but we will only bring to light those whose generations and natures older Philosophers explained, not so correctly, as it seems to me, as truth itself would require; such as, Comet, clouds, wind, thunder, etc. We will also briefly discuss rivers and fountains in passing.

***

**CHAPTER III.**
*On the composition of Comets and other Meteors placed in the upper region of the air.*

[Decorative initial M] ANIFOLD is the opinion of Philosophers concerning the generation and appearance of a Comet; while some say that it (the comet) is gradually elevated from the bowels of the earth into the uppermost region of the air by the power of the stars, from a terrestrial vapor or exhalation, thick, fatty, and viscous, and from densely compacted parts, and there it is dilated, ignited, and inflamed; and they wish it to last until all its matter is consumed by burning: Others describe it as an exhalation, not thick, but subtle, not illuminated, but shining from the light of the Sun and stars incorporated within it; and they say that meteors of this kind have their origin from the action of the stars, in the bowels of the earth, especially when the pores are constricted by cold: But to these opinions of the Philosophers, as it seems to me, many impossibilities arise; for since the nature of exhalation is hot and dry (for smoke is defined as hot and dry), it is impossible for it to pass through the cold and humid sieve and diaphragm of the middle region of the air; since there is immense contrariety between the nature of one and the other; Whence it is necessary that an immense quantity of the cold substance of the middle region of the air deny passage to the small portion of exhalation tending upwards, and violently and vehemently repress it downwards. From exhalations of this kind, therefore, rather winds or lightning or thunder and flashes arise,

--- Page 816 ---

arise, as we shall declare below, rather than Comets, and other meteors, born in the uppermost region of the air. Therefore, another philosophical explanation must be sought and given for the origin of Comets and other meteors of the same kind and location. We say therefore that a certain thicker spark of the Martian star, tending downwards, enclosed in the thicker matter of the third region of the air as if in its vehicle, due to the lightness of its body and the fiery heat of the star, both by the attractive faculty of fire and also because of the resistance of the middle region of the air which entirely prohibits its descent and passage through its regions, is compelled to hang in the middle of the uppermost region of the air. There, both by the virtue of the soul or stellar spark, and by the attractive faculty of the element of fire proportionally sustaining it, and by repulsion made through Antiperistasis from the coldness of the middle region of the air, it is always elevated in the same state and at the same distance from the earth. However, what power air, thickened by cold, has to lift solid objects upwards, and to raise and retain them by the attraction of fire, the two following experiments demonstrate.

The cause of the dissolution and vanishing of the Comet's body is the assiduous reflection of rays generating heat, and gradually increasing it daily by the continuous emanation of rays; by which virtue of heat, now increased and strengthened after many days, the body opens, the surrounding spark is liberated, and the entire composition of the Meteor is gradually destroyed by the imperceptible power of light, and dissolves into subtle air and vanishes; which also usually happens especially then, when that Martial planet generating the Comet, and nourishing and vivifying its spark, is rendered weak, or by the application or aspect of some Planet of contrary quality diminishing its vigor, or when it declines in its detriment or fall, or when the hidden matter of Mars is gradually diminished by its fiery and destructive virtue.

CAPUT IV.

On the generation of clouds.

PERIPATETICS define a cloud to be vapor elevated from the earth into the middle region of the air; and there constricted by the force of cold and as if frozen, which, driven by the varied motion of winds, is agitated here and there. But that the matter stands far otherwise in the generation of this Meteor, I will explain first by experiment, and then by sufficiently manifest Philosophical reasons. I, traveling from Venice towards Augsburg in Germany among the Alpine mountains, on the summit of a certain rock of immense height, which the solar rays vigorously struck, perceived a very subtle mist appearing, which, thickening more and more, was finally reduced into a very dense cloud, adhering only to the front peak of the mountain; but I saw the other parts of the rock free from the cloud and shining with solar rays. Therefore, I observed that the cause of this kind of Meteor originated from the wind blowing strongly against that side of the rock or mountain peak, which, driving thinner air before it with its blast, compressed it in such a way against the rock, because of the rock's hardness retaining the escaping air, so that it always added the succeeding parts of the air to the preceding ones, and because of the mountain's resistance, gradually condensed it into the consistency of a cloud; which immediately the solar rays striking the summit of the rock finally dissolved, inducing drops of rain. But perhaps someone will object, that clouds arise where moun-
Aa 2 tains

--- Page 819 ---
188 TRACTATUS I. LIB. VII.

...or rocks are minimally found: To which it must be responded that the condensation of air is produced by similar compression, although by dissimilar means or instruments; for two opposing winds blowing simultaneously, although one may be stronger than the other due to its predominance in the air, very often tend to compress and condense thinner air; and convert it into rain, according to the nature of the wind or exhalation; which two winds, if they act and resist more strongly, produce a similar roaring sound in the air, as two rivers violently falling into the same gulf or abyss with contrary motion. I also remember that while sailing the sea in a ship with sails extended, and a stronger wind blowing, I made my way and journey towards England; when again, at times, a weaker wind was blowing, I observed the opposite wind, adverse to our journey, pushing the sails back, until that wind favorable to us, overcoming the force of the other opposing wind, finally carried us happily to England: Meanwhile, therefore, various clouds were gathered, and resolved into rain. If finally we produce more evident philosophical reasons, we will perceive that those demonstrating the generation of clouds by the Peripatetics are to be held as nothing; for if the origin of a cloud were from the attraction of vapors into the uppermost region of the air, it would follow that clouds would be more frequent in summer than in winter: both because in summer the Sun with its more direct rays more easily attracts vapors upwards, and also because in warmer weather, terrestrial pores emitting such vapors allow fumes to escape without any impediment of cold obstructing the way; for we see that the air in summer is very thick due to the constant vapors rising from the earth and water; indeed, ponds, springs, and rivers are either entirely, or for a large part, converted into the substance of the air by rarefaction; just as in winter, again by thickening, when the coarser part of the air is condensed by the power of cold, the air is first converted into clouds; and then into rain. Whence ponds, springs, and rivers are refilled in winter by the change of air into water, and torrents rise: and hence the entire surface of the earth, dried in summer, becomes humid and slippery in winter. From which it is evident that not vapor immediately elevated into the middle region of the air, but the air itself condensed, is the cause and origin of the cloud's substance, and that clouds are produced more in winter than in summer, both because of the contrary blowing of opposing winds, and because the blasts of northerly winds, whose nature it is to freeze, are more frequent; although it may not always have this denomination, perhaps because of more evident blasts of an opposing wind; and finally, because the air is prepared and apt for such impressions, and the nature of the middle region of the air, due to the absence or greater distance of the Sun, is well disposed to freeze the coarser parts of the air and sustain them like ice, until they are dissolved into drops by the power of stellar rays. If, therefore, vapors are elevated during the daytime, experience constantly teaches us that they produce mists after sunset and not clouds. Finally, from the blowing of winds, various effects are produced in the generation of clouds; for where the South wind (Auster) predominates, yet the North wind (Boreas) blows, but secretly, due to the congelative disposition of the one, operating with coldness and dryness on the substance of the cloud, and the dissolutive quality of the other, which by its warm nature destroys the congelative works of its opposite, clouds are resolved into rain: But where Boreas has dominion, clouds cannot be entirely dissolved by Auster blowing imperceptibly, but are turned into snow or hail; But if Auster is still stronger, it generates partly snow and partly rain. The West wind, however, for the most part produces warmer and drier clouds, which usually sustain the solar rays and those of other stars without the dissolution of their parts; whence they appear bright and clear: But where a single and simple wind blows, or at least finds a transverse wind very weakly contrary to itself, there for the most part the air is found without clouds. If this is not enough for the wise, what is to be thought of a cloud carrying lightning in its depths, which, appearing at the outermost edge of the horizon, is perceived to move against the motion of the wind? Without doubt, such a meteor...

DE CORPORIB. IMPERFECTE MIXTIS. 189

...Without doubt, such a meteoron at the point of each horizon arises from the blowing of two oppositely blowing winds, of which one was stronger in one Horizon, and the other had predominance in the other; but that one (the stronger wind) blowing more upwards and more strongly in the hidden horizon, exciting a thundercloud, is perceived to move against the weaker wind's blowing in the visible horizon. Therefore, we conclude that a cloud is formed from the compression of the thinner parts of the air, made by the blowing of winds proceeding in opposite directions of the world; and we say, against the opinions of the Peripatetics, that wind is found both in the middle region of the air and in the lowest, since the bodies of clouds are moved by their blowing, just as the Peripatetics themselves wrote.

CAPUT V.
On Winds.

**D**ifferent ancients also wrote variously about the origin of winds, from which their uncertain knowledge about the cause of this meteor is very easily recognized. For the Peripatetics said the matter of wind was a hot and dry exhalation moving laterally around the earth; Bede, vaporous air, agitated by smoky matter emerging from the earth; Constantine defines wind as a cold and dry vapor resolved and separated from earth or water, vigorously moving the air by the power of heat; Others posited that the origin of winds was from the violent motion of clouds, pushing the air before them; Others wanted wind to have its origin from the reverberation of parts or arms of the sea coming from any region of the earth, and they say that the southern arm turning towards the north induces the East wind or Subsolanus, and so for the rest; Some others write that winds come from caves and caverns. But we are taught by a certain practice that the origin of winds is primarily derived from two things, namely, either from air enclosed, simply and violently bursting forth from the belly of the earth, or from water itself, dissipated into hot vapor by the force of central fire. But air enclosed in the earth is expelled, either by its rarefaction, caused by central heat, as is declared by the following experiment, and then because of the scarcity of matter it excites only a light wind, such as we see blowing in summer.

And in this way, according to the disposition of the Planets, various winds are induced at various times of the year, as we shall teach below.

CAPUT VI.
*On Lightning and Thunder.*

[Large decorative initial P] ERIPATETICS write that thunder and lightning occur when a hot and dry exhalation, together with a humid and watery vapor, is elevated by the heat of the Sun into the upper part of the middle aerial region; where they hold that this exhalation is surrounded and enclosed on all sides by the vapor, and condensed into a cold and dense cloud, whose intense cold the enclosed exhalation, bearing its injuries with difficulty, is driven hither and thither as if indignant, seeking an exit, and finally, by agitation and antiperistasis, like burning tow, it breaks the sides of the cloud with its fiery force, so that the cloud, thus broken and ruptured, emits a great crash, which they call *thunder*, simultaneously calling the light of the ignited exhalation *lightning, flash, and coruscation*. Indeed, we cannot disapprove of their opinions in all respects, for we say that the *patient matter*, which emits the crackling sound, is air reduced to the substance of a cloud; but the *agent form*, which induces the crash, is that sulphureous and windy matter ignited by the force of both cold and humidity; which, illuminated according to the nature of enclosed fire, seeks open air, and, to satisfy its appetite, breaks its prisons, and flies out and vanishes into a more spacious and rarefied place, where it can live more freely: Thus also we see that the substance of Saltpeter is nothing other than air congealed by cold, to which, if any portion of sulfur is added, though very small, it emits a great noise and artificial flashes, as is demonstrated by the following experiment.

From which, force by forces, and sulphurous atoms united with atoms, finally strengthened by the resistance of the very cold nitrous nature, both by the repercussion agitating the sulphurous mass, and by the active faculty of the fiery mass itself through antiperistasis, are illuminated; and the parts of sulfur, formerly operating only in potentiality, are now reduced to actuality, and are subtilized by illumination, so that from there, vigorously, due to the subtlety of their parts, they penetrate downwards to the exterior of the cloud, violently break its sides, and are perceived to emit a huge crash, which we also call thunder. Finally, we do not say that the blowing and nature of the South wind alone produces these kinds of sulfurous and drier vapors, but also other winds blowing from any quarter of the world, provided they partake of sulfurous spirits. And these things will be perceived more clearly if we carefully observe the movement of a thundering cloud vomiting forth lightning, for a cloud emitting lightning is observed to be agitated against the movement of clouds devoid of sulfur, and then for the most part a crackling sound is produced when both clouds have simultaneously come together into one mass, and have firmly and strongly enclosed the sulfurous vapor accompanying the opposing wind. Here it must also be observed that in the opposing clash of clouds, that cloud laden with sulfurous spirit also moves the contrary cloud against its own motion because of the multitude of living fire, in the manner of a very strong soul moving its own body, by the vigor of which, the strength of the other contrary cloud is repelled, no differently than when some stronger man carries a weaker one somewhere against his will and unwillingly, despite his struggles. Hence therefore the origin of the contention, in which, since the disposition of the sulfurous cloud is fiery and sulfurous, but the constitution of the cloud moving against it is very cold, the sulfurous nature is inflamed because of the reason shown in the previous demonstration concerning artificial fire in water. We conclude therefore that common experience has sufficiently clearly demonstrated that the formal origin of thunder and lightning is certain sulfurous vapors invisibly dispersed in the air, which, gathered together, are brought into action, that is, they are ignited; for while thunderbolts and lightning flashes are scattered through the air, very sulfurous odors are perceived, indeed, the true nature of sulfur is recognized even by common eyes, both in the color of its flame and in the condition of its execution. Moreover, we have seen in foreign regions more frequent thunder near those places in which sulfur mines or sulfurous mountains are found ignited by some accident, as in Sicily and around Naples; similarly in rocky regions, where solar rays are strongly concentrated against the peaks of mountains. What finally could more clearly demonstrate the origin of thunder than that horrendous production of Mount Cineritius of Puteoli, about which we spoke in the preceding chapter.

CHAPTER VII.

*How do the superior bodies act towards the production of such meteors?*

[Decorative initial 'I' in a square frame with floral patterns] N the preceding (chapters) we have only made mention of the more proximate causes of meteors: Here, however, we will briefly explain by what reason the stars and Planets produce these imperfect mixtures. Since therefore it has been determined among all Philosophers that the superior bodies continually act upon these inferior things to produce new things, it is certain that such celestial bodies are the primary causes of the production of any meteor, and of the positioning of its substance in its proper place: But what Astrologers think and strongly affirm in this matter we will briefly recount here; then we will conclude with our own opinion. Some Astrologers teach that Comets for the most part imitate the nature of Mars and Venus, whence they wish them to portend wars, heats, and commotions; others say that they have their origin from some inauspicious position of the stars, for example, by the conjunction and Eclipse of the superior Planets, and especially when Saturn, Mars, and Mercury behold the Sun or Moon with inauspicious aspects in an Eclipse, especially if some inauspicious

--- Page 828 ---
**ON IMPERFECTLY MIXED BODIES. 197**

...unfavorable conjunction of superior [planets]: Appian predicted such a Comet would come in the year 1532. They also teach that dark mists are produced and resolved into dust, when the Moon, after its conjunction or aspect with the Sun, seeks out Saturn, existing as the disposer of the sky, and views him with some aspect; and they claim that serene and white clouds mixed with redness are generated by the application of the Moon to Jupiter, who possesses dominion of the sky, after its conjunction or aspect with the Sun; and they say that rain mostly comes about by the Moon's dissolving faculty, while it sojourns in a humid mansion; and they claim that Mars, existing as the disposer of the Horoscope, generates saffron-colored clouds, and in summer time produces thunder and lightning, especially when the Moon, after its conjunction or aspect with the Sun, has viewed Mars; indeed, they claim that immense thunder and lightning arise if the Moon, after the separation of Mars, has viewed Mercury; they also assert that Venus alone, mistress of the sky, when the Moon approaches her after its separation from the Sun, produces light and long-lasting rains; finally, they claim that Mercury, stronger in the celestial scheme, when conjoined with the Moon, generates immense and rapid winds: they also assert that some winds arise from the Moon's power as it passes through a dry mansion: Also snows in winter, with some predominant aspect of Saturn with the Moon; They affirm that hail with thunder occurs when strong Saturn has viewed Mars in summer, and so forth for the rest. From these assertions of the Astrologers, we also conclude that our aforesaid opinions concerning the origin of Meteors are not fictitious, but very close to the truth itself. For in the composition of a Comet, they say the nature of *Mars and Mercury* concur; and they spoke truly: for the spark of *Martial* substance flowing down from above is, as it were, the soul and life of the Comet itself: Its body and substance, however, are entirely *Mercurial*, that is, conglomerated from the inconstant substance of the subtlest air, having the aptitude, after the manner of *Mercury*, to receive any form or impression. What also can better argue for the generation of clouds, namely, while air is thickened by the blowing of opposing winds, which, when condensed, we have called a cloud, than that they are primarily generated from the aspect and opposition of diverse Planets, exciting winds with their diverse influences into these lower regions: for in the predominant aspect of the Moon with Saturn, the humidity of one opposes the dryness of the other: Whence from such a conflict a contrary motion arises in the air, compressing it, so that a cloud is generated therefrom. Similarly, two *winds* of contrary condition are produced in summer time from the opposition, conjunction, or other malevolent aspect between predominant *Saturn* and *Mars*. For *Mars*, because of its familiarity with fire, gathers sulphurous vapors, and by its power moves them in the form of wind against the exhalation produced by Saturn, so that its own body moves against that of *Saturn* in the ethereal sky. *Saturn*, however, being cold, is opposed to *Mars* not only in motion but also in quality; Whence the coldness of *Saturn* ignites the sulphurous matter gathered by Mars no differently than that spring water ignited the other artificial mass *described in experiment 2, preceding chapter*; hence thunders exist; but because Saturn is stronger, hail also falls: Similarly, if Jupiter has dominion in the sky, and in summer time views Mars with some malevolent aspect, it induces diverse and opposing motions in the air; because the humidity of Jupiter is contrary to the dryness of *Mars*: wherefore that humidity of Jupiter, although warm, ignites the inflammable matter gathered by Mars no differently than the humidity of spittle ignited that *described in experiment 3, in the preceding chapter*, in which the humidity of spittle, penetrating and submerging itself into that fiery body, reduces that fiery power, hidden and existing only in potential, into an inflammable act; whose composition is this;

CHAPTER X.

*A brief compilation of the entire treatise into one.*

[Decorative initial Q] With what great admiration and divine speculation, after the pious contemplation of the entire Archetype, those two principles of created things are to be considered worthy: namely, the dark mass of materials, and that substantial light, given on the first day by the inexplicable and divine will of the Creator himself to the world and its parts for the creation of living things. It is not doubtful that this appears clearer than noonday light to all of you, endowed with a keener mind, and looking somewhat more deeply with your lynx-like eyes into the more hidden causes of things; since we can find absolutely nothing in this universe of things that does not partake of one of the aforementioned. For, just as those two primary substances, mentioned above, are contrary to each other in nature and disposition; so also whatever is found in this world to adhere more to one of them, all of this is likewise utterly opposed both to the opposite principle and to what proceeds from it: Therefore, there is light, to which darkness is opposed: We have GOD, the father of light, and we have the Devil, the prince of darkness; Day dawns for us and the world, to which we find night, the veil of darkness, contrary; Light produced the heavens for us, converting the purer part of the dark mass into its own substance, and darkness left us and the Macrocosm the earth, burdened with the depth of blackness and obscurity; The essence of Light infused sparks of life into us; but the body of darkness maliciously encloses, retains, and incarcerates their substance, and compels the splendor of the mind both to suffer and endure the most miserable torments of the flesh, and also, seduced by its various deceptions and snares, to deviate and err from truth and the right path, as if blinded by ignorance: Finally, from light we have fire, form, essence, perfection, life, generation, motion or action, and beauty, while from darkness we receive water, matter, privation, imperfection, death, corruption, rest, ugliness. Similarly, who doubts that whiteness, exaltation, love, virtue, good; truth, knowledge, riches, and other things of that kind, proceed from light, the messenger of the supreme Creator, when it is manifest and certain beyond all controversy that blackness, depression, hatred, vice, evil, falsehood, ignorance, poverty, and similar opposites proceed from darkness, the messenger of the Devil? Oh, how great therefore and how profound is the dimension of these principles, and how inscrutable their hidden depths! which, although they can in no way be investigated by a priori demonstration; yet God has granted us permission to contemplate them a posteriori: Indeed, happy is he who can rightly know their mysteries, about which the most profound philosophers of the Gentiles used to spend not only a year and years, but the entire span of their lives; for they were driven by so much greater application and more vehement zeal to inquire more deeply into these mysteries, the more they probably found something in them.
We conclude therefore, that if anyone wishes to judge correctly and not rashly concerning our preceding subject, he will perceive this opinion of ours to be not only probable, but also (unless I am mistaken) not far distant from truth itself: Meanwhile, however, I will most willingly adapt and submit myself to the judgments of all those more skilled in this divine Philosophy, praying them again and again, that Cc 3 with a countenance

--- Page 837 ---
206          T R A C T A T U S  I.  L I B.  V I I.
with a calm countenance they may receive these writings of ours, and the errors contained in them (which indeed I know to have crept into so profound a work, not few or insignificant) they may correct, not with a viperous tongue (as very many are accustomed to do), but, as it befits sons of light burning with fiery love, amicably and benevolently with a sounder and more skillful judgment. But you others, who in this field of Philosophy have either never, or not well, sown, I earnestly beseech you, that you do not unjustly condemn, with a mind obscured by darkness, what you justly do not understand. Meanwhile, may that immense and uncreated light, adorned with its vivid and eternally splendid virtue and grace, preserve me from the injuries of the wicked, and all of you safe and sound from the abyss of ignorance.
